response_text:
## Executive finding

**Yes—but only for a bounded part of the problem.** Compact language models are now meaningfully competitive for **closed-set, high-volume customer-support classification and routing**, particularly when fine-tuned on a stable taxonomy and allowed to abstain. Their main advantage is operational: lower and more predictable cost, higher deployable throughput, easier data residency, and often lower latency.

The evidence does **not** show that a 3–9B model can generally replace a frontier model for ambiguous, multilingual, multi-intent, policy-dependent, or rapidly changing support traffic. Public evidence is also much stronger on benchmarks than on controlled production A/B tests.

Here, “small model” means either:

- a compact encoder/classifier such as DistilBERT, ModernBERT, or a small embedding model; or
- a roughly 3–9B-parameter generative model such as Phi-4-mini, Gemma 3 4B, Llama 3.1 8B, or Qwen 2.5 7B.

“Mini,” “Flash,” and “Haiku” APIs are operationally relevant but have undisclosed parameter counts and should not automatically be treated as independently deployable SLMs.

## What the benchmarks establish

| Evidence | Result | Production interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **BANKING77**, a 77-intent customer-service benchmark | The original evaluation reported approximately **92.3% accuracy for DistilBERT** and **93.9% for RoBERTa**. SetFit subsequently reached roughly **84% with only eight examples per class** and around **94% with full training data**. | Compact supervised models can already operate near the ceiling on a stable, in-domain support taxonomy. These results are not a direct comparison with current frontier models under the same prompt and split. |
| **Meta Llama 3.1 tool-use evaluation** | Meta reported **76.1 on BFCL for the 8B model**, versus **88.5 for the 405B model**. | Small models are capable routers, but complex function selection still showed a material scale gap. This is vendor-reported, although BFCL itself is independently maintained. |
| **Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard** | Function-tuned 7B-class models have approached older GPT-4 variants on some single-turn and abstract-syntax categories. Newer multi-turn, relevance-detection, and agentic tests generally restore a frontier advantage. | Narrow routing parity is real, but it is sensitive to benchmark version. Simple function selection is much easier than handling irrelevant requests, incomplete information, and multi-step escalation. |
| **GPT-4o mini documentation** | OpenAI reported **82% MMLU**, 87.2 HumanEval, and performance above GPT-3.5-class systems at a much lower price. | Small or economical models have made large broad-benchmark gains, but MMLU and coding scores are weak evidence for support-routing reliability. |
| **LiveBench and similar independent broad evaluations** | Recent frontier families continue to lead compact 3–9B models in aggregate reasoning, instruction following, and difficult long-context tasks. | The small-model gains have not erased the general-capability gap. That gap matters when a “routing” decision requires policy interpretation or substantial inference. |
| **MMTEB/MTEB embedding evaluations** | Small specialist embedding models are often highly competitive on classification and retrieval, while no model dominates every language and domain. | A generative model is often unnecessary. An embedding classifier can be the strongest and cheapest first-stage router. |

The most important distinction is that **top-1 intent accuracy is not sufficient evidence of production readiness**. Production systems also need:

- out-of-scope and novel-intent detection;
- calibrated confidence and selective accuracy;
- per-intent recall, especially for cancellations, fraud, safety, and regulatory queues;
- multilingual and code-switched performance;
- multi-intent handling;
- resilience to taxonomy and policy changes;
- chronological rather than randomly shuffled test data.

CLINC-style evaluations and BFCL relevance-detection tests consistently show that rejecting unsupported requests is harder than choosing among known labels. A model that scores 95% on a closed test set can still be unsafe if it is confidently wrong on novel tickets.

## Benchmark gains versus operational advantages

### Accuracy

**Where small models are competitive**

- Stable taxonomies with tens to a few hundred intents.
- Sufficient historical labels or weak labels from an existing router.
- Short messages where the correct queue is mostly expressed lexically.
- Domains where the model can return “unknown” and defer difficult cases.
- High-frequency intents for which retraining data are abundant.

Fine-tuning usually matters more than another few billion parameters. A compact supervised encoder may outperform a much larger zero-shot model because its decision boundary is trained directly against the organization’s taxonomy.

**Where frontier models still have an advantage**

- New or frequently changing intent definitions.
- Sparse-label and zero-shot onboarding.
- Long conversations requiring earlier-turn context.
- Multi-intent messages and implied intents.
- Policy-dependent routing, such as deciding whether an exception applies.
- Less-resourced languages and code switching.
- Combined routing, extraction, summarization, and response planning.
- Out-of-distribution traffic and unusual paraphrases.

Broad benchmarks support this difference, but there is no accepted public benchmark reproducing a real contact center’s taxonomy, drift, escalation costs, and multilingual mix.

### Latency

For classification, a model normally emits only one label or a small JSON object. Consequently, **time to first token and input prefill matter more than output-token speed**.

- A compact encoder performs one forward pass and can commonly run in milliseconds to tens of milliseconds on suitable local hardware for short inputs.
- A quantized 3–9B decoder can fit on a single 16–24GB GPU in many configurations, although context length, KV cache, batching, and concurrency affect this substantially.
- A remote frontier API adds network, provider queueing, and rate-limit variance. It can still be fast when heavily provisioned, so smaller parameter count does not guarantee lower endpoint latency.
- Independent services such as Artificial Analysis show that some “Flash” or “mini” endpoints have very fast first-token latency and triple-digit token throughput, but the ordering changes by provider and time.

There is no public, apples-to-apples benchmark of p95 latency for small and frontier models on the same customer-support workload and concurrency level. Local SLMs have the clearest advantage when **predictable p95 latency, regional processing, or offline operation** matters.

### Throughput

Small models have a structural throughput advantage:

- less weight memory traffic;
- more replicas per GPU budget;
- larger practical batches;
- cheaper redundancy;
- the ability to pin model and serving versions.

Encoders are especially efficient because they do not autoregressively decode a response. For pure routing, they generally offer better throughput than a 7B chat model.

However, published API token rates are not capacity guarantees. Provider hardware, speculative decoding, continuous batching, quantization, and rate limits can allow a large hosted model to outperform a poorly operated small-model deployment. Throughput therefore needs to be measured at the intended prompt length and concurrency rather than inferred from parameter count.

### Cost

Using OpenAI’s documented GPT-4o-era list prices as a transparent comparison, a ticket containing **500 input tokens and a 10-token structured answer** would cost approximately:

| Model | Input/output price per million tokens | Cost per million tickets |
|---|---:|---:|
| GPT-4o mini | $0.15 / $0.60 | **$81** |
| GPT-4o | $2.50 / $10.00 | **$1,350** |

That is about a **16.7× inference-price difference** for the same token workload. Prices exclude caching, batch discounts, retries, enterprise agreements, and orchestration.

A self-hosted 3–9B model has no per-token API charge, but its true cost includes:

- GPUs or CPU capacity at peak rather than average traffic;
- redundancy and autoscaling;
- serving engineering;
- monitoring and retraining;
- security patching;
- fallback calls;
- idle capacity.

At high sustained utilization, a compact encoder or quantized SLM can be substantially cheaper than a frontier API. At low volume, the operational cost of self-hosting may erase the saving; a low-cost mini API can then be the better economic baseline.

## What deployment evidence says

### Evidence that specialist routing works in production

Uber’s published **COTA** support system used specialized ranking and classification components and reported roughly a **10% reduction in average ticket-handling time**. It predates current SLMs, but it demonstrates that high-value support routing does not inherently require frontier-scale generation.

Many current ticketing products—including Zendesk-style intent, sentiment, and language triage—also use compact classifiers or undisclosed model ensembles. Their scale is evidence for the operational pattern, but not for modern SLM/frontier parity because vendors rarely disclose architectures, matched accuracy, or fallback rates.

### Evidence for frontier-model production value

Klarna reported that its OpenAI-based assistant handled **2.3 million conversations in its first month**, reduced average resolution time from **11 minutes to 2 minutes**, and lowered repeat inquiries by 25%. This is important deployment evidence for LLM-enabled support, but:

- it was a company/vendor report rather than an independent controlled study;
- it covered a broader conversational assistant, not merely routing;
- it does not establish that a small model would have produced the same result.

### Evidence specifically comparing SLMs and frontier models

This is the weakest part of the record. Phi, Gemma, Llama, Qwen, Granite, and xLAM documentation demonstrates tool calling, structured output, long context, and single-GPU deployment. Public case studies often claim lower cost or latency. Very few disclose all of the following:

1. the exact support taxonomy and traffic mix;
2. a contemporaneous frontier baseline;
3. chronological and out-of-scope test results;
4. p50/p95 latency at matched concurrency;
5. total infrastructure and fallback cost;
6. downstream misroute or resolution outcomes.

Accordingly, claims of production parity are usually based on benchmarks, internal vendor evaluations, or promotional case studies rather than reproducible deployment evidence.

## Most defensible production architecture

A cascade captures most of the established benefit:

1. Apply deterministic rules for legally or operationally unambiguous cases.
2. Use a compact encoder or fine-tuned 3–9B model for ordinary intents.
3. Calibrate confidence on recent production data rather than raw model probabilities alone.
4. Escalate low-confidence, multi-intent, novel, high-risk, or policy-sensitive cases to a frontier model or human.
5. Monitor selective accuracy, out-of-scope false acceptance, downstream transfers, and resolution—not only classifier F1.
6. Retrain from reviewed fallbacks and test against chronological drift.

This approach is consistent with RouteLLM’s independent, though non-support-specific, result that routing most easy queries to a cheaper model can preserve much of the stronger model’s quality while sharply reducing frontier calls. Its reported savings should not be transferred directly to customer support without a local trial.

Suggested acceptance gates for a shadow deployment are:

- no more than a one-percentage-point decline in cost-weighted routing accuracy;
- no material regression on fraud, cancellation, safety, and regulatory intents;
- a measured out-of-scope false-acceptance ceiling;
- lower p95 latency under expected concurrency;
- materially lower total cost after fallback and infrastructure;
- a stable frontier/human fallback rate through at least one representative period of drift.

## Options

1. Use a frontier model for every ticket.
2. Deploy a small-model-first cascade, with calibrated frontier or human fallback.
3. Use a small model alone for all support routing.

## Sources

- Casanueva et al., **BANKING77**: [arXiv:2003.04807](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04807)
- Tunstall et al., **SetFit**: [arXiv:2209.11055](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11055)
- Meta, **Llama 3.1 model card and evaluations**: [llama.com](https://www.llama.com/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama3_1/)
- Microsoft, **Phi-3 Technical Report**: [arXiv:2404.14219](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14219)
- Microsoft, **Phi-4-mini-instruct model card**: [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct)
- Berkeley, **Function Calling Leaderboard**: [gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html)
- OpenAI, **GPT-4o mini benchmarks and launch pricing**: [openai.com](https://openai.com/index/gpt-4o-mini-advancing-cost-efficient-intelligence/)
- White et al., **LiveBench**: [arXiv:2406.19314](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19314)
- Enevoldsen et al., **MMTEB**: [arXiv:2502.13595](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13595)
- Ong et al., **RouteLLM**: [arXiv:2406.18665](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665)
- Artificial Analysis, **independent latency and throughput methodology**: [artificialanalysis.ai/methodology](https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology)
- Uber, **COTA: Improving the Speed and Accuracy of Customer Support**: [ACM Digital Library](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3219819.3219851)
- Klarna, **AI-assistant deployment announcement**: [klarna.com](https://www.klarna.com/international/press/klarna-ai-assistant-handles-two-thirds-of-customer-service-chats-in-its-first-month/)

RECOMMENDATION: 2. Deploy a small-model-first cascade, with calibrated frontier or human fallback.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Distribution shift and out-of-scope or multi-intent tickets can make a small model confidently misroute high-impact cases unless fallback is continuously calibrated and monitored.

## Bottom line

RAG is usually a better **knowledge-delivery mechanism** than fine-tuning: it is more suitable for changing enterprise facts, traceable answers, document-level access control, and deletion or correction. It is not a general replacement for fine-tuning, because fine-tuning is better suited to changing **model behavior**—such as terminology, workflow selection, output structure, abstention, and performance on stable repetitive tasks.

The strongest general architecture is therefore:

- Keep current and sensitive facts in governed repositories.
- Retrieve authorized evidence at query time.
- Use fine-tuning selectively for stable behaviors or to make a smaller model perform the task efficiently.
- Use direct database or API tools, rather than ordinary RAG, for transactional data requiring exact real-time values.

## What the evidence supports

Research since the original RAG work consistently shows that retrieval can improve knowledge-intensive question answering, especially for recent, private, or less frequently represented facts. Studies of parametric versus non-parametric memory also find that language models are less dependable on uncommon facts and that retrieval can help. Direct comparisons of knowledge injection generally favor retrieval over fine-tuning for adding new factual material.

However, this evidence is conditional:

- Retrieval helps only when the corpus contains the answer and the system retrieves the right passage.
- Irrelevant or conflicting context can reduce accuracy.
- Models sometimes ignore retrieved evidence in favor of their pretrained beliefs.
- Long-context studies show that merely placing evidence in context does not ensure it will be used correctly.
- Citation benchmarks such as ALCE show that retrieval makes citations possible but does not guarantee that every claim is supported.
- Fine-tuning experiments show that models can memorize new facts, but retention and generalization are uneven, and learning unfamiliar facts can increase hallucination or interfere with existing behavior.

Most published comparisons use open-domain QA or controlled corpora. There are relatively few independent, longitudinal enterprise studies measuring accuracy, security, operational labor, and cost together. Consequently, the evidence for the architectural distinctions is strong, while evidence for a universal cost or accuracy winner is only moderate.

## Dimension-by-dimension comparison

| Dimension | RAG | Fine-tuning | Practical conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Factual accuracy** | Usually better for document-grounded, recent, uncommon, or organization-specific facts. Failure points include retrieval misses, bad chunking, conflicting versions, distractors, and unfaithful synthesis. | Can improve narrow-domain accuracy when examples are high quality and the target is stable. Poor as a dependable store for exact facts; may memorize selectively or alter unrelated behavior. | RAG generally wins for “What does the current source say?” Fine-tuning can win for stable classification, interpretation, or recurring reasoning patterns. |
| **Freshness** | Documents can become available after ingestion or index refresh. Freshness is bounded by connector and indexing SLAs. | Knowledge is fixed at training time and requires another data, training, validation, and deployment cycle. | RAG wins for changing policies and products. For second-by-second balances or inventory, use a system-of-record API instead. |
| **Citation quality** | Can expose source IDs, passages, versions, and links. Yet a retrieved source may be relevant without supporting the generated claim. | Cannot inherently recover the source of a fact stored in weights. Training a model to emit citation-looking text improves style, not provenance. | RAG is necessary for auditable citations, but claim-level entailment and citation completeness must still be tested. |
| **Maintenance burden** | Requires connectors, parsing, deduplication, versioning, chunking, indexing, ranking, monitoring, and stale-content removal. Content can normally be corrected without retraining. | Requires curated training data, training infrastructure or vendor jobs, regression testing, model-version migration, and repeated retraining. Removing learned information reliably remains difficult. | RAG shifts maintenance into knowledge and search operations; fine-tuning shifts it into an ML lifecycle. Neither is maintenance-free. |
| **Access control** | Supports query-time authorization and document-, tenant-, row-, or classification-level filtering. Deletion and revocation are comparatively tractable. | Weights mix training examples and cannot reliably apply per-user permissions to individual learned facts. Separate models or adapters per security domain are possible but expensive. | RAG is strongly preferable for mixed-clearance or multi-tenant knowledge. Authorization must occur before evidence reaches the model, not after generation. |
| **Latency** | Adds query rewriting, embedding or lexical search, reranking, network calls, and extra context tokens. Search can be parallelized or cached, but tail latency is material. | Avoids retrieval overhead. Fine-tuning the same model does not inherently make inference faster, but enabling a smaller model can do so. | Fine-tuning has an advantage for very latency-sensitive, stable tasks. Generation may still dominate overall latency in either design. |
| **Total cost** | Lower cost of knowledge updates, but recurring costs for ingestion, search, reranking, longer prompts, observability, and operations. | Upfront and recurring costs for data curation, training, validation, and redeployment. It may reduce serving cost if a smaller tuned model replaces a larger model or long contexts. | RAG often wins for changing content and moderate usage. Fine-tuning can amortize well at high volume on stable tasks. A hybrid has the largest engineering surface but can lower per-query model and context costs. |

## Why RAG does not automatically improve factuality

A RAG answer depends on at least four independently fallible stages:

1. **Corpus coverage:** An authoritative answer must actually exist in the indexed material.
2. **Retrieval recall:** The relevant evidence must survive query formulation, filtering, retrieval, and reranking.
3. **Evidence interpretation:** The model must handle dates, exceptions, tables, negation, and conflicting versions correctly.
4. **Faithful generation:** The answer must stay within the evidence and abstain when support is insufficient.

Fine-tuning cannot repair missing or obsolete source material. Conversely, RAG cannot compensate for a model that consistently misunderstands specialized language or fails to follow the required workflow. Production systems therefore need separate measurements for retrieval recall, answer correctness, evidence support, and abstention rather than a single aggregate QA score.

## Citation quality requires more than RAG

A source appearing beside an answer can create false confidence. Citation evaluation should distinguish:

- **Citation correctness:** Does the cited passage entail the associated claim?
- **Citation completeness:** Are all significant externally verifiable claims covered?
- **Source authority:** Is the cited document approved, current, and applicable?
- **Source identity:** Did the system preserve canonical document IDs, versions, page or section locations, and links?

The model should select from citations supplied by the retrieval layer rather than inventing bibliographic text. High-risk answers may also need a verification pass that checks each claim against its cited passage.

## Access-control implications

Access control is one of the strongest arguments against storing enterprise facts through fine-tuning. A fine-tuned model does not provide a dependable mechanism for answering a fact for one employee while withholding the same learned fact from another. Machine unlearning is not yet a reliable substitute for retraining from a clean checkpoint.

RAG can enforce permissions at query time, but only if implemented correctly:

- Apply authorization before retrieval results are sent to the generator.
- Use source-system permissions or synchronized security metadata.
- Test document, chunk, row, tenant, and field boundaries.
- Protect embeddings, caches, conversation history, logs, and evaluation traces.
- Treat retrieved documents as untrusted input because they can contain indirect prompt injection.
- Propagate deletions to indexes, replicas, caches, and backups.

Fine-tuning remains acceptable where all users have the same clearance and the training data is approved for permanent inclusion in that particular model boundary.

## Where the approaches are complementary

A well-designed hybrid assigns each approach a different responsibility:

- **RAG supplies evidence:** current policies, product documentation, contracts, research, tickets, and other governed knowledge.
- **Fine-tuning supplies behavior:** terminology, tone, structured output, query reformulation, tool selection, workflow adherence, citation placement, and calibrated abstention.
- **Retriever or reranker tuning improves evidence selection:** domain examples can train search components without placing the underlying facts in the generator.
- **Tools supply deterministic state:** databases and APIs handle balances, availability, permissions, calculations, and transactions.
- **Rules supply hard constraints:** authorization, approval requirements, and compliance controls should not depend solely on learned model behavior.

This separation allows facts to be corrected or revoked without retraining while preserving a stable assistant experience.

## Decision criteria

Choose primarily **RAG** when:

- Facts change frequently or must reflect a named document version.
- Answers require citations, provenance, auditability, or rapid correction.
- Users have different permissions.
- The knowledge already exists in reasonably maintained repositories.
- Questions concern rare internal facts rather than recurring learned patterns.
- Content must be deleted or revoked on a predictable schedule.

Choose primarily **fine-tuning** when:

- The desired improvement is behavioral rather than factual.
- The task and target distribution are stable.
- There is a large, representative set of high-quality labeled examples.
- Output format, classification, terminology, or workflow execution matters more than provenance.
- Very high request volume or tight latency can justify training a smaller model.
- All permissible users can access the same learned information.

Choose a **hybrid** when:

- Answers need both current evidence and specialized behavior.
- The base model retrieves the right documents but uses them poorly.
- Search needs domain-specific query or reranking adaptation.
- A smaller tuned model can consume retrieved evidence at lower serving cost.
- The organization requires citations and permissions but also has strict style, workflow, or tool-use requirements.

Choose neither as the sole mechanism when:

- The underlying documents are incomplete, contradictory, or ungoverned.
- Exact real-time data is required; use an authorized database or API tool.
- Deterministic compliance decisions are required; use rules and human review.
- There is no representative evaluation set capable of exposing stale answers, unsupported claims, and permission leaks.

## How to decide empirically

Run a representative, time-split and permission-split evaluation comparing at least:

1. Base model with prompting.
2. RAG with hybrid lexical/vector retrieval and reranking.
3. Fine-tuned model without retrieval.
4. Selective hybrid.
5. Direct long-context input where the relevant material can fit economically.

Measure:

- Answer correctness and critical-error rate.
- Retrieval recall at the passage and document level.
- Citation entailment and completeness.
- Stale-answer and contradiction rates.
- Appropriate abstention.
- Cross-user and cross-tenant leakage.
- Prompt-injection resistance.
- Update and deletion propagation time.
- p50 and p95 end-to-end latency.
- Cost per resolved question, including infrastructure, model tokens, human escalation, evaluation, and operational labor.

The decision should be based on these production-shaped measurements rather than a generic benchmark score.

## Options

1 — RAG-first: Use retrieval as the knowledge layer and rely on prompting and evaluation without task-specific fine-tuning initially.

2 — Fine-tuning-first: Put stable domain knowledge and behavior primarily into model weights, using retrieval only exceptionally.

3 — Selective hybrid: Use RAG as the source-of-truth layer and add fine-tuning only for measured, stable behavior or efficiency gaps.

RECOMMENDATION: 3 — Selective hybrid: Use RAG as the source-of-truth layer and add fine-tuning only for measured, stable behavior or efficiency gaps.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Weak retrieval and authorization evaluation can produce authoritative-looking answers that are unsupported, stale, or exposed to the wrong user.

**Current Legal and Policy Landscape for Copyright and Generative AI in the US and EU**

**United States**  
- **Statutes:** The Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 101 et seq.) provides exclusive rights to authors; fair use (§ 107) is the primary defense for unlicensed AI training. The DMCA (17 U.S.C. § 512) provides safe harbors but raises questions about training on scraped data. No dedicated AI training statute exists.  
- **Regulatory Guidance:** The USPTO and Copyright Office have issued non-binding reports (e.g., 2024 Copyright Office report on AI and copyright) that lean toward requiring human authorship for copyright and acknowledge unresolved questions about training and outputs.  
- **Major Court Developments:**  
  - *Authors Guild v. OpenAI* (S.D.N.Y., ongoing) – class action alleging infringement in GPT training; fair use arguments central.  
  - *New York Times v. OpenAI/Microsoft* (S.D.N.Y., ongoing) – claims direct and vicarious infringement, with detailed allegations of memorization.  
  - *Thaler v. Perlmutter* (D.D.C., 2023) – affirmed no copyright for AI-generated works without human creativity, but training data issues undecided.  
  - *Kadrey v. Meta* (N.D. Cal., ongoing) – challenges use of copyrighted books for Llama training; fair use and implied license raised.  
- **Provider Policies:** OpenAI, Meta, Google, and others offer opt-out mechanisms (e.g., robots.txt, request forms) but no uniform standard. Many rely on fair use while facing mounting lawsuits.  

**European Union**  
- **Statutes:** Directive (EU) 2019/790 (Copyright Directive) Art. 3 (TDM for research organizations) and Art. 4 (TDM for other purposes, subject to rightsholder opt-out). Art. 4 requires that training on copyrighted works is allowed unless the rightsholder reserves rights “in an appropriate manner” (e.g., machine-readable opt-out). The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) imposes transparency obligations – model developers must disclose “sufficiently detailed summary” of training data (Art. 53(1)(d)).  
- **Regulatory Guidance:** The European Commission published FAQs on Art. 4 in 2024, clarifying that opt-outs can be expressed via standardised metadata (e.g., `noTextDataMining`). National implementations vary (e.g., Germany, France).  
- **Major Court Developments:** Limited case law specific to generative AI; general copyright precedents (e.g., *Infopaq*, *Funke Medien*) apply. Early challenges: *C-755/19* (pending, related to TDM).  
- **Provider Policies:** Several EU-based companies (e.g., Mistral, Aleph Alpha) commit to respecting opt-out protocols. Non-EU providers offering services in the EU must comply.  

**Settled Requirements vs. Unresolved Questions**  
- **Settled:** In the EU, Art. 4 TDM exception is the primary legal pathway for training, but it is conditional on respecting opt-outs. Transparency summaries are mandatory under the AI Act. In the US, there is no statutory exception; fair use is a defense, not a right.  
- **Unresolved:**  
  - Whether training is transformative fair use (key US litigation).  
  - Whether outputs that “memorize” parts of training data constitute infringement (NYT case).  
  - EU: What constitutes a valid machine-readable opt-out across all member states.  
  - Both: Liability for downstream outputs that infringe; who bears responsibility – developer, deployer, or user?  

**Implications for Model Developers vs. Enterprise Users**  
- **Developers:** Face direct litigation risk in US; must navigate EU opt-out compliance and transparency reporting. Licensing becomes necessary for high-risk use of copyrighted corpora.  
- **Enterprise Users:** Generally shielded from training liability if they use APIs or models from developers; must focus on output risk (e.g., reproducing copyrighted content), internal use policies, and contractual indemnities. In the EU, deployers (enterprises) also have transparency duties under the AI Act for high-risk systems.  

**Conservative Compliance Approach (Not Legal Advice)**  
- **Training Data Sourcing:** Prioritize public domain, licensed, or synthetic data. For copyrighted works, obtain licenses or rely only on EU Art. 4 with documented opt-out checks.  
- **Opt-Out Protocols:** Implement and respect machine-readable opt-outs (e.g., `robots.txt`, `noai` metadata, Spawning’s sourcing registry). Log which rights have been reserved.  
- **Documentation:** Maintain a detailed training data inventory, including provenance, licensing status, and any opt-out filters applied. This satisfies EU AI Act transparency requirements.  
- **Output Filtering:** Use technical safeguards to prevent memorization (e.g., differential privacy, de-duplication, output classifiers).  
- **Contractual Protections:** For developers, include licensing terms that transfer copyright clearance obligations upstream; for enterprise users, seek contractual warranties and indemnities from model providers.  
- **Jurisdictional Segmentation:** Consider deploying different models or training pipelines for US vs. EU markets to address divergent legal landscapes.

RECOMMENDATION: 1. Implement a conservative compliance approach that combines licensing for high-risk copyrighted materials, rigorous opt-out adherence (especially EU Art. 4), detailed documentation for transparency, and output filtering to mitigate memorization risk, while recognizing that fair use in the US remains unsettled.  
CONFIDENCE: medium  
TOP_RISK: The most immediate and unresolved legal risk is the US fair use question in ongoing lawsuits, which could retroactively impact training practices and create significant liability.

response_text:
## Bottom line

As of July 2026, the evidence does **not** support RAG as a wholesale replacement for fine-tuning. It supports a narrower conclusion:

- **RAG is generally preferable for mutable, sparse, attributable enterprise knowledge.**
- **Fine-tuning is generally preferable for stable behavior, terminology, formatting and task specialization.**
- **A hybrid is usually strongest when an assistant needs both current facts and reliable task behavior.**

Evidence is strongest for RAG’s advantages in freshness, provenance and revocability; moderate and highly system-dependent for factual accuracy; and weak for universal claims about enterprise total cost. Most published studies use public QA or synthetic benchmarks rather than realistic document permissions, OCR errors, conflicting versions and production workloads.

Here, “fine-tuning” means tuning the generator through supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization or continued pretraining. Fine-tuning an embedding model or reranker is itself commonly part of a RAG system.

## Comparison

| Criterion | RAG | Generator fine-tuning | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Factual accuracy** | Often better for new, obscure or document-specific facts—provided retrieval finds authoritative evidence and the model uses it correctly. Bad retrieval can lower accuracy. | Can perform well on narrow, stable, frequently represented knowledge and improve in-domain reasoning patterns. Exact factual recall and fact updates remain unreliable. | RAG usually wins on long-tail and recently changed facts; fine-tuning may win on stable, repeated task patterns. Neither guarantees truth. |
| **Freshness** | Documents can be added, corrected or removed without retraining, subject to connector and indexing delay. | Knowledge remains stale until another training cycle, and old knowledge can persist or conflict with the update. | Clear RAG advantage for changing knowledge. |
| **Citation quality** | Can preserve source, version, page and passage identifiers. However, models still produce unsupported, incomplete or decorative citations. | Can learn citation syntax but cannot reliably identify a source that was not supplied at inference time; fabricated citations are a substantial risk. | RAG is necessary for defensible dynamic citations, but it must be paired with claim-level grounding checks. |
| **Maintenance burden** | Requires connectors, OCR, chunking, deduplication, metadata, index rebuilding, retrieval evaluation, ACL synchronization and source lifecycle management. | Requires curated examples, training, regression testing, model-version migration and repeated tuning when data or behavior changes. | RAG shifts maintenance from model training to data and search operations; it does not eliminate maintenance. |
| **Access control** | Can enforce current user and document permissions at retrieval time and can revoke access by changing the index or entitlement system. | Knowledge encoded in shared weights cannot be reliably filtered by user or promptly deleted. Separate models or adapters per security domain are possible but burdensome. | Strong RAG advantage, although retrieval filters, caches, logs and prompt injection remain security risks. |
| **Latency** | Adds query rewriting, search, reranking, longer prompts and sometimes citation verification. Tail latency can be material. | A direct tuned-model call is normally faster and can use shorter prompts or a smaller model. | Fine-tuning usually wins under strict latency or offline constraints. |
| **Total cost** | Recurring costs include ingestion, vector or search infrastructure, reranking, extra context tokens, monitoring and data operations. | Up-front and recurring costs include data labeling, training, evaluation, retuning and serving. A smaller tuned model can be economical at high volume. | No universal winner. Knowledge churn favors RAG; stable, high-volume tasks can favor fine-tuning. Hybrid has more components but may reduce error and compliance costs. |

## What the evidence shows

### Evidence supporting RAG as a substitute for knowledge-oriented fine-tuning

1. **Retrieval improves access to tail and recently introduced facts.**  
   Work beginning with Lewis et al.’s original RAG study found that external retrieval can improve knowledge-intensive generation over purely parametric approaches. Subsequent studies found that models have particular difficulty with rare entities and facts weakly represented during pretraining, where retrieval is especially valuable.

2. **External knowledge is inspectable and reversible.**  
   An enterprise can update a policy document, invalidate an obsolete version or remove a customer record without trying to alter model weights. This is an architectural advantage, not merely a benchmark result.

3. **RAG enables evidence-based answers.**  
   Retrieval can provide exact source identifiers and passages. This makes human review, auditing and legal defensibility possible in ways that closed-book generation generally cannot match.

4. **Knowledge can remain within existing governance boundaries.**  
   A well-designed system retrieves only documents the authenticated user is entitled to see. This is much more compatible with dynamic, row-level or tenant-specific permissions than encoding the information in shared weights.

### Evidence against treating RAG as a complete replacement

1. **Retrieval recall places an upper bound on grounded accuracy.**  
   If the relevant document is not indexed, uses unexpected terminology, is buried in a table or is filtered incorrectly, the generator cannot ground its answer in it. Dense retrieval alone is often inadequate; enterprise systems commonly need keyword search, metadata filters, reranking and sometimes structured database or graph access.

2. **More context is not automatically better.**  
   Models can ignore evidence, overweight irrelevant passages or struggle when the answer is located in the middle of a long context. Contradictory document versions are particularly problematic.

3. **Citation presence is not citation correctness.**  
   ALCE and related grounding benchmarks show that fluent answers can have incomplete citations or citations that do not entail the associated claim. Citation quality therefore needs at least:
   - citation precision: whether the cited passage supports the claim;
   - citation recall: whether all externally verifiable claims are cited;
   - source quality and version validity.

4. **RAG introduces a new attack surface.**  
   Retrieved documents can contain malicious or accidental instructions, and poisoned content can manipulate generation. Retrieval filters must run before sensitive text enters the model; post-generation redaction is not a reliable security boundary.

5. **RAG does not teach stable behavior particularly efficiently.**  
   Repeating lengthy instructions and examples in every prompt is less dependable and more expensive than tuning a model to follow an organization’s output schema, tone, escalation rules or tool-use protocol.

6. **Published cost and accuracy comparisons are not broadly generalizable.**  
   Many comparisons use different base models, retrieval systems, tuning data and compute budgets. There is no credible universal result that “RAG is cheaper” or “fine-tuning is more accurate” across enterprise workloads.

## Where they are complementary

A useful division of responsibility is:

- **RAG supplies what the assistant should know now.**
- **Fine-tuning teaches the assistant how to act on what it receives.**

A strong hybrid commonly uses fine-tuning to teach the model to:

- distinguish retrieved evidence from instructions embedded inside documents;
- answer only from supplied evidence when required;
- abstain when evidence is insufficient or contradictory;
- produce the organization’s required format;
- use domain terminology and task-specific reasoning patterns;
- select tools and follow escalation policies;
- attach citations to the claims they actually support.

RAG then supplies current policies, contracts, product documentation, customer-specific records and other permission-sensitive material. Fine-tuning the embedding model or reranker on enterprise relevance judgments can further improve retrieval without putting the underlying sensitive facts into the generator’s weights.

Routing also matters. A hybrid system need not retrieve for every request:

- Retrieve for factual, document-specific or current questions.
- Skip retrieval for writing transformations, classification and other knowledge-independent tasks.
- Use authoritative APIs or databases—not free-text RAG—for balances, transactions, inventory and other exact operational state.
- Use deterministic workflows where an incorrect generative answer is unacceptable.

## Maintenance and total-cost implications

A fair annual cost comparison should include more than training and API charges:

**RAG cost**
- document connectors and change detection;
- OCR, parsing, chunking and metadata;
- index and embedding refreshes;
- ACL synchronization;
- retrieval and reranking compute;
- additional input tokens;
- grounding, security and regression evaluation.

**Fine-tuning cost**
- example creation, labeling and de-identification;
- training or adapter jobs;
- hosted-model or deployment-version management;
- regression testing after every model or dataset change;
- retuning when policy or knowledge changes;
- investigation of memorization and data-removal requests.

Fine-tuning becomes more attractive when the workload is stable, high-volume and compressible into a smaller model. RAG becomes more attractive when the corpus or permissions change frequently, queries cover a broad long-tail distribution, or the cost of an unattributed answer is high. Hybrid systems have the highest platform complexity, but may have the lowest risk-adjusted cost when errors, stale answers or unauthorized disclosure are expensive.

## Decision criteria

Choose **RAG-first** when most of the following are true:

- knowledge changes weekly or more often;
- answers must quote or cite authoritative material;
- access depends on the user, tenant, region or document;
- the corpus is broad and sparsely queried;
- deletions and corrections must take effect promptly;
- relevant facts already exist in searchable sources;
- modest additional latency is acceptable.

Choose **fine-tuning-first** when most of the following are true:

- the task and required behavior are stable;
- success is mainly classification, extraction, rewriting, formatting or tool selection;
- provenance is not required for each answer;
- representative labeled examples are available;
- strict latency, offline operation or small-model deployment matters;
- the knowledge is bounded, non-sensitive and changes infrequently.

Choose a **hybrid** when:

- current, attributable facts and specialized behavior are both required;
- the model must reliably abstain, cite, structure responses or follow domain workflows;
- retrieval quality can benefit from enterprise relevance labels;
- a smaller tuned model can offset some RAG token and serving costs;
- compliance requires both dynamic authorization and consistent response policy.

Before selecting an architecture, run all candidates on the same production-like evaluation set. Measure answer correctness, retrieval recall, claim-level citation precision and recall, abstention quality, stale-version handling, cross-user leakage, prompt-injection resistance, p50/p95 latency and fully loaded cost per successful answer.

## Practical options

1. RAG-first: use permission-aware retrieval for enterprise facts and rely on prompting for behavior.
2. Fine-tuning-first: use a tuned model for a stable, bounded task with no requirement for dynamic provenance.
3. Hybrid: use permission-aware RAG for changing, attributable enterprise facts and fine-tuning for stable behavior, format and domain skill.

## Selected evidence

- Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks,” NeurIPS 2020: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
- Mallen et al., “When Not to Trust Language Models: Investigating Effectiveness of Parametric and Non-Parametric Memories,” ACL 2023: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10511
- “Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? Comparing Knowledge Injection in LLMs”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05934
- Gao et al., “Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations” (ALCE): https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14627
- Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172
- Asai et al., “Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511
- Niu et al., “RAGTruth: A Hallucination Corpus for Developing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Language Models”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00396
- Greshake et al., “Not What You’ve Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173

RECOMMENDATION: 3. Hybrid: use permission-aware RAG for changing, attributable enterprise facts and fine-tuning for stable behavior, format and domain skill.
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: A weakly governed retrieval layer can silently return unauthorized, stale or irrelevant evidence, causing the hybrid system to produce confident, well-formatted errors.

## Bottom line

For production software engineering, no single public leaderboard is a reliable model-selection tool. The most informative public evidence comes from combining:

1. **Repository-level issue resolution:** SWE-bench Verified, newer/harder SWE-bench variants, and rolling contamination-resistant sets.
2. **Controlled code editing:** Aider’s polyglot benchmark.
3. **Fresh executable coding tasks:** LiveCodeBench and, secondarily, BigCodeBench/EvalPlus.
4. **Longer, economically meaningful work:** SWE-Lancer, Terminal-Bench, and RE-Bench/METR evaluations.
5. **Actual developer outcomes:** randomized or controlled field studies.

The decisive evaluation should nevertheless use private tasks from the organization’s own repositories. A public score is a property of the **model, agent scaffold, tools, prompt, test access, retry policy, and compute budget**, not of the model alone.

## How useful are the main public evaluations?

| Evaluation | What it measures | Production usefulness | Main limitations |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **SWE-bench Verified** | Resolving 500 human-validated GitHub issues in real Python repositories | **High as a common reference; medium for selection** | Public and increasingly saturated; only 12 repositories; test suites may not capture full intent; scores heavily depend on agent scaffold and budget |
| **SWE-bench Pro and rolling/live SWE-bench variants** | Harder, broader, or newly collected repository issues | **Potentially highest public relevance** | Some datasets or hidden tests are not fully auditable; still unlike a company’s repositories; live sets become contaminated after publication |
| **SWE-bench Multilingual** | Repository repair outside Python | **High when languages match the internal stack** | Smaller slices and uneven repository difficulty; aggregate scores can hide weak languages |
| **Aider polyglot leaderboard** | Multi-file editing in a relatively standardized edit/test loop | **High for interactive editing** | Small, exercise-like tasks; not long-horizon repository work; different Aider modes and retry settings remain consequential |
| **LiveCodeBench** | Recently released competitive-programming problems with executable tests | **Medium as a reasoning and freshness check** | Algorithmic, self-contained problems are unlike feature work, debugging, review, and maintenance |
| **BigCodeBench / EvalPlus** | Function-level generation, library use, and stronger hidden tests | **Medium-low; useful as a floor** | Public static tasks, short context, little repository navigation or tool use |
| **SWE-Lancer** | Paid freelance engineering and project-management tasks | **High external validity for autonomous work** | Limited task and repository distribution; scoring and harness still differ from an internal workflow; manager-task results are not coding results |
| **Terminal-Bench / RE-Bench / METR time-horizon evaluations** | Tool use, shell work, research engineering, and sustained autonomy | **Medium for autonomous-agent deployments** | Task mix is often systems, ML, or research-heavy rather than ordinary product engineering |
| **Security-focused suites such as CyberSecEval** | Vulnerability creation, insecure suggestions, and cyber capabilities | **Useful as a safety gate** | Synthetic coverage and benchmark leakage; cannot replace testing against the company’s actual languages and threat model |
| **HumanEval and MBPP** | Small function synthesis | **Low for model selection** | Saturated, highly exposed in training data, tiny scope, and weak correspondence to repository work |
| **Chatbot preference/Elo arenas** | General user preference | **Very low for coding selection** | Style, verbosity, and brand effects can dominate correctness; little control of tools or repositories |

### Recommended public shortlist

For an issue-to-PR assistant, prioritize:

1. A recent rolling or harder **SWE-bench-style evaluation**.
2. **SWE-bench Verified under a common scaffold**, mainly for comparability.
3. **Aider polyglot** for interactive editing.
4. **SWE-Lancer or Terminal-Bench** if substantial autonomy is intended.
5. **LiveCodeBench** as a contamination-resistant reasoning check—not as the main criterion.

For autocomplete, repository Q&A, code review, or migration assistance, these benchmarks are much less representative. Internal evaluation is essential.

## What recent results actually show

Live leaderboard ranks change too quickly to be procurement evidence, but several dated results illustrate the important patterns:

- The original 2023 SWE-bench paper reported roughly **2% resolution** by the best evaluated model. Early SWE-agent work increased this substantially through better search, editing, and tool use.
- Anthropic reported **62.3% on SWE-bench Verified for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 70.3% in a higher-compute configuration** in February 2025. The eight-point difference is itself evidence that inference budget and scaffold can matter nearly as much as changing models.
- By mid-2025, multiple vendor-reported agent systems were in the low-to-mid 70% range on SWE-bench Verified, while launch results on harder SWE-bench Pro-style evaluations remained below roughly one-quarter. This divergence suggests Verified was becoming saturated and optimized against.
- The initial SWE-Lancer results found that the best tested model solved only **26.2% of individual-contributor tasks** and **44.9% of manager tasks**. Real economically valuable work remained substantially harder than headline repository benchmarks.
- RE-Bench found AI agents competitive with or better than humans at short time budgets on selected research-engineering tasks, but experienced humans pulled ahead as more time was available. Short autonomous bursts do not establish reliable multi-hour ownership.

These results should not be arranged into a single ranking. They used different agents, prompts, tool permissions, token budgets, retry counts, model versions, and sometimes vendor-developed harnesses.

## Benchmark-design and contamination problems

### 1. Public tests measure test passing, not complete intent

SWE-bench evaluates fail-to-pass tests and checks that existing pass-to-pass tests do not regress. That is substantially better than judging text, but:

- Tests may omit edge cases, security requirements, performance constraints, or maintainability concerns.
- An alternative patch can be valid despite differing from the maintainer’s reference patch.
- Conversely, a patch can pass the supplied tests while failing the issue’s broader intent.
- Environment failures can be mistaken for model failures.

SWE-bench Verified improved the original set through human review, but validation does not make every test suite complete.

### 2. Public benchmarks inevitably become training data

SWE-bench tasks, issue descriptions, repositories, reference patches, agent trajectories, and successful solutions are publicly available. Exact-match decontamination is inadequate because models can encounter repository mirrors, discussions, paraphrases, or generated solution traces.

Rolling evaluations such as LiveCodeBench and live/rebench-style repository sets reduce this risk by selecting recent tasks. They do not eliminate it: once published, their useful uncontaminated lifetime is limited. Closed-model training-data claims are also difficult to audit.

For a private evaluation:

- Use internal issues and repository states unavailable outside the company.
- Disable internet access unless production will allow it.
- Keep acceptance tests hidden.
- Search for near-duplicate public issues.
- Rotate a portion of the suite regularly.
- Preserve a final holdout that prompt and agent developers cannot inspect.

### 3. Selection effects distort representativeness

Verified subsets tend to select reproducible, testable issues that fit containerized environments. Production work also includes underspecified requests, distributed systems, flaky integration tests, migrations, reviews, coordination, and clarification with humans. Those are systematically underrepresented.

Aggregate scores can additionally be dominated by particular repositories or task types. Report macro-averages by repository, language, task category, and difficulty rather than only a task-weighted overall average.

## Agent scaffolding must be separated from model capability

A SWE-bench leaderboard usually compares **agent systems**, not bare models. Important variables include:

- Repository retrieval and context construction
- Shell, search, IDE, and test tools
- Whether the model sees test failures
- Edit format and patch-repair logic
- System prompt and repository instructions
- Context-window and token budget
- Number of attempts or parallel trajectories
- Wall-clock limit
- Internet access
- Test-time reranking or model judging

Two complementary comparisons are needed:

### Controlled-model track

Use the same harness, tools, prompts, repository snapshot, retry policy, and budget for every model. This best answers, “Which base model should power our existing assistant?”

Run both:

- **Equal-resource:** same token/tool-call or wall-clock limits.
- **Equal-service-level:** same maximum dollar cost and latency target.

A single restriction can favor one model architecture, so both views are useful.

### Best-product track

Allow each model or vendor agent its recommended scaffold, but impose the same task, security boundary, maximum cost, and deadline. This answers, “Which complete system should we buy?”

Results must identify the exact model version and all inference settings. “SWE-bench score” without that information is not decision-grade evidence.

## Evidence from actual developer work

Public productivity studies show why benchmark success does not guarantee organizational benefit:

- A 2023 GitHub Copilot experiment with a narrow greenfield programming task reported participants completed it **55.8% faster**. This supports usefulness for well-scoped generation, but not necessarily repository maintenance.
- Three field experiments covering thousands of developers reported approximately **26% more completed tasks** with generative-AI assistance, with larger effects for less experienced developers.
- METR’s July 2025 randomized study involved 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 tasks in repositories they knew. With early-2025 AI tools, they were **19% slower**, even though they expected to be faster and believed afterward that they had been faster.

These findings are not necessarily contradictory. Effects depend on task scope, repository familiarity, developer experience, tool latency, generated-code review burden, and whether the assistant interrupts or complements the workflow. Perceived productivity and suggestion acceptance are therefore weak substitutes for measured cycle time and accepted output.

## Metrics that are decision-useful

### Correctness and completion

- **Resolved@1 under the deployed budget**
- **Resolved within the actual retry policy**, with retries and total cost disclosed
- Hidden acceptance-test success
- Existing-test and build regression rate
- Security and static-analysis failure rate
- Blinded human acceptance of the resulting patch
- Success by language, repository, and task type
- Confidence intervals clustered by repository

If retries will be used in production, report both first-attempt performance and eventual success within the allowed budget.

### Human and operational efficiency

- Developer minutes to an accepted change
- End-to-end cycle time, including review and correction
- Number and duration of required interventions
- P50 and P95 latency
- Reliability, timeout, and rate-limit incidence
- Rollback, reopened-issue, and escaped-defect rates

The economically meaningful cost measure is:

**all-in cost per accepted task = API and compute cost + developer review/correction cost, divided by accepted tasks**

Token price alone omits retries, verbosity, failed trajectories, and human cleanup.

### Quality and safety

- Maintainability and fit with local conventions
- Diff minimality where appropriate
- API and architectural compliance
- Vulnerability introduction rate
- Dependency hallucination and license-policy violations
- Prompt-injection resistance when repositories contain untrusted text
- Secret handling, data retention, residency, auditability, and model-version stability

Privacy and critical-security requirements should be hard gates, not dimensions a high coding score can offset.

## Metrics that commonly mislead

- **pass@k with large k:** Useful only if production will pay for and safely select among that many attempts.
- **Leaderboard resolved rate without budget disclosure:** May mostly reflect parallel inference or a superior agent scaffold.
- **HumanEval/MBPP pass rates:** Usually too saturated and too far from repository work.
- **Model-judge scores:** Judges can prefer verbosity, familiar styles, or outputs from their own model family.
- **Chatbot Elo:** Measures preference more than executable correctness.
- **Suggestion acceptance rate:** Can rise because suggestions are frequent or superficially convenient, even if overall work slows.
- **Lines of code generated:** More code can mean more review and maintenance burden.
- **Average score across repositories:** Conceals catastrophic weakness in an important language or domain.
- **Vendor token price:** Does not measure total cost to reach an accepted solution.
- **A point estimate without variance:** Small benchmark differences may reverse across runs or repository samples.

## Balanced evaluation framework

### Stage 1: Define the deployment target

Separate the intended workloads:

- Inline completion
- Repository Q&A
- Scoped edits and refactoring
- Test generation and debugging
- Code review
- Issue-to-PR autonomy
- Larger feature development

Weight them using observed internal workload, not an arbitrary generic coding mix.

### Stage 2: Use public benchmarks as a screen

Require credible performance on the public evaluations that match the intended workload. Do not select the winner yet.

A practical screen might include:

- Recent SWE-bench-style issue resolution
- SWE-bench Verified in a common harness
- Aider polyglot
- LiveCodeBench
- SWE-Lancer or Terminal-Bench for autonomous use
- A relevant secure-coding suite

Reject candidates with unacceptable cost, latency, privacy, or availability regardless of benchmark rank.

### Stage 3: Build a locked internal suite

Use approximately 150–300 representative tasks if feasible, sampled across repositories, languages, ages, and difficulty levels. Include recently completed real work and carefully authored prospective tasks.

Each task should have:

- A fixed repository snapshot
- Hidden functional and regression tests
- Build, lint, type, and security checks
- A maximum cost and wall-clock budget
- A rubric for architectural and maintainability requirements
- A blinded human-review procedure

Reserve a final holdout and rotate part of the suite quarterly.

### Stage 4: Run both scaffold tracks

1. **Same assistant scaffold for every model**
2. **Best vendor-native or model-specific scaffold**

Repeat stochastic tasks enough to estimate variance. Report first attempt, production-policy success, total tokens, tool calls, time, and cost. Prevent agent developers from tuning against the final holdout.

### Stage 5: Conduct a blinded production pilot

Randomize eligible tasks or developers between candidates using a crossover design where practical. Measure:

- Time to accepted change
- Review and correction time
- Completed accepted tasks per developer-week
- Defects, rollbacks, and reopened work
- Intervention and abandonment rates
- Developer satisfaction as a secondary measure

Stratify results by experience, language, and workflow. A model that helps newcomers but slows repository experts may still be valuable if routed selectively.

### Stage 6: Decide on utility, uncertainty, and gates

Use public benchmarks for screening or tie-breaking rather than as the dominant weighted component. A reasonable final decision structure is:

- **60%:** lower confidence bound on internal offline accepted-task utility
- **40%:** measured production-pilot productivity and quality
- **Hard gates:** privacy, security, reliability, latency, data governance, and maximum all-in cost

Prefer a Pareto frontier over a single opaque composite: correctness, developer time, cost, latency, and safety should remain visible. The winning system may also be a router—using a fast inexpensive model for completion and a stronger agentic model for difficult repository work.

## Principal sources

- [SWE-bench paper and leaderboard](https://www.swebench.com/)
- [OpenAI: Introducing SWE-bench Verified](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/)
- [SWE-agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793)
- [Anthropic: Claude 3.7 Sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-7-sonnet)
- [LiveCodeBench](https://livecodebench.github.io/)
- [Aider model leaderboards](https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/)
- [SWE-Lancer](https://openai.com/index/swe-lancer/)
- [METR: RE-Bench](https://metr.org/blog/2024-11-22-evaluating-r-d-capabilities-of-llms/)
- [METR: Early-2025 AI and experienced open-source developer productivity](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/)
- [GitHub Copilot productivity experiment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590)

## Decision options

1. Select the model with the highest headline public coding-benchmark score.
2. Select the best performer in one standardized public agent harness.
3. Use public benchmarks only as a screen, then select on a locked, budget-matched internal task suite and a blinded production pilot with security and operational gates.

RECOMMENDATION: 3. Use public benchmarks only as a screen, then select on a locked, budget-matched internal task suite and a blinded production pilot with security and operational gates.
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: Public benchmark gains may not transfer to your repositories, workflow, or agent scaffold, especially under contamination and different inference budgets.
