## Bottom line

For production software engineering, no public benchmark is sufficient by itself. The most useful public evidence is a **portfolio**:

1. **SWE-bench Verified plus a fresher SWE-bench variant**, run under an identical agent scaffold, for repository-level issue resolution.
2. **Aider Polyglot** for interactive, multi-language code editing.
3. **Terminal-Bench or METR task evaluations** if the assistant will operate autonomously in terminals and CI.
4. **LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench** as narrower diagnostics for coding fundamentals, freshness, and library use.
5. **SWE-Lancer and developer productivity studies** as reality checks on whether benchmark success transfers to valuable work.

For purchasing a model, public evaluations should be a screening mechanism. The decisive evaluation should be a **private, post-cutoff, production-like task set combined with a randomized developer trial**.

Public leaderboards change rapidly, so the result patterns below are more reliable than any current rank.

## Which public evaluations are most useful?

| Evaluation | Best use | Production relevance | Main limitation |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **SWE-bench Verified** | Bug fixing and issue resolution in existing repositories | High | Public answers, Python-heavy, test-passing is not necessarily a good patch, and scores depend heavily on the agent |
| **SWE-bench Live, Multilingual, Pro, or rebench-style variants** | Freshness, harder tasks, language breadth | High when the artifacts and protocol are auditable | Some sets are hidden or only partly reproducible; methodology varies |
| **Aider Polyglot** | Interactive editing across several languages | Medium-high | Small exercise-style changes; measures the Aider workflow as well as the model |
| **Terminal-Bench** | Autonomous terminal, build, debugging, and environment work | Medium-high for agents | Broad task mixture and strong scaffold dependence |
| **SWE-Lancer** | Economically meaningful freelance engineering tasks | High external realism | Task distribution may not resemble an enterprise codebase; grading and reproducibility vary by task |
| **METR time-horizon/task suites** | Long-horizon autonomous work and human comparison | Medium-high for autonomy | Smaller specialized task sets; completion time is not identical to business value |
| **LiveCodeBench / LiveBench coding** | Relatively fresh competitive-programming ability | Medium as a diagnostic | Algorithmic puzzles are unlike most repository maintenance |
| **BigCodeBench** | Function implementation and use of multiple libraries/APIs | Medium | Mostly bounded implementations rather than long-lived software changes |
| **RepoBench / CrossCodeEval** | Repository-aware completion and retrieval | High for autocomplete products | Weak proxy for issue resolution or autonomous agents |
| **EvalPlus, HumanEval, MBPP** | Fast sanity checking and regression tests | Low | Small functions, highly saturated, likely exposed in training data |
| **Chat arenas or LLM judges** | Preference and explanation quality | Low for engineering selection | Style can dominate correctness; judges can be biased or unstable |

### 1. SWE-bench is the strongest general public signal—but only under controlled conditions

The original [SWE-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770) contains 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories. [SWE-bench Verified](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) is a human-reviewed 500-task subset intended to remove ambiguous or broken tasks.

Its strengths are significant:

- The model must inspect an unfamiliar repository, localize a problem, modify multiple files when necessary, and preserve existing behavior.
- Evaluation is executable rather than based only on textual similarity.
- Tasks originated as actual software issues rather than generated coding questions.
- It exposed the importance of repository navigation and tools, not merely code completion.

The historical trajectory is also informative. The original paper’s strongest baselines resolved under 2% of tasks. By 2024, stronger models and agents were resolving a substantial fraction of Verified, and 2025 vendor system reports moved into roughly the 70% range, with some higher-compute configurations around 80%. That is genuine progress, but it also demonstrates that **the benchmark now measures advances in scaffolding, retries, context management, and test-time compute alongside model quality**.

Important limitations:

- The issue, repository history, gold commit, and often tests are public.
- The 12-repository original set is narrow and Python-centric.
- A patch may pass the available tests while being brittle, overfitted, insecure, or inconsistent with maintainers’ intent.
- Tasks with clean issue descriptions and deterministic tests are overrepresented.
- Enterprise work involving internal services, migrations, access controls, flaky CI, or stakeholder clarification is mostly absent.
- Verified improves task validity; it does **not** make the set contamination-free.

Fresh, multilingual, and more difficult SWE-bench derivatives are therefore valuable complements. However, hidden benchmarks such as some “Pro” evaluations trade contamination resistance for reduced independent reproducibility.

### 2. Aider Polyglot is useful for pair-programming behavior

The [Aider leaderboard](https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/) evaluates models using an actual code-editing workflow across multiple programming languages. It is more representative than HumanEval of a developer asking a model to change existing code, and it exposes failures in diff generation, instruction following, and edit formats.

It is especially useful when the proposed assistant is chat- or IDE-driven rather than fully autonomous. Its limitations are that the tasks are relatively bounded and that results are specifically for the Aider prompts, repository maps, retries, and editing machinery. A rank from Aider cannot safely be transferred to another IDE agent.

### 3. Terminal-Bench and METR matter for autonomous agents

[Terminal-Bench](https://www.tbench.ai/) measures whether an agent can operate in a containerized terminal, use tools, diagnose environments, and complete multi-step work. This is closer to an autonomous engineering agent than a code-generation benchmark.

METR’s [long-task research](https://metr.org/research/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/) adds a useful human baseline and measures how completion probability changes with the time a competent human would need. It provides a more decision-relevant picture of autonomy than context-window size or isolated coding scores.

For both, the result belongs to the **model-agent system**. Tool policies, command wrappers, context compaction, timeout handling, retries, and token budgets can materially alter results.

### 4. SWE-Lancer is a valuable reality check

[SWE-Lancer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12115) contains 1,488 real freelance software-engineering tasks associated with more than $1 million in payouts. Its 2025 results showed that frontier systems could capture some economic value but still failed a majority of the available work.

This contrasts with increasingly high SWE-bench Verified results. The difference is important: economically valuable tasks are often ambiguous, heterogeneous, and difficult to reduce to a clean issue-plus-tests format.

SWE-Lancer should not be treated as a universal enterprise benchmark, but it is good evidence against interpreting a high repository benchmark score as near-human engineering capability.

### 5. LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench are diagnostics, not selection criteria

[LiveCodeBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07974) continuously collects newly released programming problems and dates them, reducing—but not eliminating—contamination. It is useful for algorithmic reasoning and for testing whether an older static coding score has become saturated.

[BigCodeBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15877) uses more complex instructions and substantially more library/API functionality than HumanEval. It is useful when the assistant must compose existing libraries correctly.

Neither captures repository discovery, requirement negotiation, build systems, code review, or long-term maintainability. They are best used to diagnose why a model failed, not to decide which assistant will make a team productive.

## What recent real-world evidence says

Public benchmark progress has not translated uniformly into developer productivity.

- A controlled [GitHub Copilot study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590) with 95 developers found that participants completed a bounded HTTP-server task about **55.8% faster** with Copilot.
- Later field experiments involving thousands of developers reported approximately **26% more completed tasks**, with larger gains among less-experienced developers. Task-count outcomes, organizational context, and tool-adoption effects limit generalization.
- In contrast, METR’s [2025 randomized study of experienced open-source developers](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/) covered 246 tasks in repositories the developers already knew. Allowing early-2025 AI tools made them **19% slower**, even though participants believed the tools had helped.
- The [2024 DORA report](https://dora.dev/research/2024/dora-report/) found mixed associations between AI adoption, documentation, code quality, throughput, and stability. These are survey correlations rather than a controlled model comparison.

These findings are not necessarily contradictory. AI can perform very well on bounded implementation work while imposing overhead on experts working in complex, familiar repositories. Benefits depend on:

- Developer experience.
- Task size and ambiguity.
- Codebase familiarity.
- Review and correction cost.
- Whether work can be easily verified.
- Whether the tool is autocomplete, conversational, or autonomous.
- Organizational constraints such as CI latency and security review.

This is why **net developer time saved** is more decision-useful than either a benchmark pass rate or the number of generated lines.

## Contamination concerns

Public coding benchmarks have unusually serious contamination risks because their answers are executable commits already available online.

### Sources of contamination

- Training data may contain the issue, pull request, commit message, patch, tests, or discussions.
- Repository history can reveal the gold patch if the agent has unrestricted internet or Git access.
- “Model training cutoff” claims are difficult to audit and may not cover later fine-tuning, retrieval indexes, or synthetic data derived from the benchmark.
- Exact-string decontamination misses semantic memorization and paraphrases.
- Public leaderboards encourage repeated tuning of prompts and agents against the test set.
- A test suite itself can become a target for overfitting.

A model producing a memorized patch still passes executable tests, so test-based grading does not solve this problem.

### Practical mitigations

For the internal evaluation:

1. Use tasks created or completed after the candidate models’ plausible data cutoffs, preferably after model release.
2. Keep the task list, hidden tests, and reference solutions private.
3. Disable internet and repository-history access unless the production assistant will have them.
4. Snapshot dependencies and environments so every model receives the same state.
5. Search outputs for unusual overlap with reference commits, comments, or obsolete implementation details.
6. Include paraphrased or symbol-renamed variants for a small diagnostic subset. A large performance collapse can indicate brittle retrieval or memorization, though transformations can also change difficulty.
7. Rotate a portion of the task set after each procurement cycle.
8. Build hidden tests from the requirement independently of the reference implementation, and use mutation testing to check whether those tests are discriminating.

A useful fundamental distinction is:

- **Fully public and reproducible** benchmarks are easier to contaminate.
- **Private or continuously refreshed** benchmarks are harder to contaminate but less independently auditable.

A defensible selection process needs both.

## Agent scaffolding differences

A software benchmark score is usually not a property of the model alone. It is a result for:

> model + prompt + repository search + context selection + tools + edit format + retries + test loop + compute budget

On SWE-bench, systems such as SWE-agent, OpenHands, Agentless, Aider-style agents, and vendor-specific harnesses can produce markedly different results with the same underlying model. Differences include:

- Whether the agent is given a repository map.
- Search and symbol-indexing quality.
- Whether it can run tests after every edit.
- How failed commands and long outputs are summarized.
- Whether it generates additional tests.
- Number of attempts or independent trajectories.
- Whether an oracle or reranker selects among patches.
- Token, dollar, and wall-clock budgets.
- Temperature and model version.
- Access to the internet or Git history.

Two separate comparisons are therefore needed:

1. **Model comparison:** use the same scaffold, prompt, tools, attempt count, context budget, and execution environment for every model.
2. **Product comparison:** allow each vendor’s native agent, but impose the same dollar and wall-clock budget and report the result as a model-agent system.

Mixing these two questions produces misleading procurement decisions.

## Decision-useful and misleading metrics

### Decision-useful metrics

**Quality-adjusted resolved@1**

The percentage of tasks completed in one production-realistic run that:

- Pass independently designed hidden tests.
- Do not regress existing tests.
- Pass build, type, lint, security, and license checks.
- Receive acceptable scores from blinded human reviewers.

This should be the primary technical metric.

**Net developer time saved**

Measure task time from assignment to accepted change, including:

- Prompting and waiting.
- Reading generated code.
- Correcting failures.
- Reviewing and rerunning CI.
- Reverting or replacing poor changes.

This captures the overhead missed by coding-speed benchmarks.

**Cost per accepted task**

Use:

\[
\frac{\text{inference + infrastructure + retry + review + correction cost}}
{\text{accepted production-quality tasks}}
\]

Token price or cost per attempt alone favors cheap models that fail frequently.

**Defect and rework rate**

Track escaped bugs, security findings, review iterations, reverts, and related incidents over 30–90 days. This is a lagging but important measure.

**Latency and operational reliability**

Report median and p95 time to first useful patch, timeout rate, malformed-tool-call rate, provider errors, and rate-limit behavior.

**Stratified performance**

Break results down by language, repository size, task category, difficulty, developer experience, and context length. Aggregate success can hide a model that fails on a critical stack.

**Calibration and safe abstention**

Measure whether confidence predicts success and whether the assistant declines tasks it cannot safely perform. A lower raw completion rate can be preferable if failures are detected before review or deployment.

### Metrics that can mislead

- **Raw leaderboard rank:** often combines different agents, budgets, and model versions.
- **Pass@k without charging for k:** rewards sampling budget and assumes an oracle can identify the correct patch.
- **SWE-bench resolved rate alone:** ignores maintainability, security, task value, and human correction time.
- **Public-test pass rate:** encourages test overfitting.
- **HumanEval or MBPP accuracy:** saturated, contaminated, and too narrow.
- **Lines of code or acceptance rate:** developers may accept code temporarily and later rewrite or revert it.
- **Context-window size:** does not measure effective code retrieval or reasoning over the context.
- **Tokens per task:** lower token usage is not valuable if it increases failures or review.
- **LLM-as-judge scores:** useful for triage, but sensitive to judge identity, verbosity, and stylistic similarity.
- **Arena preference or Elo:** measures subjective user preference, not verified repository correctness.
- **Unweighted averages:** resolving ten trivial changes is not equivalent to resolving one critical defect.
- **Vendor-reported scores without artifacts:** model version, harness, retries, and failed-task exclusions may be unclear.

## Balanced evaluation framework for an internal coding assistant

### Stage 0: Establish hard gates

Before ranking quality, require:

- Acceptable data retention and training policies.
- Regional, privacy, and compliance requirements.
- Protection against repository and secret exfiltration.
- Audit logs and administrator controls.
- License and attribution handling.
- Tool allowlists and sandboxing.
- Prompt-injection defenses for repository content.
- Availability, rate limits, and version-pinning commitments.

A model that fails a hard gate should not be rescued by a higher benchmark score.

### Stage 1: Public benchmark screen

Select benchmark slices that match the intended product:

- **Repository bug fixing:** SWE-bench Verified plus a fresher or multilingual set.
- **Pair programming/editing:** Aider Polyglot.
- **Autonomous terminal operation:** Terminal-Bench and selected METR-style tasks.
- **Library/API composition:** BigCodeBench.
- **Fresh algorithmic reasoning:** LiveCodeBench.
- **Autocomplete:** RepoBench or CrossCodeEval.
- **Security-sensitive code:** a public secure-coding suite such as CyberSecEval, supplemented by CodeQL, Semgrep, dependency scanning, and internal adversarial tasks.

Run each candidate through the same scaffold first. Advance several models rather than choosing the public-benchmark winner.

### Stage 2: Private repository evaluation

Construct approximately 150–300 tasks, or enough to provide useful confidence intervals, stratified to match the expected workload. For example:

- 30% defect fixes.
- 20% small features.
- 15% tests and test repair.
- 10% refactors.
- 10% dependency or API migrations.
- 10% code review and security remediation.
- 5% documentation or operational configuration.

Include easy, medium, and long-horizon work from multiple repositories and languages. Add some tasks that require clarification or abstention rather than blindly generating a patch.

For every task:

- Freeze the initial repository state.
- Define tool and network permissions.
- Set equal dollar and wall-clock budgets.
- Use one attempt for the primary metric.
- Repeat a smaller random subset to estimate stochastic variance.
- Grade with hidden tests plus blinded human review.
- Preserve all transcripts, commands, costs, and timing.

Use paired bootstrap or another paired analysis because every candidate sees the same tasks. Report confidence intervals rather than treating a one- or two-point difference as meaningful.

### Stage 3: Randomized developer trial

Run a four- to six-week crossover or task-level randomized trial with representative developers.

Compare:

- No AI or the current assistant.
- Each finalist under its intended interface.
- Developers of different experience levels.
- New and familiar repositories.

Primary outcome:

- Time from task start to accepted merge or reviewer-approved completion.

Secondary outcomes:

- Review time.
- Number of review cycles.
- Developer interruptions and waiting time.
- Defects or reverts.
- Subjective cognitive load and trust.
- Frequency and appropriateness of assistant use.

Do not rely on self-reported speed alone; the METR result shows that perceived and measured productivity can diverge.

### Stage 4: Cost and risk normalization

A reasonable weighted decision score is:

- **40%:** quality-adjusted internal resolved@1.
- **25%:** net developer time saved.
- **15%:** total cost per accepted task.
- **10%:** latency, availability, and operational reliability.
- **5%:** maintainability, security, and calibration.
- **5%:** public-benchmark breadth and freshness.

Adjust the weights to the use case. For a security-critical organization, security should be a gate or receive much greater weight. For an autonomous background agent, cost and successful unattended completion deserve more weight than conversational quality.

### Stage 5: Canary deployment and continuous evaluation

Deploy the winner to a limited group and monitor:

- Acceptance, edit, and revert rates.
- Human time through review and merge.
- CI failures and security findings.
- Per-language and per-repository performance.
- Cost and p95 latency.
- Model-version changes.
- Incidents involving secrets, tool misuse, or unexpected network access.

Keep a rotating private holdout and rerun it before accepting model updates. Provider aliases should not be assumed to remain behaviorally stable.

## Decision options

1. Select the model with the highest SWE-bench Verified score.
2. Select the model with the highest weighted public-benchmark composite.
3. Run a fixed-scaffold, cost-normalized public benchmark screen, then select on a blinded, post-cutoff internal task trial with randomized developer measurement.

Option 1 is simple but confounds model and agent and is vulnerable to contamination. Option 2 provides broader coverage but still assumes that public benchmark weights resemble the organization’s work. Option 3 costs more initially, but directly measures transfer, developer productivity, quality, and total cost.

RECOMMENDATION: 3. Run a fixed-scaffold, cost-normalized public benchmark screen, then select on a blinded, post-cutoff internal task trial with randomized developer measurement.
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: A model selected on public leaderboards may fail on your repositories because contamination and scaffold-specific gains do not transfer.

response_text:
## Bottom line

No public benchmark is sufficient for choosing a production coding model. The strongest public evidence comes from a **portfolio**:

1. **SWE-bench Verified, Live, and Multilingual** for repository-level issue resolution.
2. **Aider Polyglot** for practical editing across languages.
3. **LiveCodeBench** for fresh, contamination-resistant code generation.
4. **Terminal-Bench** for tool use and recovery in a real terminal.
5. **SWE-Lancer** for external validity on commercially valued work.
6. **BigCodeBench/EvalPlus** as lower-cost capability checks.

The final decision should nevertheless be driven primarily by a **private evaluation on representative internal tasks**, including developer time, review burden, cost, and escaped defects.

## Decision options

1. **Choose the model with the highest current public coding-leaderboard score.**
2. **Choose from a weighted composite of standardized public coding benchmarks.**
3. **Select with a two-track evaluation: fixed-scaffold public benchmarks plus a blinded, private, cost-normalized trial on representative repository tasks.**

Option 3 is preferable because public leaderboards incompletely measure product fit and frequently compare different agents rather than just different models.

## Most useful public evaluations

| Evaluation | What it measures well | Main limitations | Production usefulness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SWE-bench Verified** | Diagnosing and fixing real GitHub issues in an existing repository; navigating code, editing multiple files, and passing regression tests | Public tasks and patches create contamination risk; Python-heavy; tests may not fully specify correctness; results depend heavily on the agent | **Highest-value public anchor**, provided the scaffold and budget are controlled |
| **SWE-bench Live** | Newer repository issues, reducing pretraining contamination and leaderboard overfitting | Still becomes public after release; environments and issue selection can be noisy | Prefer over older subsets when reproducible and temporally valid |
| **SWE-bench Multilingual** | Repository work outside Python | Smaller samples per language and repository | Important for Java, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C++, and mixed-language organizations |
| **SWE-Lancer** | Real freelance engineering work with monetary task values; includes less benchmark-like requirements | Expensive and difficult to reproduce; grading can require expert judgment; task mix may not match enterprise work | Strong evidence about external validity, but not ideal for frequent regression testing |
| **Aider Polyglot** | Editing an existing codebase, diff generation, test-driven repair, and performance across six languages | Exercism tasks and solutions are public; strongly affected by edit format, prompting, and architect/editor modes | Very useful for interactive editing assistants if run with the intended edit protocol |
| **Terminal-Bench** | Operating in a terminal, inspecting files, running tools, recovering from errors, and completing multi-step tasks | Measures the whole agent; tool descriptions, shell policy, retries, and compute can dominate | Useful when the product is an autonomous or semi-autonomous coding agent |
| **LiveCodeBench** | Executable correctness on recently released programming problems; temporal slices help expose contamination | Mostly self-contained algorithmic tasks, not repository engineering | Best public check for fresh code-generation ability, but not a proxy for software-engineering productivity |
| **BigCodeBench** | Practical function-level tasks involving libraries and APIs | Limited repository context; public tasks can eventually leak into training | Better than HumanEval for API use and implementation breadth |
| **EvalPlus: HumanEval+ and MBPP+** | Detecting superficially correct solutions through much stronger tests | Still small, function-level, and highly exposed | Useful as a cheap smoke test, not a selection benchmark |
| **RepoBench/CrossCodeEval** | Repository-aware completion and retrieval | Similarity metrics can reward copying without proving behavioral correctness | Relevant to autocomplete and retrieval, less so to autonomous issue resolution |
| **CyberSecEval/SecurityEval** | Selected secure-coding weaknesses and exploit-related behavior | Narrow vulnerability coverage; some grading is synthetic or judge-based | Use as a safety gate, supplemented by internal SAST, DAST, and adversarial tests |

For specialized assistants, add **DS-1000** for data-science code or a browser/visual benchmark for frontend work. Do not average irrelevant benchmark categories into the selection score.

## What recent results actually establish

Public figures should be treated as **source-dated snapshots**, because model versions and leaderboards change:

- The original SWE-bench paper reported only about **2% resolution** for its strongest evaluated general model. When OpenAI introduced the 500-task human-validated **SWE-bench Verified** set in 2024, a GPT-4o configuration was reported at **33.2%**.
- Anthropic reported **62.3%** for Claude 3.7 Sonnet in 2025 and **70.3% with a custom scaffold**. Regardless of later leaderboard standings, that roughly eight-point difference is direct evidence that a reported “model score” may substantially be an **agent-system score**.
- During 2025, reported SWE-bench Verified system scores entered the 70%-plus range. This represents genuine progress, but also increasing optimization against a fixed, public, relatively small test set.
- **SWE-Lancer** contains roughly 1,500 freelance tasks collectively valued at about $1 million. Its initial study found that no evaluated frontier system solved a majority of the work. This is an important counterweight to near-saturated function-level benchmarks.
- **LiveCodeBench** generally produces lower and more discriminating results on post-cutoff problem windows than old benchmarks such as HumanEval. Rankings can also change by time window, suggesting that old, aggregate scores partly measure exposure and benchmark familiarity.
- **EvalPlus** showed that many HumanEval and MBPP solutions passing their original tests fail expanded hidden tests. Original pass rates therefore overstate semantic correctness.

The important trend is not that a particular model permanently ranks first. It is that:

- Function-level benchmarks are increasingly saturated.
- Repository agents have improved rapidly.
- Scaffolding and inference budget account for a material portion of that improvement.
- Real economically meaningful tasks remain substantially harder.

## Why public scores can mislead

### 1. Contamination and benchmark overfitting

HumanEval, MBPP, Exercism, GitHub issues, accepted pull requests, and their solutions are publicly accessible. For closed models, outsiders generally cannot determine whether they appeared in pretraining, fine-tuning, retrieval corpora, or benchmark-specific training.

Even a nominally post-training-cutoff task is not automatically clean:

- Provider cutoff dates may be incomplete or apply only to base pretraining.
- Later fine-tuning and retrieval data may differ.
- Once a benchmark is published, subsequent model versions can train against it.
- Semantically equivalent solutions can be memorized without exact textual overlap.

Mitigations include:

- Prefer rolling or live benchmarks with tasks created after the tested model snapshot.
- Maintain private tasks and patches that have never been publicly posted.
- Measure suspicious similarity to known patches, including identifier choices and irrelevant edits.
- Disable internet access or log every retrieval operation.
- Ask vendors for benchmark-specific training and evaluation attestations.
- Rotate holdouts rather than reusing the same internal set for every model iteration.

A temporal split reduces contamination risk; it does not prove its absence.

### 2. Agent scaffolding differences

SWE-agent, OpenHands, Aider, vendor-native agents, and custom harnesses can differ in:

- Repository indexing and retrieval
- Editing format
- Planning prompts
- Tool descriptions
- Test execution policy
- Context compression
- Error recovery
- Retry count and parallel samples
- Token and wall-clock budgets
- Whether the agent sees test output
- Internet access and external documentation
- Use of separate planner, reviewer, or editor models

A leaderboard entry can therefore compare:

> model + prompt + tools + retrieval + inference budget + retry policy

rather than models alone.

Use two tracks:

1. **Model-controlled track:** identical scaffold, prompts, tools, context, retries, and budget. This estimates the marginal value of the model.
2. **Product-system track:** each model uses its best realistic scaffold under the same cost, wall-clock, security, and access constraints. This identifies the best deployable system.

Both are needed. The first helps with procurement and model routing; the second predicts product outcomes.

### 3. Weak or incomplete grading

Passing visible or hidden tests does not necessarily establish that a patch is suitable:

- Tests may omit edge cases.
- A patch may suppress an error rather than fix its cause.
- Unrelated behavior may regress.
- The change may introduce a vulnerability, race, resource leak, or compatibility issue.
- An enormous or unmaintainable patch can still pass.
- Some benchmark environments reward modifying tests or configuration in unintended ways.

Private evaluation should combine hidden tests with mutation testing, static analysis, security checks, performance checks, and human review.

### 4. Unrepresentative task distributions

SWE-bench emphasizes issue repair in open-source repositories. LiveCodeBench emphasizes contest problems. Aider emphasizes relatively compact edits. None adequately represents all of:

- Ambiguous requirements
- Architecture and design discussions
- Long-running migrations
- Internal frameworks
- Build and deployment systems
- Legacy code
- Code review
- Incident diagnosis
- Organizational conventions
- Maintaining a change months later

A high public score can therefore coexist with poor performance on the work that consumes most of an organization’s engineering time.

## Evidence from real developer work

Real-world studies are mixed, which is itself decision-relevant:

- A well-known GitHub Copilot controlled experiment found participants completed a small JavaScript task about **56% faster** with assistance. The task was narrow, greenfield, and had a clear endpoint.
- Larger field experiments have reported roughly **20–30% more completed tasks**, often with greater gains for less-experienced developers. These studies are more realistic but still depend on how organizations define and count work.
- A 2025 METR randomized study of experienced open-source developers working on repositories they knew found that allowing early-2025 AI tools made them about **19% slower**, despite developers expecting a speedup and afterward believing they had received one. The sample and tooling were limited, but the study directly captured prompting, waiting, checking, and rework overhead.
- SWE-Lancer’s results similarly show that success on short coding benchmarks does not translate automatically to completion of commercially valuable engineering tasks.

These findings are not necessarily contradictory. AI can accelerate boilerplate and unfamiliar syntax while slowing experts on context-heavy tasks through latency, review burden, incorrect assumptions, and disruption of an existing mental model. Consequently, perceived usefulness, code acceptance rate, and lines generated are not reliable productivity measures by themselves.

## Decision-useful metrics

### Primary metrics

1. **Accepted Task Rate at a fixed budget**  
   Fraction of tasks accepted by a reviewer after hidden tests, regression checks, and quality review, under fixed dollar and wall-clock limits.

2. **Cost per accepted change**  
   Include API charges, retries, infrastructure, developer prompting time, review time, and rework—not just token cost.

3. **End-to-end cycle time**  
   Time from task assignment to merged, deployable change. Report median and p90/p95, not only the mean.

4. **Developer time saved**  
   Measure active work, waiting, review, and correction separately. Use randomized or crossover trials when possible.

5. **Post-merge quality**  
   Reverts, escaped defects, incidents, security findings, support burden, and follow-up work at 7- and 30-day intervals.

6. **Success by task subgroup**  
   Break out language, repository size, task type, context length, developer experience, and required tool use. Aggregate scores conceal routing opportunities.

7. **Reliability and calibration**  
   Variance across runs, rate of confidently wrong answers, appropriate abstention, and ability to recognize missing information.

A useful economic summary is:

\[
\text{Expected net value} =
P(\text{accepted within budget}) \times \text{task value}
- \text{model cost}
- \text{review/rework labor}
- \text{expected defect and security loss}
\]

Report the underlying components as well as the combined value.

### Metrics that often mislead

- **HumanEval or MBPP pass@1 alone:** narrow, saturated, and contamination-prone.
- **Pass@k with a large k:** useful only if production really generates and validates that many candidates. It hides inference cost and selection difficulty.
- **One SWE-bench number:** ignores scaffold, language, budget, task mix, and contamination.
- **Unnormalized leaderboard scores:** a system using many retries and millions of tokens is not directly comparable to a one-shot system.
- **Chatbot-arena or preference Elo:** often rewards style, verbosity, and plausible explanations rather than executable correctness.
- **LLM-as-judge quality scores:** vulnerable to judge bias, model-family preference, and persuasive but incorrect output.
- **Code acceptance rate:** developers may accept boilerplate or low-risk changes while rejecting difficult ones; acceptance says little about net productivity.
- **Lines of code generated:** rewards verbosity and can be negatively associated with maintainability.
- **Token count alone:** pricing, caching, latency, tool calls, and reviewer time determine actual cost.
- **Average latency:** hides tail latency, which matters strongly in an interactive workflow.
- **Vendor-reported results without exact harness details:** usually not reproducible and may use a favorable scaffold or inference budget.

## Balanced selection framework

### Stage 1: Establish hard gates

Before ranking quality, require:

- Contractual privacy and no-training guarantees
- Data residency and retention compliance
- Acceptable software and output licensing terms
- Repository access controls and auditable tool calls
- Required context capacity
- API reliability and rate limits
- Secure-code and secret-handling thresholds
- Acceptable p95 latency and maximum per-task cost

A model failing a hard gate should not be rescued by a high coding score.

### Stage 2: Run the two public tracks

For every candidate, publish an evaluation card recording the exact:

- Model snapshot and API date
- System and user prompts
- Agent version
- Tool permissions
- Context and output limits
- Temperature and sampling policy
- Retry and parallel-sampling counts
- Wall-clock and token budgets
- Internet/retrieval access
- Cost calculation
- Task exclusions and environment failures

Use both the fixed scaffold and the best deployable scaffold. Report bootstrap confidence intervals and paired task-level differences rather than comparing rounded point estimates.

### Stage 3: Construct a private task set

Use approximately 100–300 tasks initially, stratified to match expected use:

- Bug diagnosis and repair
- Small feature implementation
- Tests and test repair
- Refactoring
- Dependency or API migration
- Code review
- Documentation tied to code
- Build, CI, and infrastructure changes
- Performance and security fixes
- Ambiguous tasks requiring clarification

Select tasks from representative repositories, including unpopular and legacy components. Keep solutions and hidden tests private. Refresh a portion every quarter and reserve a final untouched set for procurement decisions.

Count a task as successful only if it:

- Completes within the budget
- Passes hidden and regression tests
- Does not weaken tests
- Passes applicable security and performance checks
- Meets a blinded reviewer’s maintainability rubric
- Requires no more than a specified amount of human correction

### Stage 4: Run a developer trial

Randomize tasks or developers between candidates using a crossover design. Capture:

- Active development time
- Waiting time
- Prompting and context-preparation time
- Review and correction time
- Task completion and abandonment
- Developer satisfaction
- Defects and follow-up work

Do not reveal the model identity where the interface permits blinding. Developer preference is a secondary metric, not a substitute for measured outcomes.

### Stage 5: Weight the evidence

A reasonable default scorecard is:

- **45%:** private accepted-task utility, including quality and rework
- **15%:** randomized developer productivity trial
- **15%:** SWE-bench Verified plus Live/Multilingual results
- **5%:** Aider Polyglot
- **5%:** LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench/EvalPlus
- **5%:** Terminal-Bench or an equivalent tool-use evaluation
- **10%:** latency, reliability, cost, security, and operational fit

Adjust these weights to the intended product. For an autocomplete tool, increase editing and latency weights. For an autonomous issue agent, increase repository, terminal, and recovery weights. For a Java/TypeScript organization, reduce the weight assigned to Python-heavy evaluations.

Prefer a **Pareto frontier** over a single rank: quality versus cost, latency, and risk. A cheaper model may be the right default router while a stronger model handles difficult tasks.

### Stage 6: Require a meaningful winning margin

Choose a model only if it:

- Passes all hard gates
- Improves net value by a practically important margin
- Has confidence intervals inconsistent with a trivial difference
- Does not win solely on one repository or task type
- Remains favorable under plausible alternative cost and task weights

Then deploy gradually, retain a control group, and monitor cost per accepted change, review burden, reverts, and security findings. Re-evaluate after material model, scaffold, pricing, or repository changes.

## Public sources

- Jimenez et al., [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://www.swebench.com/)
- OpenAI, [Introducing SWE-bench Verified](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/)
- Jain et al., [LiveCodeBench](https://livecodebench.github.io/)
- Liu et al., [SWE-Lancer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12115)
- Aider, [LLM Leaderboards and Polyglot Benchmark](https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/)
- BigCodeBench, [Benchmark site](https://bigcode-bench.github.io/)
- EvalPlus, [GitHub repository](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus)
- Terminal-Bench, [Benchmark site](https://www.tbench.ai/)
- METR, [Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/)
- Peng et al., [The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590)

RECOMMENDATION: 3. Select with a two-track evaluation: fixed-scaffold public benchmarks plus a blinded, private, cost-normalized trial on representative repository tasks.
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: Public benchmark gains may not transfer because contamination, scaffold quality, and your repositories’ task mix can dominate the underlying model.

## Scope and bottom line

This review focuses on **production inference**: accelerators, host servers, idle capacity, data-center overhead, cooling, electricity emissions, and the embodied footprint of serving hardware. It excludes model training except where a published per-response lifecycle estimate does not separate it cleanly.

The main conclusion is that **“energy per query” is not an intrinsic property of an LLM**. It can vary by more than an order of magnitude with:

- input, output, and hidden-reasoning token counts;
- model size, quantization, and architecture;
- batching and cache-hit rates;
- accelerator generation and server configuration;
- utilization and treatment of idle capacity;
- data-center PUE, cooling, and location;
- whether estimates include host equipment, embodied hardware, or electricity-supply water.

No serving mode is automatically best. Fixed GPUs can be most efficient at sustained high load; shared autoscaling or serverless generally performs better for bursty demand—but only if unused physical capacity is actually consolidated or powered down.

## Recent estimates and why they differ

| Source and date | Reported result | Boundary and principal caveat |
|---|---:|---|
| Luccioni, Jernite & Strubell, 2024, *Power Hungry Processing* | About **0.047 kWh per 1,000 text-generation inferences**, or **0.047 Wh each**, averaged over studied open-model experiments | Short benchmark examples, generally smaller models, and experimental machine energy rather than a complete production service. Demonstrates task/model variation, not ChatGPT-scale consumption. |
| de Vries, 2023 | Approximately **564 MWh/day** for 195 million ChatGPT-like requests, equivalent to **2.9 Wh/request** | A capacity model based on older A100-era assumptions, estimated throughput, and request volume—not a production measurement. Widely repeated as if it were universal. |
| Epoch AI, 2025 | Approximately **0.3 Wh for a typical GPT-4o interaction** | Engineering estimate using newer hardware and likely token lengths. Long context can raise the result to several or tens of Wh, so 0.3 Wh is not applicable to large documents or long reasoning. |
| Google, 2025 | Median Gemini Apps text interaction: **0.24 Wh**, **0.03 gCO₂e**, and **0.26 mL water** | Operational measurement includes accelerators, hosts, allocated idle capacity, and facility overhead. It is a median across Google's model/service mix; token counts, routing, and tails are not fully exposed. Embodied hardware and off-site electricity water are not equivalent to a full lifecycle assessment. |
| OpenAI/Sam Altman, 2025 | Average ChatGPT query: **0.34 Wh** and **0.000085 US gallons**, about **0.32 mL water** | Vendor assertion without a published measurement methodology, model mix, token distribution, carbon figure, or lifecycle boundary. Numerically close to Google's operational estimate but not independently auditable. |
| Mistral AI lifecycle publication, 2025 | A 400-token Le Chat response: **1.14 gCO₂e** and **45 mL water** | Broader lifecycle methodology than the operational cooling numbers above, with different infrastructure, model, electricity, and allocation assumptions. It should not be read as evidence that the response necessarily uses 100 times Google's electricity. |
| Li et al., 2023, *Making AI Less “Thirsty”* | A 500 mL bottle for roughly **10–50 GPT-3 responses**, or about **10–50 mL/response** | Modeled older GPT-3 deployment and included both on-site cooling and off-site electricity-generation water. Location and time materially change the estimate. |

Sources: [Luccioni et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16863), [de Vries](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2023.09.004), [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/how-much-energy-does-chatgpt-use), [Google](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734), [OpenAI disclosure](https://blog.samaltman.com/the-gentle-singularity), [Mistral AI](https://mistral.ai/news/our-contribution-to-a-global-environmental-standard-for-ai), and [Li et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03271).

### Reconciliation

The apparent contradiction between approximately **0.05, 0.24, 0.3, and 2.9 Wh per interaction** largely disappears after correcting for functional unit and assumptions:

1. **Different work is called a query.**  
   A 50-token answer, a 1,000-token answer, and reasoning over a 100,000-token document cannot share a meaningful per-query value. Prefill cost grows with input length; decode cost grows with generated tokens; hidden reasoning, retries, safety models, and tool calls add unobserved work.

2. **Hardware and batching changed.**  
   A100-era capacity models are not representative of highly batched inference on newer H100/H200-class or custom accelerators. Continuous batching, paged attention, prefix caching, quantization, and optimized kernels increase tokens per joule.

3. **Marginal and average energy are different.**  
   Marginal accelerator energy answers, “What did one additional request add?” Average allocated energy also assigns idle servers, warm replicas, and control-plane overhead to requests. The former is useful for optimization; the latter is necessary for footprint accounting.

4. **Production boundaries differ.**  
   GPU-only measurements omit CPU, DRAM, storage, networking, failed requests, safety filters, idle reserve, and cooling. A PUE of 1.1 adds 10% to IT energy; a PUE of 1.5 adds 50%.

5. **Carbon is not energy.**  
   Google's 0.03 gCO₂e for 0.24 Wh implies roughly 125 gCO₂e/kWh under its accounting. The same electricity at 400 gCO₂e/kWh would produce about 0.096 g. Market-based renewable claims, location-based grid averages, and hourly marginal emissions are different quantities.

6. **Water boundaries are especially inconsistent.**  
   Google's figures imply approximately 1.08 L of direct cooling water per kWh, while OpenAI's assertion implies roughly 0.95 L/kWh. Their similarity suggests a narrow operational-water basis, although OpenAI did not publish its method. The 10–50 mL and 45 mL estimates include broader or different water effects, especially electricity-generation and lifecycle water. Water withdrawal, water consumption, and scarcity-weighted impact must also be kept separate.

7. **Medians hide expensive tails.**  
   A median consumer chat response says little about code generation, long-document analysis, agent loops, or reasoning models. For capacity and environmental reporting, p90/p99 token lengths and retries can matter more than the median.

## Comparison of serving modes

These categories overlap: an external API may internally use serverless multitenancy and autoscaling. The important distinction is who controls and can observe physical capacity.

| Mode | Hardware utilization | Electricity consequences | Water and emissions | Measurement quality |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed dedicated GPUs** | Determined by customer traffic. Often low for bursty or latency-sensitive services because enough GPUs must remain available for peak demand. Can be excellent under steady, batchable load. | Idle servers consume substantial baseline power. No cold-start or repeated model-loading penalty. Highest efficiency is possible when continuously and densely batched. | Fully determined by selected region, grid, cooling, PUE, and hardware lifecycle. Idle capacity still causes emissions and cooling demand. | Best observability: server/PDU power, utilization, tokens, and idle allocation can all be measured. |
| **Autoscaled endpoints** | Usually higher than fixed fleets when replicas track demand. Minimum replicas, cooldown periods, fragmentation, and warm pools limit improvement. | Saves energy only if removed replicas permit physical consolidation or lower-power states. Logical scale-down without physical scale-down merely moves idle energy elsewhere. | Similar location dependence. Rapid scaling can shift workload among regions, complicating carbon and water accounting. | Good if the operator exposes nodes and power; weaker for managed endpoints that report only instance-hours. |
| **Serverless inference** | Potentially highest through cross-tenant multiplexing, routing, continuous batching, and scale-to-zero. Physical utilization is normally undisclosed. | Well suited to intermittent demand. Cold starts, repeated weight loading, lost caches, and latency reserves add energy. “Zero customer instances” does not prove that provider GPUs were powered down. | Provider fleet location and cooling dominate. Shared hardware can reduce embodied impact per token if it is genuinely better utilized. | Billing milliseconds are not energy. Reliable accounting requires provider disclosure of fleet power and allocation methods. |
| **External model API** | Unknown to the customer. Hyperscalers can combine custom hardware, large batching pools, model routing, and high utilization; they may also maintain large latency reserves. | Can be efficient, but model choice overwhelms infrastructure gains: routing a simple task to a large reasoning model can consume more than a well-run small dedicated model. Hidden tokens and retries are material. | Provider decides region, electricity, cooling, and hardware refresh. Reported operational carbon may use market-based accounting and omit embodied emissions. | Lowest independent observability. Client-side power or network measurements reveal almost nothing about provider inference. |

### A useful utilization model

Let idle power be 25% of full-load power as an explicitly illustrative assumption, and let useful throughput scale linearly with utilization \(u\). Relative energy per useful token is then:

\[
\frac{0.25+0.75u}{u}
\]

Relative to full utilization, this is:

- **3.25× at 10% utilization**
- **1.25× at 50% utilization**
- **1.0× at 100% utilization**

Real low-load behavior can be worse because small batches also reduce throughput. Conversely, GPU “utilization” reported by `nvidia-smi` can appear high during memory-bound decoding while model-FLOP efficiency remains low. The operational metric that matters is therefore **useful tokens or completed requests per facility joule at a fixed latency and quality target**, not GPU busy percentage alone.

A fixed deployment's average energy per request can be expressed as:

\[
E_{\text{request}} =
\frac{\mathrm{PUE}\,[P_{\text{idle}}T+
(P_{\text{active}}-P_{\text{idle}})t_{\text{busy}}]}{N}
\]

where \(T\) is the accounting period and \(N\) is the number of successful, useful requests. This makes the break-even against an API or serverless service workload-specific rather than architectural.

## Practical measurement strategy

### 1. Define stable functional units

Report at least:

- Wh per million uncached input tokens;
- Wh per million cached input tokens;
- Wh per million visible output tokens;
- Wh per completed request within the service-level objective;
- separate distributions for short, medium, and long contexts;
- hidden/reasoning tokens, speculative tokens, retries, cancellations, and tool calls;
- quality and latency alongside energy, so an efficient but unusable model does not win.

Per-request reporting may remain as a user-facing summary, but it should be derived from a published workload distribution.

### 2. Measure the entire serving system

Preferred measurement order:

1. Rack PDU or revenue-grade server input power.
2. BMC server telemetry.
3. Accelerator power through DCGM or equivalent, plus CPU RAPL and memory estimates.
4. Software-only power models only when physical measurements are unavailable.

Sample frequently enough to capture prefill/decode bursts. Include model servers, hosts, load balancers, storage, safety models, orchestration, and an allocated share of warm and idle capacity.

Use:

\[
E_{\text{facility}}=\mathrm{PUE}\times
(E_{\text{accelerator}}+E_{\text{CPU/DRAM}}+
E_{\text{storage/network}}+E_{\text{allocated idle}})
\]

Do not multiply by PUE if power was already measured at the facility input.

### 3. Join energy telemetry to request traces

Record for every request:

- model and version;
- accelerator and precision;
- region and time;
- input, cached-input, output, and hidden-token counts;
- batch size and queue time;
- prefix/KV-cache hits;
- speculative-decoding acceptance;
- completion, cancellation, and retry status;
- latency and quality outcome.

For a shared batch, allocate energy using estimated prefill and decode work rather than dividing equally among requests.

### 4. Publish three environmental views

- **Operational location-based:** actual regional electricity times regional/hourly grid intensity.
- **Operational market-based:** contractual renewable-energy treatment, clearly labeled.
- **Lifecycle:** operational footprint plus allocated hardware manufacture, replacement, and disposal.

For water, report separately:

- direct data-center consumption;
- water withdrawal;
- electricity-supply-chain consumption;
- scarcity-weighted impact by watershed.

A litre consumed in a water-stressed region is not environmentally equivalent to a litre in a water-abundant region.

### 5. Treat external providers as a supply-chain measurement problem

Contracts or procurement questionnaires should require:

- Wh per input and output token by model/version;
- whether idle capacity and failed requests are included;
- p50, p90, and long-context results;
- location- and market-based emissions;
- PUE, direct WUE, region, and hourly matching method;
- embodied-hardware treatment;
- model routing and hidden-token policy;
- third-party assurance or reproducible benchmark results.

Without these fields, use an explicit range based on comparable hardware benchmarks rather than assigning a false-precision footprint.

## Reduction priorities

1. **Avoid unnecessary inference.** Cache deterministic and semantic results, remove duplicate calls, cap agent loops, prevent retries, and avoid generating text that users do not consume.

2. **Use the smallest model that meets measured quality.** Route simple tasks to small or distilled models and escalate only hard cases. Model selection commonly has more impact than choosing among similar data centers.

3. **Reduce token work.** Shorten system prompts, trim retrieved context, use prefix caching, limit output length, and summarize conversation history. RAG is beneficial only when retrieval and added context displace more expensive model work.

4. **Improve throughput at the required latency.** Apply continuous batching, paged attention, optimized kernels, quantization, and suitable hardware. Benchmark speculative decoding because poor draft-token acceptance can waste energy.

5. **Match capacity to demand.** Maintain dedicated capacity only for the steady base load; serve bursts with shared autoscaling. Verify that scale-down changes physical power rather than merely cloud billing.

6. **Optimize carbon and water independently.** Select low-carbon regions and hours, but avoid shifting computation into water-stressed areas. Use hourly marginal emissions for scheduling decisions and location-based emissions for inventory reporting.

7. **Extend hardware life.** Higher utilization, repair, reuse, and slower replacement reduce embodied emissions and mineral impacts. New hardware should be adopted based on lifecycle tokens-per-impact, not performance alone.

8. **Check for rebound effects.** A 50% reduction in joules per token does not reduce total energy if lower cost causes token volume to more than double.

## Decision options

1. Keep fixed dedicated GPU capacity and optimize it.
2. Adopt measurement-first shared autoscaling with model routing, while retaining dedicated capacity only for steady base load.
3. Move all inference to external APIs and rely on provider-level efficiency and disclosure.

Option 2 is the best general policy. It preserves the high efficiency and observability of dedicated infrastructure where utilization is predictably high, while using shared capacity for peaks. It should be implemented only with whole-system metering and provider disclosure; otherwise, autoscaling may reduce cost without reducing physical energy.

RECOMMENDATION: 2. Adopt measurement-first shared autoscaling with model routing, while retaining dedicated capacity only for steady base load.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Provider-reported per-query figures may omit idle capacity, hidden tokens, embodied hardware, or off-site water, making an apparently efficient option worse in practice.

parsed.recommendation: 2. Adopt measurement-first shared autoscaling with model routing, while retaining dedicated capacity only for steady base load.

## Executive summary

Inference has no single defensible “energy per query.” Recent estimates range from roughly **0.05 Wh for short generation with smaller open models** to about **4 Wh for a sparsely used 176B-parameter production endpoint**. Recent frontier-service estimates cluster near **0.24–0.34 Wh for a typical short prompt**, but these are provider measurements or models, not universal constants.

Most disagreement comes from six factors:

1. **Different work:** model size, input length, output length, precision, and quality.
2. **Marginal versus allocated energy:** incremental GPU work versus idle capacity and host energy divided across requests.
3. **Utilization:** batching, replica fragmentation, traffic shape, and whether capacity scales to zero.
4. **System boundary:** accelerator only versus CPU, memory, cooling, power conversion, networking, and hardware manufacture.
5. **Environmental accounting:** regional grid mix, market-based versus location-based emissions, and direct versus supply-chain water.
6. **Statistic and unit:** median versus mean, “query” versus token, and laboratory benchmark versus production traffic.

Consequently, **deployment labels alone do not determine impact**. A saturated dedicated GPU can outperform serverless, while an idle dedicated endpoint can be orders of magnitude worse. For intermittent demand, shared serverless or pooled APIs usually have the strongest utilization advantage, provided the provider genuinely multiplexes hardware and supplies credible environmental telemetry.

## What recent estimates actually measure

| Source | Electricity estimate | Water and emissions | Boundary and principal caveat |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Luccioni et al., *Power Hungry Processing* (2024) | Average text generation around **0.047 kWh per 1,000 inferences**, or **0.047 Wh/inference** | Carbon varied with workload and assumed grid | Predominantly smaller open models and short standardized tasks. Benchmark energy, not a fully allocated frontier production service. |
| Luccioni et al., BLOOM deployment study (2022–23) | About **3.96 Wh/request** | Roughly **1.5 gCO2e/request** | Observed API traffic on an always-available **16×A100** deployment of BLOOM-176B. Idle capacity was spread over relatively sparse traffic, making it an important dedicated-endpoint example. |
| de Vries, *Joule* (2023) | Often quoted as **2.9 Wh/ChatGPT query** | Dependent on assumed grid | A modeled division of estimated daily server energy by estimated request count—not direct ChatGPT telemetry. It reflected older hardware and serving assumptions. |
| Epoch AI (2025) | Approximately **0.3 Wh for a representative short ChatGPT query** | Not a direct water or carbon measurement | Bottom-up model using plausible modern hardware and serving efficiency. Long contexts and long outputs can raise energy by one or two orders of magnitude. |
| Google, median Gemini Apps prompt, May 2025 | **0.24 Wh/prompt** | **0.03 gCO2e** and **0.26 mL direct water** | Provider fleet measurement. It includes active accelerators, host CPU/RAM, allocated idle machines, and data-center overhead, but not a complete hardware and electricity-supply-chain LCA. |
| Sam Altman, 2025 | **0.34 Wh/query** | **0.32 mL water/query** | A provider statement without enough methodology for independent reproduction. It is broadly consistent with Google and Epoch but is not an independent measurement. |
| Li et al., *Making AI Less Thirsty* (2023) | Based on modeled GPT-3-era inference energy | **500 mL for approximately 10–50 responses**, or **10–50 mL/response** | Includes modeled onsite and offsite water and is highly sensitive to region, season, cooling, grid generation, and older serving assumptions. |
| Mistral environmental LCA (2025) | No directly comparable per-response electricity figure in the public summary | **1.14 gCO2e and 45 mL water** for a 400-output-token Le Chat response | Broader lifecycle methodology, model-specific assumptions, and infrastructure allocation. It should not be compared directly with Google’s operational direct-water figure. |

These are **different functional units**, not a confidence interval for the same query. For example:

- The approximately **85×** gap between 0.047 Wh and 3.96 Wh is largely explained by model scale, generation length, hardware generation, and whether idle service capacity is allocated.
- The drop from the older 2.9 Wh estimate to approximately 0.24–0.34 Wh is plausible given newer accelerators, quantization, continuous batching, speculative decoding, higher fleet utilization, and model-routing improvements.
- Google’s 0.26 mL and Mistral’s 45 mL differ by roughly **170×**, but one is principally direct operational cooling water while the other uses a broader lifecycle methodology. They are not contradictory measurements of an identical boundary.
- Google’s 0.03 gCO2e for 0.24 Wh implies an effective carbon intensity near 125 gCO2e/kWh. The same electricity in a 500 gCO2e/kWh region would produce about 0.12 g, before embodied emissions.

The IEA estimated that all data centers—not just AI—used about **415 TWh in 2024** and could exceed **945 TWh in 2030**. It does not provide a reliable split between LLM training, inference, conventional cloud workloads, and other AI. Multiplying a per-query estimate by a guessed worldwide query count therefore gives false precision.

## Why utilization dominates serving architecture

A useful average-energy equation is:

\[
E_{\text{request}} =
E_{\text{dynamic request}}
+\frac{P_{\text{idle system}}\times T}{N_{\text{requests}}}
+E_{\text{host/network}}
+E_{\text{cooling and power overhead}}
\]

The second term can dominate. For illustration, a service with a 1 kW whole-system baseline attributes:

- **10 Wh of baseline energy per request** at 100 requests/hour;
- **0.1 Wh per request** at 10,000 requests/hour.

The dynamic model computation has not changed; only utilization has.

GPU “utilization” also has several meanings:

- percentage of time a replica has traffic;
- accelerator kernel occupancy;
- achieved versus available memory bandwidth;
- batch fill;
- useful tokens per second;
- useful tokens per joule.

`nvidia-smi` GPU utilization alone is inadequate because LLM decoding is often memory-bound and can report activity without high computational efficiency. Generated but rejected speculative tokens and padded or discarded batches should not count as useful work.

Google’s study offers a rare production allocation: approximately **58%** of energy went to active accelerator work, **25%** to host CPU and memory, **10%** to idle machines, and **8%** to data-center overhead, with rounding. This demonstrates why accelerator-only measurements understate service energy. Most providers still do not disclose accelerator duty cycle, batch occupancy, or replica utilization.

## Comparison by deployment model

| Deployment | Utilization behavior | Environmental strengths | Environmental weaknesses | Best workload fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed dedicated GPUs** | Capacity remains powered regardless of traffic | Can achieve excellent tokens/J at sustained load; complete control over model, quantization, batching, region, and power measurement | Idle power and embodied hardware are allocated over few requests at low load; capacity is commonly sized for peaks; hardware may become obsolete early | Stable, high-volume demand with strict privacy or latency requirements |
| **Autoscaled endpoints** | Adds and removes replicas, usually retaining a minimum; responds after a utilization or queue threshold | Reduces prolonged overprovisioning while retaining operational control | Minimum replicas, cooldown windows, scale lag, and fragmented batches can remain expensive; scaling out can reduce batch efficiency | Predictable variable demand with periods long enough to amortize scaling |
| **Serverless inference** | Ideally multiplexes tenants and scales customer capacity to zero | Usually strongest option for sparse or bursty traffic; pooled warm workers can maintain high fleet utilization | Cold starts, model-weight loading, cache loss, and opaque multi-tenant allocation; “scale to zero” may apply only to billing, not physical hardware | Low-duty-cycle applications, prototypes, and bursty services |
| **External model APIs** | Provider controls routing, batching, model selection, and fleet utilization | Potentially best fleet-wide utilization and access to custom accelerators and optimized kernels; no customer-owned idle GPU | Model and hardware are opaque; per-query disclosures are usually unaudited; customer cannot choose power region or verify idle and embodied allocations | Commodity workloads where auditability, data governance, and model control are acceptable |

There is no sound universal ordering between serverless and external APIs. They can use the same physical backend, and an “autoscaled endpoint” may still reserve a private GPU. The relevant questions are whether hardware is physically shared, whether replicas reach zero, how well requests batch, and how provider-wide idle capacity is allocated.

### Likely ranking by traffic pattern

- **Sparse or unpredictable traffic:** shared serverless or a well-utilized API generally beats a private always-on endpoint.
- **Moderate variable traffic:** autoscaling usually improves on fixed capacity, but only if minimum replicas and cooldowns are aggressively controlled.
- **Sustained high traffic:** a right-sized dedicated deployment can equal or beat shared services, particularly with continuous batching and efficient quantization.
- **Strict latency with large peaks:** environmental cost rises because reserved headroom is part of the service requirement, even when unused.

## Reconciling water estimates

Water figures should identify at least three separate quantities:

1. **Direct data-center water consumption**, primarily evaporative cooling.
2. **Indirect operational water**, especially water consumed in electricity generation.
3. **Lifecycle water**, including semiconductor fabrication, hardware manufacture, and construction.

They should also distinguish **withdrawal** from **consumption**. Withdrawal may return to the watershed; evaporated or incorporated water is consumed. A liter used in a water-stressed watershed during summer is not equivalent to a liter of reclaimed water in a water-abundant region.

A credible report should therefore state:

- direct WUE in liters per kWh and its denominator;
- water source, including potable versus reclaimed;
- electricity-supply water intensity;
- watershed and season;
- withdrawal and consumption separately;
- whether hardware-manufacturing water is included.

Energy and water can trade off. Evaporative cooling may lower electricity and carbon while increasing local water consumption; dry cooling may do the reverse. “Lowest carbon” and “lowest water” regions may consequently differ.

## Measurement strategy

### 1. Define a reproducible functional unit

Do not report only “per query.” Record:

- exact model and version;
- input, cached-input, reasoning, and output tokens;
- context-window bin;
- modality;
- quantization and decoding configuration;
- quality or task-success threshold;
- latency target;
- request concurrency and batch size;
- region and measurement period.

Report at least **Wh per 1,000 useful output tokens**, **Wh per successful task**, and fully allocated **Wh per request**. Include median, p95, and mean because long contexts can dominate the mean.

### 2. Measure the entire system

For self-hosted or private endpoints:

- use rack PDU or server BMC/IPMI readings for CPU, RAM, storage, fans, and accelerator energy;
- sample GPU energy counters through NVML at sufficiently short intervals;
- measure idle power with the model loaded;
- record replica uptime, batching, cold starts, queue depth, tokens, and throughput;
- multiply IT electricity by measured or provider-specific PUE;
- avoid relying exclusively on accelerator TDP or cloud billing time.

For autoscaled and serverless systems, replay the same production trace over several diurnal cycles. Include scale-up, cooldown, cold-load energy, and failures. A short saturated benchmark conceals most autoscaling losses.

For APIs, request provider disclosure of:

- operational Wh per token or quality-normalized task;
- whether host, idle capacity, PUE, and networking are included;
- direct and indirect water;
- location- and market-based carbon;
- embodied hardware allocation;
- model-routing and version-change policy;
- independent assurance.

Price and billed token count are not reliable proxies for energy.

### 3. Report two operational views

Publish both:

- **Marginal energy:** incremental energy caused by an additional request on an already-running service.
- **Fully allocated average energy:** all service energy, including idle capacity and shared overhead, divided across served work.

Marginal figures help optimize code. Fully allocated figures support inventories and deployment comparisons. Mixing the two is the most common source of apparently contradictory estimates.

### 4. Calculate emissions transparently

Report:

\[
C_{\text{operational}} = \sum_t E_t \times CI_{\text{location},t}
\]

using time- and location-specific grid carbon intensity where possible. Report contractual or market-based Scope 2 figures separately; renewable certificates do not show that physical electricity was carbon-free when consumed.

Report embodied emissions separately and state the allocation method—for example, accelerator-hours over expected hardware life. Low utilization increases both operational idle energy and embodied emissions per useful task.

### 5. Validate under production conditions

Run an A/B replay with identical requests and quality constraints across deployment options. The test should cover:

- normal and peak traffic;
- warm and cold states;
- failures and retries;
- p95 latency;
- at least one full weekly demand cycle;
- total monthly energy, not just per-request efficiency.

The last requirement prevents efficiency gains from being hidden by rebound: cheaper, faster inference often causes many more calls and longer outputs.

## Reduction priorities

In approximate order of effectiveness:

1. **Avoid unnecessary inference:** cache safe responses, reuse embeddings and prefix states, deduplicate retries, and require explicit value from background model calls.
2. **Use the smallest model that meets a measured quality threshold:** route easy requests to compact models and escalate only when necessary.
3. **Control tokens:** cap output length, summarize history, prune retrieved documents, and avoid repeatedly sending unchanged context.
4. **Increase useful batching:** use continuous batching and prefix caching while protecting latency objectives.
5. **Optimize execution:** test FP8, INT8, or lower-bit quantization, efficient attention kernels, speculative decoding, and distillation. Measure quality and total energy; speculative decoding can waste energy when acceptance is poor.
6. **Match architecture to traffic:** scale sparse workloads to zero, consolidate moderate traffic, and reserve dedicated accelerators only when sustained utilization justifies them.
7. **Choose appropriate hardware:** a smaller or older accelerator at high utilization can outperform a large new accelerator that stays mostly idle. Evaluate tokens/J rather than TDP alone.
8. **Extend hardware life:** avoid premature replacement and include manufacture in procurement decisions.
9. **Schedule and locate flexibly:** move noninteractive work toward hours and regions with lower marginal carbon and lower water stress.
10. **Track absolute totals:** monitor monthly accelerator-hours, electricity, water, emissions, and useful tasks in addition to efficiency ratios.

## Decision options

1. Keep fixed dedicated GPUs for all inference.
2. Move all inference to autoscaled private endpoints.
3. Move all inference to serverless platforms.
4. Move all inference to external model APIs.
5. Adopt a measured, utilization-first hybrid: use a transparent shared scale-to-zero service for bursty demand, and right-size autoscaled or dedicated GPUs only for sustained demand.

Option 5 is preferable because traffic shape—not the commercial label—determines whether pooling or dedicated capacity is more efficient. It also preserves a path to dedicated deployment when measured utilization, privacy, or latency justifies it.

## Key sources

- Luccioni et al., “Power Hungry Processing: Watts Driving the Cost of AI Deployment?” FAccT 2024: https://doi.org/10.1145/3630106.3658542
- Luccioni, Viguier, and Ligozat, “Estimating the Carbon Footprint of BLOOM”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02001
- de Vries, “The Growing Energy Footprint of Artificial Intelligence,” *Joule* 2023: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2023.09.004
- Epoch AI, “How much energy does ChatGPT use?” 2025: https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/how-much-energy-does-chatgpt-use
- Google, “Measuring the Environmental Impact of Delivering AI at Google Scale,” 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734
- Li et al., “Making AI Less Thirsty,” 2023: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03271
- Mistral AI environmental assessment, 2025: https://mistral.ai/news/our-contribution-to-a-global-environmental-standard-for-ai
- IEA, *Energy and AI*, 2025: https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai

RECOMMENDATION: 5. Adopt a measured, utilization-first hybrid: use a transparent shared scale-to-zero service for bursty demand, and right-size autoscaled or dedicated GPUs only for sustained demand.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Opaque provider telemetry can make a seemingly efficient shared service impossible to verify while hiding idle capacity, broad lifecycle impacts, and rebound from rapidly growing token demand.
