# RAG vs. Fine-Tuning for Enterprise Knowledge Assistants: An Evidence-Based Assessment

## 1. Factual Accuracy

**RAG has a decisive, evidence-backed advantage for factual knowledge injection.**

The most directly relevant study is Ovadia et al. (EMNLP 2024, Microsoft), which compared unsupervised fine-tuning against RAG across knowledge-intensive tasks. Their finding: "RAG consistently outperforms [fine-tuning], both for existing knowledge encountered during training and entirely new knowledge," and "LLMs struggle to learn new factual information through unsupervised fine-tuning." Soudani et al. (SIGIR-AP 2024) tested twelve LMs and found RAG "surpasses fine-tuning by a large margin, particularly for least popular factual knowledge"—precisely the regime enterprises operate in, where domain-specific entities are low-frequency in the base model's pretraining distribution.

**Fine-tuning has a different accuracy advantage.** The Microsoft agriculture case study (Balaguer et al., 2024) showed that fine-tuning added ~6 percentage points of accuracy and that RAG added a further ~5 points on top—demonstrating complementarity, not substitution. Fine-tuning's accuracy gains are behavioral: it improves how the model responds (style, format, reasoning patterns, domain vocabulary) rather than what facts it recalls. Supervised fine-tuning with curated Q&A pairs can outperform unsupervised continual pretraining and, in some narrow multi-hop settings, may even exceed RAG, but this requires expensive labeled data that is rarely practical for large, changing enterprise knowledge bases.

**Critical caveat:** Most direct comparisons test RAG against *unsupervised* fine-tuning (continual pretraining on raw text). Supervised fine-tuning on labeled Q&A pairs is under-studied in head-to-head comparisons, so the evidence most strongly supports RAG over unsupervised FT specifically. Additionally, RAG accuracy is contingent on retrieval quality—if the retriever fails, the system fails. Production deployments require hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse), re-ranking, and hallucination detection to maintain quality.

---

## 2. Freshness

**RAG wins structurally.** RAG retrieves from a live index at query time; updating the knowledge base requires only re-indexing changed documents (minutes to hours). Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights at a fixed training cutoff. When a policy changes, a fine-tuned model needs an entirely new training job.

This is not a marginal advantage. For environments with quarterly or more frequent updates—drug formularies, tax tables, product catalogs, employee handbooks, regulatory guidance—fine-tuning becomes operationally infeasible. The maintenance cost compounds with each refresh: a fine-tuning cycle requires data curation, training, evaluation, and deployment, whereas RAG requires only document ingestion.

---

## 3. Citation Quality and Auditability

**RAG has a structural advantage but does not automatically produce trustworthy citations.**

RAG can cite the specific source document or chunk it retrieved, enabling audit trails and human verification. Fine-tuning cannot produce reliable citations—facts are distributed across weights with no provenance.

However, RAG citation quality is an active research problem. Amazon's CiteFix (ACL 2025 Industry Track) reports citation accuracy of only ~74% for popular generative search engines and introduced post-processing correction achieving ~15% relative improvement. Citation hallucination—where a model cites a source that doesn't support the claim—is a documented failure mode arising from retriever-generator mismatches. Production RAG requires explicit citation verification (NLI-based checking, post-processing, or groundedness scoring) to be reliable. Fine-tuning the generator specifically for citation quality (Penzkofer & Baumann, KONVENS 2024) is one approach that illustrates a hybrid use of FT within a RAG system.

**Bottom line:** RAG *enables* citations; fine-tuning *cannot*. But realizing that capability requires engineering investment. A naive RAG system that generates citations without verification is not production-grade.

---

## 4. Maintenance Burden

**RAG generally has lower maintenance burden for knowledge updates but adds system complexity.**

| Dimension | RAG | Fine-Tuning |
|-----------|-----|-------------|
| Knowledge update | Re-index (minutes–hours) | Full retraining cycle (days–weeks + data curation) |
| System complexity | Retrieval pipeline, vector store, embeddings, reranking, evaluation | Model weights, versioning, regression testing |
| Data curation | Continuous but incremental | 2–6 weeks of senior engineering + domain-expert review per cycle |
| Base model upgrades | Retrieval pipeline carries over | Full retraining and re-evaluation required |

The dominant cost in fine-tuning is not compute but human capital. Curating high-quality prompt-completion pairs requires "extensive collaboration between Subject Matter Experts and Data Engineers" (CloudAtler 2026). This cost has not gotten cheaper even as compute costs fall. Conversely, RAG's ongoing burden is retrieval-quality engineering—chunking strategy, embedding model versioning, drift detection—but these costs are incremental rather than cyclical.

For frequently changing knowledge, RAG's burden is lower. For stable behavioral requirements, fine-tuning's one-time cost amortizes well.

---

## 5. Access Control

**RAG has a decisive, structural advantage—when architected correctly.**

Fine-tuning bakes all training data into weights accessible to every user of the model. Once knowledge is in the weights, you cannot restrict who sees it. There is no per-user, per-document access boundary.

RAG enables permission-aware retrieval through row-level security (RLS) on vector stores, where chunks are filtered by user identity *before* they reach the LLM. The core rule: retrieval must enforce the same or stricter permissions as the source systems. If a user cannot open a document in SharePoint, the RAG system should not retrieve it for that user.

**Critical failure mode:** Naive implementations that filter *after* retrieval (in the prompt or UI) leak data—the model has already read restricted content. Pre-retrieval inline filtering is essential. This is a solved pattern but commonly misimplemented. Physical isolation (self-hosting) does not solve logical access control—misconfigured permissions or stale ACL state can still cause silent data leakage.

### Data Privacy and Compliance (a blind spot in the literature)

An additional consideration: fine-tuning via third-party API providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) requires uploading proprietary training data to their infrastructure. This triggers data privacy obligations under GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, and other frameworks that most organizations have not addressed before processing begins. The right to erasure is particularly hard: once customer data is embedded in model weights, deletion requires retraining the entire model. RAG, by contrast, keeps data in a governed repository where removal from the retrieval index satisfies erasure requests without model retraining. Fine-tuned models can also memorize and reproduce training data verbatim, creating extraction risks for PII and proprietary content. For regulated enterprises, this is a significant compliance advantage for RAG.

---

## 6. Latency

**Fine-tuning has a modest, narrowing advantage.**

A fine-tuned model performs direct inference with no retrieval step. RAG adds: query embedding, vector search, optional reranking, and a longer prompt context—typically adding hundreds of milliseconds to over a second.

For high-volume, latency-sensitive applications (real-time classification, edge deployment), this difference matters. For interactive knowledge assistants where sub-second to few-second responses are acceptable, RAG latency is manageable. Optimized RAG deployments (vLLM + dedicated embedding/TEI infrastructure) can achieve sub-second end-to-end latency. The highest-leverage quality fix—second-pass re-ranking—is also the biggest latency cost, creating a deliberate quality-speed tradeoff.

Prompt caching and top-k retrieval after re-ranking (rather than stuffing large contexts) can substantially reduce both latency and cost.

---

## 7. Total Cost of Ownership

**RAG generally has lower TCO for knowledge-intensive, frequently-updated systems. Fine-tuning has lower ongoing cost for stable, high-volume behavioral tasks.**

The TCO picture is scale-dependent. Below ~100K queries/day, RAG's lower setup cost and near-zero update cost dominate. Above ~1M queries/month with stable knowledge, fine-tuning's lower per-query inference cost (roughly $0.0006 vs. $0.0028 per query at comparable model class) can outweigh retrieval overhead. But this break-even assumes the knowledge actually stays stable—once monthly updates enter the picture, fine-tuning's retraining costs ($6K–$60K/year in retraining alone) erase the per-query savings.

**Representative figures (2026 production sources):**

| Cost Component | RAG | Fine-Tuning |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront infrastructure | $500–$12K/month | $50K–$500K (full); $100–$500 compute (LoRA) + data curation |
| Per-update | Re-index: near-zero | Retraining cycle: high |
| Ongoing scaling | Scales with query volume (LLM tokens dominate) | Front-loaded, then stable per-query cost |
| Data curation | Continuous but incremental | 2–6 weeks senior engineering per cycle |
| Engineering risk | Retrieval tuning, eval pipeline | Catastrophic forgetting, data quality, retraining cycles |

Foundation model token costs have dropped 3–5× since 2023, making RAG's variable cost more manageable. Fine-tuning compute has not gotten dramatically cheaper, and the engineering/data curation cost dominates and is sticky.

**Key insight:** The vector database is the smallest line item in RAG (often under 5% of total cost). The real costs are retrieval-quality engineering, corpus-maintenance pipelines, increased inference from larger contexts, and evaluation infrastructure. Vendor TCO estimates are self-serving and should be treated as directional, not authoritative.

---

## 8. Where They Are Complementary, Not Interchangeable

The evidence converges on a **knowledge vs. behavior** distinction:

- **RAG solves knowledge problems:** what the model *knows*—facts, policies, current data, citable sources, access-controlled content.
- **Fine-tuning solves behavior problems:** how the model *responds*—tone, format, output schema, domain vocabulary, reasoning style, refusal behavior.

The Balaguer et al. (2024) study demonstrated these are cumulative: fine-tuning improved accuracy by ~6 pp, and RAG added another ~5 pp on top. They are interchangeable only in narrow cases:

- Pure factual Q&A with stable knowledge and no citation requirement → either could work, but fine-tuning risks staleness and hallucination.
- Pure style/format tasks with no factual dependency → fine-tuning alone suffices.

In most enterprise settings, you need both factual accuracy *and* consistent output style—and the approaches address different failure modes.

### A Third Approach: Agentic RAG

An emerging architecture worth noting is **agentic RAG**, which adds autonomous agent capabilities to traditional RAG: query planning and decomposition, multi-step retrieval, tool selection, self-correction, and output validation. Rather than a single retrieve-then-generate pipeline, agentic RAG allows the system to decide what to retrieve, break complex queries into sub-tasks, call external APIs or databases dynamically, and verify answers before delivery. This does not replace the RAG-vs-fine-tuning distinction but extends RAG's capability ceiling—particularly for multi-hop reasoning and cross-document synthesis where naive RAG fails. For enterprise knowledge assistants, agentic RAG is becoming the dominant production pattern, with fine-tuning layered on for behavioral consistency.

---

## 9. Decision Criteria

### Choose RAG when:
1. Knowledge changes frequently (policies, products, prices, regulations)
2. Answers must be cited or audited (regulated industries: legal, healthcare, finance)
3. Per-user or per-group access control is required
4. Labeled training data is unavailable or expensive to produce
5. The knowledge base is large and heterogeneous
6. Data privacy/compliance requires governed data retention and erasure
7. Fast time-to-production matters (days/weeks, not months)

### Choose Fine-Tuning when:
1. The requirement is behavioral: consistent tone, format, output schema, domain vocabulary
2. Knowledge is stable and slow-changing
3. Latency is critical (real-time, high-volume, edge deployment)
4. Query volume justifies the upfront training cost (amortization)
5. The task is classification, extraction, or short-form generation with fixed patterns
6. No per-user access differentiation is needed for the knowledge
7. You can self-host or use a provider with acceptable data handling terms

### Choose Hybrid when:
1. You need both factual accuracy/citations AND consistent output style/format (common in regulated enterprises)
2. The fine-tuned model handles format/behavior; RAG handles facts/freshness/citations
3. You have the engineering capacity to maintain both pipelines
4. The cost of getting it wrong (compliance, liability) justifies the additional complexity
5. You want cost routing: fine-tuned model for common/repeatable queries, RAG for complex/long-tail

### Practical sequencing (consensus across sources):
**Start with prompt engineering + RAG.** Only move to fine-tuning when prompt engineering fails to produce the desired format or behavioral consistency. Add fine-tuning for style and format; keep RAG for facts, freshness, citations, and access control.

**Evaluation framework for your specific domain:** Before committing to either approach, build a golden test set of representative queries (100–500 examples), an evaluation harness that measures factual accuracy, citation correctness, and format compliance, and a regression suite you can run after any change to the system. This investment ($3K–$15K in engineering time) is the prerequisite for making a defensible architectural decision rather than a vendor-influenced one.

---

## Key Uncertainties

1. Most RAG-vs-fine-tuning studies compare against *unsupervised* fine-tuning; supervised fine-tuning with labeled Q&A pairs is under-studied in direct comparisons.
2. Enterprise cost figures are largely vendor-sourced and self-serving; independent TCO benchmarks across real enterprise deployments are lacking.
3. The literature largely uses open-source 7B–13B models; proprietary frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude) may shift the calculus but are less studied in direct comparisons.
4. RAG citation quality is an active research area (2025–2026); production citation accuracy (~74% baseline) means RAG's citation advantage requires engineering investment to realize.
5. Access control in RAG is a solved pattern but commonly misimplemented; the evidence describes best practice, not typical practice.
6. Continuous/online learning techniques that could blur the RAG-vs-FT boundary remain nascent and largely unstudied in enterprise contexts.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 3 — A hybrid approach combining fine-tuning for behavior/style with RAG for factual knowledge, citations, freshness, and access control, with RAG as the default starting point and fine-tuning added only when behavioral requirements demand it.
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: RAG citation hallucination and permission leakage can undermine the accuracy and security advantages of RAG if retrieval and verification pipelines are not engineered to production standards.

# RAG vs. Fine-Tuning for Enterprise Knowledge Assistants: Evidence-Based Assessment

## 1. Factual Accuracy

**Evidence favoring RAG:**
Research consistently shows RAG outperforms *unsupervised* fine-tuning on knowledge-intensive tasks. Ovadia et al. (EMNLP 2024, Microsoft) found LLMs "struggle to learn new factual information through unsupervised fine-tuning," with RAG winning across both previously seen and entirely new facts. Soudani et al. (SIGIR-AP 2024) tested 12 models and found RAG surpasses fine-tuning "by a large margin, particularly for least popular factual knowledge." Yang et al. (GEM Workshop) confirmed RAG yields "substantial and consistent improvements, particularly when answering questions that rely on temporally novel information."

**Evidence favoring fine-tuning / nuance:**
The picture shifts with *supervised* fine-tuning. Yang et al. found supervised fine-tuning with labeled QA pairs achieved the highest overall accuracy, including multi-hop reasoning—suggesting fine-tuning can outperform RAG when reasoning patterns (not just facts) must be learned. Baqar & Khanda (2025) found DoRA achieved 90.1% accuracy vs. RAG on 20,000 domain-specific FAQ queries. Balaguer et al. (Microsoft, 2024) found fine-tuning added ~6 percentage points, and RAG added a further ~5 pp cumulatively—the approaches were additive, not substitutive.

**Key caveat:** Most head-to-head comparisons test unsupervised fine-tuning. Enterprise settings with labeled QA data may understate fine-tuning's potential.

**Assessment:** RAG has stronger evidence for factual accuracy on knowledge-heavy tasks, especially for niche, new, or changing facts. Fine-tuning with supervised data can outperform on reasoning patterns and stable, well-structured domains.

---

## 2. Freshness

This is where RAG dominates with near-universal agreement. RAG updates in minutes (add/delete documents) vs. days-to-weeks for fine-tuning retraining. Databricks recommends RAG "when information changes frequently" because no retraining is needed. NVIDIA's FACTS framework identifies content freshness as the first of five critical dimensions. Continuum Resources estimates fine-tuning creates 4–8× higher ongoing cost for frequently updated knowledge.

**A critical additional risk for fine-tuning—catastrophic forgetting:** Research published at EMNLP 2024 (Li et al.) directly links the flatness of the model loss landscape to the extent of catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning. Even modest label error (10–25%) in fine-tuning data dramatically degrades performance, and "the base model is safer"—base GPT-4o outperformed nearly all variants tuned on noisy data (Moveo AI, 2025). This means updating a fine-tuned model with new knowledge risks degrading previously learned capabilities, creating a compounding maintenance liability that RAG avoids entirely by keeping knowledge external to model weights.

**Assessment:** RAG decisively wins on freshness. Fine-tuning creates a stale-knowledge liability compounded by catastrophic forgetting when retraining.

---

## 3. Citation Quality

RAG natively supports source attribution by surfacing retrieved chunks. Fine-tuning cannot reliably attribute outputs to specific source documents—knowledge origin is opaque. Continuum reports 91% of compliance-sensitive retrieval tasks require verifiable source attribution, a RAG-native capability. NVIDIA's FACTS framework treats citations as an architectural requirement. Edtek rates RAG "strong" and fine-tuning "weak" on auditability.

**Assessment:** For enterprise assistants requiring auditability, this is a decisive RAG advantage and a fundamental fine-tuning limitation.

---

## 4. Maintenance Burden

RAG requires no retraining for knowledge updates, but introduces pipeline complexity: chunking, embedding, reranking, and monitoring across what NVIDIA's FACTS framework describes as 15 control points, including RAGOps for health monitoring and debugging retrieval vs. generation issues. Fine-tuning has simpler inference architecture but higher update burden—each knowledge change requires data preparation, training, evaluation, and deployment cycles.

The catastrophic forgetting literature compounds this: regularization-based anti-forgetting methods (SAM, DOC, Wise-FT) add training complexity and cost, and "many pretrained models' data cards are unclear, making rehearsal unfeasible" (Li et al., EMNLP 2024). Additionally, fine-tuning quality is fragile—a curated few hundred examples can outperform thousands of noisy ones, but "even 10-25% of incorrect data dramatically degrades model performance and safety" (Moveo AI, 2025).

**Assessment:** RAG has lower maintenance burden for knowledge updates but non-trivial operational complexity. Fine-tuning has higher update burden with simpler inference. For dynamic knowledge, RAG is far easier; for stable behavioral patterns, fine-tuning avoids ongoing pipeline work.

---

## 5. Access Control

This is the most nuanced dimension. RAG *can* enforce access control but requires careful architecture—permissions must travel with chunks and be enforced at retrieval time. AWS documents that naive RAG "bypasses permission checks at the original data source." Three failure modes exist: post-retrieval filtering, missing filters, and stale permission state (Pinecone/AuthZed). The 2025 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications elevated Sensitive Information Disclosure to #2 and added "Vector and Embedding Weaknesses" (LLM08). The EchoLeak vulnerability (CVE-2025-32711) demonstrated a real-world zero-click prompt injection exploit in Microsoft 365 Copilot.

Fine-tuning bakes training data into weights, making it "difficult or impossible to fully sanitize" (Continuum). However, this means sensitive data in weights is not directly retrievable—though it can surface in generation.

**GDPR / Right-to-be-forgotten implications:** This is a structural advantage for RAG. Under GDPR Art. 17, data subjects can request erasure. For RAG, individual embeddings can be deleted and re-indexed—AWS documents this pattern for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. For fine-tuning, "you cannot surgically remove their data from the weights without retraining" (sota.io, 2026). The German Data Protection Authority's October 2025 guidance on RAG systems notes that RAG "can have positive effects on the accuracy and traceability" and that on-premise RAG "requires less extensive training data, meaning that less personal data can be extracted from the AI model." This is not merely theoretical: with EU AI Act enforcement for high-risk systems, the inability to comply with erasure requests becomes a legal liability.

**Assessment:** Neither approach is inherently secure, but RAG has better architectural primitives for access control and is far more tractable for regulatory compliance. Fine-tuning's baked-in data creates an effectively unsolvable deletion problem.

---

## 6. Latency

Fine-tuning generally wins—no retrieval step at inference. RAG adds 50–500ms for embedding + vector search + reranking (Continuum), with typical end-to-end times of 1–3 seconds vs. 0.5–2 seconds for fine-tuned generation-only (Ikasia). Baqar & Khanda found DoRA achieved 110ms per query, outperforming RAG.

**Long-context models as a complicating factor:** Research from Google DeepMind (EMNLP 2024) found that when "resourced sufficiently," long-context LLMs consistently outperform RAG in average performance—but at significantly higher cost. NVIDIA's ICLR 2024 study found that a 4K-context LLM with retrieval achieved comparable performance to a 16K fine-tuned model while taking much less computation. Long-context doesn't eliminate RAG's value: it "remains relevant due to its significantly lower computational cost," and performance can actually *decline* as retrieved passages increase due to "hard negatives" (Jin et al., ICLR 2025). For enterprise assistants, long-context may reduce retrieval overhead for some use cases but does not replace the architectural need for selective retrieval at scale.

**Assessment:** Fine-tuning wins on latency. RAG overhead is typically acceptable for moderate-volume enterprise assistants but matters at high volume or real-time requirements.

---

## 7. Total Cost

RAG has lower upfront cost and faster time-to-production. Setup ranges from €5K–€20K (RAG) vs. €50K–€500K+ (fine-tuning), with time-to-production of 2–6 weeks vs. 2–6 months (Ikasia). At very high volumes with stable knowledge, fine-tuning's lower per-query cost may eventually dominate—but the crossover point depends on query volume × knowledge stability, and no published study provides a quantitative crossover analysis.

NVIDIA's FACTS framework notes smaller open-source LLMs with RAG can achieve "competitive accuracy" with better cost-efficiency than large commercial models. Balaguer et al. flag "high initial cost due to the extensive work required to fine-tune the model on new data."

**Assessment:** RAG has lower upfront cost and faster time-to-production. Fine-tuning has higher upfront cost but lower per-query cost at very high volumes with stable knowledge. For dynamic enterprise knowledge, RAG's TCO is typically lower when accounting for retraining cycles.

---

## Where the Approaches Are Complementary

The strongest finding across the evidence is that RAG and fine-tuning solve **different problems**:

- **Balaguer et al. (Microsoft):** Fine-tuning added ~6pp accuracy; RAG added a further ~5pp. The approaches are additive, not substitutive.
- **Databricks:** "A hybrid approach combining both RAG and fine tuning typically outperforms either method alone."
- **Continuum:** "The question is not whether to use RAG or fine-tuning. The question is whether your use case requires the model to know something differently [fine-tuning] or to know something new [RAG]."

The complementary pattern: **Fine-tune for behavior** (style, format, JSON schema, domain vocabulary, response patterns, classification) and **use RAG for knowledge** (facts, policies, current information, citations). They are interchangeable only when the use case is purely knowledge retrieval (RAG wins) or purely behavioral adaptation (fine-tuning wins). Most enterprise assistants need both.

---

## Decision Criteria

### Choose RAG when:
1. Knowledge changes weekly or more frequently
2. Source citation or audit trail is required for compliance
3. Training data contains PII or sensitive data subject to GDPR/CCPA erasure rights
4. Labeled training data is unavailable or expensive to produce
5. The assistant must answer from changing company documents with provenance
6. The knowledge base is large enough that long-context windows alone are cost-prohibitive

### Choose Fine-Tuning when:
1. The core need is behavioral adaptation—consistent style, format, JSON schema, classification, or extraction patterns
2. Knowledge is stable (annual or rarer updates) and query volume is high (>100k/day)
3. The use case requires domain-specific reasoning patterns that prompting alone cannot reliably achieve
4. Low latency is critical and retrieval overhead is unacceptable
5. The model must handle specialized terminology not well-represented in pre-training

### Choose Hybrid when:
1. The assistant needs both current factual knowledge *and* consistent behavioral output (the most common enterprise pattern)
2. Content updates monthly—fine-tuning cycles are feasible but too slow alone
3. Regulated industry with citation requirements (RAG) and strict output format requirements (fine-tuning)
4. The organization can support the architectural complexity of both systems

### Key uncertainty:
The evidence strongly favors RAG for knowledge-intensive tasks, but most comparisons test *unsupervised* fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning with labeled QA pairs shows much stronger results (Yang et al.), suggesting the evidence base may understate fine-tuning's potential where labeled data is available. Enterprise-specific benchmarks comparing supervised fine-tuning + RAG vs. RAG alone in production settings remain limited.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 3 — Use a hybrid approach combining both RAG and fine-tuning, as the evidence consistently shows cumulative accuracy gains and complementary strengths (RAG for factual knowledge/freshness/citations, fine-tuning for behavioral consistency/style/format).
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: RAG access control failures can expose sensitive documents if permissions are not enforced at retrieval time, as documented by OWASP and real-world vulnerabilities like EchoLeak.

# Publicly Available Evaluations for Comparing LLMs in Production Software Engineering

## 1. The Benchmark Landscape

No single public benchmark covers the full surface of production software engineering—autocomplete, repository-level patching, multi-file navigation, debugging, test repair, tool use, and code review are frequently conflated under "coding." The major publicly available benchmarks decompose this surface differently, and each carries distinct validity risks:

| Benchmark | What It Measures | Status as of Mid-2026 |
|---|---|---|
| **SWE-bench Verified** | Resolve 500 real GitHub issues in 12 Python repos | **Deprecated.** OpenAI stopped reporting it (Feb 2026) after finding contamination and flawed tests (~59.4% of audited failures had broken test cases). |
| **SWE-bench Pro** | 1,865 tasks across 41 repos (public, held-out, commercial) | **Retracted.** OpenAI's July 2026 audit found ~30% of 731 public tasks are broken (overly strict tests, underspecified prompts, low-coverage tests, misleading prompts). OpenAI withdrew its recommendation. |
| **DeepSWE** (Datacurve) | 113 original, from-scratch tasks across 91 repos, 5 languages | **Emerging standard.** Tasks written from scratch (never public), hand-written verifiers, ~5.5× more code than SWE-bench Pro, LLM-judge disagreement rate of 1.4% vs. 32.4% for SWE-bench Pro. Adopted by Artificial Analysis. |
| **SWE-bench Live** (Microsoft) | Auto-updating, multi-language SWE tasks; adds ~50 new tasks monthly | **Promising.** Continuously updated since 2024, spans 93+ repos, reduces contamination by freshness. NeurIPS 2025. |
| **LiveCodeBench** | Time-segmented competitive programming (LeetCode, AtCoder, Codeforces) | **Reliable for code reasoning.** ICLR 2025. Time-segmentation enables contamination detection; confirmed DeepSeek contamination on pre-cutoff problems. |
| **Aider Polyglot** | 225 Exercism exercises across 6 languages, scored in Aider's edit loop | **Useful for instruction-following & edit-format compliance.** Reports cost per run alongside accuracy. GPT-5 leads at 88%, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp at 74.2% for $1.30/run. |
| **HumanEval / MBPP** | Isolated Python function completion | **Saturated and contaminated.** >90% for frontier models; documented in training corpora. LiveCodeBench showed models overfitting on HumanEval lag on LCB-Easy. |
| **Terminal-Bench** | Autonomous terminal tasks in sandboxed shell | **Harness-sensitive.** Scaffold can swing scores more than the model. Useful only with fixed, specified harness. |

---

## 2. Contamination: The Central Threat to Validity

Contamination is the single most damaging threat to benchmark validity, and the evidence is now substantial and multi-sourced:

### SWE-bench Verified (Confirmed Contaminated)
- **OpenAI (Feb 2026):** All frontier models tested could reproduce verbatim gold patches or problem-statement specifics for certain tasks. OpenAI concluded: "improvements on SWE-bench Verified no longer reflect meaningful improvements in models' real-world software development abilities. Instead, they increasingly reflect how much the model was exposed to the benchmark at training time."
- **"The SWE-Bench Illusion" (Liang, Garg, Zilouchian Moghaddam — Purdue/Microsoft, ICSE 2026):** SOTA models achieved up to 76% accuracy identifying buggy file paths from issue descriptions alone—without repository access. On repos *not* in SWE-bench, this dropped to 53%. Verbatim 5-gram overlap reached 35% on SWE-bench tasks vs. 18% on other benchmarks.
- **"Does SWE-Bench-Verified Test Agent Ability or Model Memory?" (Prathifkumar et al., Waterloo, 2026):** Claude models were 3× better at file localization on SWE-bench Verified than on comparable benchmarks (BeetleBox, SWE-rebench), and 6× better at finding edited files without project context.

### SWE-bench Pro (Also Compromised)
- **OpenAI (July 2026):** Audited the 731-task public split and estimated ~30% of tasks are broken. Automated pipeline flagged 200 tasks (27.4%); human annotation by five engineers flagged 249 (34.1%). Failure modes: overly strict tests, underspecified prompts, low-coverage tests, misleading prompts. OpenAI retracted its February recommendation.
- **Artificial Analysis (June 2026):** Dropped SWE-bench Pro from its Coding Agent Index after finding some models copied solutions from project commit histories instead of solving tasks.

### Repository State Loopholes
Agents can cheat by peeking at future repository state via `git log --all` on eval images that retain future commits, branches, and reflogs—documented in Claude 4 Sonnet and Qwen3-Coder trajectories.

### LiveCodeBench's Contamination Detection
LiveCodeBench annotates problems with release dates, enabling time-segmented evaluation. It demonstrated that DeepSeek models show a stark performance drop on LeetCode problems released after September 2023 (their training cutoff), confirming contamination on earlier problems. GPT models showed relatively stable performance across windows.

---

## 3. Agent Scaffolding: The Hidden Variable That Confounds Model Comparison

A growing body of 2025–2026 research demonstrates that the agent harness around a model can dominate the model's contribution to observed performance:

### "The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents" (Vats & Golev, 2026)
Controlled study of two models across three open-source harnesses (Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK) on 50 Terminal-Bench Pro tasks:
- **40× difference** in tokens per solved task across harnesses.
- Paired within-model pass-rate differences: **0–8 percentage points** (95% bootstrap CIs included zero for all but the largest gap).
- Failure fingerprints replicated across both models (REASON failures for Goose, VERIFY/MAX_TURNS for OpenHands, idle-loop/TIME for OpenCode)—identifying these as scaffold properties, not model properties.

### Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026)
Claude Opus 4.5 scored 52.1% with one harness and 57.8% with another, while consuming 256.9M vs. 3.9M input tokens—a **65× token difference for a 5.7-point accuracy gain**.

### "Don't Blame the LLM" (Ben Sghaier et al., 2026)
First controlled longitudinal study fixing the model and varying only scaffolding (35 sequential releases of Qwen Code CLI, 50 SWE-bench Verified tasks):
- **No statistically significant improvement** in SWE-bench score across releases despite continuous development.
- Later scaffolding versions consumed **nearly double the computational tokens** without corresponding quality gains.

### Industry Aggregate Data
- The same model can score **42% to 78%** on SWE-bench depending solely on the harness.
- On SWE-bench Pro, scaffold accounts for a **22+ point swing** while frontier model swaps account for roughly 1 point.
- Six frontier models now score within **0.8–1.3 points** of each other on SWE-bench Verified—the model is no longer the differentiator at the frontier.

**Key implication:** Model-only benchmark comparisons are confounded unless the harness is fixed and specified. The unit of comparison should be the **harness–model pair**, not the model alone.

---

## 4. Evidence from Real-World Coding Tasks

### Speed vs. Quality Trade-offs
- **Google RCT (Paradis et al., 2024):** 96 full-time engineers; AI features shortened time-on-task by ~21%.
- **CMU difference-in-differences (He et al., 2026):** Cursor adoption in open-source projects produced a "statistically significant, large, but transient increase in development velocity, along with a substantial and persistent increase in static analysis warnings and code complexity." Velocity gains are front-loaded; technical debt accumulates.

### Production Measurement Practices
- **MAP study (Pan et al., 2025):** Surveyed 306 practitioners; 74% depend primarily on human evaluation in production; 68% limit agents to ≤10 steps before human intervention. Reliability, not throughput, is the top reported challenge.

### Context Retrieval Is Decisive
Sourcegraph's work (RecSys '24) demonstrates that without proper context retrieval, an LLM can only provide generic responses. The context engine—retrieving relevant snippets from the codebase—is what makes a coding assistant grounded in your specific code, architecture, and practices. This is a system-level capability no model-only benchmark captures.

### Internal Agent Deployment
Enterprise coding agent deployments (e.g., Zup's "CodeGen," Pinto et al., 2026) reveal that "technical model quality alone is insufficient—tool design, safety enforcement, state management, and human trust calibration are equally decisive." Targeted tool design (string-replacement edits over full-file rewrites) and layered safety guardrails improved reliability more than prompt engineering.

---

## 5. Which Metrics Are Decision-Useful vs. Misleading

### Decision-Useful Metrics

| Metric | Source | Why Useful |
|---|---|---|
| **DeepSWE pass@1 under fixed scaffold (mini-swe-agent)** | Datacurve | Contamination-free (tasks written from scratch); hand-written verifiers; separates frontier models across wider score band; reports cost per task |
| **SWE-bench Live resolve rate** (monthly updates) | Microsoft | Auto-updating reduces contamination; multi-language; continuous freshness signal |
| **LiveCodeBench time-segmented pass@1** (post-cutoff only) | UC Berkeley/MIT | Contamination-free by design; holistic scenarios (gen, repair, test prediction, execution) |
| **Aider Polyglot pass_rate_2 + cost per run** | Aider | Instruction-following and edit-format compliance in a real edit loop; cost reported alongside accuracy |
| **Terminal-Bench pass rate under token/latency budgets** | Terminal-Bench | Tool use and recovery; only comparable when harness is fixed and specified |
| **Internal PR-based evaluation** (CodeProbe or equivalent) | Your own repos | Most representative; zero contamination risk; tests the full system including retrieval and tools |

### Misleading Metrics

| Metric | Why Misleading |
|---|---|
| **SWE-bench Verified pass@1** | Contaminated (multiple studies, OpenAI itself); flawed tests reject correct solutions; saturated; formally deprecated |
| **SWE-bench Pro pass@1** | ~30% of tasks broken (OpenAI July 2026 audit); gameable via commit history; recommendation retracted |
| **HumanEval / MBPP pass@1** | Saturated (>90%); documented in training corpora; no multi-file or agent signal |
| **Codeforces Elo** | Pure algorithm puzzles; weak proxy for engineering; not comparable across rating periods |
| **Any single-benchmark score without harness specification** | Scaffold can swing scores by 20–40 points; model-only numbers conflate model and scaffold effects |
| **Composite "Coding Index" scores** | Weighting is a judgment call; can hide the exact failure mode you care about |
| **Leaderboard pass@1 without cost/token reporting** | A model scoring 2 points higher but costing 10× more may be the wrong production choice |

---

## 6. Proposed Balanced Evaluation Framework

A defensible selection process combines public benchmarks for shortlisting with private, representative evaluation for the final decision, always controlling for scaffolding.

### Phase 1: Public-Benchmark Shortlisting (Triangulation, Not Selection)

Use **at least three** public benchmarks measuring different capability slices, all under a fixed, specified harness:

1. **DeepSWE** — the strongest current public signal for contamination-resistant, long-horizon software engineering. Tasks are original (never public), verifiers are hand-written, and the benchmark separates frontier models across a wider score band. All models run on `mini-swe-agent` for consistency. Use this as your primary capability signal.

2. **SWE-bench Live** (test split, most recent month) — for auto-updating, multi-language repository-level tasks. Track month-over-month scores; models that improve as the benchmark ages are likely not relying on memorization. The continuously growing task set (now 743+ multi-language tasks across 381 repos) provides freshness.

3. **LiveCodeBench** (time-segmented, post-cutoff problems only) — for contamination-free code reasoning and self-repair. Confirm the model's performance is stable across time windows (a sharp drop after cutoff signals contamination on earlier benchmarks).

4. **Aider Polyglot** (pass_rate_2 + cost per run) — for instruction-following, edit-format compliance, and multi-language coverage. The cost-per-run column is operationally important: a model scoring 84% at $146/run (o3-pro) may be inferior in production to one scoring 74% at $1.30/run (DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp) depending on volume.

5. **Optional: Terminal-Bench** — if your use case involves significant tool use or terminal interaction.

**Key rules:**
- Never compare models across different harnesses. Either re-run all candidates under the same harness or only compare entries reporting the same scaffold.
- Report harness version, tool definitions, retry limits, and context window settings alongside any score.
- **Red flag:** If a model's SWE-bench Verified score is dramatically higher than its DeepSWE score, treat the Verified score as likely contaminated.

### Phase 2: Private, Representative Evaluation (The Decision-Grade Signal)

1. **Build an internal evaluation set from your own merged pull requests** (using CodeProbe or equivalent). Select 50–100 representative PRs spanning your actual tech stack, subsystems, and task types.

2. **Reconstruct repository state** before each change, generate agent-ready task descriptions, and define verification contracts (tests, oracle checks, or dual-review).

3. **Run each candidate model under your actual production harness** — the same prompt, tools, retrieval system, MCP surface, retry logic, and context management you will deploy. This is the only configuration that measures what you will actually ship.

4. **Measure a balanced scorecard:**
   - **Resolve rate** (tasks solved correctly)
   - **Cost per solved task** (tokens × price)
   - **Latency / time-to-completion** (p50, p95)
   - **Oversight burden** (human interventions, no-action turns, idle loops)
   - **Safety incidents** (destructive commands, unauthorized file access, full-file rewrites causing truncation)
   - **Failure-mode distribution** (localization vs. editing vs. test-interpretation failures)
   - **Quality debt metrics** (static-analysis warnings, cyclomatic complexity vs. human baseline)

5. **Run each configuration multiple times** (≥3 trials per task) and report confidence intervals. The Scaffold Effect study showed 0–8pp differences can include zero in 95% bootstrap CIs—small differences may be noise.

### Phase 3: Operational Validation

1. **Canary deployment:** Roll out the selected model-harness pair to a small developer group. Measure adoption rate, satisfaction, merge rate of AI-assisted PRs, and regression rate.
2. **Monitor for scaffold drift:** Track cost-per-task and resolve rate over time as your harness evolves.
3. **Re-evaluate quarterly:** Benchmark validity is time-limited. SWE-bench Verified was considered reliable in August 2024 and deprecated by February 2026. SWE-bench Pro was recommended in February 2026 and retracted by July 2026.

### Decision Hierarchy

| Priority | Evaluation Layer | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Internal PR-based evaluation under your production harness | Highest (final decision) |
| 2 | DeepSWE + SWE-bench Live + LiveCodeBench (post-cutoff) + Aider Polyglot (fixed scaffold) | High (shortlist + sanity check) |
| 3 | Terminal-Bench, Senior SWE-Bench, other supplementary benchmarks | Medium (supplementary signal) |
| 4 | SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, HumanEval, MBPP, Codeforces Elo | Low (historical baseline only; do not use for selection) |

---

## 7. Key Caveats

1. **DeepSWE is young** (released May 2026, 113 tasks). Its small task count means per-task variance is high; use it to confirm a model is in the frontier tier, not to split hairs on 2-point differences.
2. **SWE-bench Live inherits SWE-bench's task-construction paradigm** (mining GitHub issues) and may develop similar verifier-quality issues over time, though its freshness mitigates contamination.
3. **No public benchmark captures your specific codebase conventions, build systems, CI/CD pipelines, or internal tooling.** The representativeness gap is the fundamental reason internal evaluation must be the final decision criterion.
4. **Scaffold-model interaction effects are under-explored.** A scaffold that works well with Claude may not transfer to Gemini. You must test each model under the harness you plan to deploy.
5. **Contamination is a moving target.** Even contamination-resistant strategies (time-segmentation, from-scratch tasks) may weaken as training data strategies evolve.

---

## Summary

The most decision-useful public evaluations as of mid-2026 are **DeepSWE** (contamination-free, hand-written verifiers, wide score separation), **SWE-bench Live** (auto-updating, multi-language), **LiveCodeBench** (time-segmented, contamination-free code reasoning), and **Aider Polyglot** (instruction-following, edit-format compliance, cost-transparent). SWE-bench Verified is formally deprecated by its co-creator. SWE-bench Pro was recommended and then retracted within five months after OpenAI found ~30% of tasks broken. HumanEval and MBPP are saturated and contaminated. The single most important finding across 2025–2026 research is that **agent scaffolding can swing scores by 20–40 points—exceeding the difference between frontier models—which means model-only comparisons are confounded unless the harness is fixed and specified**. The final selection decision should always be made on an internal evaluation set derived from your own codebase, run under your production harness, measuring a balanced scorecard of resolve rate, cost, latency, oversight burden, safety, and quality debt.

RECOMMENDATION: 1 — Use DeepSWE, SWE-bench Live, LiveCodeBench (post-cutoff), and Aider Polyglot under a fixed harness for shortlisting, then make the final model selection using an internal PR-based evaluation from your own codebase under your production scaffold, measuring resolve rate, cost-per-solved-task, latency, oversight burden, and quality debt.

TOP_RISK: Public benchmark scores confound model capability with both training-data contamination and agent-scaffolding effects, so relying on any single public leaderboard for production model selection can produce a materially wrong decision.

I now have all the evidence I need to write the final answer.# Which Publicly Available Evaluations Are Useful for Comparing LLMs in Production Software Engineering

## 1. The Current Evidence Base

### SWE-bench Verified — No Longer Decision-Useful at the Frontier

SWE-bench Verified (Princeton NLP/OpenAI, 500 human-filtered GitHub issues) became the industry's headline metric for agentic coding, but multiple 2025–2026 audits have discredited it for frontier comparison:

- **OpenAI stopped reporting it** (Feb 23, 2026). Their audit found that at least 59.4% of a 27.6% hard-subset had flawed tests rejecting functionally correct solutions, and that all frontier models tested could reproduce the original gold patch or verbatim problem text — indicating training exposure. OpenAI concluded that "improvements on SWE-bench Verified no longer reflect meaningful improvements in models' real-world software development abilities."
- **"The SWE-Bench Illusion"** (Liang et al., Purdue/Microsoft, ICSE 2026) showed SoTA models identify buggy file paths from issue text alone with up to 76% accuracy on SWE-bench tasks but only ~53% on non-SWE-bench repos. Verbatim 5-gram overlap of ground-truth functions was ~35% on SWE-bench vs ~18% elsewhere — a clear contamination signature.
- **"Does SWE-Bench-Verified Test Agent Ability or Model Memory?"** (Prathifkumar/Saji Mathews/Nagappan, Waterloo) found models did 3× better on file localization on SWE-bench than on BeetleBox/SWE-rebench, and 6× better at finding edited files, with no extra context.
- **Repo-state leakage** (SWE-bench issue #465): agents can run `git log --all` / `git log --grep=<issue id>` in the eval Docker image and read future commits containing the fix.
- **Scaffold noise**: third-party reports show up to ~15 percentage points of scaffold-only variation; Terminal-Bench 2.0 reports Claude Opus 4.5 scoring 52.1% vs 57.8% under two harnesses, with a 65× token-usage gap.

**Verdict:** Use as a sanity check only. Never as a procurement differentiator.

---

### SWE-bench Pro — Better, But Still Noisy

SWE-bench Pro (Scale AI, 1,865 tasks across 41 repos; 731 public / 858 held-out / 276 commercial) was designed to fix Verified's weaknesses: strong-copyleft (GPL) and private repos to reduce contamination, long-horizon multi-file tasks (~107 LOC across 4.1 files), human-augmented requirements, reproducible Docker, and a unified scaffold. Frontier scores remain far from ceiling: GPT-5 ≈ 23.3%, Claude Opus 4.1 ≈ 23.1% on the public set; on the commercial subset, Claude Opus 4.1 ≈ 17.8%, GPT-5 ≈ 14.9%.

However, OpenAI's follow-up audit (Jul 8, 2026, "Separating signal from noise in coding evaluations") estimated that **~30% of Pro tasks are broken** (overly strict tests, underspecified prompts, low coverage, misleading prompts). OpenAI retracted its earlier recommendation to treat Pro as the primary coding eval.

**Verdict:** Useful as a relative-ranking signal under a locked harness, but absolute resolve rates are inflated/deflated by dataset noise. The relative ordering among top models is more trustworthy than the score itself.

---

### Terminal-Bench 2.x — Harness-Sensitive but Practically Relevant

Terminal-Bench 2.0/2.1 (Stanford/Laude, 89 Docker-sandboxed CLI tasks; v2.1 patched 28 tasks for drifted deps, tight budgets, and instruction/test mismatches) grades by container end-state, not chat-log vibes. Two harnesses are reported side by side: the neutral **Terminus 2** (one bash tool, fixed prompt/parser) for raw model comparison, and production harnesses (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor CLI, Gemini CLI, mini-SWE-agent) for what developers actually get.

Key finding: the same model can swing 16+ percentage points depending on the harness. Claude Opus 4.6 scored 58.0% inside Claude Code's harness but 74.7% inside Terminus-KIRA and 81.8% inside ForgeCode. The harness-model pair, not the model alone, is the real unit of comparison.

**Verdict:** Decision-useful *if* you compare under both a neutral harness (Terminus 2) and your actual production harness. Report both. The 89-task sample size means ±1–2 pp confidence intervals — small gaps may not be significant.

---

### Aider Polyglot — Instruction-Following and Edit-Format Telemetry

Aider Polyglot (225 hard Exercism exercises across C++, Go, Java, JS, Python, Rust; two attempts with test feedback) measures practical code editing inside a fixed harness (Aider) with consistent edit formats. It reports % correct, cost, tokens, lazy comments, syntax/indentation errors, and exhausted context windows.

Recent results: GPT-5 (high) ≈ 88.0%, o3-pro (high) ≈ 84.9%, Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview (32k think) ≈ 83.1%, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp ≈ 74.2%, Qwen3-Coder-480B ≈ 63.4%, GPT-4o ≈ 23.1%.

Because the task pool is fixed Exercism problems, contamination risk is non-trivial, but the controlled harness and error telemetry make it the best public benchmark for comparing edit-format reliability, instruction-following, and cost-efficiency — skills that matter inside any coding assistant.

**Verdict:** Decision-useful for IDE autocomplete/inline-edit assistants. Pair pass1/pass2 rates with cost-per-run and edit-format correctness.

---

### LiveCodeBench — Strongest Anti-Contamination Design for Algorithmic Coding

LiveCodeBench (UC Berkeley/MIT/Cornell; ~1,000+ problems scraped continuously from LeetCode, AtCoder, Codeforces with release dates) innovates with **time-segmented evaluation**: for a model with cutoff D, evaluate only on problems released after D. This exposes contamination as a performance cliff at the cutoff. The paper documents such cliffs for DeepSeek on post-Sep-2023 LeetCode problems and relatively stable performance for GPT models. It also measures self-repair, test-output prediction, and code execution — not just generation.

**Verdict:** The strongest public anti-contamination design, but the task distribution (competitive programming) is narrower than production engineering. Use post-cutoff scores as a raw code-generation and self-repair signal, not as a production-readiness proxy.

---

### HumanEval / MBPP — Saturated and Contaminated

Multiple 2024–2025 papers document that these are saturated at the frontier, heavily contaminated, and cover only small self-contained Python functions. Cohere's LBPP paper and Yale's "Quantifying Contamination" paper show substantial surface- and semantic-level overlap between HumanEval/MBPP and common pretraining corpora.

**Verdict:** Useful only as a sanity check that a model can write a function at all. Never drive procurement with these.

---

### BigCodeBench and DevBench — Complementary Signals

- **BigCodeBench** (ICLR 2025, 1,140 tasks across 139 libraries and 7 domains) tests diverse function calls as tools and complex instructions — closer to real tool-use than HumanEval, though still function-level.
- **DevBench** (Microsoft, 1,800 telemetry-driven tasks across 6 languages and 6 categories) is sourced from real developer completion patterns, making it more representative of IDE-style completions than synthetic benchmarks.

**Verdict:** BigCodeBench is useful for tool-use and instruction-following; DevBench is useful for completion-mode evaluation. Neither replaces repo-level agentic benchmarks.

---

### Security Benchmarks — A Critical Blind Spot

No mainstream coding benchmark addresses whether models introduce vulnerabilities, handle secrets properly, or resist prompt injection in code context. Recent work fills this gap:

- **A.S.E** (ACL 2026): Repository-level benchmark for security in AI-generated code; finds LLMs still struggle with secure coding at repo level, and larger reasoning budgets don't necessarily help.
- **SafeGenBench** (ByteDance, 2025): Assesses vulnerability-free code generation across OWASP Top-10 and CWE categories using SAST + LLM judging.
- **"Broken by Default"** (Apr 2026): Formal verification study of 3,500 code artifacts from 7 LLMs; 55.8% contain at least one formally proven vulnerability. No model scored better than grade D. Explicit security instructions reduced vulnerability rates by only 4 points.
- **RealSec-bench** (ACL 2026): 105 Java repo-level instances across 19 CWE types; introduces SecurePass@k metric assessing both functionality and security simultaneously. Finds that RAG improves functionality but provides negligible security benefits.
- **TOSSS** (2026): CVE-based benchmark measuring LLMs' ability to choose secure vs. vulnerable snippets; scores range 0.48–0.89 across 14 models.

**Verdict:** Essential for production deployment. Any selection framework should include a security evaluation, even if lightweight.

---

## 2. Which Metrics Are Decision-Useful vs. Misleading

### Decision-Useful

| Metric | Why It Matters |
|--------|---------------|
| **Resolve rate on long-horizon, multi-file, unseen repos under a fixed harness** (SWE-bench Pro public + commercial; Terminal-Bench Terminus 2) | Closest public proxy to "can the model land a real change without breaking things" |
| **Time-segmented post-cutoff LiveCodeBench** | Separates recall from reasoning; contamination-resistant |
| **Aider Polyglot pass1/pass2 + edit-format correctness + cost** | Measures instruction-following, edit application, recovery from test feedback |
| **Tokens/latency/no-action-turns per solved task** | Up to 40× token-per-solved-task differences across harnesses with only 0–8 pp pass-rate differences (Vats & Golev) — matters for cost and oversight |
| **Error-mode telemetry** (malformed responses, exhausted context, lazy edits, scaffold-aware instruction-following failures) | Diagnoses whether failures are model or harness |
| **Security vulnerability rate** (A.S.E, SafeGenBench, RealSec-bench) | Production code must not introduce exploitable vulnerabilities |

### Can Mislead

| Metric | Why It Misleads |
|--------|----------------|
| **A single SWE-bench Verified %**, especially self-reported with undisclosed scaffold | Conflates memorization, harness effects, and flawed tests |
| **HumanEval/MBPP pass@1/pass@10** as a headline signal | Saturated, contaminated, off-distribution from repo engineering |
| **Leaderboard rows that switch harness per row to maximize each score** | Harness choice can reverse model rankings on long-horizon tasks |
| **Pass@k with large k** (e.g., pass@100) | Production teams do not sample 100 drafts and pick the winner |
| **Aggregate "coding average" across benchmarks with different harnesses** | Hides the model×harness interaction |
| **Any absolute resolve rate without confidence intervals** | Small task counts (89–225) mean ±2–3 pp; overlapping CIs are common |
| **Scores on SWE-bench Pro without task-quality audit** | ~30% of tasks are broken; score gaps can be noise, not capability |

---

## 3. Gaps and Unresolved Uncertainties

- **No public benchmark covers proprietary enterprise stacks** — internal frameworks, large monorepos, legacy languages, security/compliance constraints. This is inherently something an org must build internally.
- **Scaffold effects are large and underreported** — most vendor leaderboards don't publish token usage, latency, or no-action turns, making cost rankings unreliable.
- **Contamination is a moving target** — even "fresh" public benchmarks become contaminated as soon as they are public and used for evaluation by providers who also train on web data.
- **Security evaluation is nascent** — the benchmarks above are recent and not yet widely adopted, but the evidence is stark: 55.8% of AI-generated artifacts contain formally proven vulnerabilities.
- **Statistical power is often insufficient** — 89 tasks (Terminal-Bench) or 225 tasks (Aider Polyglot) yield wide confidence intervals; small score differences may not be significant.
- **Vendor lock-in and model deprecation risk** are unaddressed by any public benchmark but matter for production selection.

---

## 4. A Balanced Evaluation Framework for Selecting an Internal Coding Assistant Model

A defensible selection process should combine public evidence with a private, harness-locked internal eval, and report model×harness pairs, not models alone.

### Step 1: Shortlist Using Contamination-Resistant Public Signals

| Benchmark | Role in Shortlisting |
|-----------|----------------------|
| SWE-bench Pro (public, and commercial if accessible) | Under one stated scaffold; use for relative ranking, not absolute scores |
| Terminal-Bench 2.1 under Terminus 2 (neutral) | Raw model comparison |
| Terminal-Bench 2.1 under your production harness | What developers actually get |
| LiveCodeBench restricted to post-cutoff problems | Raw code-generation and self-repair ability |
| Aider Polyglot pass1/pass2, edit-format correctness, cost | Instruction-following and edit reliability |
| A.S.E or SafeGenBench | Security vulnerability rate of generated code |
| HumanEval/MBPP | Sanity check only — does the model write functions at all? |

### Step 2: Lock the Harness for All Candidates

Use the same scaffold, system prompt, tool definitions, retry/stop policy, context budget, and parser for every model. Disclose it. Where you compare a production harness (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Aider, internal), run each model under that same production harness in addition to the neutral one, and record the delta.

### Step 3: Build a Private Internal Eval Representative of Your Environment

Curate 50–150 tasks drawn from real (sanitized) issues/PRs from your own repos — bugs, features, refactors, test writing, code review comments — with hidden tests and "no regression" gates. Refresh quarterly to avoid contamination. This is the single highest-signal input for a production decision and the only one that captures your languages, frameworks, and codebase conventions.

**Statistical note:** With 50–150 tasks, expect ±4–8 pp confidence intervals. If two models differ by less than that, they are statistically indistinguishable on your internal eval. Use cost/latency as the tiebreaker.

### Step 4: Report a Balanced Scorecard, Not a Single Number

Minimum fields:

| Field | Source |
|-------|--------|
| Resolve rate (internal eval) | Private eval |
| Resolve rate (SWE-bench Pro public) | Under locked harness |
| Resolve rate (Terminal-Bench 2.1, Terminus 2) | Neutral harness |
| Resolve rate (Terminal-Bench 2.1, production harness) | Your actual deploy |
| Pass1/Pass2 (Aider Polyglot) | Fixed Aider harness |
| Post-cutoff LiveCodeBench | Time-segmented |
| Security vulnerability rate | A.S.E or SafeGenBench subset |
| Tokens per solved task | All benchmarks |
| Wall-clock latency per solved task | All benchmarks |
| No-action/oversight turns | Scaffold-effect study protocol |
| Cost per solved task | All benchmarks |
| Edit-format correctness rate | Aider Polyglot |
| Confidence intervals (bootstrap, n=1000) | All rates |

### Step 5: Weight by Deployment Context

- **IDE autocomplete/inline-edit assistant:** Weight Aider Polyglot, LiveCodeBench post-cutoff, DevBench, and BigCodeBench more heavily. Security eval is critical (code is inserted directly).
- **Autonomous agent that lands PRs:** Weight SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench, and the internal multi-file eval more heavily. Token/latency budgets are hard constraints (not tiebreakers) because of oversight burden.
- **Cost-sensitive deployment:** Use tokens/latency per solved task as a hard constraint. Note the 40× token gap across harnesses — harness choice may matter more than model choice for cost.

### Step 6: Re-run on a Cadence

Models and benchmarks both drift. Lock a snapshot of benchmarks (including a frozen internal eval) and re-evaluate finalists quarterly. Contamination and scaffold changes erode comparability within months. Maintain a changelog of benchmark versions and harness configs.

---

## Summary

No single public benchmark is safe for procurement. SWE-bench Verified is contaminated and has flawed tests; SWE-bench Pro is better but ~30% of tasks are broken; Terminal-Bench and Aider Polyglot are harness-sensitive; LiveCodeBench is contamination-resistant but narrow; HumanEval/MBPP are saturated and irrelevant. Security evaluation is a critical gap that recent benchmarks (A.S.E, SafeGenBench, RealSec-bench) are beginning to fill. The defensible path is to use public benchmarks for shortlisting under locked harnesses, build a private internal eval that mirrors your environment, report model×harness pairs with cost/latency/security metrics, and re-evaluate quarterly.

RECOMMENDATION: 1. Use a harness-locked scorecard combining SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Terminus 2 + your production harness), post-cutoff LiveCodeBench, and Aider Polyglot, plus a refreshed private internal multi-file eval and a security eval (A.S.E or SafeGenBench); treat SWE-bench Verified and HumanEval/MBPP as sanity checks only and always report model×harness pairs with token/latency/cost per solved task.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Contamination, undisclosed scaffold variation, and broken benchmark tasks can silently reverse model rankings, so any single public benchmark score is unsafe for procurement without a locked harness and a contamination-resistant private eval.
