response_text:
# Publicly Available Evaluations for Comparing Production Coding LLMs

## 1. Inventory of the Main Public Benchmarks

### HumanEval / MBPP (and variants) — Not Decision-Useful
These oldest code-generation benchmarks are saturated, contaminated, and measure only single-function Python synthesis with no repository context, no edit loop, and no tool use. Peer-reviewed analyses document "substantial overlap between popular code generation benchmarks and open training corpus" (Riddell et al., ACL 2024). Cohere's "On Leakage of Code Generation Evaluation Datasets" (EMNLP-Findings 2024) argues HumanEval/MBPP have become mandatory for competitive launches, producing direct leakage, indirect leakage via synthetic data, and overfitting during checkpoint selection. LiveCodeBench (ICLR 2025) confirms time-segmented evaluation detects contamination across GPT-4o, Claude, DeepSeek, and Codestral, with stark performance drops after model cutoffs.

**Verdict:** Not decision-useful for production SE selection in 2025/2026 beyond a basic sanity check.

### SWE-bench Verified — Contaminated and Deprecated
The de facto agentic SE benchmark since ICLR 2024: models receive a repo snapshot + issue and must produce a patch passing the repo's test suite. Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index reports SWE-bench jumped from 4.4% (2023) to 71.7% (2024) for the top system.

However, OpenAI formally abandoned SWE-bench Verified in February 2026, stating it "no longer measures frontier coding capabilities." Their audit found:
- **59.4% of audited problems** in a representative subset had flawed test cases that rejected functionally correct submissions.
- **All frontier models tested** could reproduce the original human-written gold patch or verbatim problem-statement specifics for certain tasks, indicating training-data contamination.
- Models that had seen problems during training were more likely to succeed because they had additional information needed to pass underspecified tests.

Independent academic studies corroborate this:
- **"The SWE-Bench Illusion"** (Liang, Garg, Moghaddam; Purdue + Microsoft, arXiv 2506.12286, June 2025): SoTA models achieve up to 76% accuracy identifying buggy file paths from issue text alone, without repo access—vs. only up to 53% on repos not included in SWE-bench. Verbatim 5-gram overlap in function reproduction was up to 35% on SWE-bench Verified vs. up to 18% on other benchmarks.
- **"Does SWE-Bench-Verified Test Agent Ability or Model Memory?"** (Waterloo, arXiv 2512.10218): Claude models perform ~3× better on file localization on SWE-bench-Verified than on BeetleBox/SWE-rebench, and ~6× better at finding edited files—strong evidence of training exposure to SWE-bench specifically.
- **PatchDiff / ICSE 2026** (Wang, Pradel, Liu): Differential patch testing on three SoTA tools found 7.8% of patches counted as correct while failing the developer-written test suite; 29.6% induced behavior different from ground truth; 28.6% of behaviorally divergent patches were certainly incorrect. Net inflation of reported resolution rates: ~6.4 absolute percentage points.

**Verdict:** OpenAI itself stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified and recommends SWE-bench Pro. Reading a 70%+ score as "solves 70% of your tickets" is a category error.

### SWE-bench Pro (Scale AI, Sep 2025) — Most Contamination-Resistant Public Agentic SE Benchmark, But Noisy
Designed to fix SWE-bench's limitations: 1,865 instances across 41 repos (11 public, 12 held-out, 18 commercial), sourced from GPL/strong-copyleft and private repos to resist contamination, with human-augmented task statements, averaging 107.4 LOC across 4.1 files. Frontier models score far lower: GPT-5 23.3%, Claude Opus 4.1 23.1% on the public split; on the private commercial subset GPT-5 drops to 14.9% and Claude Opus 4.1 to 17.8%.

However, in July 2026, OpenAI audited SWE-bench Pro and estimated **~30% of tasks are broken** (27.4% flagged by automated pipeline, 34.1% by human annotation), with issues including overly strict tests, underspecified prompts, low-coverage tests, and misleading prompts. OpenAI retracted its prior recommendation to use SWE-bench Pro as a primary coding eval.

**Verdict:** Currently the most contamination-resistant public agentic SE benchmark, but absolute scores should be treated as noisy (±10 pp); rely on relative ordering across models run identically.

### Aider Polyglot — Strong Fixed-Scaffold Instruction-Following Signal
225 Exercism exercises across C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, Rust; the model must emit structured edits inside Aider's real edit loop and gets a second attempt with failing-test output. Epoch AI describes it as measuring "coding abilities across [six languages]… as well as their ability to edit files and correct their mistakes," with pass rate after second attempt as the primary metric.

Current leaders (Aug 2025): GPT-5 (high) at 88.0%, o3-pro (high) 84.9%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 83.1%, Grok-4 79.6%, Claude Opus 4 72.0%, and best open-weight DeepSeek V3.2-Exp at 74.2%. Aider also reports cost-per-run and "percent cases well formed" (edit-format compliance), which are operationally meaningful.

**Verdict:** The best public proxy for instruction-following + reliable editing in a pair-programming loop, with a fixed scaffold so model comparisons are valid. Still single-file, self-contained exercises—not repo-scale feature work.

### LiveCodeBench — Contamination-Resistant Algorithmic/Repair Signal
Time-segmented contest problems (LeetCode, AtCoder, Codeforces, May 2023–Aug 2024+), with scenarios for generation, self-repair, execution, and test-output prediction. The ICLR 2025 paper demonstrates that time-segmented evaluations serve as a robust approach to evade contamination; they successfully detect contamination across GPT-4o, Claude, DeepSeek, and Codestral.

**Verdict:** Useful as a contamination-resistant algorithmic/coding signal and for measuring repair capability, but competitive-programming-flavored, not production SE.

### Chatbot Arena Coding / WebDev Arena — Weak Vibes Signal
Human pairwise preference on coding prompts. The Coding leaderboard shows Anthropic's Opus 4.x thinking variants and GPT-5.x at the top; WebDev Arena (React/Tailwind sandbox) also ranks frontier models highly. These are subject to documented biases: the "Leaderboard Illusion" paper (Cohere/AI2/Princeton/Stanford/Waterloo/UW, 2025) showed undisclosed private testing and selective score disclosure.

**Verdict:** A weak, possibly gameable prior. Treat as a UX/formatting tie-breaker, not a production-readiness signal.

### Other Notable Benchmarks
- **LiveBench** (monthly refresh, objective scoring): Good for contamination-resistant coding and agentic coding evaluation, with cost-per-successful-task reporting. Top models still score below 70%, so it discriminates at the frontier.
- **BigCodeBench**: Library-aware code generation with 100+ libraries. Top score ~35.5% vs. human 97%. Useful for checking breadth of API knowledge.
- **Terminal-Bench / Terminal-Bench Pro**: Terminal-task agent benchmarks. Useful for measuring agent reliability in tool-use-heavy environments, provided the harness is fixed and reported.
- **Scale SEAL**: Curated private datasets evaluated by domain experts, making them immune to training-data contamination. Good for triangulation, but proprietary and not auditable by external researchers.

## 2. Agent Scaffolding: A First-Order Confound

This is the single most under-appreciated issue for a buyer comparing "models."

- **SWE-bench's own data** shows scaffolded-vs-bare-API gaps of ~16 points for the same model (Claude Opus 4 with Anthropic scaffold 58.7% vs. bare-API simple loop 42.1%; o3 scaffolded 51.8% vs. bare 38.4%). The leaderboard now lets you filter by agent and explicitly warns to compare like with like.
- **The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents** (arXiv 2607.22585): Across Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK on Terminal-Bench Pro, harness choice induces up to a **40× difference in tokens per solved task**, while paired within-model pass-rate differences stay 0–8 pp (95% CIs mostly include zero). Failure fingerprints replicate across models, indicating scaffold-level biases that are largely model-independent. The authors argue the unit of comparison should be **harness–model pairs, not models alone**.
- **Don't Blame the LLM** (arXiv 2607.03691): Controlled longitudinal study of 35 sequential Qwen Code CLI releases against fixed SWE-bench Verified tasks with fixed LLM: no statistically significant improvement in resolve rate across releases, while later scaffold versions consume nearly double the tokens and tool calls. Quality regressions practitioners report after "model updates" are often actually scaffold regressions.
- **Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness** (arXiv 2605.23950): Formalizes the "Binding Constraint Thesis"—for long-horizon tasks evaluated across models with comparable frontier capability, the agent execution harness is often a stronger determinant of agent performance than the model it wraps. Reports up to 15 percentage points of scaffold-only variation on SWE-bench Verified.
- **Harness-Bench** (arXiv 2605.27922): Introduces a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating configuration-level harness effects, finding substantial variation in completion, process quality, efficiency, and failure behavior across model–harness pairings.

**Implication:** Any leaderboard that ranks by model name while the harness varies (or is undisclosed) is not a model comparison. SWE-bench Pro's results are reported "under a unified scaffold" (SWE-Agent), which is a meaningful improvement; Aider Polyglot also fixes the scaffold.

## 3. Real-World Evidence from Production Coding Tasks

RCTs and field studies show AI assistance produces real but modest and heterogeneous productivity gains:

- **Cui et al. (Microsoft, Accenture, Fortune 100; n=4,867)**: IV estimates give 26.08% (SE 10.3%) increase in weekly completed tasks from Copilot access; less experienced developers gained more. Published in *Management Science*, Feb 2026. AEA-registered.
- **Paradis et al. (Google, n=96)**: ~21% reduction in time on a complex enterprise task (wide CI); developers who spend more hours on code activities per day benefit more.
- **A 2025 difference-in-differences study of Cursor adoption** found a significant but transient increase in development velocity, coupled with a significant and persistent increase in static analysis warnings and code complexity—the increased complexity acted as a drag on long-term velocity. This quality-debt dynamic is not captured by any current benchmark.
- **Bakal et al. (Zoominfo, 400+ developers)**: Copilot acceptance rate ~33% (suggestions) and 20% (lines of code), 72% satisfaction; language-specific variation.
- **1mg/DeputyDev (n=300 engineers, 1 year)**: 31.8% reduction in PR review cycle time; ~40% of code shipped to production AI-generated by month 6; 85% satisfaction for code review, 93% want to continue.

These production numbers do not correlate cleanly with SWE-bench percentages. A SWE-bench score is "evidence of benchmark capability, not a forecast of how much engineering work an agent will complete inside your organization." Tasks are 12 Python repos, not your enterprise stack; resolution criteria (pass/fail tests) differ from acceptance criteria (reviewers, style, security, cross-system effects); and productivity is bottlenecked by review, integration, and ownership—not by raw ticket resolution.

## 4. Which Metrics Are Decision-Useful vs. Misleading

### Decision-Useful
- **SWE-bench Pro public split pass-rate under a fixed scaffold** — the most contamination-resistant public signal for agentic repo-scale SE, with the caveat that ~30% of tasks are broken, so treat absolute levels as noisy and rely on relative ordering across models run identically.
- **SWE-bench Verified drop from full SWE-bench** — useful as a hardness-resistance indicator (models with low drop are genuinely better on hard problems, not inflated by easy ones), but no longer reliable as an absolute capability number due to memorization.
- **Aider Polyglot pass rate after second attempt + percent cases well formed + cost-per-run** — the best public proxy for instruction-following + reliable editing in a pair-programming loop, with a fixed scaffold so model comparisons are valid.
- **LiveCodeBench post-cutoff slices** — contamination-resistant generation + self-repair signal.
- **LiveBench Coding/Agentic Coding** — monthly refresh, objective scoring, still discriminating at the frontier. Cost-per-successful-task is practically relevant.
- **Token-per-solved-task and latency under a fixed harness** — operationally critical for cost; a 40× token gap between harnesses for the same model is a deployment-deciding metric that no public leaderboard captures.

### Can Mislead
- **HumanEval / MBPP absolute scores** — saturated, contaminated, single-function; near-useless for model selection.
- **SWE-bench Verified absolute pass-rate** — OpenAI itself says it no longer measures frontier coding capability; contaminated and test-flawed.
- **SWE-bench Pro absolute scores without acknowledging ~30% broken tasks** — relative ordering is informative; absolute level is inflated downward and noisy.
- **Chatbot Arena Coding / WebDev Arena raw Elo** — subject to selective private testing and undisclosed variant submission (Leaderboard Illusion); vibes-biased toward formatting/length.
- **Any model-only leaderboard where the scaffold varies** — conflates model capability with harness quality (the scaffold-effect studies show up to 28 pp and 40× token differences from scaffold alone).
- **"Pass@1" without test-quality audits** — PatchDiff analysis shows ~6.4 pp inflation in SWE-bench from plausible-but-incorrect patches.
- **"Lines of code generated" or "characters accepted"** — rewards verbosity and boilerplate; inversely correlates with code quality.

## 5. Proposed Balanced Evaluation Framework for Selecting an Internal Coding Assistant

A defensible selection process cannot rely on any single public number. I recommend a layered framework:

### Layer 1 — Public-Signal Shortlisting (cheap, fast, ~1 week)
Use a **fixed internal scaffold** (your actual tooling or a standard one like SWE-Agent) and test candidate models on:
- **SWE-bench Pro public split under SWE-Agent** as the primary agentic SE filter (treat absolute scores ±10 pp as noise; use for relative ranking).
- **Aider Polyglot pass-rate + well-formedness + cost** as the instruction-following/edit-reliability filter.
- **LiveCodeBench post-cutoff slices** as a contamination-resistant generation sanity check.
- **LiveBench** (latest monthly release) Coding + Agentic Coding for contamination-resistant capability and cost-per-successful-task.
- **Chatbot Arena Coding/WebDev Elo** only as a weak tie-breaker for UX/formatting, never as a primary signal.

### Layer 2 — Contamination-Aware Interpretation
- Discount SWE-bench Verified scores heavily; if a vendor reports them, require SWE-bench Pro numbers too.
- When reading SWE-bench Pro, remember ~30% broken tasks; prefer rankings from audits over raw pass rates.
- Prefer benchmarks with time-stamped or held-out splits (LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Pro held-out/commercial, LiveBench).

### Layer 3 — Fixed-Scaffold Comparison
- Re-run the top 2–3 shortlisted models under *your own* scaffold (or at least a single open scaffold like OpenHands or mini-SWE-agent) on a fixed task set.
- Report pass-rate **and** tokens-per-solved-task **and** latency **and** no-action-turn rate. The scaffold-effect literature shows these can vary by 40× for the same model.
- Treat the comparison unit as harness–model pair, not model.

### Layer 4 — Internal Private Eval (the decisive layer)
- Build a private, contamination-free eval from your own codebase: 50–200 resolved issues/PRs with held-out test suites, covering your languages and frameworks. This is the only signal that directly predicts production value.
- Include reviewer-acceptance criteria (not just test pass) to capture the gap PatchDiff exposes (plausible-but-incorrect patches).
- Track production metrics that field studies use: PR cycle time, acceptance rate, rework rate, downstream defect rate within 30 days of merge, developer satisfaction, context window exhaustion rate, re-read ratio.

### Layer 5 — Pilot with Human-in-the-Loop
- Run a 4–8 week pilot with a randomized or cohort-design subset (cf. Cui et al., Paradis et al.) measuring weekly completed tasks, cycle time, and satisfaction. Expect 20–30% task-throughput gains for less-experienced developers, with wide CIs; do not assume lab RCT effect sizes transfer without your tooling and codebase.
- **Kill criteria**: If downstream defect rate increases >20% or team velocity drops, re-evaluate.

### Suggested Weighting
- **Internal pilot results: 50%** (predicts actual utility on your stack)
- **External benchmark composite: 30%** (validates generalizability and detects contamination)
- **Cost/latency: 20%** (determines deployability at scale)

### Decision Rule
A model should only be selected if it (a) clears the public-signal thresholds in Layer 1, (b) survives contamination-aware interpretation in Layer 2, (c) is competitive under a fixed scaffold in Layer 3, (d) wins on the internal private eval in Layer 4, and (e) shows real productivity gains in the Layer 5 pilot. Public benchmarks should inform the shortlist, not the decision.

RECOMMENDATION: 1 — Use a layered framework: shortlist with SWE-bench Pro (fixed scaffold) + Aider Polyglot + LiveCodeBench post-cutoff, discount contaminated SWE-bench Verified, compare harness–model pairs (not models alone) on pass-rate, tokens-per-solved-task, and latency, and make the final decision on a private internal-codebase eval plus a 4–8 week randomized pilot measuring PR cycle time, acceptance rate, and developer satisfaction.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Contamination and scaffold confounds mean any single public benchmark score can overstate or misstate real production capability, so selecting on public numbers alone risks buying benchmark performance rather than engineering value.

# Environmental Impact of Serving Large Language Models in Production: Inference-Focused Analysis

## 1. Why Inference, Not Training, Is the Growing Environmental Concern

While training GPT-3 consumed ~1,287 MWh and emitted ~550 tonnes CO₂, inference is now recognized as the dominant lifecycle contributor. Recent estimates suggest inference can account for up to **80–90% of total lifecycle energy use** for deployed models. As models serve billions of prompts daily, the per-query footprint—though individually small—accumulates to enormous aggregate impacts. Scaling a single GPT-4o query (0.43 Wh) to 700 million queries/day yields annual electricity comparable to 35,000 U.S. homes, freshwater evaporation matching the drinking needs of 1.2 million people, and carbon emissions requiring a Chicago-sized forest to offset.

---

## 2. Per-Prompt Electricity, Water, and Emissions Estimates

### Electricity

| Source | Model | Energy/Query | Notes |
|--------|-------|-------------|-------|
| Google (Aug 2025) | Gemini (median text prompt) | **0.24 Wh** | Full-stack: TPU 58%, CPU/RAM 25%, idle machines 10%, DC overhead 8% |
| Epoch AI (2025) | GPT-4o | **~0.30 Wh** | Assumes ~200B params, MoE with ¼ active, pessimistic bounds |
| Sam Altman (2025) | ChatGPT | **~0.34 Wh** | Self-reported, method unspecified |
| Jegham et al. (2025) | GPT-4o (short query) | **0.42–0.43 Wh** | Infrastructure-aware benchmarking across 30 models |
| Jegham et al. (2025) | o3 / DeepSeek-R1 (long prompt) | **>33 Wh** | Reasoning models: 70× GPT-4.1 nano |
| AI Energy Score v2 (2025) | Reasoning models avg. | **30× non-reasoning** | 150–700× for specific models with reasoning toggled on |
| Older 2023 estimate | ChatGPT | **2.9 Wh** | Now considered ~10× overestimated |

### Water

| Source | Estimate | Boundary |
|--------|----------|----------|
| Google (2025) | **0.26 mL/prompt** | On-site cooling only |
| UC Riverside (2023) | **2.2 mL/request** (US avg. on-site) | On-site cooling |
| UC Riverside (2023) | **10–47.5 mL/request** (total, incl. electricity generation) | Full lifecycle: on-site + off-site power plant cooling |
| Washington Post (2024) | **~519 mL per 100-word email** | Full lifecycle including generation, transmission |

**Key reconciliation:** Google's 0.26 mL figure is on-site only, while UC Riverside's higher figures include both on-site and off-site (power plant cooling) water. Comparing them directly is "apples to oranges"—as UC Riverside's Shaolei Ren emphasized. If one includes off-site water from electricity generation, total water consumption per prompt is roughly 10–180× higher depending on grid mix and data center location.

### Emissions

| Source | Estimate | Method |
|--------|----------|--------|
| Google (2025) | **0.03 gCO₂e/prompt** | Market-based accounting with RECs |
| GreenLLM (2024) | **~4 gCO₂e/prompt** (ChatGPT) | Operational + embodied carbon, location-based |
| Jegham et al. (2025) | Scaled to 700M/day → Chicago-forest-equivalent | Region-specific multipliers |

---

## 3. Comparing Deployment Modes

### Fixed Dedicated GPUs

- **Hardware utilization:** Typically 5–15% for early-stage or spiky workloads; can reach 60–80% for sustained high-volume.
- **Idle power waste ("Model Parking Tax"):** A 2026 study (Vadari) measuring 335,267 idle-state samples across 14 H100 GPUs found that simply having a CUDA context loaded forces a discrete DVFS transition consuming **+26–66 W above bare idle** (26–50 W on HBM architectures, 66 W on GDDR6). The marginal VRAM effect is negligible (<0.02 W/GB). The CUDA context accounts for >98% of the parking tax regardless of model size. On a 4×H100 node, this is ~208 W continuously—just for readiness.
- **Execution-idle:** A 2026 study (Lei et al.) found that in academic AI clusters, GPUs in "execution-idle" state (allocated, program loaded, near-zero activity) account for **19.7% of in-execution time and 10.7% of energy**. Unlike CPUs, GPU power remains elevated even when a loaded program is fully idle—CPU-based energy intuition does not transfer.
- **Environmental impact:** Highest idle-to-active ratio. Wastes energy on readiness, but eliminates cold-start latency. Embodied carbon is amortized only if utilization is sustained.

### Autoscaled Endpoints

- **Utilization:** Better than fixed-dedicated because capacity scales with demand, reducing idle waste during quiet periods.
- **"Utilization Fallacy":** A 2025 study (Sinha et al., UT Austin / HotCarbon) demonstrated that **higher GPU utilization via spatial sharing does not always improve carbon efficiency**. The outcome depends on which models are co-located, fluctuations in energy sources, request rates, and input/output requirements. Frequency tuning on shared GPUs can improve carbon efficiency but must be tailored to the specific model combination. Manufacturing 350,000 A100s emits ~7.54 million kgCO₂ (21.56 kgCO₂/GPU), so co-location strategies that extend GPU lifetimes matter as much as utilization metrics.
- **DynamoLLM (2024):** Dynamically reconfiguring inference clusters (instance count, model parallelism, GPU frequency) under SLO constraints conserves **52% energy, 38% operational carbon, and 61% cost** while meeting latency targets.

### Serverless Inference

- **Utilization:** Near-zero idle waste—GPUs spin up on request and release on completion. No "parking tax."
- **Break-even analysis (DigitalOcean, 2026):** Serverless is cheaper than self-hosted GPUs until the GPU is **22–48% busy**. Dedicated managed inference is 30% more expensive than self-hosted, with break-even at ~29% duty cycle. Most startups keep GPUs only 5–10% busy, making serverless 2–4× cheaper.
- **Cold start penalty:** 5–30 seconds for 70B models on self-managed serverless; managed platforms have reduced this to milliseconds via checkpoint/restore and warm pools. The environmental cost of cold starts (loading model weights from storage) must be weighed against the savings from eliminating idle power.
- **Environmental trade-off:** Serverless minimizes operational energy by eliminating idle waste, but the per-request overhead of model loading adds energy. Net-positive when utilization is low; can be net-negative at high sustained utilization due to repeated load/unload cycles and the serverless pricing premium (20–40% per GPU-hour).

### External APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.)

- **Transparency deficit:** Providers do not disclose per-model inference data. Emissions are aggregated across entire cloud infrastructures without disaggregation by model or workload.
- **Google's disclosure (2025):** The most transparent estimate to date—0.24 Wh, 0.03 gCO₂e, 0.26 mL per median prompt—using a full-stack methodology including idle machine capacity (10% of total energy) and DC overhead (8%). However, it uses market-based carbon accounting with RECs, which can understate location-based emissions by 10–100×.
- **Scalability insight:** Google reported a **33× reduction in energy and 44× reduction in carbon** for the median Gemini prompt over 12 months through software/hardware efficiency improvements—suggesting that API providers can optimize fleet-level efficiency faster than individual deployers.

---

## 4. Reconciling Conflicting Estimates: Key Assumptions Driving Differences

| Assumption | Low estimate | High estimate | Impact |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|--------|
| **System boundary** | GPU-only energy | Full stack (GPU + CPU + RAM + cooling + PUE + idle capacity) | 1.7–3× difference (Google: TPU is only 58% of total) |
| **Carbon accounting** | Market-based (RECs offset emissions) | Location-based (physical grid mix) | 10–100× difference in reported emissions |
| **Water boundary** | On-site cooling only | On-site + off-site (power plant cooling) | 10–180× difference |
| **Model architecture** | Dense, quantized (INT4/FP8) | Dense bf16 | 2–4× energy difference |
| **Model type** | Standard generation | Reasoning (chain-of-thought) | 30–700× difference |
| **MoE vs. dense** | MoE (fraction of params active) | All params active | 2–4× |
| **Grid carbon intensity** | Renewable-rich region (50 gCO₂/kWh) | Coal-heavy region (800+ gCO₂/kWh) | 16× in emissions per Wh |
| **Idle allocation** | Exclude idle machine capacity | Include idle (10% of total at Google scale) | ~10% addition |
| **Batch size** | Optimized batching | Single-request serving | 2–5× in per-token energy |
| **Embodied carbon** | Exclude manufacturing | Include (21.56 kgCO₂/A100) | Significant for short-lived deployments |

---

## 5. Practical Measurement Strategies

1. **CodeCarbon / AI Energy Benchmarks:** Open-source tools (used by AI Energy Score) that wrap inference calls and measure GPU energy via nvidia-smi or RAPL. Good for relative comparisons but may miss host CPU/RAM/cooling overhead.

2. **AI Energy Score (HuggingFace/MLCommons, v2 Dec 2025):** Standardized benchmarking across 10 tasks on H100 hardware. Now includes reasoning models. Uses controlled datasets and reproducible methodology. The EU AI Act Code of Practice explicitly calls for inference energy benchmarks—this framework is positioned as the standard.

3. **MLPerf Power (MLCommons):** Measures performance-per-watt for standardized inference workloads (Llama 2 70B, Llama 3.1 405B). Architecture-neutral and reproducible but focuses on throughput, not per-prompt energy.

4. **ML.Energy Leaderboard (University of Michigan):** Community-driven, tracks energy consumption of AI models; praised by Google researchers as complementary.

5. **Google's full-stack methodology:** The gold standard for production measurement—includes active AI accelerator power, host CPU/RAM, idle machine capacity, and DC overhead (PUE). Organizations should replicate this boundary even if they lack Google's instrumentation granularity.

6. **DCGM telemetry (NVIDIA):** Per-second GPU power telemetry for production clusters. The "Model Parking Tax" study used 335,267 samples over 18 days to characterize idle power—organizations should instrument at similar granularity.

7. **Per-model traffic tracking:** Most teams lack per-model utilization data, defaulting the deployment-mode decision to instinct. Instrument per-model request rates and GPU duty cycles before choosing serverless vs. dedicated.

---

## 6. Practical Reduction Strategies

### Hardware & Architecture
- **Model quantization:** INT4/FP8 vs. bf16 reduces energy 2–4× with minimal quality loss for most serving scenarios.
- **MoE architectures:** Mixture-of-experts activates a fraction of parameters per token, reducing per-query FLOPs 2–4×.
- **Model routing (Hybrid LLM):** Route simple queries to small/distilled models, reserve frontier models for complex queries—can reduce energy 40–60% with comparable accuracy.
- **Reuse older GPUs (GreenLLM):** Disaggregating prefill/decode phases onto older GPUs reduces total carbon (embodied + operational) by up to **40.6%** while meeting >90% of latency SLOs. Extends hardware lifetime, amortizing embodied carbon (21.56 kgCO₂/A100).

### Scheduling & Orchestration
- **Carbon-aware scheduling:** Route inference requests to regions with low-carbon electricity. Spatiotemporal variability in carbon intensity (50–800 gCO₂/kWh) creates massive optimization opportunities. Sprout (2024) achieves >40% carbon reduction using generation directives and global grid data.
- **DynamoLLM-style dynamic reconfiguration:** Automatically reconfigure instance count, model parallelism, and GPU frequency under SLO constraints—52% energy savings, 38% carbon reduction, 61% cost reduction.
- **DVFS frequency tuning:** The Utilization Fallacy paper shows frequency tuning on shared GPUs can improve carbon efficiency, but only when tailored to the specific model combination and carbon-intensity context.
- **CUDA_DISABLE_PERF_BOOST flag:** NVIDIA's flag eliminates the model parking tax within measurement noise on Hopper and Ampere—zero-cost reduction of 26–66 W/GPU idle power.
- **Workload consolidation:** Consolidate low-traffic models onto shared GPUs to reduce the number of idle GPUs paying the parking tax. But apply carbon-aware co-location, not just utilization maximization.

### Deployment Mode Selection
- **Below ~30% sustained utilization:** Serverless is both cheaper and lower-carbon (no idle waste).
- **30–50% utilization:** Managed dedicated inference or autoscaled endpoints with aggressive scale-to-zero.
- **Above 50%:** Self-hosted or dedicated GPUs with batching optimization, quantization, and carbon-aware scheduling.
- **Hybrid:** Keep critical models warm on dedicated GPUs for primary traffic; push long-tail and experimental models to serverless.

### Regulatory & Transparency
- **EU AI Act Code of Practice:** Signed by OpenAI, Microsoft, Google—calls for inference energy benchmarks. Organizations should adopt the AI Energy Score methodology for internal and external reporting.
- **Disclose both on-site and total water consumption:** Following UC Riverside's framework, not just on-site figures.
- **Use location-based carbon accounting** alongside market-based figures to avoid greenwashing through RECs.

---

## 7. Embodied Carbon and E-Waste

Manufacturing 350,000 A100 GPUs emits an estimated **7.54 million kgCO₂ (21.56 kgCO₂/GPU)**. E-waste from generative AI could reach 1.2–5.0 million tons between 2020–2030. Rapid hardware turnover for inference (where models are frequently upgraded) accelerates obsolescence. Reusing older GPUs for disaggregated inference phases (prefill on new, decode on old) is a concrete strategy that addresses both embodied carbon and e-waste simultaneously.

---

## 8. Summary Table: Deployment Mode Environmental Profile

| Dimension | Fixed Dedicated | Autoscaled | Serverless | External API |
|-----------|----------------|------------|------------|--------------|
| Idle energy waste | High (parking tax: 26–66 W/GPU) | Moderate (scales down but not to zero) | Near-zero (scales to zero) | Hidden (provider's idle capacity) |
| Execution-idle waste | High (19.7% of execution time) | Moderate | Low (short sessions) | Hidden |
| Embodied carbon amortization | Poor if underutilized | Better (shared fleet) | Best (high utilization across tenants) | Unknown |
| Cold-start energy | None | Low (warm pools) | High (model loading per request) | None (always warm) |
| Transparency | Full (you measure) | Full | Partial (provider metrics) | Low (aggregated, self-reported) |
| Best utilization range | >50% | 30–70% | <30% | Any (but opaque) |

---

RECOMMENDATION: 3 — Adopt a hybrid deployment strategy with carbon-aware scheduling: use serverless for workloads below ~30% sustained GPU utilization, autoscaled dedicated endpoints for 30–50%, and fixed dedicated GPUs with DVFS tuning, quantization, and model routing above 50%, while measuring full-stack energy (including idle capacity and DC overhead) using the AI Energy Score methodology and reporting both location-based and market-based emissions.
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: The "utilization fallacy"—increasing GPU utilization through spatial sharing without carbon-aware co-location can increase rather than decrease total emissions, especially when shared workloads are mismatched or grid carbon intensity is high.

# Environmental Impact of Serving LLMs in Production: An Inference-Focused Analysis

## 1. Why Inference Now Dominates the Lifecycle Footprint

Early sustainability research focused on training (GPT-3: ~1,287 MWh, ~550 tCO₂e, ~700 kL water). But inference now dominates the lifecycle footprint of large-scale LLM deployments. Recent estimates suggest inference can account for up to 90% of a model's total lifecycle energy use, because it runs continuously while training is episodic. LLMCO2 (Fu et al., Oct 2024) estimates that ~121 days of serving GPT-4 inference produces carbon emissions equal to one full training run; this break-even is shrinking as daily request volume grows. Google's first-party production paper (Vahdat/Dean et al., Aug 2025) states that "the cumulative footprint of serving billions of queries now dominates the life-cycle of many deployments and can exceed training by a wide margin."

---

## 2. Per-Prompt Electricity Estimates: A Wide Spread

| Source | Model / workload | Electricity per prompt | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google production measurement (Aug 2025) | Median Gemini Apps text prompt | **0.24 Wh** | Full-stack: accelerators + host CPU/DRAM + idle capacity + PUE overhead |
| Jegham et al. "How Hungry is AI?" (May 2025) | GPT-4o, short query | **0.42–0.43 Wh** | Infrastructure-aware benchmarking, 30 models |
| Same | Claude-3.7 Sonnet | ~0.9 Wh (short) / varies (long) | Ranked highest eco-efficiency |
| Same | o3 / DeepSeek-R1, long prompt | **>33 Wh** | ~70× GPT-4.1 nano; reasoning models far more intensive |
| Luccioni et al. (2023, widely cited) | GPT-3 ChatGPT query | ~1.3–2.4 Wh (early estimates) | Pre-2024 hardware; superseded by newer numbers |
| GreenLLM (Shi et al., Dec 2024) | ChatGPT prompt | ~4 gCO₂e cited; implies ~1–3 Wh depending on grid | Uses older multiplier |

### Reconciling the differences

The gap between Google's 0.24 Wh and Jegham's 0.42 Wh for roughly comparable models is driven by:

1. **System boundary.** Google's number is a full-stack production measurement including idle machines, host CPU/RAM, and PUE. Google notes that "many current AI energy consumption calculations only include active machine consumption," which understates the real footprint. Google's own data shows that AI accelerators (TPUs) account for just 58% of total energy—host CPU/DRAM adds 25%, idle machines 10%, and data center overhead (PUE) 8%. Jegham's framework also attempts full-stack but relies on *statistical inference* of hardware configurations rather than direct instrumentation. Hoxha et al. (Oct 2025) reproduced this gap quantitatively, finding a narrow/comprehensive ratio of ≈0.417, meaning accelerator-only measurements miss ~58% of energy.

2. **Time period.** Google reports a **33× energy reduction** for the median Gemini prompt over 12 months due to software/hardware co-design. Jegham's data captures a point-in-time cross-section. Any estimate older than ~6 months may be substantially outdated.

3. **Model versioning.** Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) that generate long chain-of-thought traces consume **70× more** than compact models per long prompt—this dwarfs any infrastructure-level variation.

4. **Precision/quantization.** FP8 serving roughly halves per-token energy vs. BF16 (vLLM optimization playbook, 2026). Commercial APIs likely run lower precision than academic benchmarks.

5. **Grid carbon intensity (CI) assumptions.** Location-based vs. market-based accounting changes CO₂e by 2–5× depending on renewable energy credits.

**Bottom line:** For a current-generation dense LLM (GPT-4o / Gemini-class), a realistic full-stack short-prompt range is **0.2–0.5 Wh**. Reasoning models can push this to **10–35 Wh per long prompt**.

---

## 3. Water Consumption

Water comes from two sources: **onsite evaporative cooling** (data center cooling towers) and **offsite electricity generation** (thermoelectric plant evaporation).

- **Google (2025):** Median Gemini prompt = **0.26 mL** (≈ 5 drops), including both onsite + offsite water.
- **Jegham et al. (2025):** 700M GPT-4o queries/day → annual freshwater evaporation matching drinking needs of **1.2 million people**.
- **African data center water dataset (Shumba et al., 2025):** Writing a 10-page report with Llama-3-70B consumes **~0.66 L**; GPT-4 for the same task up to **~59 L** (2024-era estimates; authors note >30× efficiency improvements since). Country-level variation is huge: hydro-dominant grids (Ethiopia, Congo) have *higher* water intensity than gas-reliant grids (Libya, Tunisia), inverting common assumptions about renewable energy and water.
- **Hoxha et al. (Oct 2025):** Grid carbon intensity and electricity water intensity are only **weakly correlated**, so optimizing for carbon alone can increase water use. For 500M GPT-4o queries/day, baseline consumption is 1.196 ML water/day, reducible to 0.490 ML with dual-objective optimization.

Water per Wh varies by roughly **10× across regions** depending on cooling technology and grid mix—making location a first-order lever, not a second-order detail.

---

## 4. Hardware Utilization: The Idle-Power Problem

### Execution-idle is not like CPU idle

Lei et al. ("The Energy Cost of Execution-Idle in GPU Clusters," 2026) measured per-second telemetry on a large academic AI cluster and found:

- GPUs remain at **high power even when visible activity is near zero** (unlike CPUs, which scale down).
- Execution-idle accounts for **19.7% of in-execution time and 10.7% of energy** across diverse workloads and GPU generations.
- In serving traces, idle intervals can account for up to **65% of total energy**.

This means **utilization is the single biggest controllable lever** for inference carbon.

### The "Model Parking Tax"

Vadari ("The Model Parking Tax," 2026) provided the first cross-architecture measurement of idle GPU power as a function of VRAM allocation, combining 18 days of production telemetry (335,267 samples, 14 H100 GPUs) with controlled experiments on three GPU architectures. Key finding: idle GPU power is **piecewise constant** across all architectures—the CUDA context forces a discrete DVFS transition consuming +26–66 W over bare idle, while the marginal VRAM effect is <0.02 W/GB on every device tested. The CUDA context accounts for >98% of the parking tax regardless of memory technology. Cold-start breakeven intervals are **1–5 minutes** depending on request arrival rate and loading latency—not model size.

### The utilization fallacy

Sinha et al. (HotCarbon 2025, UT Austin) show that "higher GPU utilization → better carbon efficiency" is **not always true**. Spatial sharing (co-locating models via MIG) can increase utilization while *increasing* per-request CO₂ if the co-located models are mismatched. Carbon-aware GPU sharing and frequency tuning—tailored to the specific model combination—outperforms naive utilization maximization.

---

## 5. Deployment-Mode Comparison

| Mode | Idle power waste | Utilization at scale | Typical break-even | Environmental profile |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed dedicated GPUs** (static provisioning for peak) | High — GPU draws 50–70% of TDP even idle (execution-idle) | 10–20% common (PromptMetrics/Modal 2026); 39–50% even at P95 provisioning (operator-level autoscaling study, Nov 2025) | N/A — always provisioned | Worst per-token efficiency at low/variable load; best throughput-per-watt at sustained high load |
| **Autoscaled endpoints** (model-level autoscaling) | Moderate — scales replicas with traffic, but treats model as monolith | Better than static; ~40% GPU reduction demonstrated with operator-level autoscaling | Replaces fixed when traffic is bursty | Cuts idle waste significantly; operator-level autoscaling (Cui et al., Nov 2025) achieved **40% fewer GPUs, 35% less energy** at same SLO |
| **Serverless inference** (pay-per-token, scale-to-zero) | Near-zero when idle (provider absorbs idle across tenants) | High on provider side (multi-tenant batching); low from customer's perspective | Cheaper than self-host until **22–48% sustained utilization** (DigitalOcean 2026); **29%** vs. dedicated managed; **51–66%** at current RunPod pricing (PromptMetrics 2026) | Best for bursty/low-volume; avoids idle power entirely; but multi-tenant efficiency is opaque to customer |
| **External API** (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) | Zero customer-side idle; provider amortizes across all tenants | Highest aggregate batching; Google reports 33× efficiency gains in 12 months | N/A — usage-based | Lowest per-query energy *if* provider is efficient; least transparency; carbon/water depends on provider's data center region and grid mix |

### Key reconciliation

The "30% rule" (dedicated beats serverless above 30% utilization) is now **stale**. Current pricing pushes the break-even to **40–66%** depending on GPU type and provider (PromptMetrics 2026, RunPod pricing verified July 2026). This means more workloads should default to serverless/external API on environmental grounds than older guidance suggested. DigitalOcean's testing (July 2026) confirmed: serverless is 2–4× cheaper than dedicated when GPUs run below 10–20% utilization, which is the common reality for most teams.

### DynamoLLM (HPCA 2025)

Microsoft Azure's DynamoLLM dynamically reconfigures inference clusters (instance count, model parallelism, GPU frequency) under SLO constraints, achieving **52% energy savings, 38% operational carbon reduction, and 61% cost reduction** at the service level. This demonstrates that *dynamic* dedicated clusters can approach serverless efficiency at high utilization by exploiting the distinct compute properties of prefill (compute-bound, frequency-sensitive) vs. decode (memory-bound, frequency-insensitive) phases.

### Festina (2026)

For serverless multi-tenant LLM serving on shared GPUs, Festina (Wang et al., 2026) provides a profiling-guided, power-aware control plane that jointly coordinates request placement, SM partitioning, and GPU operating points under TTFT/TBT SLOs. It reduces energy consumption by up to **56%** while maintaining SLO attainment within a 2% margin.

---

## 6. Aggregated Scale Estimates

Jegham et al. (2025) scaling a single 0.42–0.43 Wh GPT-4o short query to **700M queries/day**:

- **Electricity:** comparable to **35,000 U.S. homes**
- **Water:** annual drinking needs of **1.2 million people**
- **Carbon:** requiring a **Chicago-sized forest** to offset

Hoxha et al. (2025) for **500M GPT-4o queries/day**: 0.344 GWh, 1.196 ML water, 121 tCO₂ (location-based) per day at median—reducible to 0.145 GWh, 0.490 ML, and 25 tCO₂ with their SLO-aware bi-objective optimization.

Google (2025) does not disclose absolute daily totals but emphasizes per-prompt efficiency improvements (33× energy, 44× carbon in one year) and notes that absolute volume growth can outpace per-prompt gains—a "growing paradox."

---

## 7. Assumptions Driving Conflicting Estimates

| Assumption | Impact on estimates | Where they diverge |
|---|---|---|
| **System boundary** (accelerator-only vs. full-stack with idle, host, PUE) | Accelerator-only understates by ~2.4× (Hoxha: comprehensive/narrow ratio ≈ 0.417) | Google (full-stack, measured) vs. older academic (accelerator-only) |
| **Hardware inference** (which GPU, how many, utilization rate) | 10× variation | Jegham statistically infers; Google measures directly |
| **Grid carbon intensity** (location-based vs. market-based) | 2–5× CO₂e difference | Market-based with RECs can show near-zero; location-based shows actual grid emissions |
| **Water intensity** (onsite + offsite; regional grid mix) | Up to 10× | Hydro grids: high offsite water; arid regions: high onsite |
| **Query volume** (daily requests × prompt length) | Linear scaling dominates all other factors | 270M (2023) → 700M (2025) → projected billions |
| **Model type** (dense vs. reasoning/CoT) | Up to 70× per-prompt | o3/DeepSeek-R1 >> GPT-4o > Gemini |
| **Precision** (BF16 vs. FP8 vs. INT4) | ~2× energy | Commercial APIs likely lower precision than academic benchmarks |
| **Time frame** | 33× efficiency gain in 12 months (Google) | 2024-era estimates already significantly outdated |

---

## 8. RAG Pipeline Overhead (A Blind Spot in Prior Work)

Most inference energy studies treat LLM calls in isolation, but production systems increasingly use RAG. Recent research reveals significant hidden energy costs:

- **Workflow fungibility** (Pan et al., NeurIPS 2025 Workshop): RAG configurations with ≤3% accuracy difference can vary by up to **20.2× in energy per query**. Pairing Llama3-8B with stronger retrievers matches Llama3-70B accuracy while using 5.42× less energy.
- **RAG-specific energy optimization** (Guo et al., ICSE-SEIS 2026): Across 200+ hours of trials, techniques like increasing similarity thresholds and reducing embedding sizes reduced RAG energy by up to **60%** with no accuracy loss. Indexing strategies and reranker choices also matter significantly.
- **In-storage retrieval** (REIS, 2025): The retrieval stage of RAG is a significant performance bottleneck; in-storage processing can improve retrieval energy efficiency by **55×** compared to server-grade systems.

This means any measurement framework that ignores retrieval, embedding, and reranking components is systematically underestimating the true per-query energy of production AI systems.

---

## 9. Multimodal Inference (Another Blind Spot)

Google's study explicitly excluded image and video generation. Tri-serve (Jia et al., 2026) identified three classes of power inefficiency in multimodal inference serving: (1) inter-stage dependency stalls running at maximum frequency despite being idle, (2) anti-correlation between auto-boost frequency and arithmetic intensity, and (3) thermal throttling. Their software DVFS controller achieved **22% energy efficiency improvement** with no latency or throughput impact. Multimodal inference likely has significantly higher per-request energy than text-only, but no major provider has disclosed production measurements.

---

## 10. Practical Measurement Strategies

1. **Full-stack boundary:** Include accelerator power + host CPU/DRAM + idle/provisioned capacity + PUE overhead. Hoxha et al. show comprehensive/narrow ratio ≈ 0.417, meaning accelerator-only measurements miss ~58% of energy.

2. **Per-second GPU telemetry:** Use nvidia-smi/DCGM per-second power draws, not TDP × GPU-hours. Execution-idle states (Lei et al.) are invisible at coarse granularity.

3. **Phase-aware measurement:** Prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) have very different power profiles. LLMCO2 shows that equation-based models are unreliable for inference precisely because of "lower and highly variable model FLOPS utilization." DynamoLLM confirms: requests with large input tokens are frequency-sensitive; requests with few input tokens and many output tokens can have frequency reduced with minimal performance impact.

4. **Location-based carbon accounting by default:** Use real-time grid CI (e.g., Electricity Maps, WattTime) for the actual data center region. Report market-based as a sensitivity only. Hoxha et al. enforce this distinction.

5. **Water = onsite (WUE) + offsite (EWIF):** Track Water Usage Effectiveness (L/kWh for cooling) + electricity water intensity factor (L/kWh for generation). These are weakly correlated with carbon and must be tracked separately.

6. **Include RAG overhead:** Measure the full pipeline—embedding generation, vector search, reranking, and LLM generation—not just the LLM call. The retrieval stage can dominate energy in knowledge-intensive applications.

7. **Attributional vs. consequential:** For internal optimization, use attributional (what did this query consume). For capacity decisions, use consequential (what happens to grid mix if we add load here vs. there).

---

## 11. Practical Reduction Strategies (Ranked by Impact)

### Tier 1 — Utilization (highest impact)

1. **Continuous batching at high concurrency:** The single biggest lever. vLLM optimization playbook (2026): going from concurrency 1 to 256 yielded **73× throughput and 104× energy efficiency** (0.14 → 14.5 tokens/joule). No other optimization comes close.

2. **Default to serverless/external API for bursty workloads:** Eliminates idle power entirely below ~40–50% sustained utilization. DigitalOcean, PromptMetrics, and GMI Cloud all converge on this. Most teams run at 10–20% utilization—serverless is 2–4× more efficient there.

3. **Operator-level autoscaling** (not model-level): Cui et al. (Nov 2025) → 40% fewer GPUs, 35% less energy at same SLO. Treat the model as a DAG of operators, not a monolith.

4. **Dynamic reconfiguration (DynamoLLM):** 52% energy, 38% carbon, 61% cost reduction via runtime frequency tuning, instance count, and parallelism adjustment under SLO.

5. **Energy-aware serverless scheduling (Festina):** 56% energy reduction in multi-tenant serverless via coordinated request placement, SM partitioning, and GPU operating point control.

### Tier 2 — Model and serving optimization

6. **Model routing by complexity:** Use small models for simple queries, reserve large/reasoning models for hard ones. The 70× gap between GPT-4.1 nano and o3 per long prompt makes routing the highest-impact model-level decision.

7. **RAG workflow optimization:** Exploit workflow fungibility—choosing the right retriever-generator combination can yield 5–20× energy savings at near-identical accuracy (Pan et al., NeurIPS 2025).

8. **Quantization (FP8/INT4):** ~2× energy reduction with minimal quality loss (vLLM playbook: "legitimate free lunch on L40S" with perplexity gate).

9. **Speculative decoding:** Up to 2.8× latency reduction (vLLM), which reduces wall-clock energy per token; most effective at low-medium QPS.

10. **Prefix caching:** Avoids recomputation of shared prompt prefixes; up to 5.4× latency reduction for long-context workloads (AMD/vLLM on MI300X); 30–60% throughput gain on shared system prompts.

### Tier 3 — Location and infrastructure

11. **Carbon-aware routing:** Route requests to regions with lower real-time grid CI. Hoxha et al. (2025) SLO-aware bi-objective framework: **57–59% energy, 59–60% water, 78–80% CO₂ reduction** via region/batch/phase-aware MILP optimization.

12. **Dual-objective carbon + water optimization:** Because grid CI and electricity water intensity are only weakly correlated, optimizing carbon alone can increase water. Hoxha et al. explicitly balance both.

13. **Hardware lifecycle extension (GreenLLM):** Disaggregate prefill onto older GPUs → **40.6% carbon reduction** including embodied carbon, while meeting SLOs for >90% of requests.

14. **Power oversubscription (POLCA, Microsoft ASPLOS 2024):** Inference workloads offer substantial headroom; 30% more servers can be deployed in existing power-limited clusters with minimal performance loss, deferring new data center construction.

### Tier 4 — Workflow and demand-side

15. **Prompt engineering / context trimming:** Bloated system prompts and retry loops are a major (often dominant) cost driver (PromptMetrics 2026). Reducing prompt tokens reduces energy linearly.

16. **Caching and deduplication:** Avoid redundant inference for repeated or near-identical queries.

17. **Human-in-the-loop gates:** Circuit-breaker patterns that prevent runaway agent loops (retry storms, abandoned outputs) can cut token spend significantly. The same gate that provides audit trail compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Articles 12 and 19) also caps budget and energy.

---

## 12. Key Uncertainties and Caveats

- **Provider opacity:** Commercial AI providers do not disclose model-specific inference data. Jegham et al. and LLMCO2 both rely on statistical inference or public API benchmarks. Google's 2025 disclosure is the first major first-party production measurement; it has not been independently replicated. It also covers only text prompts, excluding multimodal workloads.

- **Rapid efficiency gains:** Google's reported 33× energy improvement in 12 months means any estimate older than ~6 months may be substantially outdated. The African water dataset authors explicitly flag this.

- **Embodied carbon:** Manufacturing 350,000 A100 GPUs ≈ 7.54M kgCO₂ (21.56 kgCO₂/GPU). Embodied carbon is rarely included in inference estimates but can be 20–50% of total lifecycle for short-lived hardware. GreenLLM and Sinha et al. are among the few to address this.

- **Water data quality:** Onsite WUE data is rarely publicly available; offsite EWIF depends on grid mix assumptions that change seasonally.

- **RAG and pipeline overhead:** Most estimates capture only the LLM forward pass. In production, retrieval, embedding, reranking, and agent orchestration can add significant energy—up to 20× variation between equivalent-accuracy RAG configurations.

- **Jevons paradox:** Per-prompt efficiency gains (Google's 33× in one year) may be offset by increased query volume. Google and Jegham both note this "growing paradox." Reasoning models like o3 and DeepSeek-R1 consume 70× more per prompt, potentially overwhelming efficiency gains at the system level.

- **Regulatory uncertainty:** Emerging mandatory disclosure regimes (EU AI Act logging requirements, evolving carbon reporting standards) may force measurement standardization, but no universal standard exists yet.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 3 — Default to serverless inference or external APIs for bursty/low-utilization workloads, and only migrate to autoscaled dedicated GPUs (with continuous batching, FP8 quantization, and operator-level autoscaling) once sustained utilization exceeds ~40–50%, while routing requests carbon- and water-aware across regions and measuring full-stack energy with per-second GPU telemetry.
