# Environmental Impact of Serving Large Language Models in Production: Inference-Focused Analysis

## 1. Why Inference Dominates the Lifecycle Footprint

Training happens once or rarely; inference runs continuously at global scale. The gap is now quantified:

- **Meta reports inference constitutes up to 70% of its AI power consumption**; Google attributes 60% of its ML energy to serving; AWS estimates 80–90% of its cloud compute demand is inference, not training ([Fernandez et al., ACL 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1563.pdf); [Google AI paper, Aug 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734)).
- **LLMCO2** (Fu et al., 2024) estimates that **121 days of GPT-4 inference equals the emissions of training GPT-4 itself**—inference overtakes training within ~4 months ([arXiv:2410.02950](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02950)).
- **Jegham et al. (2025)** find that scaling a single GPT-4o short query (0.43 Wh) to 700 million daily queries yields annual impacts comparable to 35,000 U.S. homes' electricity, 1.2 million people's annual drinking water (evaporation), and carbon requiring a Chicago-sized forest to offset ([arXiv:2505.09598](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09598)).

**Key assumption:** The training-to-inference crossover depends on query volume and model class. A lightly used model may never break even; a heavily used one does so in months.

---

## 2. Per-Prompt Estimates: Reconciling the Numbers

### Electricity (Wh per prompt)

| Source | Model | Prompt type | Energy/prompt |
|--------|-------|-------------|---------------|
| Google (Aug 2025, measured) | Gemini Apps (median text) | Short text | **0.24 Wh** (full-stack); **0.10 Wh** (active chip only) |
| OpenAI (Altman disclosure, mid-2025) | ChatGPT average | Average query | **~0.34 Wh** |
| Epoch AI (bottom-up, Feb 2025) | GPT-4o typical | Typical query | **~0.3 Wh** |
| Jegham et al. 2025 | GPT-4o short | 100 in / 300 out | **0.42–0.43 Wh** |
| Jegham et al. 2025 | GPT-4.1 nano | Short | **~0.006 Wh** |
| Jegham et al. 2025 | o3 / DeepSeek-R1 | Long prompt | **>33 Wh** (reasoning models, ~70× nano) |
| ML.Energy (MIT) | Llama 3.1 8B | Answer | **~0.032 Wh** (~114 J) |
| ML.Energy (MIT) | Llama 3.1 405B | Answer | **~1.86 Wh** (~6,706 J) |
| Dauner & Socher (2025, A100 measured) | 14 LLMs, MMLU | 500 MC + 500 FR | Varies with size/token output; reasoning models substantially higher |

**Reconciling the "3 Wh per query" controversy:** The widely cited 2023 de Vries estimate of ~3 Wh per ChatGPT query was **explicitly refuted by Epoch AI**, which found it ~10× too high for a typical GPT-4o query ([Epoch AI, Feb 2025](https://epoch.ai/blog/how-much-energy-does-chatgpt-use); [Nature Scientific Reports, Dec 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-31896-0)). The gap arises from three conflating assumptions:

1. **Full-stack vs. active-chip-only:** Google's 0.24 Wh includes host CPU/RAM (25%), idle backup machines (10%), and data center overhead/PUE (8%). Active-chip energy is only 0.10 Wh—just 58% of the total. Early estimates counted only the chip, systematically underestimating by 2–3×.
2. **Reasoning vs. standard models:** o3 and DeepSeek-R1 generate long internal "thinking" token chains, consuming 70× more energy than nano models. The emissions.dev API applies a 6× thinking-ratio multiplier for o3. This is a new category that didn't exist before late 2024.
3. **Batch size and utilization:** At batch size 1, GPU SM utilization falls below 5%, making per-token energy up to 44× worse than at saturated batch sizes. Many estimates assume ideal batching that real workloads don't achieve.

### Water (mL per prompt)

| Source | Estimate |
|--------|----------|
| Google (Gemini, measured, Aug 2025) | **0.26 mL** (~5 drops) |
| OpenAI (Altman disclosure) | **~0.32 mL** (0.000085 gallons) |
| Washington Post / UC Riverside (2024, worst-case) | **up to 519 mL** for a 100-word email in a hot Texas data center; as low as 235 mL elsewhere |
| African Data Center dataset (2024) | GPT-4 medium email: ~2.9 L; Llama-3-70B: ~0.13 L |

**Reconciliation:** The "bottle of water per email" headline is a **worst-case scenario in a hot-climate, fossil-heavy-grid data center**, not a representative figure. Google's measured 0.26 mL is ~2,000× lower. The discrepancy is driven by:
- **Grid water intensity:** Hydroelectric grids (Ethiopia, Congo) paradoxically have high water consumption due to reservoir evaporation, while natural-gas-heavy grids (Libya, Tunisia) can have lower water intensity ([arXiv:2412.03716](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03716)).
- **On-site vs. off-site water:** Off-site water (electricity generation) often dominates total water use. The Washington Post figure conflates both.
- **Cooling technology:** Evaporative cooling in hot climates dramatically increases on-site water; hyperscalers increasingly use air cooling or recycled water.

### Carbon (gCO₂e per prompt)

| Source | Model/Scenario | Estimate |
|--------|----------------|----------|
| Google (measured) | Gemini median text | **0.03 gCO₂e** |
| Jegham et al. (implied) | GPT-4o short, Azure grid | **~0.15 gCO₂e** (0.43 Wh × 0.3528 kg/kWh) |
| emissions.dev API | GPT-5.2, 5K in + 2K out | **1.20 gCO₂e** (0.90 operational + 0.30 embodied) |
| Dauner & Socher (2025) | A100, 480 g/kWh factor | Varies; larger models and reasoning models substantially higher |

**Reconciliation:** Carbon per prompt varies by **grid carbon intensity** (30 g/kWh in Norway to 850 g/kWh in coal-heavy regions) and **PUE** (1.08–1.12 for hyperscalers vs. 1.5–2.0 for typical on-premise). Google's 0.03 gCO₂e reflects both low-PUE data centers and aggressive carbon-free energy procurement (though RECs are "accounting, not physics"—the physical grid mix where servers run may still be fossil-heavy at certain hours).

---

## 3. Deployment Mode Comparison

### A. Fixed Dedicated GPUs

**Characteristics:** You own/rent a GPU 24/7. Power flows whether or not requests arrive.

- **Idle power is 30–60% of peak** for modern GPUs. An idle A100 draws ~250 W; active ~300 W.
- **Scenario from cost analysis:** An A100 serving only 10 prompts/day for 24h uptime produces **2,810 gCO₂e/day**, of which 99.98% is idle energy—**281 gCO₂e per 1,000 prompts**, vs. 7.5 gCO₂e for an efficient laptop running the same workload.
- **Break-even threshold:** A dedicated H200 GPU ($3.44/hr) breaks even with serverless pricing only at **~72% sustained utilization**. Below that, serverless is cheaper and more energy-efficient per token ([DigitalOcean analysis](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/llm-inference-cost)).
- **Embodied carbon:** Manufacturing 350,000 A100s emits ~7.54 million kgCO₂ (21.56 kgCO₂ per GPU). Poor utilization means this embodied carbon is amortized over fewer useful tokens ([UT Austin / HotCarbon 2025](https://ut-sysml.ece.utexas.edu/publications/prints/hotcarbon2025_sinha.pdf)).

**Verdict:** Worst environmental efficiency at low utilization. Best only when traffic is steady and high (>70%).

### B. Autoscaled Endpoints

**Characteristics:** Managed endpoint that scales replica count up/down. Reduces but does not eliminate idle capacity.

- Google's methodology explicitly accounts for **idle machines kept ready for failover and traffic spikes** as part of the full-stack footprint (10% of total energy in their measurement).
- **Energy-aware scheduling** (e.g., Festina) shows DVFS and workload consolidation on shared GPUs can reduce energy by up to 56% while maintaining SLOs.
- **Scale-to-zero** eliminates idle power but introduces cold-start latency and model-loading energy.
- Carbon efficiency depends on scaling aggressiveness and grid carbon intensity at the moment of scaling decisions.

**Verdict:** Better than fixed dedicated at moderate utilization, but still carries idle overhead unless scale-to-zero is used.

### C. Serverless Inference

**Characteristics:** Pay-per-token; provider owns all infrastructure and scaling.

- Serverless is cheaper (and thus more energy-efficient per token) than self-hosted GPUs until the GPU is **22–48% busy**. For dedicated managed endpoints, the break-even is ~29% duty cycle ([DigitalOcean](https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/serverless-vs-dedicated-vs-self-hosted-llm-inference-cost)).
- **Multi-tenant GPU sharing** achieves higher aggregate utilization than single-tenant setups. This is the core efficiency advantage.
- **The "Utilization Fallacy"** (Sinha et al., HotCarbon 2025): Higher GPU utilization via spatial sharing does **not always** improve carbon efficiency. The outcome depends on which models are co-located (different power-performance curves) and the grid mix at that moment. Carbon-aware GPU sharing—not just utilization maximization—is needed.
- Serverless shifts environmental cost to the provider's shared fleet; the provider's PUE, grid mix, and fleet utilization are the dominant variables.

**Verdict:** Generally the most energy-efficient per token for low-to-moderate, bursty traffic.

### D. External APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google)

**Characteristics:** Call a proprietary API; no visibility into underlying infrastructure.

- **Google's measured figures** (0.24 Wh, 0.03 gCO₂e, 0.26 mL per Gemini prompt) are the only first-party, full-stack, production-measured numbers available. Google claims a **33× reduction in energy and 44× reduction in carbon** per prompt over 12 months ([Google blog, Aug 2025](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/infrastructure/measuring-the-environmental-impact-of-ai-inference)).
- **OpenAI's figure** (~0.34 Wh per query) is a company disclosure without detailed methodology.
- External APIs benefit from hyperscaler efficiency: PUE as low as 1.08–1.12, advanced cooling, increasingly renewable energy procurement. However, RECs are accounting, not physics.
- **Reasoning models via API** (o3, DeepSeek-R1) are dramatically more expensive: >33 Wh per long prompt. The emissions.dev API applies a 6× thinking-ratio multiplier for o3.
- **Embodied carbon** is amortized across billions of queries, making per-query embodied carbon very low.
- **Network transfer energy:** A 2025 study from Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam found that fetching LLM content from a remote server uses **3.5–8.9× less client-side energy** than on-device generation, but HTTP overhead (handshake, connection, data transfer) adds a non-trivial per-request energy cost at scale. For a typical API request transferring ~5 KB of text, this is negligible compared to inference energy, but for latency-sensitive applications transferring large context windows repeatedly, it compounds ([Nguyen et al., CAIN 2025](https://doi.org/10.1109/cain66642.2025.00016)).

**Verdict:** Can be highly efficient due to hyperscale optimization and clean energy procurement, but transparency is limited. Reasoning model APIs are the most energy-intensive option per prompt.

---

## 4. Hardware Utilization: The Pivotal Variable

The single most important variable across all deployment modes is **GPU utilization**:

- A GPU at 30% utilization uses nearly the same power as one at 90%, but produces 1/3 the useful output. Improving utilization from 40% to 80% effectively halves environmental impact per unit of work ([Civo](https://www.civo.com/blog/sustainable-gpu-cloud-efficiency-utilization)).
- **At batch size 1, GPU SM utilization falls below 5%**, making per-token energy 44× worse than at saturated batch sizes.
- **Idle GPUs are the hidden cost** of dedicated and autoscaled-with-min-replicas deployments. Google's full-stack accounting reveals idle machines account for 10% of total per-prompt energy.
- **Fernandez et al. (ACL 2025)** showed that proper application of inference efficiency optimizations (vLLM, continuous batching, quantization, model parallelism) can reduce total energy use by **up to 73%** from unoptimized baselines ([ACL 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1563.pdf)).

---

## 5. Reconciling Conflicting Global Estimates

| Source | Global AI Carbon (2025) | Global AI Water (2025) |
|--------|------------------------|------------------------|
| de Vries-Gao (Joule, 2025) | **32.6–79.7 Mt CO₂** | **312.5–764.6 billion L** |
| Jegham et al. (GPT-4o @ 700M/day) | "Chicago-sized forest" | 1.2M people's annual drinking needs |
| Google (direct measurement) | 0.03 gCO₂e per prompt (Gemini only) | 0.26 mL per prompt (Gemini only) |

**Why they differ:**
1. **Scope:** de Vries-Gao uses company-wide environmental disclosures and approximates AI's share from data center growth; the 32.6–79.7 Mt range reflects this uncertainty. Jegham et al. scale a single model's per-prompt cost to estimated daily query volume. Google measures its own production fleet directly.
2. **Grid mix assumptions:** de Vries-Gao acknowledges company disclosures are insufficient to separate AI from non-AI workloads.
3. **Efficiency improvements over time:** Google's 33× efficiency improvement in one year means any static estimate becomes stale rapidly. The African Data Center paper explicitly notes its 2024 estimates are "historical reference values, not representative of current performance."

---

## 6. The Jevons Paradox: A Critical Blind Spot

Luccioni, Strubell, and Crawford (ACM FAccT 2025) directly address how Jevons' Paradox applies to AI: efficiency gains may paradoxically spur increased consumption. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella himself invoked the paradox after DeepSeek's efficiency breakthrough ("As AI gets more efficient and accessible, we will see its use skyrocket"). This is documented in cloud computing broadly—Google's data center energy increased 3.7× from 2016 to 2022 despite massive efficiency improvements ([Sharma, arXiv:2411.11540](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11540); [Luccioni et al., arXiv:2501.16548](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16548); [Wu, Nature Cities 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44284-025-00289-9)).

**Implication:** Per-query reductions are necessary but insufficient. Total consumption depends on demand elasticity. A 33× efficiency improvement that enables 50× more queries is a net increase. Teams should measure absolute energy/carbon, not just per-query intensity, and consider demand management as a reduction lever.

---

## 7. Emerging Regulatory Landscape

The **EU AI Act** (Regulation 2024/1689, in force August 2024) requires energy disclosure for training but **does not currently require inference energy disclosure**—a critical gap identified by ACM Europe TPC and Hacker et al. (2024). Key gaps include:

- No inference-phase energy requirements in Annexes IV, XI, XII
- No disclosure of indirect GHG emissions
- No AI-specific water consumption requirements
- No standardized methodology for energy reporting
- No public registry for climate metrics

ACM recommends mandating inference-phase energy disclosure, cumulative server-level reporting, AI-specific water use estimates, and sustainability impact assessments in Articles 9 and 55. These amendments, if adopted, would make inference environmental reporting mandatory for high-risk AI systems in the EU ([ACM Europe TPC Policy Brief, June 2025](https://www.acm.org/binaries/content/assets/public-policy/europe-tpc/acm_climate_disclosure_final.pdf); [Hacker et al., arXiv:2409.07471](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07471)).

---

## 8. Additional Reduction Strategies: Speculative Decoding and Distillation

### Speculative Decoding

Speculative decoding uses a small "draft" model to generate candidate tokens that a large "target" model verifies in parallel, reducing latency. However, the energy implications are nuanced:

- **A 2026 EACL study** (Dutta et al.) found that some speculative decoding methods (COGA with VICUNA-13B target) actually **consume more energy than vanilla decoding** despite lower latency, because the draft model + verification overhead exceeds the energy saved from reduced wall-time ([EACL 2026 Findings](https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-eacl.249.pdf)).
- **Disaggregated Speculative Decoding (DSD)** (Shi et al., IEEE CAL 2025) addresses this by assigning draft models to older GPUs and target models to newer GPUs, requiring only token/probability transfers. The GreenLLM framework built on DSD reduces carbon emissions by up to **40.6%** while meeting latency SLOs ([IEEE CAL 2025](https://www.computer.org/csdl/journal/ca/2025/02/11230830/2bqyKQIVmE0)).
- **Implication:** Speculative decoding is not automatically energy-efficient. The draft model size, acceptance rate, and hardware assignment must be co-optimized for energy, not just latency.

### Model Distillation

Distillation trains a smaller "student" to mimic a larger "teacher," reducing inference cost. Key findings:

- **Puzzle** (Bercovich et al., ICML 2025) uses NAS + blockwise distillation to derive Nemotron-51B from Llama-70B, achieving **2.17× inference throughput speedup** while retaining 98.4% of benchmark accuracy—fitting on a single H100 instead of requiring multi-GPU ([ICML 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/bercovich25a.html)).
- **DistiLLM** (Ko et al., ICML 2024) achieves up to 4.3× speedup over prior KD methods while building high-quality student models ([ICML 2024](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/ko24c.html)).
- **End-to-end energy accounting** (Lambert & Luccioni, ICML 2026) warns that distillation's upstream costs—teacher-side data generation, logit caching, evaluation—can rival or exceed student training energy. Claims of distillation efficiency that omit these costs are unreliable ([arXiv:2605.13981](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13981)).
- **Implication:** Distillation is one of the most impactful approaches for cutting inference energy at scale, but total lifecycle energy (including the distillation process itself) must be measured, not just student inference energy.

### Carbon Arbitrage Risk

A 2026 framework by Luo & Cheng identifies that relaxing inference latency constraints can enable geographic relocation of inference to cheaper, lower-carbon regions, but **migration frictions—egress costs, state locality, legal constraints, capacity limits—can sharply reduce or reverse realized benefits**. A 2026 IEEE study finds that realistic reductions from carbon-aware geographic load shifting are only **~5%**, insufficient to compensate for data center growth ([Vanderbauwhede, arXiv:2509.07043](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07043); [Luo & Cheng, arXiv:2604.27855](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27855)). The risk is "carbon arbitrage"—routing inference to regions with cheaper but dirtier electricity if cost is optimized without carbon constraints.

---

## 9. Practical Measurement Strategies

### Instrumentation

| Tool | What it measures | Granularity |
|------|-----------------|-------------|
| **RAPL** (Intel/AMD) | CPU/GPU package power | Per-code-segment |
| **NVIDIA DCGM** (`dcgmi`) | GPU power, utilization, temperature | Per-GPU, time-series |
| **pyJoules** | Energy of code segments across CPU/GPU | Per-function |
| **CodeCarbon** | Carbon estimates from device power + regional CI | Per-run (lacks prompt-level granularity for APIs) |
| **EcoLogits** | Per-call energy for supported provider SDKs | Per-API-call |
| **Perun framework** | GPU device power consumption with emission conversion | Per-task |

### Estimation Tools

- **emissions.dev LLM API:** Estimates CO₂e from token usage, model tier, provider, grid intensity. Covers 80+ models, includes reasoning model detection and embodied carbon.
- **AI Energy Score / ML.Energy leaderboard:** Standardized benchmarks for per-task energy on consistent hardware.
- **FUEL framework** (Wu et al., ACL 2025): Functional unit-based evaluation comparing models on standardized tasks.
- **LLMCO2** (Fu et al., 2024): GNN-based prediction for inference carbon footprint, accounting for prefill/decode phases.
- **Green Software Foundation SCI for AI** (ISO/IEC 21031:2024 extension): Reference implementation for measuring LLM inference carbon footprint end-to-end, with API cost as complementary lens ([GSF GitHub](https://github.com/Green-Software-Foundation/reference-implementations/tree/main/specifications/sci-for-ai/gsf/llm-inference)).

### What to Measure (Google's full-stack methodology as gold standard)

1. **Per-request energy (Wh):** GPU power × inference time, including host CPU/RAM overhead and PUE.
2. **Sustained utilization (%):** Over 24h windows, not peak. The single most important variable.
3. **Grid carbon intensity** at the time and location of inference (use real-time APIs like Electricity Maps).
4. **Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE):** Both on-site (cooling) and off-site (electricity generation).
5. **Embodied carbon:** Amortize GPU manufacturing emissions over expected lifetime token throughput.
6. **Absolute total consumption:** Not just per-query intensity, to detect Jevons paradox effects.

---

## 10. Practical Reduction Strategies

### Model-Level
1. **Choose the smallest model that meets quality requirements.** Llama 3.1 8B uses ~114 J/answer vs. 6,706 J for 405B—a 59× difference.
2. **Quantize:** INT4/FP8 quantization significantly lowers energy per token. FUEL case studies show quantization is among the most effective levers.
3. **Avoid reasoning models when not needed.** o3 and DeepSeek-R1 consume 70× more than nano models per long prompt.
4. **Use distillation to create smaller, capable models.** Puzzle achieves 2.17× throughput with 98.4% accuracy retention—but measure end-to-end distillation energy, not just student inference.
5. **Prompt caching:** emissions.dev reports 90% energy reduction on cached input tokens.

### Serving-Level
6. **Maximize batch size under latency SLOs.** Batch size 1 wastes 44× more energy per token than saturated batching. Continuous batching (vLLM) is essential.
7. **Use serverless for bursty/low traffic.** More energy-efficient than dedicated GPUs below 22–48% utilization.
8. **Consolidate workloads.** Energy-aware consolidation reduces static GPU power by migrating workloads and powering down unused GPUs (Festina: up to 56% reduction).
9. **Apply DVFS.** Tune GPU operating points based on workload phase and load.
10. **Consider speculative decoding carefully.** DSD with heterogeneous GPU assignment can reduce carbon by up to 40.6%, but naive speculative decoding can increase energy.
11. **Carbon-aware scheduling:** Route inference to regions/times with lower grid carbon intensity—but beware of "carbon arbitrage" to dirty grids and note that realistic geographic shifting yields only ~5% reductions.

### Infrastructure-Level
12. **Choose data centers with low PUE and clean grid.** PUE 1.1 vs. 1.5 means 36% less overhead energy.
13. **Scale-to-zero for non-production workloads.** Eliminates idle power at the cost of cold-start latency.
14. **Monitor and report using full-stack methodology** (active power + host + idle + PUE + WUE). Active-chip-only accounting underestimates by 2–3×.
15. **Track absolute consumption, not just per-query intensity.** Per-query improvements that enable total usage growth (Jevons paradox) yield net increases.
16. **Prepare for regulation.** EU AI Act amendments will likely mandate inference energy disclosure; proactive measurement avoids compliance scrambling.

---

## 11. Summary Comparison Table

| Deployment mode | Energy efficiency | Water efficiency | Utilization profile | Embodied carbon/query | Best for |
|----------------|-------------------|------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|----------|
| **Fixed dedicated GPU** | Poor at <50% util; good at >70% | Same as grid WUE | Steady high traffic only | High at low util | Predictable, high-volume workloads |
| **Autoscaled endpoint** | Moderate; idle replicas waste energy | Same | Variable traffic with floor | Moderate | Production with SLAs |
| **Serverless inference** | Best for bursty/low traffic; multi-tenant sharing | Provider-dependent | Bursty, spiky | Low (amortized) | Startups, variable traffic |
| **External API** | Hyperscaler-optimized; limited transparency | Provider-dependent | Any | Lowest (billions of queries) | Teams without infra; reasoning models |

---

## 12. Key Uncertainties

1. **Provider opacity:** Only Google has published full-stack, production-measured per-prompt figures. OpenAI's 0.34 Wh is a disclosure without methodology. All third-party estimates rely on inferred hardware configurations.
2. **Rapid efficiency improvements:** Google's 33× energy reduction in 12 months means any estimate older than ~6 months may be substantially outdated.
3. **Water estimates are highly location-dependent:** The same model in Norway vs. Texas can vary by 2,000× in water consumption per query.
4. **Embodied carbon is often excluded.** Most per-prompt estimates exclude hardware manufacturing; emissions.dev includes it (0.3 g for a GPT-5.2 query), but most academic studies do not.
5. **Reasoning models are a step-change.** o3 and DeepSeek-R1's 33+ Wh per long prompt represents a new category of energy-intensive inference.
6. **Jevons paradox undermines per-query optimism.** Per-query efficiency gains may increase total consumption if demand is elastic.
7. **Regulatory landscape is evolving.** EU AI Act currently omits inference energy; amendments are under discussion.

RECOMMENDATION: 7. Use serverless inference or external APIs for bursty workloads, choose the smallest quantized model that meets quality needs, and measure full-stack energy with RAPL/DCGM plus real-time grid carbon intensity to enable carbon-aware routing and workload consolidation.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Provider opacity and Jevons paradox effects mean per-query efficiency gains may not translate to net environmental reductions, so continuous full-stack measurement of absolute consumption rather than one-time per-query calculation is essential.

## Analysis

**The bottleneck is prefill, not decode.** With a 60,000-token shared prefix and an average output of only 200 tokens, roughly 99% of the computation before the first token is spent processing the repository prefix. Since time-to-first-token (TTFT) is the sole complaint, the optimization must reduce prefill latency — not generation speed.

**Prefix caching is the textbook fit.** It stores the computed KV-cache for the shared prefix so that subsequent requests reusing that prefix skip re-processing all 60,000 tokens, collapsing prefill to just the short user-specific suffix. The workload has three properties that make this maximally effective:

1. **High prefix reuse** — 80% of requests hit the same repository revision within a five-minute window, so cache-hit rates will be very high under steady traffic.
2. **Large, stable prefix** — the 60k-token prefix is identical across requests, meaning a cache hit eliminates nearly all prefill work.
3. **Short variable suffix** — the user-specific request is tiny, so after a cache hit only a few hundred tokens need prefill.

**Why the other options are inferior:**

- **Prompt-compression (2)** reduces prefill cost but discards information from the repository context and still recomputes the (slightly smaller) prefix every request. Caching eliminates far more prefill work with zero information loss.
- **Smaller-long-context-model (3)** lowers per-token prefill cost but sacrifices quality and still recomputes the full 60k prefix each time.
- **Speculative-decoding (4)** accelerates the *decode* phase (time per output token), not prefill. With only 200 output tokens and TTFT as the sole complaint, this doesn't address the bottleneck.
- **Repository-RAG (5)** replaces the full prefix with retrieved chunks, risking missed cross-file dependencies, and still requires prefill of retrieved chunks on every request — without leveraging the high temporal locality nearly as effectively.

**Top risk and practical caveat:** A 60,000-token KV cache is memory-heavy. If GPU HBM cannot retain the cached prefix alongside concurrent decode batches, eviction will push effective hit rates below the naive 80% estimate, partially diluting the TTFT improvement. In practice this is manageable by sizing cache capacity to the expected working set (a handful of hot revisions) and using block-granular caching — but a single differing token early in the prefix invalidates all subsequent cached blocks, so the prefix must be byte-identical (including any system prompt, formatting, or metadata) for a hit.

RECOMMENDATION: 1. prefix-caching
CONFIDENCE: high
TOP_RISK: The 60,000-token KV cache may be evicted under GPU memory pressure, pushing effective hit rates below the expected 80% and diluting TTFT improvement.

# Legal and Policy Landscape: Copyrighted Material in Generative-AI Training and Retrieval Systems (US & EU)

*This analysis is informational only and is not legal advice. Statutes, court rulings, and regulatory materials are current as of the dates cited; the landscape is evolving rapidly.*

---

## 1. United States

### 1.1 Statutory and Regulatory Baseline

**Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 106):** The exclusive rights of reproduction, derivative works, distribution, public performance, and display are prima facie implicated when copyrighted works are copied to train AI models. There is no specialized statutory exception for AI training; the general fair use doctrine (17 U.S.C. § 107) governs, applying a four-factor balancing test: (1) purpose and character of the use (including transformativeness and commerciality), (2) nature of the copyrighted work, (3) amount and substantiality used, and (4) effect on the potential market for or value of the original.

**DMCA § 1202 (CMI removal):** Actionable where a defendant intentionally removes copyright management information and distributes works knowing it will induce or conceal infringement. Plaintiffs are actively testing this theory in news-content cases (e.g., *NYT v. OpenAI*).

**US Copyright Office AI Report, Part 3 (pre-publication, May 9, 2025):** Nonbinding but influential. Key conclusions:
- Use of copyrighted works for AI training constitutes prima facie infringement.
- Fair use is "a matter of degree"; models trained to produce content sharing the original's audience appeal are at best modestly transformative.
- The "human learning analogy" (i.e., comparing LLM training to a student reading books) is "mistaken" as a blanket defense.
- Guardrails against infringing outputs weigh in favor of fair use.
- Knowing use of pirated or illegal sources weighs against fair use.
- The Office does not currently recommend new compulsory licensing but discusses voluntary and statutory licensing models.
- RAG/retrieval systems are addressed separately from training and involve ongoing copying that may require an independent fair use analysis. Where RAG systems summarize copyrighted works rather than providing hyperlinks to original sources, outputs are less likely to be considered transformative.

### 1.2 Major Court Developments

**Bartz v. Anthropic, No. C 24-05417 WHA (N.D. Cal. June 23, 2025):** Judge Alsup held Anthropic's LLM training on lawfully purchased books was "exceedingly transformative" fair use; digitization of purchased print books to enable search/storage was also fair use. However, use of pirated copies from Library Genesis (LibGen), Books3, and Pirate Library Mirror (PiLiMi) was "inherently, irredeemably infringing" and not fair use. The court found Anthropic downloaded over seven million pirated books, with CEO Dario Amodei acknowledging the preference to "steal" books to avoid "legal/practice/business slog." Piracy claims proceeded to trial.

**Settlement (preliminarily approved September 25, 2025):** Anthropic agreed to pay approximately **$1.5 billion** — about $3,000 per book for an estimated 500,000 works downloaded from piracy sites. Judge Alsup called the settlement "fair." The release covers only past acquisition, retention, and use for training; it does not cover future conduct or infringing outputs. Anthropic also agreed to destroy datasets containing the allegedly pirated material. This is believed to be the largest copyright recovery in history.

**Kadrey v. Meta, No. 23-cv-03417 VC (N.D. Cal. June 25, 2025):** Judge Chhabria granted summary judgment for Meta on fair use for training on plaintiffs' books (including from shadow libraries), finding the use "highly transformative." However, he emphasized the ruling was narrow and fact-specific. Critically, he warned that "in most cases" involving Meta-style training without permission, "the answer will likely be yes" — i.e., infringement — if plaintiffs develop a proper record on market harm. He introduced the concept of "indirect market substitution": LLMs can flood markets with substitute content even without verbatim reproduction of specific works, potentially dramatically undermining the incentive for human creation. The case continues on BitTorrent "seeding" (distribution) claims. Notably, the court revealed that Meta's head of generative AI discussed spending up to $100 million on licensing but abandoned the effort because publishers generally do not hold subsidiary rights to license books for AI training and no collective licensing organization exists.

**New York Times Co. v. Microsoft/OpenAI, No. 23-cv-11195 (SHS) (S.D.N.Y. 2025):** Judge Stein allowed core direct infringement and contributory infringement claims to proceed; dismissed "hot news" misappropriation claims; partially allowed DMCA § 1202(b)(1) CMI removal claims (Daily News and Center for Investigative Reporting, not NYT on CMI specifics). OpenAI's statute-of-limitations defense rejected.

**Other developments:** Record label cases (UMG v. Udio settled October 2025 with licensing component); visual arts cases (*Andersen v. Stability AI*; *Getty v. Stability AI* resolved with licensing); numerous settlements in 2025 signal a trend toward licensing plus settlement.

### 1.3 Provider Policies and Market Signals

- **OpenAI:** Publicly argues fair use and TDM exceptions are "critical" to training; told the White House (March 2025) that restricting access to copyrighted data would cause the US to "forfeit" the AI race to China. Simultaneously pursuing major licensing deals: News Corp deal valued at over $250 million over five years (May 2024), plus agreements with AP, Financial Times, Dotdash Meredith, Axel Springer, Reddit, and others.
- **Google:** Similar fair use position; offers two-pronged customer indemnity covering both training data and generated output.
- **Anthropic:** Updated consumer terms (August 2025) allowing use of Free/Pro/Max conversations for training unless user opts out; commercial/API/enterprise terms exclude training use by default.

### 1.4 Settled vs. Unresolved in the US

**Relatively settled:**
- Unauthorized copying for training is prima facie infringement (reproduction right implicated).
- Use of pirated sources weighs heavily against fair use (*Bartz*, Copyright Office).
- Fair use is fact-specific and requires case-by-case analysis.
- DMCA § 1202 claims can survive motion to dismiss where CMI removal is plausibly intentional.
- Training on lawfully purchased/acquired books can constitute fair use where outputs do not reproduce protected expression (*Bartz*).

**Unresolved:**
- Whether LLM training generally is fair use — neither *Bartz* nor *Kadrey* resolved this broadly; both are district court decisions subject to Ninth Circuit appeal.
- How "indirect market substitution" (*Kadrey*) will be weighed in Factor Four — the concept that LLMs can flood markets with substitute content even without verbatim output.
- Whether model weights themselves can be infringing (Copyright Office notes a "strong argument" where outputs are substantially similar).
- Scope of contributory infringement for user-generated infringing outputs.
- Whether training on lawfully accessed web content (not pirated) is fair use — the central question in *NYT* and similar cases.
- Status of RAG/retrieval systems as distinct from training — USCO Part 3 addresses RAG separately, noting it involves ongoing copying that may require its own fair use analysis; courts have not squarely addressed RAG.
- State-level legislation (e.g., Tennessee's ELVIS Act, California AI transparency measures) may create additional compliance layers.

---

## 2. European Union

### 2.1 Statutory Framework

**Copyright in the Digital Single Market (CDSM) Directive (EU) 2019/790:**
- **Article 3:** Mandatory TDM exception for scientific research (research organizations and cultural heritage institutions); no opt-out.
- **Article 4:** General TDM exception for "lawfully accessible works" for any purpose, subject to a rightsholder opt-out. The exception applies "on condition that the use…has not been expressly reserved by their rightsholders in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means in the case of content made publicly available online" (Article 4(3)).
- **Article 15:** Press publishers' related rights — protects "very short extracts" beyond individual words, relevant to AI outputs that reproduce portions of press content.

**AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), in force August 1, 2024; GPAI provisions applicable from August 2, 2025:**
- **Article 53(1)(c):** GPAI providers must put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, in particular to identify and comply with opt-outs expressed under Article 4(3) CDSM, "including through state of the art technologies."
- **Article 53(1)(d):** GPAI providers must draw up and make publicly available a "sufficiently detailed summary" of training content, using a template provided by the AI Office.
- **Article 53(2):** Open-source GPAI models are mostly exempted, but the transparency/training-summary obligation still applies.
- **Article 55:** Additional obligations for GPAI models with systemic risk (model evaluations, risk mitigation, incident reporting).
- **Recital 107:** Summary should balance transparency for rightsholders with protection of trade secrets.

### 2.2 Regulatory Guidance and Templates

**AI Office GPAI Code of Practice (July 2025):** Voluntary compliance mechanism; adherence can provide presumption of compliance with Article 53 obligations.

**Training Content Summary Template (July 24, 2025):** Mandatory format with three sections:
1. General information (model identity, modalities, training data size, languages).
2. Data sources (web crawling, licensed datasets, user data, synthetic data, etc.).
3. Processing and governance (provenance, opt-out compliance, retention, copyright, removal of illegal content, data protection).

Updates required every six months for material changes. **Transitional deadline:** Existing models have until August 2, 2027 to comply. New models placed on the market after August 2, 2025 must comply immediately.

**Guidelines on Scope (July 18, 2025):** Establish indicative criterion that a model is considered GPAI when training compute exceeds 10²³ FLOP and it can generate language, text-to-image, or text-to-video. Non-EU providers are subject to obligations when a GPAI model is "placed on the market" in the EU, including through integration into apps or AI systems.

**European Parliament JURI Committee Study (July 2025):** Identifies structural mismatch between AI training and TDM exceptions; calls for input/output distinction, harmonized opt-out, transparency, and equitable licensing models. The Parliament's June 2025 motion for a resolution (2025/2058(INI)) calls for clearer provisions or a dedicated exception for generative AI training.

### 2.3 Key Pending Litigation: CJEU Case C-250/25

**Like Company v. Google Ireland (C-250/25):** Lodged April 3, 2025, by the Budapest District Court — the first case to bring generative AI before the CJEU. A Hungarian press publisher alleges Google's Gemini chatbot reproduced substantial portions of its copyrighted articles. Four preliminary questions:
1. Does display of text partially identical to press content in chatbot responses constitute "communication to the public" under Article 15 CDSM and Article 3(2) InfoSoc?
2. Does LLM training constitute "reproduction" under Article 2 InfoSoc?
3. If so, does it fall within the Article 4 TDM exception?
4. Can reproduction of press content by a chatbot in response to user prompts be attributed to the chatbot provider?

This case could fundamentally reshape the EU analysis. Academic commentary (e.g., Dornis & Stober 2025 in *IIC*) argues that AI model training may involve reproduction under Article 2 InfoSoc, while dissemination of AI-generated outputs may trigger communication to the public under Article 3, particularly when protected content is recognizably reproduced or outputs serve as functional substitutes.

### 2.4 Interpretive Uncertainties

- **Does Article 4 CDSM cover generative AI training?** The directive defines TDM as "automated analytical technique aimed at analysing text and data…to generate information which includes but is not limited to patterns, trends and correlations." Whether model training falls within this or is a different activity is contested.
- **What counts as "machine-readable" opt-out?** The German LAION case (under appeal to BGH) and Hamburg court approach suggest opt-outs must be "machine-actionable" — automatically detectable and executable. The European Commission launched a consultation in 2025 to move from "machine-readable" to verifiable, interoperable signals.
- **Territorial scope of Article 53(1)(c):** Whether non-EU providers must comply with EU opt-out signals when training outside the EU but placing models on the EU market — the Guidelines indicate yes, but enforceability remains uncertain.
- **Pre-release obligations:** Whether Article 53 applies to training conducted before August 2, 2025, or only to models placed on the market after that date.
- **Intersection with GDPR:** Training data containing personal information creates dual compliance obligations under both copyright and data protection law.

### 2.5 Settled vs. Unresolved in the EU

**Relatively settled:**
- EU has a statutory TDM exception with a rightsholder opt-out (Article 4 CDSM).
- GPAI providers placing models on the EU market must comply with Article 53 transparency and copyright-policy obligations from August 2, 2025.
- A training-content summary must be published using the AI Office template.
- Scientific research TDM (Article 3) has no opt-out and is mandatory.
- Open-source models are not exempt from the training-summary obligation.

**Unresolved:**
- Whether generative AI training qualifies as "TDM" under Article 4 (pending C-250/25).
- Technical standard for a valid opt-out (machine-readable vs. machine-actionable).
- Territorial and temporal scope of Article 53 obligations.
- Whether Member States can impose additional copyright requirements beyond CDSM/AI Act (maximal harmonization debates).
- Whether EU copyright protects AI-generated content (no authorship without human creativity per *Infopaq* and *Painer*, but ownership/related rights are contested).
- Practical enforceability of Article 53 for non-EU providers — how the AI Office can compel compliance from providers outside the EU who place models on the EU market through API access.

---

## 3. Implications: Model Developers vs. Enterprise Users

### Model Developers

**US:** Face direct infringement liability for training copies; fair use is the primary defense but is fact-specific. Pirated source use has generated multi-billion-dollar exposure (Anthropic's $1.5B settlement). Should expect licensing demands, litigation, and potential statutory damages ($750–$30,000 per work, up to $150,000 for willful infringement). The *Kadrey* court's "indirect market substitution" theory means even non-verbatim outputs can trigger Factor Four harm if they flood markets with substitute content. The emerging secondary market for AI training data licenses (e.g., OpenAI–News Corp deal at $250M+ over five years, Shutterstock, Financial Times, AP, Axel Springer) signals growing pricing norms for voluntary licensing.

**EU:** Must implement Article 53 policies and publish training summaries from August 2, 2025 (transitional deadline August 2, 2027 for existing models). Must honor Article 4(3) opt-outs using "state of the art" technologies. Noncompliance risks administrative fines, market withdrawal, and civil copyright claims. Need to track evolving opt-out standards and CJEU guidance from C-250/25. The practical enforceability against non-EU providers remains an open question, but the Guidelines indicate that placing a model on the EU market (including through API integration) triggers obligations.

### Enterprise Users (Deployers)

**US:** Generally not direct training infringers, but face:
- **Output liability risk:** If prompts elicit infringing outputs, users may be direct infringers; developers may be contributorily liable (*NYT v. OpenAI* allowed contributory claims to proceed).
- **RAG/retrieval risk:** Enterprise RAG systems that reproduce copyrighted content in responses may infringe independent of training; USCO treats RAG as a separate use requiring its own analysis. Where RAG systems summarize rather than link to originals, outputs are less likely to be transformative.
- **Indemnity reliance:** Provider indemnity programs have significant carve-outs:
  - **OpenAI ("Copyright Shield"):** Excludes claims where customer knew or should have known output was infringing; where customer disabled filtering/safety features; where output was modified or combined with non-OpenAI products; where customer lacked rights to input; and trademark claims.
  - **Microsoft ("Customer Copyright Commitment"):** Requires customers to implement all required mitigations specified in Azure OpenAI documentation; excludes modified outputs and requires use of configured safety systems.
  - **Google Cloud:** Two-pronged indemnity covering both training data and generated output.
  - **Anthropic:** Expanded copyright indemnity for authorized use of services and outputs (January 2024).

**EU:** Enterprise deployers of high-risk AI systems have separate Article 26 obligations, but copyright liability for outputs is governed by general EU/national copyright law. Deployers should verify provider compliance with Article 53 summaries and opt-out policies, since downstream liability may attach if providers used infringing training data. The C-250/25 case may clarify whether chatbot outputs that reproduce press content trigger communication-to-the-public liability for the provider.

---

## 4. Conservative Compliance Approach (Not Legal Advice)

### For Model Developers

1. **Source hygiene:** Avoid pirated or "shadow library" sources (LibGen, PiLiMi, Books3). Use lawfully purchased, licensed, or clearly public-domain/CC-licensed content. Document provenance meticulously. The *Bartz* settlement price (~$3,000/work for ~500,000 works) provides a reference point for piracy exposure.

2. **Opt-out compliance (EU):** Implement a robust, documented system to detect and honor Article 4(3) CDSM opt-outs, including machine-readable signals (e.g., TDMRep, robots.txt with TDM directives, structured metadata). Track evolving "machine-actionable" standards and Commission guidance. Document the "state of the art" technologies used.

3. **Training content summaries (EU):** Prepare and publish Article 53(1)(d) summaries using the AI Office template; update every six months for material changes. For existing models, transitional compliance deadline is August 2, 2027. Include data sources, processing methods, opt-out compliance measures, and copyright/data protection governance.

4. **Guardrails and output filtering:** Implement technical measures to prevent near-verbatim or substantially similar outputs of training works; document these measures (weighs toward fair use under USCO analysis and supports transformativeness arguments). Configure RAG systems to summarize and cite rather than extract verbatim.

5. **Licensing where feasible:** Enter voluntary licensing deals for high-value or clearly protected content (news, books, music, stock images). The OpenAI–News Corp deal ($250M+ over five years) and other publisher deals signal growing market norms. Consider collective or extended collective licensing mechanisms where available — though the *Kadrey* court noted the current absence of collective licensing organizations for book authors' AI training rights.

6. **Data minimization and retention limits:** Retain training copies only as long as necessary; avoid permanent "digital libraries" of questionable provenance (*Bartz* distinguished lawful purchase-digitization from piracy retention).

7. **Contractual protections:** Provide customer indemnities only where source hygiene and output controls are robust; exclude liability for customer-directed prompts that reproduce works.

8. **US litigation readiness:** Assume training-copy infringement as a baseline; preserve evidence of transformative purpose, market analysis, guardrails, and licensing efforts. Anticipate Ninth Circuit appeals of *Bartz* and *Kadrey*.

### For Enterprise Users

1. **Provider due diligence:** Require representations/warranties that training data was lawfully sourced and EU Article 53-compliant; request training summaries; verify indemnity scope and carve-outs.

2. **Output controls:** Configure RAG/retrieval systems to avoid verbatim or near-verbatim reproduction of source documents; use summarization and citation rather than extraction. The USCO specifically flags that RAG outputs that summarize rather than link are less likely to be transformative.

3. **Prompt governance:** Prohibit prompts that request reproduction of specific copyrighted works (lyrics, book chapters, articles); log and monitor high-risk prompts. Note that provider indemnities typically exclude claims where the customer knew or should have known output was infringing.

4. **Indemnity understanding:** Review provider indemnity terms carefully — most exclude willful customer misuse, unmodified model outputs only, disallowed prompts, and outputs combined with non-provider products. Microsoft requires implementation of all specified mitigations; OpenAI excludes modified or combined outputs.

5. **EU deployment documentation:** For high-risk or GPAI deployments, maintain Article 26 compliance records; verify provider conformity documentation and Article 53 summaries.

6. **Jurisdictional scoping:** For EU deployments, ensure provider compliance with Article 53 and CDSM opt-out regime; for US deployments, prioritize indemnity scope and output-liability allocations.

7. **Insurance:** Consider dedicated IP/media liability insurance covering AI-output infringement claims.

8. **Monitor C-250/25:** The CJEU's ruling in *Like Company v. Google Ireland* could reshape both training and output liability in the EU; maintain adaptability in compliance programs.

---

## 5. Key Caveats

- **No appellate precedent yet** on fair use for AI training in the US; both *Bartz* and *Kadrey* are district court decisions subject to Ninth Circuit review.
- **The Anthropic settlement** is not precedential on liability but signals pricing for piracy exposure (~$3,000/work).
- **CJEU C-250/25** could fundamentally reshape the EU analysis; compliance programs should be adaptable.
- **Opt-out technical standards** remain in flux; the EU Commission consultation and BGH review of LAION may change expectations.
- **RAG vs. training** is analytically distinct; most case law addresses training, not retrieval-augmented output. USCO Part 3 flags RAG separately but courts have not addressed it squarely.
- **Model weights as infringing** remains a contested theory; USCO finds a "strong argument" where outputs are substantially similar.
- **Collective licensing infrastructure** is absent for many content types — the *Kadrey* court noted no organization exists for collective licensing of book authors' AI training rights, creating a structural barrier to large-scale licensing.
- **State-level US legislation** (e.g., Tennessee's ELVIS Act, California AI transparency measures) may create additional compliance layers not addressed in federal copyright law.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 1 — Adopt a conservative, documented compliance program combining lawful sourcing, EU Article 53 transparency, opt-out honoring, output guardrails, licensing where feasible, and jurisdictional due diligence, while treating this as risk mitigation rather than a guarantee of non-liability.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Courts or regulators may determine that training on copyrighted works without a license is infringement where market harm or output substitution is shown, exposing developers to substantial damages and enterprise users to output-liability and indemnity-gap risk.

# Copyright in Generative-AI Training and Retrieval Systems: United States and European Union

*This analysis is informational only and does not constitute legal advice. The legal landscape is evolving rapidly through litigation, regulatory guidance, and legislative action.*

---

## 1. United States

### 1.1 Statutory Framework

**Exclusive Rights (17 U.S.C. § 106)**: Unauthorized reproduction, distribution, public display, performance, or creation of derivative works constitutes *prima facie* infringement. Copying copyrighted works to build training datasets, create retrieval indices, or generate outputs triggers these rights unless an exception applies. This baseline is **settled**.

**Fair Use (17 U.S.C. § 107)**: The primary defense invoked by AI developers. Courts weigh four factors: (1) purpose and character of the use, including transformativeness and commerciality; (2) nature of the copyrighted work; (3) amount and substantiality used; (4) effect on the potential market. Application to GenAI training is **fact-intensive and unresolved at the appellate level**.

**DMCA § 1202**: Prohibits intentional removal or alteration of copyright management information (CMI). Plaintiffs increasingly allege that stripping metadata from training corpora violates § 1202(b)(1). Courts have allowed these claims to proceed in several cases.

**No statutory text-and-data-mining exception**: Unlike the EU, US copyright law provides no TDM exception. Fair use is the sole statutory defense (alongside licensing).

### 1.2 US Copyright Office Guidance

The Copyright Office released Part 3 of its AI report in pre-publication form on May 9, 2025. While not binding law, it is influential and cited by courts and Congress.

Key positions:
- Data collection, training, and RAG all "implicate the right of reproduction" and may constitute *prima facie* infringement.
- Fair-use transformativeness is "a matter of degree"; training to produce content competing for the same audience is "at best, modestly transformative."
- The human-learning analogy is "mistaken"; AI creates "perfect copies" with near-instant analysis.
- Use of guardrails weighs *in favor* of fair use; knowing use of pirated/illegal sources weighs *against*.
- Model weights *may* embed reproductions where outputs are substantially similar—a "strong argument" that weights themselves infringe in some cases.
- The Office declined to recommend a statutory licensing regime, citing the early state of voluntary licensing markets.

Part 2 (January 29, 2025) confirmed that purely AI-generated outputs are not copyrightable; human authorship is required for registration.

### 1.3 Major Court Developments

**Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence (D. Del., Feb. 11, 2025)**
Judge Bibas reversed his prior 2023 order and granted Thomson Reuters summary judgment on fair use, holding Ross's use of Westlaw headnotes to train a competing legal-research AI was *not* fair use. The court found Ross's use was commercial and non-transformative, and that it caused market harm by building a direct competitor. This is the **first major ruling against an AI trainer on fair use**, though its scope is narrowed by the specific facts: direct competitor, small curated dataset, non-generative output. Issues regarding other headnotes and the Key Number System remain for trial.

**Bartz v. Anthropic (N.D. Cal., June 23, 2025)**
Judge Alsup held Anthropic's use of lawfully purchased books to train Claude was "quintessentially transformative" fair use, analogizing to a reader aspiring to be a writer. No infringing outputs were alleged. Print-to-digital conversion of lawfully bought books was also fair use. However, downloading millions of books from "shadow libraries" (pirated sources like Books3) was *not* fair use; summary judgment was denied on those copies, with willfulness left for trial. The case subsequently settled, with reports indicating Anthropic agreed to pay up to approximately $1.5 billion.

**Kadrey v. Meta (N.D. Cal., June 25, 2025)**
Judge Chhabria granted Meta's cross-motion for partial summary judgment on fair use for training Llama on copyrighted books, including shadow-library copies. Training was found "highly transformative"—extracting statistical patterns differs from books' purpose of being read. Unlike *Bartz*, the court treated shadow-library downloads together with training as a single fair-use analysis. However, the opinion contains stark warnings: "in most cases the answer will likely be yes" (infringement), because GenAI can "dramatically undermine the market" for human-created works. The court noted that future litigants presenting stronger evidence of market impacts could reach different results. DMCA claims were also rejected, with the court holding fair use is a full defense to infringement.

**New York Times Co. v. Microsoft/OpenAI (S.D.N.Y., April 4, 2025)**
Judge Stein denied most of OpenAI/Microsoft's motion to dismiss. Direct infringement, contributory infringement, and DMCA § 1202 claims (for Daily News and Center for Investigative Reporting) survive. The court found contributory infringement plausibly alleged—OpenAI had reason to know ChatGPT could reproduce articles and skirt paywalls. "Hot news" misappropriation claims were dismissed; CIR's abridgement claim was rejected for lack of substantial similarity. This case is heading toward discovery and potentially trial, and could establish precedent on both training-copying and output-liability theories.

**Dow Jones & Co. v. Perplexity (S.D.N.Y., Aug. 21, 2025)**
Judge Failla denied Perplexity's motion to dismiss/transfer. Critically, she framed **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) itself as the mechanism of infringement**: copying works into a retrieval index and "repackaging" them in answers. The court recognized infringement theories on both input (copying into RAG index) and output (verbatim/substitutive reproductions) ends, plus trademark misattribution/hallucination claims. This signals that RAG systems face **distinct, potentially aggravated liability** beyond training-only claims.

**Advanced Local Media LLC v. Cohere (S.D.N.Y., Nov. 13, 2025)**
Judge McMahon denied Cohere's motion to dismiss. News publishers plausibly stated direct infringement claims, including for "substitutive summaries" generated by Cohere's RAG-enabled Command models—even where verbatim copying was not alleged. Secondary infringement (inducement/contributory) and trademark claims based on hallucinated articles bearing publisher marks also survived. Key holding: "substitutive summaries" can infringe at the pleading stage; RAG retrieval of paywalled/site content is actionable.

**Summary of US case trajectory:**
- District courts are splitting on fair use, but common themes are emerging:
  - Training *can* be transformative fair use where outputs do not substitute and sources are lawful (*Bartz*).
  - Use of pirated/shadow-library sources is a major vulnerability (*Bartz*; Copyright Office Part 3).
  - RAG raises separate and potentially broader infringement exposure than training (*Perplexity*, *Cohere*).
  - Output-side infringement (verbatim, near-verbatim, substitutive summaries, hallucinated attributions) is increasingly viable (*NYT*, *Cohere*).
  - Direct competitor scenarios are highly unfavorable for fair use (*Thomson Reuters*).
- No appellate decision yet; Ninth Circuit appeals in *Bartz* and *Kadrey* are likely. Supreme Court guidance is unlikely before 2026–2027.

### 1.4 Provider Policies and Positions (US)

- **OpenAI**: Public position that fair-use access to copyrighted data is "a matter of national security"; has licensing deals with several publishers; offers IP indemnification to enterprise customers ("Customer Copyright Commitment") subject to conditions (use within scope, no known-likely infringement, no tampering with safety systems).
- **Anthropic**: Did not press a copyright-policy ask in its March 2025 submission; commercial terms state Anthropic will not train on customer content and assigns output rights to customer. Settled *Bartz* for substantial sum, signaling cost of pirated-source exposure.
- **Microsoft**: "Customer Copyright Commitment" extends IP indemnity to Copilot and Azure OpenAI outputs *if* the customer implements required guardrails/metaprompts and uses services unmodified and within scope.
- **Google Cloud**: Two-prong indemnity (training data and generated output) covering allegations that training data use infringes, and that generated output infringes.

Common features: indemnities are conditional, often exclude trademark and DMCA § 1202 claims, and require customers to use built-in filters/guardrails. Enterprise customers should not assume blanket protection.

---

## 2. European Union

### 2.1 Statutory Framework

**Copyright Directive (Directive (EU) 2019/790, "DSM Directive")**
- **Article 3**: Mandatory TDM exception for research organizations and cultural heritage institutions.
- **Article 4**: Broader TDM exception for any purpose, subject to (i) lawful access and (ii) **opt-out**: rights holders may "expressly reserve" their rights "in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means in the case of content made publicly available online" (Art. 4(3)). Recital 18 confirms TDM covers AI development. Therefore, in the EU, training on copyrighted content without consent is permitted *unless* the rightsholder has opted out *and* the provider had lawful access.

**AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)** — GPAI provisions in force **August 2, 2025**:
- **Article 53(1)(c)**: GPAI model providers placing models on the EU market must put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, "in particular to identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, a reservation of rights expressed by rightsholders pursuant to Article 4(3)" DSM Directive.
- **Article 53(1)(d)**: Providers must publish a "sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training" using the AI Office template, to enable rightsholders to exercise rights.
- **Article 55**: Additional obligations for "systemic-risk" GPAI models (notably those with ≥10^25 FLOP training compute).
- **Extraterritorial reach**: Applies to any GPAI model "placed on the EU market," regardless of where the copyright-relevant acts occurred. Guidelines indicate a model is placed on the EU market when integrated into apps/systems made available there.

**InfoSoc Directive (2001/29/EC)**: Exclusive rights (reproduction, communication to the public, making available) remain the baseline; TDM exceptions carve into them.

**Database Directive (96/9/EC) sui generis right**: May apply to substantial extractions from databases; relevant for structured/crawled corpora.

### 2.2 Regulatory Guidance and Code of Practice

- **AI Office Guidelines on GPAI scope (July 18, 2025)**: Non-binding but enforcement-informing. Indicative GPAI threshold: training compute > 10^23 FLOP for language/text-to-image/text-to-video. "Lifecycle" begins at large pre-training; downstream significant modifications may create a new provider.
- **Template for public summary of training content (July 24, 2025)**: Three sections—(1) general information; (2) list of data sources (including crawlers, top 10% of scraped domains, datasets, user and synthetic data); (3) data processing aspects (opt-out compliance, removal of illegal content). Covers pre-training through post-training; does *not* cover operational/RAG data unless the model actively learns from it.
- **GPAI Code of Practice (July 10, 2025) — Copyright Chapter**: Co-regulatory instrument drafted by independent experts. Key commitments:
  - **Commitment 1**: Adopt and maintain a forward-looking copyright policy, including classification of data sources and measures to identify and comply with Article 4(3) opt-outs.
  - **Commitment 2**: Implement state-of-the-art technologies to identify opt-outs (e.g., robots.txt, metadata, terms-of-service signals).
  - Adherence to the Code does not constitute conclusive compliance but is a way to demonstrate it; 26 GPAI providers had signed as of late 2025.

### 2.3 Open Questions in the EU

- **Lawful access scope**: What counts as "lawful access" for web-scraped content—is access via a public webpage enough, or must the scraper respect paywalls, CAPTCHAs, and terms of service? No CJEU ruling yet; the Hamburg Regional Court's *LAION v. Kneschke* decision is the only direct ruling, and the forthcoming *GEMA v. OpenAI* decision from Munich may provide further guidance.
- **Opt-out modalities**: What is "appropriate" reservation—robots.txt, meta tags, TOS clauses, or all of the above? Consensus is emerging (the Code expects multiple signals) but no CJEU ruling yet.
- **Retroactivity**: Article 53(1)(c) applies to models placed on the EU market after August 2, 2025; treatment of pre-existing models already in distribution is contested.
- **Extraterritoriality**: Non-EU providers whose models are integrated into EU-deployed systems are covered; how aggressively the AI Office will enforce against non-EU upstream providers is uncertain.
- **Trade-secret tension**: The training-summary template balances transparency against trade secrets; the level of detail required is contested.
- **RAG and operational data**: The template expressly excludes operational/RAG data unless the model "actively learns" from it—but what counts as active learning is undefined.

---

## 3. Settled vs. Unresolved Questions

| Issue | United States | European Union |
|---|---|---|
| Copying copyrighted works without consent is *prima facie* infringement | **Settled** | **Settled** (exclusive rights; exception only via TDM Art. 4) |
| Training can in principle be fair use / TDM exception | Defense available; outcomes fact-specific and split | **Largely settled** for training (conditional on lawful access + no opt-out) |
| Knowing use of pirated/shadow-library sources is high-risk | **Strongly indicated** (*Bartz*; Copyright Office Part 3) | Lawful access requirement effectively bars pirated sources |
| Outputs that reproduce/substantially similar to training works infringe | **Settled in principle** (*NYT*, *Cohere*) | **Settled in principle** (Art. 2 InfoSoc reproduction; making available) |
| RAG creates distinct copying acts | **Increasingly recognized** (*Perplexity*, *Cohere*) | Template excludes operational RAG from training-summary duty, but copyright exclusive rights still apply to RAG reproductions |
| DMCA § 1202 CMI-stripping claims | Viable (*NYT*, *Cohere*)—case-specific | No direct equivalent; related moral-rights regimes vary by Member State |
| Whether model weights themselves infringe | **Disputed**; Copyright Office says "strong argument" in some cases | Open; not yet litigated at CJEU |
| Categorical fair use / TDM exception for training | **Unresolved** (split district court decisions; no appellate ruling) | **Largely resolved** for training (conditional); RAG and fine-tuning less clear |
| Inducement/contributory liability for AI providers | Viable at pleading stage (*NYT*, *Cohere*) | Less developed; possible under national implementations of Enforcement Directive |
| Extraterritorial reach of obligations | Case-by-case (personal jurisdiction) | **Settled** in AI Act text; enforcement uncertain |
| Training-summary transparency duty | No federal requirement | **Settled** (Art. 53(1)(d), template effective Aug. 2025) |
| Opt-out/reservation compliance duty | No federal opt-out regime (contractual only) | **Settled** (Art. 53(1)(c) + Art. 4(3) DSM) |

---

## 4. Implications for Model Developers vs. Enterprise Users

### 4.1 Model Developers

**US exposure**: Developers face the highest litigation risk. Key vulnerabilities include:
- Use of pirated/shadow-library sources (the *Bartz* settlement suggests massive settlement value).
- Outputs that substitute for or reproduce training works.
- RAG systems that copy and republish source content.
- DMCA § 1202 claims for CMI stripping.
- Contributory/inducement liability for user misuses the provider reasonably anticipated.

**EU exposure**: Developers must implement (i) a copyright compliance policy, (ii) state-of-the-art opt-out identification technologies, (iii) public training-data summaries via the AI Office template, (iv) lawful-access controls, (v) systemic-risk obligations if applicable. Non-compliance risks AI Office enforcement and Member State penalties.

**Cross-border**: A model trained lawfully in the US may still be non-compliant if placed on the EU market without opt-out compliance and training summaries. The extraterritorial reach of the AI Act means non-EU providers are not insulated.

### 4.2 Enterprise Users / Deployers

**US exposure**: Direct infringement risk for outputs they generate, publish, or distribute; secondary risk if they configure/promote systems to produce infringing outputs. Provider indemnities help but are conditional (must use guardrails, stay within scope, not knowingly induce infringement; trademark and DMCA claims typically excluded).

**EU exposure**: Less direct training liability (the GPAI provider bears Art. 53 duties), but deployers of high-risk AI systems have separate AI Act obligations. Deployers using RAG over third-party content still face copyright exposure for reproductions and communications to the public.

**Procurement considerations**: Enterprise users should verify:
- Provider indemnity scope and exclusions.
- Whether provider has a copyright compliance policy and opt-out process (EU Art. 53(1)(c)).
- Whether provider has published a training summary (EU Art. 53(1)(d)).
- Guardrail/filter requirements to maintain indemnity.
- RAG data source provenance and licensing.

---

## 5. Commentary Representing Multiple Perspectives

**AI developer perspective**: Without broad fair-use access (US) or a functioning TDM exception (EU), the volume and diversity of content necessary for cutting-edge models is practically impossible to license individually. Licensing markets are nascent; requiring blanket licensing would throttle a transformative technology and disadvantage US/EU innovation globally. The *Bartz* and *Kadrey* courts recognized transformative purpose; the human-learning analogy, while imperfect, captures the functional reality that models extract patterns rather than reproduce originals.

**Rightsholder perspective**: Unlicensed training corrodes the creative ecosystem by using entire bodies of copyrighted work—without consent or compensation—to produce content that competes with the originals. The *Thomson Reuters* decision correctly recognizes that building a competing product from copyrighted expression is not transformative. Market-dilution theory is real: if GenAI floods markets with substitutes, the incentive to create is diminished. Opt-out mechanisms are inadequate in practice because they place the burden on rightsholders rather than users.

**Public-interest perspective**: The public benefits from both technological innovation and a thriving creative community. Some balance—whether through voluntary licensing, statutory mechanisms, or carefully calibrated exceptions—is necessary. The Copyright Office's reluctance to recommend compulsory licensing reflects the early state of markets but leaves a policy vacuum. RAG-specific concerns are distinct from training concerns: RAG systems that retrieve and republish copyrighted content are functionally closer to search engines than to training, and existing search-engine jurisprudence may inform but not fully resolve these questions.

---

## 6. Conservative Compliance Approach (Not Legal Advice)

### For Model Developers

1. **Prefer licensed or clearly lawfully acquired sources**; document provenance at dataset level. Avoid shadow libraries, pirated torrents, and sources known to host infringing copies.
2. **Implement and document opt-out compliance** using state-of-the-art technologies (robots.txt recognition, meta-tag scanning, TOS review, opt-out registries, internal tooling to remove opted-out works). Critical for EU market placement under Art. 53(1)(c) and Art. 4(3) DSM.
3. **Maintain a written copyright compliance policy** and keep it updated (EU Code of Practice Commitment 1; useful for US fair-use factor-one narrative).
4. **Publish a sufficiently detailed training-content summary** via the AI Office template if placing GPAI models on the EU market; balance trade-secret concerns with template requirements.
5. **Deploy guardrails**: output filters, prompt classifiers, memorization testing, watermarking/provenance where feasible. The Copyright Office and provider indemnities both credit guardrails.
6. **Audit for memorization/regurgitation**; remove or curate near-duplicate training examples; track and remediate reported infringing outputs.
7. **For RAG systems**: treat retrieval indices as reproductions; obtain licenses for paywalled/proprietary sources; respect robots.txt and terms of service; avoid "substitutive summaries" that replace the original's market; provide clear attribution and link-backs.
8. **Preserve CMI**: do not strip metadata from training/retrieval sources; address DMCA § 1202 exposure.
9. **Contractual protections**: obtain representations and warranties from data suppliers regarding lawfulness of acquisition and opt-out status; carry IP indemnity for downstream customers with appropriate conditions.
10. **Monitor litigation**: track Ninth Circuit appeals in *Bartz*/*Kadrey*, *NYT v. OpenAI* trial, *Perplexity* and *Cohere* proceedings, and any CJEU referrals on Art. 4 DSM.

### For Enterprise Users

1. **Use commercial/enterprise tiers** of major providers with IP indemnities; read the conditions (scope, guardrails, exclusions, termination rights).
2. **Implement provider-required mitigations** (content filters, metaprompts, safety systems) to preserve indemnity coverage.
3. **Do not knowingly prompt or configure systems to reproduce third-party works**; avoid "write me the NYT article on X"–style prompts; monitor for and remediate verbatim or substitutive outputs.
4. **For RAG-over-third-party-content**: license the corpus, respect robots.txt/paywalls, attribute sources, and avoid outputs that substitute for the originals.
5. **Maintain internal policies** on acceptable AI use, output review, and takedown response; train staff on copyright and DMCA exposure.
6. **Vet fine-tuning datasets** for provenance, licenses, and opt-outs; fine-tuning on customer/proprietary data is generally lower risk than on scraped third-party content.
7. **EU-specific**: confirm the upstream GPAI provider has published a training summary and has a compliant copyright policy; document this in procurement records.
8. **Preserve CMI** in any internal corpora used for fine-tuning or RAG.
9. **Insurance**: consider specialized IP/media liability coverage; verify whether general policies exclude AI-related claims.
10. **Document everything**: provenance, licenses, opt-out compliance, guardrail deployments, and incident response—these records are central to both fair-use narratives and EU compliance demonstrations.

---

## 7. Key Uncertainties to Watch

- **Ninth Circuit appeals** in *Bartz* and *Kadrey*—may unify or deepen the fair-use split.
- **NYT v. OpenAI** trial—first major training+output case to a jury.
- **Perplexity / Cohere**—RAG-specific liability theories maturing.
- **Copyright Office Part 3 final publication** and any congressional response.
- **CJEU referral** on Art. 4 DSM opt-out modalities (none yet; likely within 1–2 years; *GEMA v. OpenAI* may prompt one).
- **AI Office enforcement actions** under Art. 53—first cases will set the practical compliance bar.
- **EU "omnibus" simplification proposals**—may modify GPAI timelines/obligations.
- **State-level US laws**—e.g., California, Texas, Tennessee proposals on AI training and publicity rights.
- **Whether model weights are infringing articles**—open in both jurisdictions; could reshape developer liability if answered affirmatively.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 1. Adopt a conservative, dual-regime compliance posture: license or lawfully acquire training/retrieval sources, implement and document state-of-the-art opt-out compliance, deploy guardrails and memorization audits, preserve CMI, publish EU training summaries, obtain provider indemnities and verify their conditions, and avoid RAG and output patterns that substitute for or reproduce third-party works.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Use of pirated/shadow-library sources and RAG systems that copy and republish copyrighted content are the highest-probability pathways to infringement liability under current US case law and EU lawful-access requirements.

## Analysis

### Option 1 — on-device-quantized-model: **Fails the 3 GB memory budget**

A 4.2 GB quantized model file already exceeds the 3 GB app memory limit on disk, and runtime memory is always larger. Real-world benchmarks confirm this: an 8B Q4_K_M model (~4.9 GB on disk) peaks at ~5–6 GB even with KV cache quantization and short context, and well over 9 GB with longer context windows and FP16 KV cache. The KV cache, activation buffers, and runtime framework overhead all add on top of the weight footprint and are not reduced by weight quantization. Even with aggressive mmap or KV cache compression, a 4.2 GB model would peak far above 3 GB during active generation. **This option is non-viable.**

### Option 3 — platform-native-model-api alone: **Leaves 40% of users without the feature**

Platform-native APIs (e.g., Apple Foundation Models, Android AICore) are attractive because the system model does **not** count against the app's memory budget or bundle size — Apple's WWDC25 Foundation Models session explicitly confirms it "won't increase your app size" and runs entirely on-device with no network calls. However, the native API is available on only **60% of the target install base**. Selecting this option alone means 40% of users get no summarization capability at all.

### Option 2 — extractive-plus-small-generator alone: **Viable but universally lower quality**

The published TTFT numbers split: Provider A wins on median (180ms vs. 310ms), Provider B wins on tail (480ms vs. 620ms). The critical factor is whether B's prefix caching materially reduces TTFT on cached turns. Research evidence is strong on this point:

If B's caching delivers even a 50-70% TTFT reduction on the 55% of requests that hit cache, its effective p50 TTFT on cached turns drops to ~90-155ms—**below Provider A's 180ms**. But this assumes the stated 310ms is a cold-cache baseline; if it already reflects mixed hit/miss traffic, the improvement is smaller. We don't know, and no independent benchmark covers this workload.

Provider B's 61 vs. 42 tokens/s (45% higher) directly reduces per-turn generation time. For a 6-turn agent conversation, this compounds: each turn's generation phase is meaningfully shorter. This advantage is unambiguous and doesn't depend on caching.

|----------|---------------------------|-----------------|
