## 1. The Current Benchmark Landscape — Verified Status

### A. HumanEval and MBPP — Retired from Decision-Making

These benchmarks are saturated (frontier models exceed 90% pass@1) and contaminated. Riddell et al. (ACL 2024) quantified substantial n-gram overlap with training corpora; Matton et al. (EMNLP 2024) identified three contamination channels (direct leakage, indirect synthetic-data leakage, checkpoint-selection overfitting). Their LBPP benchmark showed SOTA models perform up to 43% worse on genuinely unseen problems. **No frontier-model selection decision should be driven by these scores.**

### B. SWE-bench Verified — Officially Deprecated by Its Co-Creator

This is the most consequential finding. On **February 23, 2026**, OpenAI published a detailed analysis and **stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified scores**, recommending the industry follow suit. Two failure modes were documented:

1. **Broken tests**: OpenAI audited 138 problems (27.6% of the 500-task dataset) that their o3 model couldn't consistently solve across 64 runs. At least **59.4% of these had flawed test cases** — 35.5% enforced implementation details never mentioned in the problem description; 18.8% tested functionality that was never specified. Functionally correct solutions were being rejected.

2. **Training contamination**: All tested frontier models (GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash) could reproduce gold patches verbatim or quote problem-specific details from commit history they should never have seen. Contaminated models gain an unfair advantage on underspecified tests by "remembering" implementation details not present in the problem statement.

Microsoft Research's "The SWE-bench Illusion" (Liang et al., 2025) independently confirmed repository-level memorization: models achieved **76% accuracy identifying buggy file paths from issue descriptions alone** for SWE-bench repos, but only **<53%** for structurally similar non-SWE-bench repos — a logically near-impossible task without prior exposure. Prathifkumar et al. found models performed **3× better** at file localization on SWE-bench Verified than on comparable benchmarks.

UTBoost (Zhu & Kang, ACL 2025) showed that 26 of 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks have insufficient tests; augmenting with generated tests detected 15.7% more incorrect patches and **changed leaderboard rankings for 24% of agents**.

**Verdict: SWE-bench Verified is no longer a valid metric for comparing frontier models.** It may retain limited value only under the most constrained conditions (bash-only mini-SWE-agent track, with contamination diagnostics run), but its creators have explicitly said improvements "no longer reflect meaningful improvements in real-world software development abilities."

### C. SWE-bench Pro — The Current Best Public SE Benchmark (With Caveats)

Scale AI released SWE-bench Pro in September 2025: 1,865 tasks (731 public, 858 held-out, 276 commercial) across 41 repositories, multi-language (Python, JS/TS, Go, Rust, Java), with tasks averaging 107.4 lines across 4.1 files. Contamination resistance is by design — public/held-out tasks use **strong copyleft (GPL) licenses** whose legal complexity makes inclusion in proprietary training corpora unlikely; the commercial subset uses private codebases entirely.

At launch, GPT-5 scored 23.3% and Claude Opus 4.1 scored 23.1% — far below the 70%+ on SWE-bench Verified, confirming the difficulty gap. The benchmark evaluates under a **unified SWE-Agent scaffold**, addressing the harness-conflation problem.

**Critical caveat (a blind spot the panel missed):** On **July 8, 2026**, OpenAI published an audit of SWE-bench Pro finding that **~30% of tasks are broken** (27.4% flagged by automated pipeline, 34.1% by human annotation). The four issue categories: overly strict tests, underspecified prompts, low-coverage tests, and misleading prompts. Additionally, SWE-bench Pro scores rose from 23.3% to 80.3% in eight months, suggesting it is saturating faster than expected. SWE-bench Pro remains the best available public SE benchmark, but its scores require the same skepticism applied to Verified — always audit task quality and check for saturation trends.

### D. SWE-bench-Live — Continuously Updated, Contamination-Resistant

Microsoft Research's SWE-bench-Live (NeurIPS 2025 D&B) addresses staleness directly: 1,319 tasks from GitHub issues created since 2024, spanning 93 repositories, with ~50 new verified issues added monthly. Now expanded to multi-language (743 tasks across C/C++, C#, Java, TS/JS, Go, Rust from 381 repos) and multi-OS (61 Windows tasks). The RepoLaunch automated curation pipeline enables continuous updates without manual bottlenecks.

The paper reports a **"substantial performance gap"** compared to static SWE-bench even under controlled evaluation conditions — direct evidence that stale benchmark scores are inflated. The continuously-updated test split is the most contamination-resistant design available for a public benchmark, though it has fewer model evaluations and the automated pipeline may introduce its own selection biases.

### E. LiveCodeBench — Contamination Detection Gold Standard

LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., ICLR 2025) continuously collects problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces with release-date annotations, enabling **time-segmented evaluation**. Its key empirical contribution: DeepSeek models show a stark performance drop on LeetCode problems released after their training cutoff, while GPT models remain relatively stable — a direct contamination detection mechanism. However, it tests competitive programming, not repository-level software engineering.

### F. Aider Polyglot — Multi-Language Code Editing Fidelity

Aider's polyglot benchmark tests 225 challenging Exercism exercises across 6 languages (C++, Go, Java, JS, Python, Rust), measuring not just pass rate but **edit format compliance** and cost — whether a model can produce correctly-formatted edits that automated tooling can apply without human cleanup. This captures a failure mode (malformed edits) that standard benchmarks ignore and that directly affects production assistant usability. However, a June 2025 GitHub issue (#4201) noted signs of test-set overfitting, and these are self-contained exercises, not repository-level tasks.

---

## 2. Agent Scaffolding: The Hidden Variable That Can Dwarf Model Choice

Multiple 2026 papers demonstrate that the agent harness — context management, tool configuration, retry logic, stopping conditions — is often a **stronger determinant of benchmark performance than the model itself**:

- **Zhang et al. (2026), "Stop Comparing LLM Agents Without Disclosing the Harness"**: Formalizes the "Binding Constraint Thesis." For comparable frontier models on long-horizon tasks, harness-induced variance exceeds model-induced variance, including **model ranking reversal in 6 of 9 comparisons** on a SWE-bench subset. Swapping the scaffold moved scores 6–54 points; model-paper advances typically move 2–4 points. Holding the model fixed while changing only the harness raised Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 from 69.7% to 77.0%.

- **Vats & Golev (2026), "The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents"**: Across 300 trials (3 harnesses × 2 models × 50 Terminal-Bench Pro tasks), harness choice induced up to **40× difference in tokens per solved task**, while paired pass-rate differences stayed within 0–8 pp. Failure-mode fingerprints replicated across models (REASON failures for Goose, VERIFY/MAX_TURNS for OpenHands-SDK), proving these are scaffold properties, not model properties.

- **Claw-SWE-Bench (Zheng et al., 2026)**: On a multilingual SWE-bench-style benchmark, model choice changed Pass@1 by 29.4 pp; harness choice changed it by 27.4 pp under fixed models — nearly equal magnitude. One model went from 19.1% to 73.4% by changing nothing but the adapter.

**Implication**: Any leaderboard score that does not disclose the harness configuration is incomplete and potentially misleading. A vendor's custom multi-rollout, RAG-augmented, review-pipeline agent is not comparable to a minimal bash-only setup. The SWE-bench Pro leaderboard's use of a unified SWE-Agent scaffold is a meaningful improvement; the SWE-bench Verified "bash-only" mini-SWE-agent track is the most model-isolating configuration on that deprecated benchmark.

---

## 3. Evidence from Real-World Coding Tasks

Production evidence provides a crucial reality check against benchmark scores:

### Studies showing productivity gains:
- **Google RCT** (Paradis et al., 2024): 96 engineers, randomized controlled trial. AI significantly shortened task time, best estimate ~21% reduction (large confidence interval). Benefits larger for developers with more coding hours.
- **Microsoft/Accenture RCT** (Cui et al., 2025): 4,867 developers, 26% increase in completed tasks, but gains concentrated in less experienced developers.
- **1mg.com/DeputyDev** (Kumar et al., 2025): 300 engineers, 1 year. 31.8% reduction in PR review cycle time, 93% desire to continue, adoption scaling from 4% to 83% peak.
- **Zoominfo Copilot** (Bakal et al., 2025): 400+ developers, 33% suggestion acceptance rate, 72% developer satisfaction.

### Studies showing slowdown or mixed effects:
- **METR RCT** (Becker et al., 2025): 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks. AI tools **increased completion time by 19%** (CI: +2% to +39%) — a significant slowdown. Developers expected 24% speedup and believed they got 20% speedup even while being slower. The study attributes this to debugging poor AI suggestions and integration friction in mature codebases.
- **METR February 2026 update**: Their follow-up study (August 2025 onward) found the 2025 slowdown result is now outdated — early 2026 tools likely show speedup — but the new experiment's data is **unreliable due to selection effects**: developers increasingly refuse to work without AI, biasing the sample. Among original participants, estimated speedup of 18% (CI: -38% to +9%); among new recruits, -4% (CI: -15% to +9%). The selection problem itself is telling: developers find AI sufficiently valuable that they won't participate in no-AI conditions.
- **Cursor DID study** (He et al., 2025): Cursor adoption caused a transient velocity increase followed by persistent increases in static analysis warnings and code complexity, causing long-term slowdown.
- **BNY Mellon** (Chen et al., ICSE-SEIP 2026): 2,989-person survey. Self-reported usefulness conflicts; productivity factors are heterogeneous and under-measured.

### Critical insight from Meta/REAP (Jha et al., 2026):
Solve rates of 42.9–58.2% across 5 frontier models on production-derived tasks. Public benchmarks diverge from production in language distribution, prompt style, and codebase structure. Industrial codebases are polyglot (majority Hack, Java, C++ at Meta — not Python-heavy like SWE-bench). "Offline evaluation using existing benchmarks offers speed and reproducibility, but public benchmarks differ from production workloads in multiple ways."

**Bottom line from production evidence**: Gains are real but heterogeneous — contingent on developer experience, task type, codebase maturity, and language. The 20–30% productivity range (from optimistic studies) and the 19% slowdown (from METR) bracket a wide uncertainty interval. Benefits accrue most to less experienced developers on familiar task types; experienced developers on complex, unfamiliar codebases may see no benefit or slowdown. No production study cleanly isolates model quality from tool integration quality.

---

## 4. Which Metrics Are Decision-Useful vs. Misleading

### Decision-Useful

| Metric | Why It's Useful | Caveats |
|---|---|---|
| **SWE-bench Pro Pass@1 (unified scaffold)** | Tests long-horizon, multi-file, multi-language enterprise tasks under a fixed harness; ~25% ceiling provides discrimination | ~30% of tasks broken (OpenAI July 2026 audit); saturating rapidly (23%→80% in 8 months) |
| **SWE-bench-Live Resolve Rate** | Continuously updated, post-2024 tasks, multi-language, contamination-resistant by design | Newer, fewer model evaluations; automated curation may introduce biases |
| **LiveCodeBench (post-cutoff time window)** | Gold standard for contamination detection; identifies memorization vs. genuine capability | Competitive programming, not repository-level SE |
| **Aider polyglot pass rate + edit format compliance + cost** | Tests multi-language code editing; reports production-relevant cost and format fidelity | Self-contained exercises; signs of overfitting |
| **Tokens per solved task / USD per task** | Real deployment cost; distinguishes "cheap and good enough" from "expensive overkill" | Needs paired-task design; harness-dependent |
| **Latency to first correct edit** | Developer wait time; flow-state disruption | Infrastructure-dependent |
| **Acceptance rate (internal A/B)** | Directly observed production metric | Confounded by tool integration quality |
| **PR cycle time, developer satisfaction, escalation rate (internal pilot)** | Outcome metrics benchmarks predict weakly | Requires 4–8 week minimum; team heterogeneity |

### Misleading

| Metric | Why It Misleads |
|---|---|
| **HumanEval / MBPP pass@1** | Saturated (>90%), contaminated; measures 164/974 isolated snippets, not engineering |
| **SWE-bench Verified pass rate** | Officially deprecated by OpenAI (Feb 2026): 59.4% of hard tasks have broken tests; all frontier models contaminated; scores reflect memorization, not capability |
| **Any leaderboard score without harness disclosure** | Harness-induced variance can exceed model-induced variance (up to 54-point swings); model rankings can reverse |
| **Single-number % Resolved without test-quality audit** | UTBoost showed 15.7% of "correct" patches are actually incorrect; OpenAI showed ~30% of SWE-bench Pro tasks are broken |
| **Pass@1 on any frozen benchmark without time-segmenting** | Cannot distinguish learning from memorization |
| **Raw token counts without per-solved-task normalization** | A model that uses 40× more tokens but has the same pass rate is not "better" — it's more expensive |

---

## 5. Proposed Balanced Evaluation Framework

For selecting a model for an internal coding assistant, I recommend a **four-tier framework** weighted toward production-derived evidence:

### Tier 1: Public Benchmark Screening (weight: 20%) — Fast triage of 5–10 candidates

1. **SWE-bench Pro (public split, unified SWE-Agent scaffold)** — primary model discrimination signal. If all candidates score <15%, your tasks may be harder than autonomous agents can reliably handle, suggesting an "assistant" (human-in-the-loop) interaction model rather than an autonomous agent. Apply the OpenAI audit's task-quality findings: treat any single score as ±5–10 pp uncertain due to broken tasks.
2. **SWE-bench-Live (test split, most recent monthly update)** — contamination-resistant, multi-language, continuously fresh. Prioritize this over SWE-bench Pro if the candidate model's training cutoff may overlap with GPL-licensed Pro tasks.
3. **LiveCodeBench (post-cutoff window only)** — contamination check. If a model scores dramatically better on SWE-bench Pro than on LiveCodeBench post-cutoff, suspect memorization of code patterns rather than generalizable skill.
4. **Aider polyglot** — multi-language code editing fidelity, with edit-format compliance and cost as secondary metrics.

**Red flags**: Model scores 70%+ on SWE-bench Verified but <30% on SWE-bench Pro → memorization. Model scores well on SWE-bench Pro but <40% on Aider polyglot → may resolve issues but cannot produce clean inline edits. Model scores well on all public benchmarks but cannot pass file-path identification on your internal repos → benchmark overfitting.

### Tier 2: Contamination and Harness Auditing (weight: 10%) — Gating filter

5. **Run the file-path identification diagnostic** from "The SWE-Bench Illusion": ask the model to identify buggy files from issue descriptions alone, without repository access. If it scores >50% on SWE-bench tasks but <30% on your internal repos, it has memorized SWE-bench, not learned general SE skill. Downweight all its public benchmark scores.
6. **Run UTBoost or equivalent test augmentation** on a sample of benchmark tasks to verify that pass/fail scores are robust to test coverage gaps.
7. **Fix and disclose the harness**: strip git history (reflogs, branches, origins, tags) to eliminate repo-state loopholes (documented September 2025 in SWE-bench issue #465, affecting Claude 4 Sonnet, Qwen3-Coder, and GLM 4.5 runs). Report the exact harness configuration (agent loop, tools, retry logic, context window management, stopping conditions) alongside every score. If a vendor cannot disclose their harness, treat their score as a model+harness composite, not a model score.

### Tier 3: Internal Task-Based Evaluation (weight: 40%) — Highest decision weight

8. **Construct a SWE-bench-Live-style benchmark from your own repositories**: 50–100 recent, merged PRs with passing tests, post-training-cutoff, across your primary languages. Use Meta's REAP methodology for curation (fail-to-pass tests from CI, multi-run stability checks, automated test-relevance validation). This eliminates contamination, matches your codebase distribution, and tests the actual task distribution.
9. **Measure beyond pass rate**: per-task token cost, latency, number of tool calls, number of no-action turns (a "wait tax" on developers — Vats & Golev showed these are a harness property, not a model property), and whether patches pass **augmented** tests (not just original tests, which may be insufficient per UTBoost findings).
10. **Test code understanding/explanation tasks**: give models internal code and ask for summaries, bug identification, and impact analysis. IBM's study found code understanding is the top production use case, but SWE-bench-family benchmarks do not test it.
11. **Run all candidates under a single fixed harness** to isolate model effects. Report results as harness-model pairs, not model-only scores.

### Tier 4: Production Pilot with Human-Centered Metrics (weight: 30%) — Final validation

12. **A/B test with 50–100 developers over 4–8 weeks**, modeled on the Google RCT design. Measure:
    - **Task completion rate** (submitted code that builds and passes tests)
    - **PR cycle time** (per Kumar et al.: 31.8% reduction is a strong benchmark)
    - **Reviewer acceptance rate** of AI-authored code (Zoominfo: 33% suggestion acceptance)
    - **Developer satisfaction** and "continue using" intent (DeputyDev: 93% desire to continue)
    - **Escalation rate** (human had to take over)
    - **Code quality regression**: track static analysis warnings, cyclomatic complexity, and churn over time (the Cursor DID study showed a transient velocity gain followed by persistent quality degradation and long-term slowdown)
13. **Track adoption curves and heterogeneous effects**: benefits are not evenly distributed. Measure by developer experience level, language, task type, and codebase maturity. The METR study's 19% slowdown for experienced developers on mature codebases is a real risk; the Microsoft/Accenture study's 26% gain concentrated in less experienced developers is the optimistic case. Your population will fall somewhere on this spectrum.
14. **Be aware of selection effects**: METR's February 2026 update showed that as AI tools improve, developers increasingly refuse to participate in no-AI conditions, biasing any controlled study toward underestimating AI's value. Design your pilot to account for this — use within-subject comparisons where possible, and track voluntary no-AI refusal rates as a signal of perceived value.

### Why this weighting:
- **Tier 3 (40%)** receives the highest weight because internal, production-derived benchmarks eliminate contamination, match your codebase, and test your actual task distribution — the single most decision-useful signal per Meta/REAP.
- **Tier 4 (30%)** is the only source of real human productivity signal, but it is expensive, slow, and confounded by integration quality and selection effects.
- **Tier 1 (20%)** is useful for triage and cross-checking but every public benchmark has documented contamination or task-quality issues.
- **Tier 2 (10%)** functions as a gating filter — if a model fails contamination or harness audits, downweight its Tier 1 scores regardless of magnitude.

---

## 6. Key Uncertainties

1. **SWE-bench Pro is also degrading.** OpenAI's July 2026 audit found ~30% of SWE-bench Pro tasks are broken, and scores rose from 23.3% to 80.3% in eight months — suggesting faster-than-expected saturation. No public benchmark appears durable. Continuous internal benchmark curation is not optional; it is the only long-term solution.

2. **The METR 19% slowdown may be outdated but its methodology is broken.** METR's February 2026 update suggests early-2026 tools likely show speedup, but selection effects (developers refusing no-AI conditions) make controlled measurement increasingly impossible. This means the production productivity evidence is itself unreliable — neither the optimistic studies (Google 21% speedup) nor the pessimistic study (METR 19% slowdown) can be taken at face value.

3. **Harness-model boundary is regime-dependent.** The "Binding Constraint Thesis" applies when frontier models are roughly comparable. For models with large capability gaps, model choice still matters significantly. The panel's evidence shows both effects are large (~27–29 pp each for model and harness on Claw-SWE-Bench) — the relative importance depends on which models you're comparing.

4. **Production gains are heterogeneous and no study isolates model quality from integration quality.** A model that scores well on benchmarks may underperform in production due to poor IDE integration, context-retrieval failures, or edit-format mismatches — and vice versa.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 4 — Balanced hybrid framework: use SWE-bench Pro (unified scaffold) and SWE-bench-Live for contamination-resistant public triage, audit for memorization and broken tests, build an internal SWE-bench-Live-style benchmark from your own repos with augmented tests and disclosed harness configs as the highest-weight signal, and validate with a 4–8 week A/B pilot measuring acceptance rate, PR cycle time, code quality regression, and developer satisfaction.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: All public coding benchmarks have documented contamination or task-quality defects, and harness engineering can swing scores by more than model choice, so any selection based primarily on public leaderboards risks choosing a well-benchmarked model that underperforms on your actual codebase and internal scaffold.

# Environmental Impact of Serving Large Language Models in Production

## 1. The Shift from Training to Inference

The sustainability spotlight has moved decisively from one-time training to continuous inference. A 2025 scoping review cited by the WEF finds inference accounts for roughly **60–70%** of combined AI electricity consumption, with training at 20–40% and model development ≤10%; other analyses place inference as high as **65–90%** of lifecycle energy (Jegham et al., 2025; Hoxha et al., 2025). The structural reason is simple: a frontier model is trained once but served billions of times. Google's August 2025 production study—the first from a hyperscaler to disclose measured, full-stack per-prompt metrics—notes that "with these AI models now serving billions of user prompts globally, the energy, carbon emissions, and water impacts associated with generating responses at scale represents a significant and rapidly growing component of AI's overall environmental cost" (Elsworth et al., 2025).

A parallel concern is the **scale paradox** (Jegham et al., 2025): although per-query costs have fallen sharply, global adoption drives disproportionate aggregate impact. At 700 million queries/day, a single short GPT-4o query (0.43 Wh) scales to electricity use comparable to 35,000 U.S. homes, freshwater evaporation matching the annual drinking needs of 1.2 million people, and carbon emissions requiring a Chicago-sized forest to offset.

---

## 2. Reconciling Conflicting Per-Prompt Estimates

### The headline conflict

The most widely circulated conflict is the ~10× spread in "energy per ChatGPT query":

| Source | Estimate (text prompt) | System boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Alex de Vries, 2023 (widely cited) | ~3 Wh/query | Older hardware (A100-era), pessimistic token counts, no MoE |
| Epoch AI, Feb 2025 (bottom-up) | ~0.3 Wh (GPT-4o) | Updated chips, MoE active params, ~500 output tokens |
| Sam Altman, mid-2025 (OpenAI disclosed) | ~0.34 Wh; ~0.32 mL water | OpenAI production average |
| Google, Aug 2025 (Gemini, measured) | 0.24 Wh; 0.03 gCO₂e; 0.26 mL water | **Full stack**: active accelerator + host CPU/RAM + idle capacity + data-center overhead (PUE) |
| Google, active-chip-only subset | 0.10 Wh | Accelerator only, no idle/host/overhead |
| Jegham et al., May 2025 | 0.43 Wh (GPT-4o short); up to 33+ Wh (o3/DeepSeek-R1 long) | Inferred hardware + region-specific PUE/WUE/CIF |
| Washington Post / UC Riverside, Sep 2024 | up to 519 mL water per 100-word email | Worst-case hot-climate Texas DC; Scope 1+2+3 water |
| ML.Energy / MIT Tech Review | 114 J (Llama-3.1 8B) to 6,706 J (Llama-3.1 405B) per answer | Direct GPU measurement |

### What drives the 10× gap between 3 Wh and 0.24–0.43 Wh

1. **Hardware generation**: de Vries assumed older, less-efficient chips; H100/H200/B200 and Google TPUs are substantially more efficient per FLOP.
2. **Model architecture**: GPT-4o is likely a mixture-of-experts model with ~100B active parameters, not the ~175B dense model assumed in the 3 Wh estimate (Epoch AI, 2025).
3. **Token-count assumptions**: de Vries overestimated output tokens; Epoch AI uses ~500.
4. **Software efficiency**: Google reports a **33× energy and 44× carbon reduction** for the median Gemini text prompt over 12 months, driven by model, compiler, and serving-stack improvements (Elsworth et al., 2025). ML.ENERGY's longitudinal analysis confirms that vLLM software optimizations alone reduced energy per token by 15–41% on identical Llama 3.1 hardware over one year (ML.ENERGY Blog, 2026).
5. **System boundary**: active-chip-only estimates are roughly 2.4× lower than full-stack (Google: 0.10 vs 0.24 Wh). Many alarming estimates use only active power, while many provider disclosures include idle + host + PUE. Google's own breakdown shows TPUs account for just 58% of total electricity; host CPU/RAM is 25%, idle backup machines 10%, and data-center overhead 8% (MIT Tech Review, 2025).

### What drives the water gap (519 mL vs 0.26 mL)

- **Scope**: the 519 mL figure includes Scope 1 (on-site evaporative cooling) + Scope 2 (electricity-generation evaporation) + Scope 3 (embedded water), in a hot, water-stressed Texas region. Google's 0.26 mL is a median across its global fleet with optimized cooling and water replenishment.
- **Regional WUE**: water usage effectiveness varies dramatically by climate and cooling technology. A data center in a cool, humid region may use negligible Scope 1 water; one in Arizona may use orders of magnitude more.
- **Median vs worst case**: headlines cite the upper bound; providers cite medians.
- **Cooling technology**: neither liquid nor air cooling differences are typically disaggregated in public disclosures, yet they are critical for data-center-level WUE optimization—a blind spot in most estimates.

---

## 3. Comparison Across Deployment Modes

### A. Fixed Dedicated GPUs (always-on)

- **Electricity**: dominated by idle/execution-idle power at low utilization. The "model parking tax" study (Vadari, 2026) finds a CUDA context forces +26–66 W over bare idle on H100/A100/L40S, regardless of VRAM allocation; the CUDA context accounts for >98% of the parking tax. The "execution-idle" study (Lei et al., 2026) finds execution-idle accounts for **19.7% of in-execution time and 10.7% of energy** in academic GPU clusters.
- **Hardware utilization**: low average utilization (often <30% for dedicated single-model deployments). The "1/W Law" (Chen et al., 2026) shows tokens-per-watt varies by 40× across deployments of identical hardware depending on context window; a GPU serving a single 4K-context request idles near 43% TDP, while large batches approach 86% TDP.
- **Emissions**: high operational carbon if the grid is fossil-heavy; embodied carbon amortized over longer life. Nguyen et al. (2025) find older GPUs (T4) can be more energy-efficient than newer ones (RTX 6000 Ada) at batch size 1, but newer GPUs win at larger batches—so a dedicated always-on box may paradoxically be dirtier per token than a shared, older GPU.
- **Best for**: steady, high-volume traffic where utilization stays high.

### B. Autoscaled Endpoints

- **Electricity**: reduces idle waste by scaling down during low traffic, but incurs cold-start energy. Vadari (2026) derives a cold-start breakeven of **1–5 minutes** depending on request arrival rate and loading latency. Below that breakeven, keeping a model warm is cheaper than reloading.
- **Hardware utilization**: higher average utilization than fixed dedicated, but bursts can strand capacity. Autoscaling typically targets 50–70% utilization to preserve headroom.
- **Emissions**: better than fixed dedicated for variable workloads, but the benefit depends on how aggressively the scaler downscales and how clean the grid is at the autoscaler's home region.
- **Best for**: predictable diurnal or weekly traffic patterns.

### C. Serverless Inference (multi-tenant GPU sharing)

- **Electricity**: the most elastic option; platforms like Azure, Hugging Face, and Run:ai multiplex many models across shared GPUs. Festina (Wang et al., 2026), an energy-aware serverless scheduler coordinating request placement, SM partitioning, and DVFS, reduces cluster energy by **up to 56%** while holding SLO attainment within 2%.
- **Hardware utilization**: highest average utilization, but sharing introduces contention. The "utilization fallacy" paper (Sinha et al., HotCarbon 2025) warns that higher utilization does **not** always improve carbon efficiency—the outcome depends on which models are co-located, because power draw is nonlinear and DVFS state is device-wide.
- **Emissions**: best when the platform is carbon-aware; CarbConscious (Gupta et al., 2026) reports **35–52% carbon reductions** for mixed-latency LLM workloads via temporal + spatial shifting while maintaining 99.5% SLA. Cross-region migration under grid constraints yields ~13% carbon and ~15% cost reductions (Hankendi & Coskun, 2026).
- **Best for**: spiky, unpredictable, or multi-model workloads.

### D. External APIs (managed provider)

- **Electricity**: per-prompt figures are now measured and disclosed by leading providers: Google Gemini 0.24 Wh (full-stack), OpenAI 0.34 Wh. These are substantially lower than independent 2023 estimates. However, **transparency is incomplete**: providers disclose medians but not distributions, regional breakdowns, or water by scope.
- **Hardware utilization**: hyperscale providers run at very high utilization via massive batching and custom silicon (TPUs), which is hard to match on self-hosted single-tenant GPUs.
- **Emissions**: depends on the provider's power purchase agreements and REC strategy. Hyperscaler "near-zero carbon" claims often rely on **RECs that are accounting, not physics**—the physical grid mix where the server runs may still be fossil-heavy. For honest reporting, use location-based (grid-average) carbon intensity, not market-based (REC-adjusted).
- **Best for**: low-to-medium volume, variable demand, or when internal GPU ops expertise is lacking.

---

## 4. Assumptions That Drive Differences Across Studies

| Assumption | Effect on estimate |
|---|---|
| System boundary (active-chip vs full-stack) | ~2.4× (Google: 0.10 vs 0.24 Wh) |
| Model size & active parameters (MoE) | 50×+ (Llama 8B vs 405B; GPT-4.1 nano vs o3) |
| Context length (1/W law) | tokens/W halves each time context doubles |
| Output token count | linear in decode FLOPs |
| Hardware generation | H100 vs A100 vs T4 can differ 2–3× per token |
| Batch size | newer GPUs dominate at high batch; older can win at batch=1 |
| Regional PUE (1.1–1.6) | 10–50% overhead |
| Regional WUE (cool vs hot, dry) | orders of magnitude in water |
| Carbon intensity factor (50–800+ gCO₂e/kWh) | 16× spread in operational carbon |
| Idle allocation method | marginal vs average attribution changes per-prompt cost at low load |
| Carbon accounting (market vs location) | REC-based can understate physical emissions |
| Quantization (INT4/INT8) | ML.ENERGY longitudinal shows 39% energy reduction at batch 256 for FP8 Llama-405B; but de-quantization penalties on prosumer GPUs without native INT4 support can make INT4 *less* energy-efficient than FP16 (IEEE CAL, 2026) |

---

## 5. Practical Measurement Strategies

1. **Instrument the full stack**, not just the GPU: measure GPU power (NVML/DCGM), host CPU/RAM (RAPL/IPMI), and apply data-center PUE. Google's methodology explicitly includes idle backup capacity and host overhead—omitting them understates real footprint by ~2.4×.
2. **Attribute idle power per-prompt**, not just active power. Use marginal attribution (energy delta from serving one more request) for routing decisions and average attribution (total fleet energy ÷ total prompts) for reporting. The execution-idle and parking-tax studies show idle can be >10% of served energy.
3. **Use real-time carbon intensity APIs** (electricityMaps, WattTime, energy-charts) for location-based operational carbon, not annual averages. Carbon intensity varies 5–10× within a day in renewable-heavy grids.
4. **Track water across all three scopes**: Scope 1 (on-site evaporative cooling), Scope 2 (evaporation from electricity generation), Scope 3 (embedded in hardware). Use site-specific WUE; do not assume a global average. Separate liquid vs. air cooling in your accounting.
5. **Standardize with open benchmarks**: ML.Energy leaderboard (University of Michigan), AI Energy Score (Hugging Face), CodeCarbon, Zeus/Perseus for per-token profiling. These enable apples-to-apples model comparison.
6. **Log prompt-level metadata**: model ID, input/output token counts, context length, batch size, region, latency. The 1/W law shows context length is a first-order energy driver; without it, per-prompt numbers are meaningless.
7. **Disclose distributions, not just medians**: a median of 0.24 Wh can hide a 95th-percentile of 5+ Wh for long reasoning prompts. Providers should publish percentiles.
8. **Measure multimodal separately**: multimodal LLMs introduce "modality inflation"—vision encoders and visual token expansion raise energy by 17–94% over text-only baselines for identical inputs (Moghadampanah et al., 2025). Image generation (~0.63 Wh) and especially video generation (~944 Wh for 5 seconds) are 10–100× more energy-intensive than text (MIT Tech Review / ML.Energy).

---

## 6. Practical Reduction Strategies (Ranked by Leverage)

1. **Model right-sizing**: choose the smallest model that meets quality bar. Llama-3.1 8B uses ~114 J vs 405B's ~6,706 J per answer (MIT Tech Review/ML.Energy). Distilled, quantized (INT4/INT8), and MoE models (e.g., Qwen3-235B-A22B) can cut active FLOPs by 5× with comparable quality. On data-center GPUs with native low-bit tensor cores, FP8 quantization delivers up to 39% energy reduction (ML.ENERGY, 2026). On prosumer GPUs without native INT4 support, verify that quantization actually saves energy—de-quantization penalties can negate gains (IEEE CAL, 2026).
2. **Context-length routing**: route long-context requests to high-concurrency pools and short-context to others. The 1/W law shows two-pool routing gives ~2.5× better tok/W on homogeneous H100 fleets—more than upgrading to B200 (1.7×).
3. **Batch size optimization**: increase batching to push GPUs from ~43% TDP (single request) toward 86% TDP (full batch). This is the cheapest utilization lever.
4. **Carbon-aware scheduling**: defer non-urgent inference to lower-carbon windows or regions. CarbConscious: 35–52% carbon reduction. Cross-region migration: ~13% carbon, ~15% cost (under grid constraints). The Hoxha et al. (2025) bi-objective framework achieves 57–59% energy, 59–60% water, and 78–80% location-based CO₂ reductions through time-resolved, SLO-aware joint optimization of region, batch size, and hardware.
5. **Serverless with energy-aware schedulers**: Festina-style joint placement + SM partitioning + DVFS reduces energy up to 56%. This outperforms naive autoscaling.
6. **DVFS / frequency tuning**: scale GPU clock down during execution-idle or light decode. The utilization-fallacy paper shows frequency tuning is a carbon lever but must be tailored to co-resident model mix. DVFS from 2842 MHz to 180 MHz achieves ~42% energy savings with only 1–6% latency increase (Maliakel et al., 2026).
7. **Hardware selection by workload**: older, lower-TDP GPUs (T4) are more energy-efficient at batch size 1; newer GPUs (H100/B200) dominate at high batch. Match hardware to traffic profile, and amortize embodied carbon by extending GPU life.
8. **Region selection by grid mix**: prefer regions with carbon intensity <100 gCO₂e/kWh (e.g., Quebec, Norway, Pacific Northwest hydro) over >500 gCO₂e/kWh (coal-heavy). This is a 5–10× operational carbon lever.
9. **Avoid REC-only claims**: use location-based carbon accounting for honest sustainability reporting; supplement with additional real decarbonization (PPAs, on-site renewables) rather than paper offsets.
10. **Cold-start management**: for serverless, weigh the 1–5 minute breakeven. For models with request gaps shorter than breakeven, keep warm; for longer gaps, allow cold-start.
11. **Grid-interactive demand response**: AI inference workloads contain enough operational flexibility to participate in grid demand response. A field demonstration in Phoenix (Colangelo et al., 2025) achieved 25% power reduction for three hours during peak grid events while maintaining AI QoS—turning a liability into a grid-stabilizing asset.

---

## 7. Unresolved Uncertainties

- **Provider opacity**: Google and OpenAI have disclosed medians but not distributions, regional breakdowns, or water-by-scope. Independent verification of proprietary model footprints remains impossible.
- **Embodied carbon amortization**: estimates of GPU manufacturing emissions range from 10.3 kg (T4) to 26.6 kg (RTX 6000 Ada) to 21.56 kg per A100 (Meta fleet). The amortization period and reuse market are unsettled.
- **Rebound effects**: no empirical study has quantified whether efficiency gains increase total consumption (Jevons' paradox) at AI scale.
- **Reasoning models**: o3 and DeepSeek-R1 consume 33+ Wh per long prompt (Jegham et al.), but adoption rates and average prompt lengths for these models are not publicly tracked.
- **Regulatory pressure**: the EU AI Act (in force Aug 2024) requires GPAI model providers to document "known or estimated energy consumption" (Annex XI), with compliance deadlines of Aug 2027 for pre-Aug-2025 models and immediate obligations for models launched after that date. This will drive measurement adoption but the implementing standards are not yet finalized.
- **Fine-tuning and continuous learning**: sit between training and inference in the lifecycle but are not addressed in most inference-focused studies.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 1 Adopt a full-stack, prompt-level measurement system and route inference to serverless or carbon-aware autoscaled endpoints using the smallest quantized/MoE model that meets quality, with context-length routing and DVFS-based consolidation as the primary levers.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Provider opacity and REC-based carbon accounting obscure real physical emissions, making independent verification and honest sustainability reporting impossible without first-party instrumentation.

# Copyright and Generative AI: Legal and Policy Landscape in the United States and European Union

## I. United States: Statutory Framework and Regulatory Guidance

### Core Statute
The Copyright Act of 1976 (17 U.S.C. §§ 101–810) governs all copyright questions. No provision expressly addresses AI training. The central legal question is whether copying copyrighted works to train generative-AI models qualifies as **fair use** under 17 U.S.C. § 107, which requires weighing four factors: (1) purpose and character of use (including transformativeness and commerciality); (2) nature of the copyrighted work; (3) amount and substantiality used; and (4) effect on the potential market for or value of the original.

The Supreme Court's 2023 decision in *Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith*, 598 U.S. 508, reshaped the first factor by requiring that a secondary use have a "further purpose or different character" from the original to qualify as transformative. Commercial uses that remain "substantially the same" as the original's purpose weigh against fair use. This decision narrows the defense AI developers previously built on *Authors Guild v. Google* (2d Cir. 2015), which held that digitizing books for searchable snippets was transformative fair use.

The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), 17 U.S.C. § 1202, separately prohibits intentional removal or alteration of copyright management information (CMI) with intent to induce or conceal infringement.

### U.S. Copyright Office Report (May 2025)
On May 9, 2025, the U.S. Copyright Office released Part 3 of its Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, titled *Generative AI Training* (pre-publication version). The Report:

- Surveys the technology lifecycle (data collection, training, memorization, RAG, outputs) and analyzes prima facie infringement at each stage.
- Applies all four fair-use factors in depth, finding that some training uses are "likely transformative"—particularly for research and analysis where outputs do not reproduce protected expression—but that using pirated works or producing competing expressive outputs weighs heavily against fair use.
- Recommends **no immediate government intervention**: neither a broad fair-use exemption nor a statutory licensing scheme. Instead, it concludes that voluntary licensing markets should develop organically, while flagging extended collective licensing as a potential future mechanism.

The day after the Report's release, Register of Copyrights Shira Perlmutter was dismissed by the Trump administration. The D.C. Circuit subsequently ruled 2-1 on September 10, 2025 that the President lacks authority to unilaterally remove her, but the political signal created regulatory uncertainty about future copyright policy direction. The Trump administration also revoked Executive Order 14110 (October 2023), which had directed the Copyright Office to study AI-copyright issues.

### Provider Advocacy and Stakeholder Commentary
OpenAI and Google filed comments with the White House in March 2025 framing fair-use access to copyrighted training data as a "matter of national security," arguing that licensing requirements would cede the AI race to China. Anthropic notably did not join this copyright advocacy, focusing instead on national-security risk assessment.

Copyright-holding industries—publishers, record labels, visual artists—argue that unlicensed training is market-destroying and that *Warhol* undermines AI companies' fair-use claims. The Copyright Alliance and creator groups have filed amicus briefs emphasizing licensing-market harm.

Academic commentary is divided. Scholars like Edward Lee argue that scaling datasets for technological development has a "further purpose" supporting fair use. Critics like Jacqueline Charlesworth counter that generative AI's purpose is to exploit expressive content, distinguishing it from *Google Books* and prior intermediate-copying precedents.

---

## II. European Union: Statutory Framework and Regulatory Guidance

### Copyright Directive (EU) 2019/790 (DSM Directive)
The EU framework establishes two text-and-data-mining (TDM) exceptions:

- **Article 3**: A mandatory exception for reproduction and extraction by research organizations and cultural heritage institutions, for scientific research, with lawful access. This cannot be overridden by contract.
- **Article 4**: A broader exception allowing TDM for any purpose (including commercial), **provided** that rightholders have not reserved their rights "in an appropriate manner" (including machine-readable means such as robots.txt, metadata, or terms of service). This is the critical provision for AI training.

The opt-out mechanism under Article 4(3) is the cornerstone of EU copyright compliance for AI. Rightsholders may reserve TDM rights, and AI providers must identify and respect these reservations using "state of the art technologies."

### EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
The AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024, with GPAI model obligations becoming applicable on August 2, 2025. Key provisions:

- **Article 53(1)(c)**: Requires providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models to "put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, and in particular to identify and comply with, including through state of the art technologies, a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790."
- **Article 53(1)(d)**: Requires a "sufficiently detailed summary" of training content, using a template published by the European AI Office.

These obligations apply to all GPAI providers placing models on the EU market, regardless of where training occurs—a significant extraterritorial reach.

### Regulatory Guidance and Code of Practice
On July 10, 2025, the EU AI Office published the final voluntary **Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models**, comprising three chapters: Transparency, Copyright, and Safety & Security. The Copyright Chapter offers providers practical measures to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1)(c), including implementing a copyright policy, web-crawler identification, and opt-out compliance mechanisms. The Code explicitly states that adherence does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance with Union copyright law—enforcement remains for national courts and ultimately the CJEU.

On July 24, 2025, the AI Office published the mandatory **Template for the Public Summary of Training Content**, implementing Article 53(1)(d). The Template requires disclosure of: model/provider metadata; organized listing of data source categories (public datasets, licensed datasets, crawled/scraped content, user data, synthetic data, other); and processing/governance aspects addressing copyright compliance, removal of illegal content, and data protection obligations. Summaries must be updated every six months or upon material change.

The GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) independently applies when training data contains personal data, requiring a lawful basis for processing and adherence to purpose limitation and data minimization principles.

---

## III. Major Court Developments

### United States

**1. Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence** (D. Del., Feb. 11, 2025)
The first federal decision squarely rejecting fair use for AI training. Judge Bibas (sitting by designation from the Third Circuit) revised his 2023 opinion and granted summary judgment to Thomson Reuters on direct infringement and fair use. The court found that Ross's use of 2,243 Westlaw headnotes to train a competing legal-research AI was commercial, non-transformative, and designed to supplant the market for the originals. The court distinguished prior intermediate-copying cases (*Sega v. Accolade*, *Authors Guild v. Google*) because the copied works were not computer programs and the purpose was competitive substitution. The court expressly noted it was not ruling on generative AI, leaving open whether its reasoning extends to models with different purposes than their training inputs.

**2. New York Times Co. v. OpenAI / Daily News v. OpenAI** (S.D.N.Y., April 4, 2025)
Judge Stein denied motions to dismiss contributory infringement claims, holding plaintiffs adequately alleged that OpenAI knowingly enabled third-party infringement and that ChatGPT lacked substantial noninfringing uses as configured. On DMCA § 1202(b)(1) claims, the court allowed claims by Daily News and Center for Investigative Reporting (finding adequate pleading of intentional CMI removal with requisite scienter) but dismissed the NYT's own DMCA claim for failure to adequately plead intent. Section 1202(b)(3) claims were dismissed across all actions. Direct infringement claims were permitted to proceed; "hot news" misappropriation claims were dismissed.

**3. Dow Jones v. Perplexity AI** (S.D.N.Y., Aug. 21, 2025)
Judge Failla denied Perplexity's motion to dismiss or transfer, holding that RAG-based copying states a plausible copyright claim. The court identified infringement at two stages: first, by "copying a massive amount of Plaintiffs' copyrighted works as inputs into its RAG index," and second, by providing outputs containing "full or partial verbatim reproductions of Plaintiffs' copyrighted articles." The court treated RAG itself as the mechanism of infringement—not merely background plumbing—framing the indexing and repackaging of third-party content as direct copying. Trademark claims based on hallucinated attributions also survived.

**4. Other pending cases**
*Getty Images v. Stability AI* (D. Del. and UK High Court) and *In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation* (N.D. Cal.) are in earlier procedural stages. *Doe 1 v. GitHub* (N.D. Cal.) saw DMCA § 1202 claims survive in part.

### European Union

**5. GEMA v. OpenAI** (Munich I Regional Court, Nov. 11, 2025)
A landmark first-instance ruling that AI memorization of copyrighted works constitutes reproduction under copyright law, and the TDM exception does not cover training that results in memorization. The court found that GPT-4 and GPT-4o had "fixed" nine well-known German song lyrics in model parameters such that simple prompts elicited near-verbatim reproductions. Key holdings:

- **Memorization as reproduction**: The presence of protected texts encoded in model parameters, retrievable via simple prompts, constitutes fixation/reproduction under Article 2 InfoSoc Directive and § 16 German Copyright Act. The fact that encoding takes the form of probability weights does not preclude classification as a copy.
- **Output as further infringement**: Reproducing original elements in outputs constitutes additional reproduction; making outputs available to users constitutes communication to the public under § 19a UrhG. Responsibility rests with the provider, not users, because the provider controls architecture, data selection, and training.
- **TDM exception rejected**: The court rejected OpenAI's reliance on § 44b UrhG (implementing DSM Directive Article 4), holding that the TDM exception permits only preparatory copies for analytical purposes and does not extend to memorization or reproduction of entire works. Once an LLM produces reproducible works, the exploitation interests of rightsholders are affected and the TDM exception's scope is exceeded.
- The court did not refer the matter to the CJEU. The judgment is not yet final; OpenAI may appeal.

**6. LAION v. Kneschke** (Hamburg Regional Court)
Addressed the TDM exception for dataset collection, with the Hamburg court finding LAION's activities potentially covered. An appeal decision is scheduled for December 10, 2025.

---

## IV. Settled Requirements vs. Unresolved Questions

### Settled Requirements

| Jurisdiction | Settled |
|---|---|
| **US** | Copyright subsists in original works; reproduction and derivative-work rights are implicated when works are copied into datasets, during training, and when weights memorize protectable expression. Fair use is a four-factor, case-specific test with no per se rule for AI training. Outputs substantially similar to copyrighted training works can infringe. Standing requires registered copyright. |
| **US** | DMCA § 1202 prohibits intentional CMI removal with intent to induce or conceal infringement; some AI training preprocessing may implicate this. |
| **EU** | Commercial TDM is lawful unless a rightsholder has reserved rights via machine-readable means (DSM Directive Art. 4). Research TDM is permitted with lawful access (Art. 3). |
| **EU** | GPAI providers placing models on the EU market must implement a copyright compliance policy (AI Act Art. 53(1)(c)) and publish a training-content summary using the AI Office template (Art. 53(1)(d)). |
| **EU** | Rightsholders can opt out of TDM; providers must use "state of the art technologies" to identify reservations. |
| **EU** | GDPR independently applies to personal data in training sets. |

### Unresolved Questions

| Jurisdiction | Unresolved |
|---|---|
| **US** | Whether *any* generative-AI training on copyrighted works is fair use—no Circuit Court ruling exists on training per se. Whether *Ross* reasoning extends to generative AI with purposes different from training inputs. |
| **US** | Whether trained model weights themselves constitute infringing copies or derivative works when memorization occurs. |
| **US** | The legal status of RAG systems that retrieve, copy, and repackage third-party content in real time (plausibly infringing per *Dow Jones v. Perplexity*, but merits untested). |
| **US** | Whether there is an "opt-out" obligation for scraped data, and what constitutes adequate notice. |
| **EU** | Whether generative-AI training falls within the definition of "text and data mining" at all—*GEMA v. OpenAI* suggests the TDM exception does not cover training resulting in memorization. |
| **EU** | What precisely constitutes an "appropriate manner" of reservation under Article 4(3), and what "state of the art technologies" for detection are required. |
| **EU** | The territorial scope of Article 53(1)(c)—whether it applies to training done entirely outside the EU. |
| **EU** | Whether opt-outs can apply retroactively to works already ingested (BGH "Anastasia" case, with pending CJEU reference questions). |
| **EU** | How national courts will enforce against providers; no CJEU ruling yet on TDM and GPAI. |

---

## V. Implications: Model Developers vs. Enterprise Users

| Dimension | Model Developers | Enterprise Users |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary exposure** | Direct copyright infringement for training-data ingestion; contributory infringement for enabling user prompting that generates infringing outputs; DMCA § 1202 liability for CMI removal during preprocessing. | Vicarious or contributory liability if knowingly deploying systems that systematically output infringing material; contract breach if violating platform terms; potential direct liability for custom RAG configurations over third-party corpora. |
| **RAG / retrieval liability** | Developers operating RAG indices face direct claims for copying source works into vector databases (*Dow Jones v. Perplexity*). | Enterprises configuring custom RAG over proprietary or third-party corpora may face direct infringement for the retrieval and display steps. |
| **EU obligations** | Must implement Article 53 copyright policies, publish training summaries, and respect TDM opt-outs regardless of training location if placing on EU market. Must navigate *GEMA* holding that TDM exception may not cover training resulting in memorization. | As "deployers" under the AI Act, must comply with transparency and documentation obligations for high-risk systems; may face downstream liability if using non-compliant models. |
| **Fair use uncertainty** | Cannot rely on fair use as a blanket defense; must assess factor-by-factor for each training dataset and output category. | Generally do not invoke fair use themselves; depend on developer indemnification and warranties. |
| **Licensing burden** | Must negotiate or subscribe to licensed datasets; emerging market for AI-training licenses (Getty Images, Shutterstock, Axel Springer, Reddit, AP). | Can require contractual representations that models were trained on licensed or lawfully accessed data; should scrutinize scope. |
| **Indemnification** | May offer limited indemnity to enterprise customers—typically covering outputs, not training-data claims. | Should scrutinize scope; most provider indemnities exclude training-data claims, creating a significant gap. |
| **Insurance** | D&O insurers increasingly excluding AI IP risks; coverage for training infringement is rare. | General liability policies often exclude IP; specialized AI liability insurance is nascent and expensive. |

---

## VI. A Conservative Compliance Approach

This section outlines three strategic postures. This is descriptive, not legal advice.

**Option 1: Maximum Fair-Use Reliance with Output Guardrails**
Proceed on the assumption that broad training is fair use, relying on *Authors Guild v. Google* and technological-progress arguments. Implement output-filtering guardrails to reduce infringing generations, document the transformative purpose, and maintain a litigation reserve. This posture accepts maximum legal risk, betting that appellate courts will extend fair use to generative training while the EU trajectory (per *GEMA*) remains adverse.

**Option 2: Comprehensive Licensing-First Approach**
License all copyrighted training inputs, avoid all TDM-restricted works in the EU, and maintain chain-of-title documentation for every dataset. Use only public-domain, Creative Commons, or contractually cleared materials. This minimizes litigation risk but incurs significant cost and may limit model capability where licensing markets are thin or slow to develop.

**Option 3: Segmented Risk-Based Compliance with Geographic and Use-Case Differentiation**
Prioritize licensed or public-domain data for **high-risk categories** (expressive works: fiction, photography, music, journalism) where market substitution is most likely and rights-holder litigation is most active. Rely on lawfully accessed, publicly available data for **low-risk, factual categories** where fair-use arguments are stronger. In the **EU**, implement a rigorous TDM opt-out compliance program using machine-readable detection tools, respecting robots.txt and emerging standards; account for the *GEMA* holding by implementing deduplication and memorization-testing to ensure models do not reproduce protected works verbatim. Maintain **training-data provenance records**, publish the AI Office-mandated summary, and deploy **output guardrails** to block substantially similar reproductions. Secure **contractual indemnification and representations** from upstream model providers that are tailored to training-data claims, not just output claims. Conduct periodic **output audits** and maintain an insurance or reserve strategy for residual risk. Consider **jurisdictional segmentation**—deploying different models or inference configurations depending on deployment jurisdiction—until U.S. and EU laws converge.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 3 - Adopt a segmented risk-based compliance posture that prioritizes licensed or public-domain training data for high-risk expressive categories, deploys state-of-the-art opt-out compliance for all EU-facing models, implements output-filtering guardrails and memorization testing, and secures contractual indemnification from upstream providers, while maintaining detailed provenance documentation.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: U.S. appellate courts could reject fair use for generative-AI training entirely in pending cases, and EU courts (per GEMA v. OpenAI) may hold that the TDM exception never covers training resulting in memorization, forcing retroactive licensing or liability for unlicensed training data used in deployed models.

# Environmental Impact of Serving LLMs in Production: An Inference-Focused Analysis

## 1. Why Inference Now Dominates the Lifecycle

Training was the initial focus of AI sustainability debates, but inference has become the dominant lifecycle contributor for deployed models. Recent estimates suggest inference can account for up to 80–90% of a model's total lifecycle energy use. LLMCO2 (Fu et al., 2024) estimates that roughly 121 days of serving GPT-4 inference produces emissions comparable to training GPT-4—and as daily request volumes rise, this crossover period is shrinking. A single LLM query may consume only 0.3–1 Wh, but at hundreds of millions of requests per day, aggregate demand reaches utility scale.

---

## 2. Recent Per-Prompt Electricity, Water, and Emissions Estimates

### Electricity

| Source | Model / Setting | Per-prompt energy | Boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Google** (Aug 2025, Elsworth et al.) | Median Gemini Apps text prompt | **0.24 Wh** | Full serving stack: active accelerators + host CPU/RAM + idle capacity + PUE + water |
| **OpenAI** (Altman, Jun 2025) | "Average" ChatGPT query | **~0.34 Wh** | Unspecified; methodology not published |
| **Epoch AI** (Feb 2025) | GPT-4o | **~0.3 Wh** | ~1 second of H100 at ~1,500 W partial utilization, ~500 output tokens |
| **Jegham et al.** (2025) | GPT-4o short query | **0.43 Wh** | Infrastructure-aware model with region-specific multipliers |
| **Jegham et al.** (2025) | o3 / DeepSeek-R1 long prompt | **>33 Wh** | Same; reasoning models generate many more tokens |
| **Luccioni et al.** (2023) | BLOOM 176B via API | ~2–4 Wh (batch size 1) | Bottom-up hardware profiling; older models, no production batching |

The spread from ~0.24 Wh (Google Gemini) to >33 Wh (reasoning models)—a factor of over 140×—is driven primarily by **output token count**, **model size/precision**, and **reasoning depth**, not by measurement error alone. Google also reports a **33× reduction in energy** and **44× reduction in carbon footprint** for the median Gemini prompt over a 12-month period, demonstrating how rapidly software and hardware efficiency gains shift the numbers.

### Water

| Source | Estimate | What is counted |
|---|---|---|
| **Google** (2025) | **0.26 mL** per median Gemini prompt | Site + source water, comprehensive boundary |
| **OpenAI** (Altman, 2025) | **~0.32 mL** per query | Direct on-site cooling only; no methodology published |
| **UC Riverside** (Li et al., 2023) | **~10–25 mL** per query (GPT-3 era) | On-site cooling + some indirect (electricity generation) |
| **Washington Post / UC Riverside** (2024) | **~519 mL** for a 100-word GPT-4 email | Full lifecycle including electricity generation and training supply chain |

The ~1,500× range (0.26 mL to 519 mL) is almost entirely a **boundary problem**: cooling-only estimates count only evaporative cooling at the data center, while full-lifecycle estimates add the water consumed by power plants generating the electricity used by the data center. Neither is "wrong"—they measure different things. Regional Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) ranges from ~0.18 L/kWh (AWS US) to ~1.20 L/kWh (some Chinese data centers), producing a ~6× difference from location alone.

### Carbon

Per-prompt carbon depends on the **grid carbon intensity** where inference runs. Google reports 0.03 gCO₂e per median Gemini prompt, reflecting both efficiency gains and clean energy procurement. For 500M GPT-4o queries/day, Hoxha et al. (2025) show comprehensive-boundary totals of ~0.344 GWh electricity, ~1.196 ML water, and ~121 tCO₂ (location-based) per day—reducible to 0.145 GWh, 0.490 ML, and 25 tCO₂ with optimization. Grid intensity ranges from ~30 gCO₂e/kWh (Norwegian hydro) to ~850 gCO₂e/kWh (coal-heavy regions), meaning the same query can vary >25× in carbon depending on location.

---

## 3. The "Model Parking Tax": Idle GPU Power

A critical and underappreciated factor is the energy cost of keeping GPUs warm. Vadari (2026, "The Model Parking Tax") provides the first cross-architecture measurement of idle GPU power as a function of VRAM allocation, combining 18 days of production telemetry (335,267 samples, 14 H100 GPUs) with controlled experiments on H100, A100, and L40S.

Key findings:
- The CUDA context forces a discrete DVFS transition consuming **+26–66 W over bare idle** (26–50 W on HBM architectures, 66 W on GDDR6).
- The marginal VRAM effect is negligible: **<0.02 W/GB** on every device tested.
- The CUDA context accounts for **>98% of the parking tax** regardless of memory technology.
- Cold-start breakeven intervals are **1–5 minutes** depending on arrival rate and loading latency—not model size.

NVIDIA's `CUDA_DISABLE_PERF_BOOST` flag (driver series 580+) can eliminate the parking tax, dropping H100 idle from 128.6 W to 73.1 W (bare idle) with no measurable latency impact. This is an immediate, zero-cost intervention for operators.

---

## 4. Deployment Mode Comparison

### A. Fixed Dedicated GPUs

- **Utilization**: Typically 30–60% for production inference; often 5–15% for early-stage or spiky workloads. Lim et al. (CMU 2024) found that Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on datacenter GPUs running inference averages only ~2% of theoretical peak—98% of compute capacity sits idle.
- **Idle power**: An H100 draws ~100–150 W at bare idle, and with a CUDA context active, 121–128 W regardless of whether requests arrive. On a 4×H100 node, the parking tax is ~200 W continuously.
- **Environmental profile**: Worst per-query efficiency when utilization is low because idle power is paid continuously. Self-hosting only beats serverless on cost/efficiency when utilization exceeds ~22–48% (depending on GPU type). Below that, the idle parking tax makes dedicated GPUs 2–4× worse per useful token.
- **Embodied carbon**: Manufacturing an H100-class GPU emits an estimated 150–200 kg CO₂. A dedicated GPU with low utilization has very high embodied carbon per useful token.

### B. Autoscaled Endpoints

- **Utilization**: Better than fixed dedicated because capacity scales with demand, but production systems still require provisioned idle capacity for traffic spikes and failover. Google explicitly includes "idle machines" (10% of total energy) in its comprehensive measurement methodology.
- **Energy profile**: Intermediate between fixed and serverless. Autoscaling reduces idle waste but cannot eliminate it without risking latency SLO violations. DynamoLLM (Stojkovic et al., 2025, HPCA) showed dynamic reconfiguration (GPU frequency scaling, instance count, model parallelism) can conserve 52–53% energy and reduce operational carbon 38% under SLOs.
- **PUE advantage**: Managed endpoints in hyperscale data centers benefit from low PUE (1.08–1.12), versus typical on-premise PUE of 1.6–2.0.

### C. Serverless Inference

- **Utilization**: Serverless GPU platforms target **80–90% utilization** by aggregating demand across users and time zones, versus 30–60% for dedicated instances.
- **Energy per useful work**: Moving from 35% dedicated to 85% serverless utilization can more than halve energy per useful teraflop. Zero idle energy when not invoked eliminates the parking tax entirely.
- **Cold-start tradeoff**: The breakeven for keep-warm vs. cold-start is 1–5 minutes. For sporadic traffic (<1 request per 1–5 minutes), serverless is clearly optimal; for sustained streams, reloading wastes energy.
- **Festina** (Wang et al., 2026): A power-aware serverless scheduler that reduces energy consumption by up to **56%** while maintaining SLO attainment within a 2% margin. It coordinates request placement, SM partitioning, and GPU operating points under TTFT/TBT SLOs.
- **Caveat—the utilization fallacy**: Sinha et al. (HotCarbon 2025) showed that higher GPU utilization does **not always** improve carbon efficiency. Spatial sharing of GPUs can increase utilization while increasing total CO₂ if co-located models have mismatched resource profiles.

### D. External APIs

- **Transparency**: Google's 2025 disclosure is the most comprehensive first-party dataset. OpenAI's 0.34 Wh / 0.32 mL figure is a single blog-post sentence without methodology. Anthropic discloses nothing model-specific.
- **Grid mix and RECs**: Hyperscalers often claim near-zero carbon via Renewable Energy Certificates, but the physical generation mix where the server runs may still be fossil-heavy. "RECs are accounting, not physics." For accurate reporting, location-based grid intensity should be used rather than market-based REC-adjusted figures. Google's 0.03 gCO₂e uses market-based accounting; location-based would be ~3× higher.
- **Practical footprint**: External APIs shift environmental accounting to the provider but do not eliminate it. For high-volume workloads, self-hosting on a clean grid can have lower actual physical emissions than a cloud region relying on RECs but physically powered by fossil fuels.
- **Scale advantages**: Google reported a 33× energy reduction and 44× carbon reduction per prompt in one year through stack-wide optimization—improvements individual deployments cannot match.

**Comparative ranking by operational carbon per useful token** (for identical model and throughput):
1. **External APIs at scale** (best batching, provider optimization, renewable procurement)
2. **Serverless** (zero idle under low utilization; efficient multi-tenant sharing)
3. **Autoscaled endpoints** (moderate idle overhead)
4. **Fixed dedicated GPUs** (best only at sustained >50% utilization with aggressive batching)

This ranking inverts when **embodied carbon** is weighted: external APIs amortize hardware across billions of requests, while a dedicated GPU with low utilization has very high embodied carbon per useful token.

---

## 5. Reconciling Conflicting Estimates: The Assumptions That Drive Differences

| Driver | How it changes estimates | Magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| **System boundary** | Accelerator-only vs. full-stack (host CPU/RAM + idle + PUE). The narrow-to-comprehensive ratio is consistently ~0.417 (i.e., accelerator-only captures ~42% of total). | ~2.4× |
| **Query definition** | "Average query" is undefined. A 10-token greeting vs. a 5,000-token reasoning chain differ by >100×. | >100× |
| **Water boundary** | Cooling-only (0.26–4 mL) vs. cooling + electricity-generation water (10–519 mL). | ~1,500× |
| **Precision** | FP16 vs. INT8 vs. INT4. Gains are significant in compute-bound (prefill) phases but limited in memory-bound (decode) phases. | ~2× |
| **Batching and concurrency** | Batch size 1 vs. 64 reduces carbon per token by 11× with only 2× latency increase (Lim et al., CMU 2024). | ~11× |
| **Grid carbon intensity** | ~30 gCO₂e/kWh (Norway hydro) to ~850 gCO₂e/kWh (coal-heavy regions). | >25× |
| **Hardware generation** | H100 vs. B200 vs. older A100; Google's 33× efficiency gain over 12 months. | Up to 33× |
| **Utilization pattern** | A GPU idle 92% of the day inflates per-prompt emissions by 10–50× vs. one running near-continuously. | 10–50× |
| **Carbon accounting method** | Location-based (physical grid mix) vs. market-based (REC-adjusted) can change reported carbon by an order of magnitude. | ~3–10× |

No single "answer" exists. Google's 0.24 Wh and Jegham's 0.43 Wh for short GPT-4o queries are reconcilable: Google includes fleet-wide optimization (speculative decoding, disaggregated serving, high batching) that external benchmarks cannot capture. Jegham's 1.79 Wh for a long GPT-4o query reflects a different operating point on prompt length. The accelerator-to-comprehensive ratio of ~0.417, confirmed by Hoxha et al., provides a translation key between studies using different boundaries.

---

## 6. Practical Measurement Strategies

1. **Adopt a comprehensive serving boundary**: Follow Google's methodology—include active accelerator power, host CPU/DRAM, idle/provisioned capacity, and data center overhead (PUE). Accelerator-only measurements understate true footprint by ~2.4×.

2. **Use standardized benchmarks**: The **AI Energy Score** (HuggingFace) provides star-rated energy efficiency comparisons on standardized hardware. The **ML.ENERGY Benchmark** (NeurIPS 2025) measures energy, latency, and quality for LLMs on H100 and B200. **TokenPowerBench** provides phase-aligned energy attribution to prefill and decode stages.

3. **Instrument at token/phase granularity**: Separate prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases. Tools: NVIDIA DCGM (`dcgmi`), `pyJoules`, Intel RAPL for host power, and the Zeus library for GPU energy profiling.

4. **Track water with dual boundaries**: Report both site-only (evaporative cooling) and site+source (including electricity-generation water) using region-specific Electricity Water Intensity Factors (EWIF).

5. **Use location-based carbon accounting**: Cite the grid region's actual carbon intensity (from electricityMaps or WattTime) rather than market-based RECs, especially for sustainability disclosures under CSRD or SEC rules.

6. **Include embodied carbon**: Amortize GPU manufacturing emissions (~150–200 kg CO₂ per H100) over expected device lifetime and usage. The CMU finding of 2% MFU suggests massive overprovisioning—deploying inference-optimized hardware with less compute but sufficient memory bandwidth can reduce embodied carbon substantially.

7. **Normalize by useful work**: Use tokens per joule or gCO₂eq per useful token, not per wall-clock hour. This prevents conflating throughput with efficiency.

---

## 7. Practical Reduction Strategies (Ranked by Demonstrated Impact)

| Strategy | Demonstrated reduction | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Model selection / routing** (small models for routine tasks, frontier for hard tasks) | 50–500× energy for blended workloads; GPT-4.1 nano uses 70× less energy than o3 | Jegham et al., 2025 |
| **Request arrival shaping / batching** | Up to **11×** carbon per token (batch 1→64, 2× latency increase) | Lim et al., CMU 2024 |
| **Bi-objective carbon+water optimization** (region routing, batching, phase-aware hardware) | **57–59%** energy, **59–60%** water, **78–80%** CO₂ | Hoxha et al., 2025, Sustainability 17(23):10473 |
| **Serverless with energy-aware scheduling** (Festina) | Up to **56%** cluster energy reduction, SLO parity within 2% | Wang et al., 2026, arXiv:2606.30391 |
| **Dynamic frequency/instance scaling** (DynamoLLM) | **52–53%** energy, 38% carbon, 61% cost under SLOs | Stojkovic et al., 2025, HPCA |
| **CUDA_DISABLE_PERF_BOOST** (eliminate parking tax) | H100 idle: 128→73 W (zero-cost, zero-latency-impact) | Vadari, 2026; SGLang issue #27567 |
| **Carbon-aware geographic routing** | **35%** emission reduction today (56% by 2035) | Chien et al., HotCarbon 2023 |
| **Renewable-powered regions** | Up to **69.2%** renewable offset potential | Özcan et al., 2025 |
| **Hardware reuse / disaggregation** | Up to **40.6%** total carbon reduction | GreenLLM, Shi et al., 2024 |
| **Quantization (INT8/INT4)** | Significant in compute-bound phases; limited in memory-bound decode | Multiple studies |
| **Speculative decoding and KV caching** | Major contributor to Google's 33× annual efficiency gain | Google, 2025 |

---

## 8. Recommendation Options

**Option 1:** Adopt a comprehensive-boundary measurement framework (active accelerators + host CPU/RAM + idle capacity + PUE + site+source water + location-based carbon), then apply a layered reduction strategy: (a) route to the smallest sufficient model, (b) use continuous batching and request arrival shaping, (c) deploy on serverless or autoscaled infrastructure with energy-aware schedulers, (d) choose low-carbon-intensity regions, (e) apply quantization and phase-aware hardware disaggregation, (f) enable CUDA_DISABLE_PERF_BOOST to eliminate the parking tax on dedicated GPUs.

**Option 2:** Default to external APIs from providers with audited energy disclosures (e.g., Google's Gemini methodology), and rely on their efficiency gains; self-host only when sustained utilization exceeds ~30–40%.

**Option 3:** Prioritize single-lever optimization: move all inference to serverless GPU platforms to maximize utilization and minimize idle waste, accepting cold-start tradeoffs.

**Option 4:** Focus exclusively on model-level optimizations (quantization, pruning, distillation) without changing deployment infrastructure.

---

RECOMMENDATION: 1 Adopt a comprehensive-boundary measurement framework (active accelerators + host CPU/RAM + idle capacity + PUE + site+source water + location-based carbon), then apply a layered reduction strategy: (a) route to the smallest sufficient model, (b) use continuous batching and request arrival shaping, (c) deploy on serverless or autoscaled infrastructure with energy-aware schedulers, (d) choose low-carbon-intensity regions, (e) apply quantization and phase-aware hardware disaggregation, (f) enable CUDA_DISABLE_PERF_BOOST to eliminate the parking tax on dedicated GPUs.

### Why prefix-caching (Option 1) is the highest-impact choice

**The dominant cost is prefill, not generation.** A 60k-token prefix means prefill computes attention across tens of thousands of tokens before the first output token appears. With only ~200 output tokens, generation time is comparatively trivial. Prefix caching stores the KV cache from the already-computed prefix, so on a cache hit the engine skips straight to processing the short user-specific suffix (a few hundred tokens). TTFT drops from "prefill 60k tokens" to "prefill ~200 tokens" — potentially a 100x+ reduction in time-to-first-token for the 80% of requests that share the revision.

**Why the other options are inferior for this specific scenario:**

| Option | Why it's weaker |
|---|---|
| **Prompt-compression** (2) | Adds its own preprocessing latency and risks information loss; doesn't exploit the exact-repeat pattern the way caching does. |
| **Smaller long-context model** (3) | Major engineering change with quality risk; the bottleneck is redundant prefill, not model capacity. |
| **Speculative-decoding** (4) | Targets tokens-per-second during *generation*, not TTFT. With 200-token outputs, it barely helps. |
| **Repository-RAG** (5) | Adds retrieval latency, risks missing relevant context, and still requires prefilling whatever chunks are retrieved. Strictly more complex than caching an exact prefix. |

If that tail matters, a secondary mitigation (e.g., warming the cache on new commits) can be layered on top.
