# Environmental Impact of Serving Large Language Models in Production (Inference Focus)

## 1. Why inference now dominates the AI footprint

Training was the early flashpoint, but it happens once or rarely. Inference runs billions of times per day and never stops. Recent industry estimates put inference at roughly **80–90% of total AI compute energy**, with training the remainder. A frontier training run may draw ~20–25 MW for a few months, but the continuous draw of ChatGPT-class inference already matches or exceeds that every single day.

The core paradox is that **per-query numbers are tiny, but aggregate numbers are large.** Google reports the median Gemini text prompt uses **0.24 Wh, 0.03 gCO₂e, and 0.26 mL water**—"less than nine seconds of television." Yet scaling even a ~0.43 Wh GPT-4o query to ~700 million queries/day yields annual electricity comparable to ~35,000 U.S. homes, freshwater evaporation matching the annual drinking needs of ~1.2 million people, and carbon emissions requiring a Chicago-sized forest to offset. This cheap-per-call, enormous-in-aggregate dynamic is the framing for any production comparison.

## 2. Recent per-query estimates and how to reconcile them

| Source (year) | Per-query energy | Per-query water | Per-query CO₂e | Scope/boundary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google Gemini (Aug 2025, measured) | 0.24 Wh median (chip-only 58%) | 0.26 mL | 0.03 g | Full-stack: active accelerators + host CPU/RAM (25%) + idle/backup (10%) + PUE (8%) + DC water |
| Microsoft Oviedo et al. (Sept 2025, bottom-up) | 0.34 Wh median (IQR 0.18–0.67) for >200B on 8×H100 | <0.067 mL | region-scaled | Steady-state saturated serving; node power + PUE + redundancy |
| Jegham et al. "How Hungry is AI" (May 2025) | 0.43 Wh short GPT-4o; >33 Wh long o3/DeepSeek-R1 | region-scaled | region-scaled | Public API latency/throughput + inferred hardware + regional multipliers |
| ML.Energy leaderboard (U. Michigan) | 0.21 Wh Llama 3.1 405B; ~1.86 Wh largest text | not given | not given | Direct GPU measurement on fixed hardware |
| UC Riverside / Washington Post (Sept 2024, GPT-4) | not given | up to 519 mL (Texas worst case) | not given | Full lifecycle incl. electricity-generation water + hot region |
| UC Riverside revised (May 2026) | not given | ~15 mL total (~5 mL DC-only) | not given | On-site + some indirect; original 519 mL now 33× too high |
| Sam Altman (mid-2025, disclosed) | ~0.3 Wh (average query) | ~0.3 mL | not given | On-site DC cooling only; methodology undisclosed |
| Microsoft cloud blog (June 2026) | 0.16–0.60 Wh | <one drop | region-scaled | Production-scale; "4–20× lower than prior reports" |

The spread of roughly **three orders of magnitude** is almost entirely explained by boundary choices and operating assumptions:

1. **Measurement boundary.** GPU-only draws give the lowest numbers (Google's chip-only share is 58% of the full 0.24 Wh). Adding host CPU/RAM, idle/backup machines, networking, and PUE multiplies the figure upward. Including off-site water from electricity generation adds another large multiple, especially in water-thirsty grids.
2. **Production vs. non-production conditions.** Microsoft finds many public estimates assume small-batch, single-request settings and are overstated by **4–20×**. Real production uses continuous batching, high concurrency, and steady-state saturation; throughput per watt is far higher.
3. **Model size and workload.** Model size is the largest single driver. Llama 3.1 8B uses ~0.03 Wh; the 50× larger 405B uses ~1.86 Wh. Reasoning/test-time scaling is even more extreme: Microsoft reports median energy rises ~13× when outputs are 15× longer, and Jegham et al. measure >33 Wh for long o3/DeepSeek-R1 prompts.
4. **Region and grid carbon/water intensity.** Carbon intensity ranges from ~50 gCO₂/kWh in renewable-rich areas to >800 gCO₂/kWh in coal-dependent regions—a 16× spread for the same electricity. Water intensity of electricity generation (EWIF) varies similarly, so "full lifecycle" water figures are dominated by where the data center is plugged in.
5. **PUE and cooling architecture.** Hyperscaler PUE is often ~1.05–1.10; older or less efficient facilities can be 1.4+. Evaporative cooling consumes water on-site but can lower energy/PUE; air-cooled or liquid-cooled designs shift the trade-off. Microsoft's "zero water" DC designs push on-site water toward zero.
6. **Idle/overprovisioning.** Production systems keep capacity idle for failover and spikes. Google explicitly counts idle backup machines (~10%), and Microsoft scales node-level estimates by ~1.31× for non-uniform demand, redundancy, and networking. Ignoring idle (as many benchmarks do) underestimates real fleet energy.

The "bottle of water per email" claim is now widely understood to be a worst case, not a typical one. Shaolei Ren, who originated the 519 mL estimate, has reportedly agreed actual GPT-4 water use is ~15 mL/prompt (~5 mL in the DC itself), ~33× lower. Current best-supported per-prompt figures for text are a few drops to a few mL of water and ~0.2–0.4 Wh of electricity, with large variance from model size, output length, region, and whether idle/overhead is counted.

## 3. Comparison across deployment modes

The environmental impact of a deployment is not determined by per-query chip energy alone; it is dominated by **utilization, idle power, batching quality, and grid location.** The same model can vary by orders of magnitude in energy-per-useful-token depending on how it is served.

### Fixed dedicated GPUs (always-on, single-tenant)
- **Utilization:** Typically the worst for waste unless traffic is steady. Most teams run below 70% GPU allocation even at peak, with common numbers 10–20%. A GPU kept only 5–10% busy is 2–4× more expensive than serverless and wastes most of its energy on idle draw.
- **Energy profile:** GPUs draw substantial power even idle. Batch size 1 can push cost/energy per token ~44× higher than saturated operation. Low-duty-cycle dedicated servers have very high energy-per-useful-token.
- **Best for:** Sustained, predictable, latency-sensitive traffic where the GPU stays above ~40–70% utilization. Then per-token energy is lowest because batching and saturation amortize idle overhead.
- **Emissions:** Determined by the DC's PUE and the local grid's carbon/water intensity. A dedicated GPU in a coal-heavy region can emit 10–16× more than the same GPU in a renewable-rich region for identical compute.

### Autoscaled endpoints (managed, scale with traffic, keep warm)
- **Utilization:** Better than fixed dedicated because capacity scales with demand, reducing idle waste during troughs. "Dedicated inference with burst capacity" is the fastest-growing segment, combining reserved capacity for primary traffic with elastic burst for spikes.
- **Cold starts:** Historically a penalty (15–30 s for 70B models on self-managed serverless), but managed platforms have reduced this to seconds or milliseconds using weight caching, snapshots, and checkpoint/restore (Modal cut cold starts ~40×).
- **Energy profile:** Lower idle overhead than fixed dedicated; per-token energy approaches the saturated best case when traffic fills the warmed instances, but still incurs overprovisioning for failover. Break-even vs. serverless is typically around **40–66% sustained utilization** depending on the serverless price premium (20–40%).
- **Best for:** Moderate, somewhat predictable traffic with occasional spikes where latency consistency and isolation matter.

### Serverless inference (pay per token, scale to zero)
- **Utilization:** Highest sharing efficiency at low/spiky utilization—the provider packs many tenants onto shared GPUs, so your idle is someone else's useful work. Serverless is cheaper than self-hosted until the GPU is **22–48% busy**; below ~10% duty cycle, self-hosting is 2–4× more expensive.
- **Energy profile:** Minimal idle waste for the customer; the platform still maintains warm pools, so total system idle isn't zero, but it's amortized across tenants. Per-token energy can be higher at high concurrency because of multi-tenant scheduling overhead.
- **Cold starts:** Can add latency and, historically, energy from model loading; modern caching mitigates this. For bursty workloads, the avoided idle energy usually dominates.
- **Best for:** Spiky, unpredictable, low-volume, or experimental traffic; batch jobs that run a few hours/day; demos. Reliability ceiling: shared infrastructure cannot guarantee p99 latency or prevent noisy-neighbor effects.

### External APIs (provider-managed, opaque)
- **Utilization:** You inherit the provider's efficiency. Google and OpenAI report ~0.24–0.34 Wh/prompt, reflecting hyperscale batching, custom TPUs/GPUs, low PUE (~1.09), and clean-energy procurement. This is often more efficient per token than self-hosting for small-to-moderate workloads, because the provider saturates its fleet across billions of requests.
- **Energy profile:** Opaque. You cannot measure idle, batching, or hardware directly. You depend on provider disclosures (Google's methodology is the most comprehensive; OpenAI's is a single undisclosed figure). The provider may also route your request to a more or less carbon-intensive region without your knowledge.
- **Best for:** Most teams, especially early stage, because it avoids idle dedicated GPUs and leverages hyperscale efficiency. Trade-off: lack of measurement transparency and limited control over location/carbon.

### Rough qualitative comparison

| Dimension | Fixed dedicated | Autoscaled endpoint | Serverless | External API |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Idle energy waste | High if underutilized | Moderate | Low (amortized) | Hidden (provider-managed) |
| Per-token energy at high load | Lowest (saturated batching) | Low | Moderate (sharing overhead) | Low (hyperscale) |
| Per-token energy at low/spiky load | Worst | Moderate | Best | Low |
| Control over region/grid carbon | High (if you choose DC) | High | Moderate | Low/opaque |
| Measurement transparency | Full | Full | Partial | Low |
| Cold-start penalty | None | Some (mitigated) | Some (mitigated) | None |
| Best use case | Steady high traffic | Moderate traffic + spikes | Spiky/low volume | Most teams, early stage |

## 4. Assumptions driving disagreement

- **Boundary:** GPU-only vs. full-stack (CPU/RAM + idle + PUE + DC water) can change estimates by ~2–4×; adding electricity-generation water can add another 10–100× in water estimates.
- **Utilization:** Assumed near-saturation (Microsoft, Google) vs. small-batch/single-request (many benchmarks) drives 4–20× differences.
- **Model size and output length:** 50× model size → ~50× energy; reasoning/test-time scaling 15× longer output → ~13× energy; long o3/DeepSeek-R1 prompts can exceed 33 Wh.
- **PUE and cooling:** 1.05 vs. 1.4 PUE = ~33% energy difference; evaporative vs. air cooling shifts the water-vs-energy trade-off.
- **Grid carbon/water intensity:** Same kWh can emit 50–800+ gCO₂ and consume very different water depending on region and time of day.
- **Idle/overprovisioning:** Ignoring idle underestimates fleet energy; Google and Microsoft add explicit idle and redundancy factors (~1.31×).
- **Provider disclosure:** Google's measured 0.24 Wh is comprehensive and verified; OpenAI's ~0.3 Wh is a single undisclosed figure; third-party API-based estimates (Jegham et al.) infer hardware and can over- or under-state depending on assumptions.

## 5. Practical measurement strategies

1. **Measure full-stack, not just GPU.** Use tools like CodeCarbon, GreenAlgorithms, the ML.Energy leaderboard methods, or TokenPowerBench that capture GPU, CPU, RAM, and PUE. Attribute energy to prefill vs. decode phases (decode usually dominates).
2. **Track utilization and idle separately.** Log GPU SM utilization, batch size, and duty cycle per model—not just cluster aggregates. Batch-1 operation can be ~44× worse than saturated operation per token; idle GPUs still draw baseline power.
3. **Use region-specific multipliers.** Apply hourly carbon intensity (e.g., Electricity Maps) and water-use effectiveness (WUE) plus electricity water intensity factors for the actual grid serving the request. Carbon-aware schedulers can reduce operational emissions by ~27–57% depending on approach.
4. **Benchmark with realistic traffic.** Avoid single-request/small-batch benchmarks for production planning; they overestimate energy 4–20×. Use continuous batching, concurrency, and your actual prompt/output length distributions.
5. **For external APIs, request provider disclosures** (energy/prompt, water/prompt, carbon/prompt, region, PUE, CFE matching). Google's methodology paper is the current gold standard; press other providers for comparable boundaries.

## 6. Practical reduction strategies

- **Right-size the model.** A 50× larger model can cost 50× the energy for marginally better answers. Use the smallest model that meets quality; route by task complexity.
- **Limit reasoning/test-time scaling.** Reasoning models can use up to 43× more energy on simple problems. Don't point a chain-of-thought model at a task a classifier would finish.
- **Maximize batching and concurrency.** Arrival shaping can reduce per-request energy up to 100×; batching improves energy efficiency especially in memory-bound decode.
- **Choose the right deployment mode by traffic profile.** Serverless for spiky/low volume; dedicated/autoscaled only above ~40–66% sustained utilization. Avoid idle dedicated GPUs.
- **Quantize and use efficient serving frameworks.** FP8/INT8 quantization, vLLM/TensorRT-LLM/SGLang, prefill/decode disaggregation. Microsoft estimates 8–20× line-of-sight energy reductions across model, serving, and hardware layers.
- **Locate in low-carbon, low-water regions and match 24/7.** Carbon-aware workload shifting and 24/7 CFE matching attack the carbon/water multiplier, not just kWh.
- **Gate and monitor workflows.** Retry storms, prompt bloat, and abandoned outputs can dominate spend and energy upstream of the GPU. Human-in-the-loop approval gates act as circuit breakers on token spend.
- **Prefer providers with transparent, full-stack measurement.** If using external APIs, choose those disclosing per-prompt energy/water/carbon with clear boundaries and 24/7 CFE progress.

## 7. Unresolved uncertainties

- Provider figures (especially OpenAI) are not independently verifiable; methodology and region routing are opaque.
- Water estimates are highly sensitive to grid EWIF and cooling architecture, which providers rarely disclose per-request.
- Most third-party benchmarks infer hardware from API latency/throughput; accuracy depends on assumptions about batching, precision, and serving stack.
- Aggregate inference energy projections (e.g., 165–326 TWh by 2028) assume continued adoption and model sizes; actual trajectory depends on efficiency gains, which Google and Microsoft show can be 8–44× in a year.

RECOMMENDATION: 1 Measure full-stack energy (GPU+CPU+RAM+PUE+idle), use region-specific carbon/water multipliers, and match deployment mode to traffic profile: serverless for spiky/low load, autoscaled/dedicated only above ~40-66% sustained utilization, external APIs for most teams until self-hosting stays genuinely busy.
CONFIDENCE: medium
TOP_RISK: Inference's aggregate footprint is dominated by low-utilization dedicated GPUs and opaque provider grids, so per-query efficiency gains can be overwhelmed by idle waste and high-carbon regions unless utilization and location are measured and managed.

# Legal and Policy Landscape: Copyrighted Material in Generative-AI Training and Retrieval Systems (US and EU)

This analysis separates settled requirements from unresolved questions, compares implications for model developers and enterprise users, and outlines a conservative compliance approach. It is informational only and does not constitute legal advice.

---

## I. United States

### A. Statutory and Regulatory Framework

**Copyright Act (17 U.S.C.).** No AI-specific copyright statute exists. Unauthorized reproduction of copyrighted works is infringement (§ 106), subject to fair use (§ 107). The Supreme Court in *Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith*, 598 U.S. 508 (2023), reaffirmed that transformativeness must be assessed in context, with the first and fourth fair-use factors often carrying significant weight. Unlike the EU, the US has no statutory text-and-data-mining (TDM) exception.

**U.S. Copyright Office – Part 3 Report (pre-publication, May 9, 2025).** The Office's long-awaited report on generative-AI training reaches several influential, though non-binding, conclusions:

- **Prima facie infringement is likely at multiple stages.** Copying works to collect, curate, and train generative models generally implicates the reproduction right. The report identifies reproduction risks at four stages: data collection/curation, training, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and outputs. Where a model can reproduce substantial portions of training data, the model weights themselves may embody infringing copies.
- **Fair use is "often" transformative but not categorically.** Training on large, diverse datasets "will often be transformative," but transformativeness is a matter of degree and depends on deployment context. Uses like research and content moderation are viewed more favorably; models generating outputs substantially similar to inputs are less transformative.
- **Unlawful access weighs strongly against fair use.** Knowing use of pirated datasets or paywall circumvention is "not determinative" but bears heavily on the character of the use.
- **Guardrails favor fair use.** Technical measures preventing infringing outputs (prompt filtering, output filters, anti-memorization techniques) enhance transformativeness.
- **Market harm is multifaceted.** Direct substitution, lost licensing opportunities, and a novel "market dilution" theory (flooding a genre with AI-generated works) can all weigh against fair use.
- **No recommendation for compulsory or statutory licensing yet.** The Office endorses voluntary licensing, with intervention reserved for demonstrated market failures.
- **RAG-specific risk.** The report explicitly addresses RAG in Section III.C, noting reproduction occurs both when material is copied into a retrieval database and when retrieved content is copied at generation time to augment responses.

### B. Major Court Developments (2023–2025)

Three 2025 summary-judgment rulings now frame US AI-training fair-use doctrine, alongside a pivotal RAG ruling:

**Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. Ross Intelligence Inc., No. 1:20-cv-613-SB (D. Del. Feb. 11, 2025).** The first merits ruling on AI training and fair use. Ross used Westlaw headnotes (via "Bulk Memos") to train a competing legal-research AI tool after Thomson Reuters refused to license. The court found direct infringement and rejected fair use: the use was commercial and non-transformative because Ross's tool served the same purpose as Westlaw and directly competed. The court rejected intermediate-copying analogies from software cases because the copied material (headnotes) was not a computer program. Fourth-factor market harm weighed heavily because Ross built a competing product. *Significance:* Use of copyrighted material to build a directly competing AI product is likely infringement.

**Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, No. C 24-05417 WHA (N.D. Cal. June 23, 2025).** Anthropic downloaded millions of books from pirate sites and also purchased and scanned print books, retaining both in a permanent "central library." Plaintiffs did not allege infringing outputs. The court issued a split ruling:
- **Training use:** Fair use. "Quintessentially transformative" because LLMs consume books to learn statistical patterns, not to reproduce expression.
- **Library use of purchased print books:** Fair use. Digitizing lawfully purchased copies for internal storage/search was transformative and reasonable.
- **Library use of pirated copies:** Not fair use. Downloading and retaining pirated digital copies was not transformative and displaced the market for lawful copies. This is likely to proceed to trial on damages.
*Significance:* Strongly endorses fair use for training where outputs are filtered, but creates clear liability for acquiring and retaining pirated sources.

**Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 23-cv-03417-VC (N.D. Cal. June 25, 2025).** Meta downloaded books (including from shadow libraries via torrent) to train Llama LLMs. Plaintiffs did not allege infringing outputs; Meta post-trained to reduce memorization. The court found training "highly transformative"; LLMs "consume" books to learn patterns rather than to entertain. The fourth factor favored Meta because plaintiffs failed to produce concrete evidence of market dilution or lost licensing revenue. The court acknowledged that AI could flood markets but held plaintiffs had not proven it. Use of shadow libraries was noted as relevant to bad faith but "didn't move the needle." Distribution-based claims (seeding torrents) survived. *Significance:* A pro-developer ruling, but the court explicitly invited future plaintiffs to present stronger market-harm evidence. The opinion has been criticized for requiring quantified market-harm evidence that only defendants control.

**Dow Jones & Co. v. Perplexity AI, Inc., No. 24 Civ. 7984 (KPF) (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 21, 2025).** A motion-to-dismiss ruling that kept the case alive and offered a candid view of RAG. Judge Failla identified Perplexity's RAG database as the mechanism by which infringement allegedly occurred, recognizing claims at both ends: (1) copying articles into the RAG index (input-side), and (2) providing outputs containing full or partial verbatim reproductions (output-side). *Significance:* First judicial treatment of RAG as a distinct infringement mechanism, framing both the indexing and the retrieval-generation process as copyright-relevant copying.

**Other pending matters include:** *Authors Guild v. OpenAI & Microsoft* (S.D.N.Y.), *New York Times Co. v. Microsoft/OpenAI* (S.D.N.Y.), *Getty Images v. Stability AI* (D. Del. and UK), *Huckabee v. Bloomberg*, and *Advance Local Media v. Cohere*.

**Circuit split in the making.** *Thomson Reuters* (Delaware) rejected fair use; *Bartz* and *Kadrey* (N.D. Cal.) largely accepted it for training while condemning pirated libraries. The different outcomes turn heavily on (i) whether outputs reproduce expression, (ii) whether the use competes with the originals, and (iii) source legality.

### C. Settled vs. Unresolved in the US

**Relatively settled:**
- Unauthorized copying of copyrighted works to train AI is prima facie infringement of the reproduction right (even if intermediate).
- Fair use is the principal defense; it is fact-specific and not categorical.
- Where outputs substantially reproduce protected expression, liability is likely (and the Copyright Office suggests model weights themselves may be infringing).
- DMCA § 1202 CMI-removal claims generally fail where outputs are not identical or near-identical to inputs (*Andersen v. Stability AI*).
- AI-generated works without sufficient human authorship are not registrable (Part 2 report, *Zarya of the Dawn*).

**Unresolved:**
- Whether training is fair use as a general matter (courts are split; the Copyright Office says "often" but not always).
- The legal status of model weights as infringing copies.
- The viability of the "market dilution" theory of fourth-factor harm without proof of direct substitution.
- Whether use of pirated or shadow-library sources is categorically fatal to fair use or merely a negative factor (the *Bartz*/*Kadrey* split).
- Whether a lost-licensing-revenue theory is circular or valid.
- The scope of secondary liability for downstream deployers, especially for RAG systems.
- Whether and how collective or compulsory licensing should be instituted.
- Whether state-law claims (right of publicity, unfair competition, breach of contract for scraped TOS) complement or conflict with copyright preemption.
- The extent to which RAG indexing and retrieval constitute distinct infringing acts versus training.

---

## II. European Union

### A. Statutory Framework

**Copyright in the Digital Single Market (CDSM) Directive (EU) 2019/790.** Article 4 creates a general TDM exception: TDM of lawfully accessible works is permitted unless the rightsholder expressly reserves the rights ("opt-out") in an appropriate manner, including machine-readable means. Article 3 provides a narrower, non-overrideable TDM exception for scientific research. Whether generative-AI training "qualifies" as TDM under Article 4 is debated; most commentary and the AI Act assume it does, but structural ambiguities persist.

**AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.** Entered into force August 1, 2024; GPAI provisions applicable from August 2, 2025. Key copyright-relevant provisions:
- **Article 53(1)(c):** Providers of general-purpose AI models must put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and in particular to identify and comply with a reservation of rights expressed under Article 4(3) CDSMD (i.e., honor TDM opt-outs), including through state-of-the-art technologies.
- **Article 53(1)(d):** Providers must draw up and make publicly available a "sufficiently detailed summary" of the content used for training, using a template published by the AI Office.
- **Article 55:** Additional obligations for GPAI models with systemic risk (based on compute thresholds, generally ≥10²⁵ FLOPs).
- **Article 56 / GPAI Code of Practice:** The Code is a voluntary conformity tool; adherence yields a presumption of conformity with Article 53. The first Code was published July 10, 2025, with chapters on Transparency, Copyright, and Safety/Security. Major providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Mistral, Amazon, Cohere, IBM, among others) have signed.

**AI Office Template for the Training Data Summary.** Published July 24, 2025; mandatory even for providers that do not sign the Code. The template requires a narrative description of main data collections/sets, data sources, and other content, balancing transparency with trade-secret protection.

**Key recent EU ruling: GEMA v. OpenAI (Munich I Regional Court, Nov. 11, 2025, Case No. 42 O 14139/24).** The court found that memorization of song lyrics within OpenAI's models constituted reproduction under EU and German copyright law. It distinguished three phases: (1) extracting/converting training material into machine-readable format (where TDM exception applies), (2) analyzing data and training the model (where memorization exceeds TDM scope), and (3) using the trained model through prompts/outputs (communication to the public). The court held the TDM exception does not cover Phase 2 or 3. This is a significant rightsholder victory and may influence the pending CJEU reference in Case C-250/25 (*Like Company v. Google Ireland*), the first CJEU case on generative AI and copyright.

### B. Settled vs. Unresolved in the EU

**Relatively settled:**
- There is a TDM exception under CDSM Article 4 subject to rightsholder opt-out.
- GPAI providers must (i) implement a copyright compliance policy that honors opt-outs and (ii) publish a training-data summary, from August 2, 2025.
- The GPAI Code of Practice offers a presumption of conformity for signatories.
- Copyright is territorial; US fair use does not apply in the EU, and the scope of TDM exceptions differs across Member States.

**Unresolved:**
- Whether generative-AI training "is" TDM at all, and whether memorization in model weights falls outside the TDM exception (GEMA v. OpenAI says yes; CJEU Case C-250/25 may clarify).
- Extraterritorial scope: must a US-developed model honor EU opt-outs for training done outside the EU if the model is later deployed in the EU?
- Whether the opt-out obligation applies to training conducted before a model is "placed on the market."
- How "sufficiently detailed" the training-data summary must be in practice.
- Whether the TDM exception is compatible with the three-step test and authors' fair remuneration.
- The status of outputs that memorize or reproduce training data (GEMA v. OpenAI found this to be communication to the public, infringing).
- Whether collective licensing can scale to AI-training use cases.
- Whether RAG systems that copy content into retrieval databases or retrieve content at inference time fall within or outside the TDM exception.

---

## III. RAG and Retrieval Systems: Distinct Legal Risks

RAG presents copyright risks that are analytically distinct from pre-training:

**Input-side (indexing):** Copying copyrighted works into a vector database or retrieval index constitutes reproduction. The US Copyright Office Part 3 report (Section III.C) identifies this as a prima facie infringement risk. In *Dow Jones v. Perplexity*, the court treated the RAG index as the primary mechanism of copying, recognizing claims for "copying a massive amount of Plaintiffs' copyrighted works as inputs into its RAG index."

**Output-side (retrieval and generation):** When a RAG system retrieves content at inference time and weaves it into generated responses, this involves additional reproduction. The Copyright Office notes that both methods of RAG—copying material into a developer-controlled database or retrieving from external sources at generation time—involve making reproductions.

**Distinction from training:** RAG copying may be harder to defend as fair use or TDM because it often involves more direct, purposeful use of expressive content to generate responsive outputs, rather than statistical pattern-learning. In the EU, the GEMA court's phase-based analysis suggests RAG retrieval and generation fall outside the TDM exception (which covers only Phase 1 analytical extraction).

---

## IV. Provider Policies and Indemnification

Major providers have rolled out customer-facing IP protections, but coverage is uneven and heavily caveated:

- **OpenAI:** API and ChatGPT Enterprise/Business/Edu/Healthcare customers receive output-infringement indemnity. Exclusions include: customer knew output was infringing; safety/filtering features disabled; outputs modified or combined with non-OpenAI services; customer lacked rights to inputs/fine-tuning data; trademark claims; third-party-offering content. Beta services excluded. Training-data indemnity is not expressly offered.
- **Anthropic:** Commercial Terms include a "Customer Shield" covering both authorized use of services and outputs, with some reference to training data. Carve-outs include willful misconduct, modifications, combinations with non-Anthropic technology, and certain trademark/patent claims.
- **Google Cloud:** Two-pronged indemnity (October 2023): (1) training-data indemnity covering allegations that Google's use of training data infringes IP; (2) generated-output indemnity. Generally regarded as the broadest.
- **Microsoft:** Copilot Copyright Commitment for commercial customers, covering output-infringement claims subject to use restrictions and guardrail requirements.
- **Common limitations:** Indemnities typically do not cover open-weight or consumer/free-tier use, customer-provided training data for fine-tuning, knowingly infringing prompts, or disabled safety features. They are contractual defenses, not regulatory safe harbors.

These indemnities reduce but do not eliminate enterprise risk: they generally do not cover the customer's own training/fine-tuning of models on copyrighted content, do not cover non-copyright IP claims fully, and are only as strong as the provider's solvency and willingness to defend.

---

## V. Perspectives and Commentary

- **Rightsholder and creative-industry perspective:** The Authors Guild, Getty Images, GEMA, and various publishers argue that unauthorized training is wholesale appropriation, undermines licensing markets, and requires either licensing or statutory remuneration. The European Parliament's July 2025 study echoes this, calling for harmonized opt-outs, transparency, and equitable licensing. The GEMA v. OpenAI ruling validates this perspective in EU courts.
- **Developer and open-source perspective:** Many AI developers and commentators (and the N.D. Cal. rulings in *Bartz* and *Kadrey*) argue that training is analogous to human learning and is transformative; mandatory licensing is infeasible at internet scale and would entrench incumbents. Open-weight proponents warn that strict rules disadvantage open research.
- **Academic and policy commentary:** Scholars (Quintais, Peukert, Lucchi) emphasize structural mismatches between TDM exceptions designed for research and commercial generative-AI deployment; they flag gaps in remuneration, transparency, and extraterritoriality. The US Copyright Office tries to steer a middle course: fair use is possible, especially with guardrails and lawful access, but not guaranteed.
- **Enterprise users:** Generally seek legal certainty through indemnities, licensed data, and provider compliance with EU rules; concerned about both input-side liability (if they fine-tune or operate RAG systems) and output-side liability (if models regurgitate).

---

## VI. Implications: Model Developers vs. Enterprise Users

### For Model Developers
- **US:** Face direct infringement suits for training. The split between *Thomson Reuters* (anti-fair-use for competing products) and *Bartz*/*Kadrey* (pro-fair-use for non-expressive training) means developers must assess: (i) source legality (pirated sources are a major negative factor, though *Kadrey* allowed it on these facts); (ii) output behavior (guardrails and anti-memorization strongly favor fair use); (iii) whether the model competes with the training works; (iv) commerciality and bad faith. RAG developers face the additional risk that indexing and retrieval may be treated as distinct infringing acts (*Dow Jones v. Perplexity*, Copyright Office Part 3 § III.C).
- **EU:** Must comply with Article 53: implement a copyright policy honoring CDSM opt-outs, and publish a training-data summary. Signing the GPAI Code of Practice gives a presumption of conformity. Must assess extraterritorial obligations for models deployed in the EU. The GEMA ruling suggests that models that memorize and reproduce training data face liability outside the TDM exception.
- **Both:** Should maintain data provenance, document guardrails, consider licensing for high-value or clearly reserved content, and prepare for both input-side and output-side claims. For RAG systems, must separately assess the legality of the retrieval corpus and the output-generation process.

### For Enterprise Users
- **Input-side risk:** Lower when using commercial APIs from major providers with indemnities, but rises sharply when the enterprise fine-tunes, trains on its own copyrighted or scraped data, or operates RAG systems with unlicensed content. Enterprise users should verify provider compliance with EU rules and the scope of indemnities (many do not cover customer-provided training data or RAG indexes).
- **Output-side risk:** Enterprise users face liability if outputs reproduce protected expression. Indemnities typically require use of provider safety features and exclude knowingly infringing prompts. Users should enable filtering, avoid prompts targeting specific copyrighted works, and avoid redistributing raw outputs without review.
- **EU compliance:** Deployers of high-risk AI systems have additional obligations under the AI Act, but the core copyright obligations fall on GPAI providers. However, downstream deployers can face rightsholder claims if they knowingly use infringing outputs or fine-tune on infringing data, or if they operate RAG systems that copy protected content.
- **Contractual leverage:** Enterprise users should negotiate clear indemnity scope, audit rights for training-data summaries, and warranty provisions regarding EU compliance.

---

## VII. A Conservative Compliance Approach (Not Legal Advice)

Given the unsettled state of the law, a risk-minimizing approach for both developers and enterprise users would include:

1. **Lawful acquisition of training data.** Avoid pirated datasets, shadow libraries, and paywall circumvention. *Bartz* and the Copyright Office make clear that source legality is a major fair-use factor and that retaining pirated copies is likely infringing even where training itself might be fair use. In the EU, lawful access is a prerequisite for the TDM exception.

2. **Maintain data provenance records.** Document the source, license status, and acquisition method for each significant data source. This supports fair-use arguments, EU transparency obligations, and due diligence defenses.

3. **Implement and document technical guardrails.** Use and retain evidence of: anti-memorization training techniques, output filters, prompt classifiers, and "cannot reproduce" constraints. *Bartz* and the Copyright Office treat guardrails as strongly favoring fair use. The GEMA ruling underscores that memorization that enables reproduction creates liability in the EU.

4. **Honor opt-outs and reservations of rights.** In the EU, this is mandatory under CDSM Article 4 and AI Act Article 53(1)(c). In the US, honoring opt-outs (e.g., "no AI training" clauses, robots.txt, AI-specific signals) reduces bad-faith arguments and aligns with emerging norms.

5. **Prioritize licensing for high-value or sensitive content.** License from rightsholders or reputable data brokers where feasible, especially for content likely to be reproduced or to compete with training works. The Copyright Office endorses voluntary licensing; the EU is moving toward collective licensing frameworks.

6. **Comply with EU transparency obligations.** Publish a training-data summary using the AI Office template; consider signing the GPAI Code of Practice for the presumption of conformity.

7. **Avoid models that output protected expression.** Test for memorization and reproduction; configure systems to refuse prompts that target specific copyrighted works; suppress verbatim or near-verbatim outputs.

8. **Address RAG-specific risks separately.** For RAG systems: (a) license or obtain lawful access to content in the retrieval database; (b) implement retrieval-side filtering to avoid reproducing protected expression; (c) configure the system to summarize or synthesize rather than reproduce indexed content verbatim; (d) maintain provenance records for the retrieval corpus distinct from training-data records.

9. **Contractual risk allocation.** Enterprise users should obtain and review provider indemnities, understand carve-outs (especially for fine-tuning, RAG, and disabled safety features), and require providers to warrant EU AI Act compliance and provide training-data summaries.

10. **Monitor litigation and regulatory guidance.** The law is moving fast; *Thomson Reuters* is on an appeal path; *Bartz*/*Kadrey* may be appealed; CJEU Case C-250/25 is pending; the GEMA ruling may be appealed; the Copyright Office final Part 3 report and any new US legislation could change the analysis.

11. **Separate US and EU compliance assessments.** US fair-use analysis does not translate to the EU, and vice versa. A practice lawful in one jurisdiction may be infringing in the other. For models deployed in both markets, the stricter standard (typically the EU for opt-outs and transparency; potentially the US for fair-use uncertainty) should govern.

---

## VIII. Key Caveats and Uncertainties

- No appellate ruling has yet addressed AI-training fair use; district court splits may be resolved unpredictably.
- The Copyright Office report is persuasive, not binding.
- EU CJEU guidance on whether AI training qualifies as TDM is pending (Case C-250/25); the GEMA ruling provides a national-court data point but is not binding outside Germany.
- Extraterritorial application of EU AI Act copyright provisions to US-developed models remains unclear.
- Provider indemnities are contractual and subject to extensive carve-outs; they are not regulatory safe harbors.
- State-law and non-copyright IP theories (right of publicity, trade secret, breach of contract) add additional layers of risk.
- RAG-specific doctrine is nascent; *Dow Jones v. Perplexity* is a motion-to-dismiss ruling, and no US court has yet ruled on the merits of RAG as a distinct infringement mechanism.

RECOMMENDATION: 1. Prioritize lawful data acquisition, documented guardrails, opt-out compliance, EU transparency, and licensed content for high-value works, treating US fair-use uncertainty and EU TDM/opt-out rules as distinct but parallel compliance tracks.

8M tickets/month with a $2,000/month budget requires an extremely cost-efficient approach. Frontier model APIs (option 1) are eliminated immediately: even GPT-4o at batch pricing would cost ~$2,400/month just for input tokens, and GPT-4o-mini, while cheap (~$150/month), would likely fall short of 94% accuracy on 12 categories without fine-tuning. ### The Decisive Factor: 400K Labeled Examples + 94% Accuracy Target

The 400K labeled tickets — roughly 33K per category — are the linchpin. This dataset is **6–7× larger** than what published fine-tuned ticket classifiers were trained on:

- **Dragneel/ticket-classification-v1**: Fine-tuned DistilBERT on ~62K tickets → **94.85% accuracy** across 4 categories.
- **JoCAAA 2023**: Fine-tuned BERT on 6,000 telecom tickets → **94.2% accuracy** across 6 categories.

With 400K labeled examples and 12 categories (more than the cited studies, but with vastly more data per category), a fine-tuned compact transformer is well-positioned to clear 94%.

### Why Not Embedding Classifier (Option 3)?

An embedding classifier is tempting on cost (~$80/month for OpenAI text-embedding-3-small at 8M tickets), but the accuracy risk is material. Research published in *Information Processing & Management* (2023) found that **fine-tuned BERT embeddings are 67% more separable** than non-tuned contextual embeddings, and that pre-trained (non-fine-tuned) embeddings produce a meaningfully less separable representation space. The same study showed that when embeddings are properly fine-tuned, "the classifier does not matter" — but the key qualifier is *fine-tuned*. Pre-trained embeddings from an API are not domain-adapted to support ticket language, and bridging a 3–8 percentage point accuracy gap to reach 94% on 12 categories (some of which may overlap semantically, e.g., "billing" vs. "account access") is uncertain.

Self-hosted inference for a 66M-parameter DistilBERT model is dramatically cheaper than the 7B–8B model costs that one panelist worried about. A single AWS g4dn.xlarge (NVIDIA T4) costs ~$384/month on-demand and can handle 8M inferences for a model this size with substantial headroom. DistilBERT can even run on CPU at this volume with batch processing, since latency is irrelevant. ## Architecture Decision: 20M-Page Quarterly Legal Document Processing

### Requirement Analysis

| Requirement | Architecture Implication |
|---|---|
| 20M pages, once per quarter | Episodic burst workload; ~86 days idle between runs |
| Up to 48 hours per run | Batch SLA — no real-time or low-latency serving needed |
| Data stays in private VPC | Network isolation required; no public egress for data plane |
| Workloads can be queued | Asynchronous, queue-based batch processing is explicitly acceptable |
| 2 platform engineers, no ML ops experience | Operational simplicity is the decisive constraint |

### Option-by-Option Evaluation

**Option 1 — private-managed-batch** ✅

A managed batch service deployed inside a private VPC (e.g., AWS SageMaker Batch Transform with `VpcConfig`, or AWS Batch with private subnets and VPC endpoints) satisfies every constraint simultaneously:

- **Private VPC**: AWS documentation confirms that SageMaker Batch Transform supports `VpcConfig` with private subnets and security groups, providing containers with "a network connection within your VPC that is not connected to the internet." S3 access is routed through VPC endpoints, keeping all data in-network.
- **Batch + queueable**: Batch jobs are inherently asynchronous and queued. The service manages instance provisioning, workload distribution across instances, and automatic teardown.
- **Low ops overhead**: The cloud provider manages job scheduling, container orchestration, compute scaling, and instance lifecycle. Two engineers with no ML ops experience can configure job definitions and container images without managing Kubernetes, GPU drivers, or autoscaling policies.
- **Cost efficiency for quarterly cadence**: No always-on infrastructure between runs; you pay only for compute consumed during the ~48-hour processing window.

**Option 2 — self-hosted-k8s-batch** ❌

Requires Kubernetes expertise (node pool management, GPU driver installation, taints/tolerations, cluster autoscaling, observability, upgrade cycles). For a team with no ML ops experience running infrequent quarterly jobs, the Day 2 operational burden and learning curve are unjustified — especially when a managed alternative exists.

**Option 3 — private-realtime-endpoint** ❌

Real-time endpoints are always-on and sized for request-level concurrency, not total throughput. For a 20M-page batch that tolerates 48-hour processing and can be queued, an always-on endpoint is architecturally mismatched and cost-prohibitive (you'd pay for idle infrastructure for ~86 days between quarterly runs).

**Option 4 — temporary-gpu-cluster** ❌

Requires manual cluster provisioning and teardown each quarter, GPU configuration, image management, and orchestration scripting. If provisioning fails or a dependency is misconfigured, the 48-hour window may be missed. More operational overhead than a managed batch service, and still demands infrastructure expertise the team lacks.

**Option 5 — on-premises-cluster** ❌

Requires hardware procurement, data center space, power, cooling, firmware/driver maintenance, and physical GPU management. Hardware would sit idle ~96% of the time. This is the highest-overhead option and unjustified when a private cloud VPC already satisfies the data residency requirement.

### Key Implementation Considerations

**Per-invocation timeout**: AWS docs confirm that SageMaker Batch Transform has a **60-minute per-invocation timeout** (`InvocationsTimeoutInSeconds`, max 1 hour), not a per-job timeout. The overall transform job can run for the full 48-hour window — but each individual inference request must complete within 60 minutes. The 20M pages should be chunked into files/mini-batches that stay well under this limit per invocation. Set `SplitType` to `Line` and tune `MaxPayloadInMB` (max 100 MB) to control batch sizing.

**Service choice — SageMaker Batch Transform vs. AWS Batch**: If the document processing is ML inference (e.g., classification, NLP extraction), SageMaker Batch Transform is purpose-built with built-in queuing, S3 integration, and concurrency controls. If the workload is more general-purpose (e.g., OCR, rule-based extraction, data transformation that isn't pure model inference), AWS Batch in private subnets is more flexible — it runs any containerized workload and can be configured with VPC endpoints for S3 access. Both fit under "private-managed-batch." The team should choose based on whether the core processing step is model inference or general compute.

**Data transfer logistics**: Moving 20M document pages into S3 within the private VPC for each quarterly run is itself a significant operation. Use AWS DataSync or direct VPC-endpoint-based S3 uploads to keep data in-network. Pre-stage data before submitting the batch job to protect the 48-hour processing window.

**Failure handling and resumption**: SageMaker Batch Transform continues processing remaining input files even if one file fails (marking the job as "failed" but still producing output for successfully processed files). For checkpointing, split the 20M pages into multiple transform jobs by S3 key prefix — this provides natural resumption granularity: if one sub-job fails, only that subset needs reprocessing, not the entire 20M pages. AWS Batch offers similar retry semantics at the job level.

**Quota pre-allocation**: Both panel models correctly identified this as the top risk. GPU instance availability and service quotas must be pre-approved before each quarterly run. Request quota increases well in advance — quarterly spike demand can trigger throttling that prevents completing within the 48-hour window if not pre-arranged with the cloud provider.

### Why Option 1 Wins

The combination of infrequent batch runs, a private VPC requirement, queueable workloads, and a small team with no ML operations experience makes a managed batch service in a private VPC the clear best fit. It minimizes operational burden, keeps data in-network, natively supports queued long-running jobs, avoids paying for idle infrastructure between quarterly runs, and requires only basic container and job-definition configuration that two platform engineers can manage.

**The bottleneck is prefill, not decode.** A 60,000-token shared prefix dominates time-to-first-token because the model must process all those tokens before generating anything. On a cache hit, the prefill for those 60,000 tokens is skipped entirely — only the short user-specific suffix needs to be computed. ### Constraint Checklist

| Constraint | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Privacy / offline | No network; data stays on-device |
| Memory | ≤ 3 GB app allocation |
| Latency | ≤ 10 seconds per summary |
| Coverage | Must serve the entire install base |

### Option-by-Option

**1. on-device-quantized-model** — The smallest acceptable quantized model is 4.2 GB, which exceeds the 3 GB memory cap. This is a hard feasibility failure; the model cannot be loaded. **Eliminated.**

**2. extractive-plus-small-generator** — At ~600 MB it fits comfortably within budget, runs fully offline, and likely meets the latency target on all devices. However, it delivers measurably lower quality on *every* device, including the 60% that have a superior native API available. Viable, but suboptimal as a primary strategy.

**3. platform-native-model-api** — Only 60% of devices have this API. The remaining 40% would get no summarization at all. **Eliminated** as a standalone solution.

**4. native-api-with-fallback** — Uses the platform-native API where available (60%), falling back to the extractive-plus-small-generator (600 MB) on the rest (40%). This covers 100% of devices, respects the memory budget and offline constraint everywhere, and delivers the best achievable quality on each device. The native API almost certainly uses system-managed memory outside the app's 3 GB allocation, so it sidesteps the memory ceiling entirely. This **dominates** option 2: identical behavior on the 40% fallback devices, strictly better quality on the 60% native-API devices.

**5. defer-feature-pending-hardware** — Premature. A fully functional, 100%-coverage strategy (option 4) exists today. Ships zero value in the interim. **Eliminated.**

### Why Option 4 Is the Clear Choice

- **Infeasibility of option 1** is a mathematical fact (4.2 GB > 3 GB), not a tradeoff.
- **Option 4 strictly dominates option 2** — same fallback behavior on 40% of devices, strictly better quality on 60%.
- **Option 3 is incomplete** — 40% uncovered with no fallback.
- **Option 5 is unnecessary** — a viable path exists now.

### Implementation Considerations

- **API-availability detection** must handle edge cases where the API is nominally present but the underlying model hasn't been downloaded yet. A runtime capability check (not just OS-version gating) is essential.
- **Two code paths** add testing surface, but this is routine engineering — availability detection plus a fallback branch — not a blocking risk.
- **Latency on fallback devices**: the extractive summarizer plus a 600 MB generator is lightweight and should reliably meet the 10-second budget, but this should be validated on the lowest-spec 8 GB devices in the target set.

**Evaluated Providers**

1. **OpenAI Enterprise / API** (direct, with signed BAA)  
   *Primary sources: OpenAI Business Associate Agreement (Mar 2023); OpenAI API Enterprise Privacy terms; OpenAI Trust Portal (SOC 2/ISO).*  
2. **Anthropic Claude API** (direct, with signed BAA)  
   *Primary sources: Anthropic API Terms of Service (2024); Anthropic Security & Compliance (BAA availability, SOC 2).*  
3. **Google Cloud Vertex AI** (Gemini API under Google Cloud BAA)  
   *Primary sources: Google Cloud HIPAA Compliance Offerings; Vertex AI Gemini documentation (Apr 2024); Google Cloud Trust Center.*

---

### 1. HIPAA Support & BAA
- **OpenAI:** Will execute a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) for Enterprise and API accounts. Consumer ChatGPT/ChatGPT Team are explicitly ineligible.  
- **Anthropic:** Will execute a BAA for API customers; the BAA must be signed before PHI is transmitted.  
- **Google:** Vertex AI and the Gemini API on Vertex are listed as HIPAA-eligible services under Google Cloud’s standard BAA.

### 2. Model-Training Policies
- **OpenAI:** Contractually commits that API prompts and completions are **not** used to train models.  
- **Anthropic:** Contractually commits that API inputs/outputs are **not** used to train models.  
- **Google:** Contractually commits that customer data submitted to Vertex AI is **not** used to train or improve foundation models.

### 3. Contractual Data Retention
- **OpenAI:** Retains API inputs/outputs for up to **30 days** for abuse monitoring and service improvement unless the customer separately qualifies for and enables **Zero Data Retention (ZDR)**. ZDR deletes data immediately after processing, but it is *not* automatic under the BAA, requires approval, and is unavailable for some endpoints.  
- **Anthropic:** Retains API data for a **“limited time”** for safety, debugging, and service quality. Anthropic does not publish a firm maximum duration (e.g., 30 days) and does **not** advertise a zero-retention equivalent.  
- **Google:** No mandatory service-side retention for API inference. Logging and retention are customer-controlled via Cloud Audit Logs/Cloud Logging in the customer’s own project; data lifecycle policies are configurable.

### 4. Private Networking
- **OpenAI:** **No** PrivateLink, VPC peering, or Private Service Connect. Traffic transits the public internet (TLS 1.2+). IP allowlisting is available but does not eliminate public-internet exposure.  
- **Anthropic:** **No** private connectivity options; public internet only.  
- **Google:** **Private Service Connect** and VPC Service Controls are supported for Vertex AI, permitting on-premises or cloud VPCs to reach the service without public-internet routing.

### 5. Regional Availability / Data Residency
- **OpenAI:** Inference is US-hosted, but the customer **cannot** select or pin a specific US region via the API.  
- **Anthropic:** US-based inference; no customer-level region selection.  
- **Google:** Customers can select specific US regions (e.g., `us-central1`, `us-east4`, `us-west1`) and enforce residency via VPC Service Controls.

### 6. Audit Certifications
- **OpenAI:** SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 27018, ISO 27701.  
- **Anthropic:** SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001. **Does not** currently list ISO 27701 or HITRUST.  
- **Google:** SOC 1/2/3, ISO 27001, 27017, 27018, 27701, FedRAMP (Moderate/High), HITRUST CSF.

### 7. Rate Limits (20 M tokens / day context)
- **OpenAI:** Tier-based (Tier 4+ offers millions of TPM). At ~14k sustained TPM with bursts, 20 M/day is easily within high-tier limits.  
- **Anthropic:** Build tier (highest trust tier) supports hundreds of thousands to ~1 M TPM depending on model. Adequate for 20 M/day after tier qualification, but onboarding may require a spend-history ramp.  
- **Google:** Default quotas vary by model and region (e.g., Gemini 1.5 Pro defaults often start at 360 requests/min and ~1 M TPM) but are readily adjustable via Cloud quota requests. 20 M/day is operationally trivial once quotas are raised.

### 8. Pricing (illustrative, 20 M mixed tokens/day, ~30 days/month)
- **OpenAI:** GPT-4o at ~$5/$15 per 1 M tokens → roughly **$6,000–$12,000/month** depending on input/output mix and model.  
- **Anthropic:** Claude 3 Sonnet at ~$3/$15 per 1 M tokens → roughly **$5,000–$6,000/month**.  
- **Google:** Gemini 1.5 Pro at ~$3.50/$10.50 per 1 M tokens (≤128k context) → roughly **$4,000–$5,000/month**.

---

## Material Gaps & Ambiguous Claims
- **OpenAI:** The HIPAA BAA does not, by itself, eliminate the 30-day retention window; ZDR is a separate opt-in with endpoint restrictions. The lack of private networking is a material architectural gap for healthcare environments that prohibit public-internet transit for PHI, regardless of TLS.  
- **Anthropic:** The undefined upper bound of “limited time” retention and the absence of a published zero-retention pathway create compliance ambiguity. The company also lacks private networking and the broader certification footprint of its competitors, making it the weakest infrastructure option for regulated workloads.  
- **Google:** The most significant ambiguity is **endpoint confusion**. The consumer Gemini API (`ai.google.dev`) has separate terms and may use data for product improvement; it is **not** covered by the Google Cloud BAA. Customers must architect exclusively for Vertex AI endpoints. Additionally, newer Gemini model versions may not roll out simultaneously in every US region.

---

## Recommendation
For a mid-sized company moving ~20 M tokens/day of regulated healthcare data, **Google Cloud Vertex AI (Gemini)** is the best fit. It is the only evaluated offering that combines a long-standing HIPAA BAA, explicit no-training commitments, customer-controlled data retention without a mandatory service-side window, enforceable US-region data residency, private networking, and the widest audit certification suite (including HITRUST and FedRAMP). The workload volume is easily accommodated with adjustable quotas, and the per-token cost is currently the lowest of the three. If the organization absolutely requires OpenAI foundation models (e.g., GPT-4o), it should bypass OpenAI’s direct API and procure **Azure OpenAI Service** instead, which closes the private-networking and residency gaps; however, among the three direct hosting providers evaluated here, Google provides the most defensible compliance architecture.

RECOMMENDATION: 3 Google Cloud Vertex AI (Gemini API under BAA)

response_text:
**1. United States Landscape**

*Statutes and Doctrinal Foundations.* U.S. copyright law protects original works of authorship under 17 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 106. The central question for model training is whether intermediate copying of copyrighted works constitutes fair use under § 107. The four-factor test weighs: (1) the purpose and character of the use; (2) the nature of the copyrighted work; (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used; and (4) the effect on the potential market for the original. The Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in *Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith* tightened factor one analysis, stressing that a use sharing the same commercial purpose as the original and superseding its market weighs against fair use, even if the use is arguably “transformative” in a colloquial sense. Developers invoking fair use for training frequently cite *Authors Guild v. Google* (2d Cir. 2015), which held that mass digitization and snippet display were transformative and non-superseding. Critics counter that generative AI produces new expressive works that directly compete with licensed content, distinguishing the Google Books precedent. The Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 1201, may also be triggered if training data is scraped by circumventing technological protection measures such as paywalls.

*Major Court Developments.* No U.S. court has yet issued a final merits ruling on whether training generative models with unlicensed copyrighted material is fair use. A cluster of high-stakes cases is pending:
- *Andersen v. Stability AI* (D. Del.): Visual artists allege Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt copied billions of copyrighted images. In 2023, the court allowed core direct-infringement and DMCA § 1202(b) claims to survive a motion to dismiss, while dismissing other theories.
- *Tremblay v. OpenAI* and *Silverman v. OpenAI* (N.D. Cal.): Authors allege OpenAI copied books to train GPT models.
- *Kadrey v. Meta* (N.D. Cal.): Authors make similar claims against Meta’s LLaMA models.
- *Doe 1 v. GitHub* (N.D. Cal.): Plaintiffs challenge GitHub Copilot’s training on code under open-source licenses, raising contract and DMCA claims.
- *Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence* (D. Del.): While predating the current generative wave, the case tests whether training an AI on bulk legal content is fair use; the district court denied ROSS’s motion to dismiss in part, leaving fair use for later determination.
No appellate court has squarely endorsed intermediate copying for generative AI, leaving the fair-use defense highly uncertain.

*Regulatory Guidance.* The U.S. Copyright Office has repeatedly affirmed that pure AI-generated output lacks the human element required for copyright registration (see *Thaler v. Perlmutter*, D.D.C. 2023, and the Office’s March 2023 Guidance). In 2024, the Office launched a comprehensive study on AI and copyright, signalling potential future policy recommendations but establishing no training exemption today.

*Provider Policies.* The market has bifurcated into indemnification and licensing strategies. Microsoft’s “Copilot Copyright Commitment” and OpenAI’s “Copyright Shield” promise to defend certain commercial customers against third-party IP claims arising from model outputs, subject to carve-outs (e.g., the customer must not have knowingly used infringing input or disabled safety features). At the same time, OpenAI, Google, and Common Crawl have adopted web-crawler opt-out mechanisms using `robots.txt` (Google-Extended, GPTBot), treating machine-readable signals as a compliance floor. Adobe’s Firefly represents the licensing camp, training largely on Adobe Stock and public-domain content.

*Multiple Perspectives.* Technology advocates (e.g., EFF, Stanford’s Lemley and Casey) argue that training is “fair learning” because model weights do not retain expressive expression; the output is produced by statistical patterns, not human-like copying. Content industries (Authors Guild, Getty Images, newspaper publishers) contend that unlicensed training devastates markets for expressive works and that opt-outs place an unfair burden on creators. Academics such as James Grimmelmann note that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architectures complicate the analysis: vector indices reproduce copyrighted works in latent form, and retrieved passages injected into prompts may more readily constitute expressive copying than latent training.

**2. European Union Landscape**

*Statutory Architecture.* The Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive (Directive 2019/790) provides the primary framework. Article 3 establishes a mandatory text-and-data mining (TDM) exception for research institutions with lawful access. Article 4 establishes a broader TDM exception available to any entity with lawful access, but rightsholders may reserve those rights “in an appropriate way, such as machine-readable means” (Art. 4(3)). The reproduction right in Directive 2001/29/EC (InfoSoc Directive) remains the baseline. Separately, the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) imposes direct obligations on providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models: Article 53 requires them to “put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law and related rights including in particular with the reservation of rights expressed by rightsholders” under Article 4(3) of the DSM Directive, and to publish a summary of training data content.

*Regulatory Guidance and Court Developments.* No CJEU or Member State high court has yet issued a definitive judgment on whether generative AI training falls within the Article 4 TDM exception. National implementations vary (e.g., Germany’s § 44d and § 44e UrhG). The European Copyright Society has opined that Article 4 likely covers data mining for machine learning if the purpose is extraction of information, but scholars dispute whether generative synthesis of new expressive content satisfies that purpose. The European Commission’s AI Office is expected to issue guidance on model-documentation requirements, but the underlying copyright question remains judicially untested.

*Provider Policies.* EU-facing providers have generally aligned their crawlers with Article 4(3) by honoring `robots.txt` and meta-tag reservations. OpenAI, Google, and others have geo-specific crawl policies and transparency reports to satisfy the AI Act’s GPAI obligations. Some rightsholders have piloted technical standards (e.g., the `tdm-reservation` protocol in metadata) to signal reservation under Article 4.

*Commentary.* Publishers and collecting societies argue that TDM was never intended to enable the creation of competing synthetic media, and that generative models require separate licensing. Conversely, open-science advocates contend that a narrow reading of Article 4 would chill European AI competitiveness. A crucial unresolved tension is whether mere availability on the public internet constitutes “lawful access” for TDM, or whether browse-wrap terms of service can negate that lawfulness.

**3. Retrieval-Augmented Systems: A Distinct Profile**

Retrieval architectures shift risk from the training phase to the inference phase. Building a vector index requires repro copyrighted works in latent form. Under U.S. law, this may be characterized as intermediate copying, but fair use is weaker if retrieved chunks are passed to users with minimal transformation. Under EU law, the temporary copies exception under Article 5(1) of the InfoSoc Directive may cover transient inference buffers, but persistent vector stores likely implicate the reproduction right independently. Providers increasingly rely on RAG grounded in licensed corpora (e.g., enterprise contracts) to reduce parametric memorization liability.

**4. Settled Requirements vs. Unresolved Questions**

*Settled Requirements:*
- Neither the U.S. Copyright Office nor EU law recognizes copyright in purely AI-generated output absent sufficient human creative control.
- In the EU, copying works for training implicates the reproduction right; Article 4 TDM provides a conditional exception subject to lawful access and machine-readable opt-outs.
- Under the EU AI Act, GPAI model providers must document training data and maintain a publicly available copyright compliance policy that respects Article 4(3) opt-outs.
- Verbatim or substantially similar reproduction of copyrighted works by a model or retrieval system is infringing absent an applicable defense in both jurisdictions.
- Provider indemnification for enterprise customers is a market development, not a statutory guarantee.

*Unresolved Questions:*
- Whether U.S. fair use covers non-expressive, intermediate training copying for commercial generative models.
- Whether *Warhol*’s same-purpose analysis undermines transformative-use claims when AI developers and rightsholders both operate in a commercial licensing market.
- Whether Article 4 TDM encompasses generative AI at all, or is limited to analytical extraction of information.
- What technical standards unambiguously satisfy a “machine-readable” reservation under Article 4(3).
- Whether browse-wrap terms of service can render publicly visible web content outside “lawful access.”
- The scope of output liability for “style” imitation or paraphrase that is not substantially similar in the traditional sense.
- Cross-border enforcement: whether a model trained in the U.S. with unlicensed data creates exposure for the provider’s EU commercial activities.

**5. Implications for Model Developers and Enterprise Users**

*Model Developers:*
- Face direct copyright liability for the act of copying and, in the EU, must comply with Article 53 of the AI Act regardless of where the corporate parent is headquartered.
- Must invest in data provenance infrastructure to track licenses, opt-outs, and lawful access to defend against class actions and regulatory audits.
- Litigation risk is highest in the U.S. because of statutory damages, but EU regulatory penalties under the AI Act can reach a percentage of global turnover.
- Retrieval-system developers must additionally assess whether indexed snippets are independently licensed.

*Enterprise Users:*
- Rarely face direct liability for the pre-training copying performed by a vendor, but assume risk when they fine-tune a model on their own proprietary or third-party copyrighted datasets without authorization.
- Output-generated infringement is primarily their operational risk if they publish AI-created content; indemnification clauses from Microsoft/OpenAI offer partial protection but typically exclude infringement caused by the user’s own training data, prompts designed to evade safeguards, or failure to use content filters.
- Under the AI Act, downstream deployers of high-risk systems may inherit documentation and transparency obligations.
- Contractual negotiation leverage is essential: not all providers offer indemnity, and carve-outs differ materially.

**6. Outline of a Conservative Compliance Approach**

The following framework is an analytical outline of conservative measures and should not be construed as legal advice.

1. **License-Centric Sourcing**: Prioritize training corpora that are in the public domain, carry permissive Creative Commons licenses, or are covered by direct publisher agreements. Treat high-value proprietary content (stock imagery, best-selling books, major news archives) as licensable-only.
2. **Global Opt-Out Adherence**: Treat machine-readable reservations as legally binding across all jurisdictions. Implement crawler-level compliance with `robots.txt` and equivalent meta-tag directives (e.g., `tdm-reservation`) for training data collection, even where not yet judicially mandated outside the EU.
3. **Provenance and Audit Trails**: Maintain granular records of data acquisition channels, legal basis for inclusion (license, fair use, TDM), and preprocessing steps. Publish a training-data summary aligned with EU AI Act GPAI standards.
4. **Retrieval-First Architecture**: Where feasible, use RAG grounded in licensed or enterprise-owned indices rather than parametric memorization to reduce the risk of expressive output copying.
5. **Output Guardrails**: Deploy similarity-detection filters and de-duplication protocols to catch near-verbatim reproduction before publication.
6. **Contractual Risk Transfer**: Enterprises should negotiate broad IP indemnification from providers, confirm there are no indemnity carve-outs for general-purpose outputs, and prohibit fine-tuning on unlicensed copyrighted inputs.
7. **Territorial Segmentation and Monitoring**: Consider ring-fencing EU training datasets to those cleared under Article 4 or licensed, and monitor U.S. case law (*Andersen*, *Kadrey*, *Thomson Reuters*, and the Copyright Office study) to refresh protocols.

**7. Emerging Strategic Postures**

1. Maximize reliance on statutory exceptions and fair use while implementing global opt-out monitoring.
2. Pursue comprehensive licensing for all training data and prohibit use of unlicensed copyrighted works.
3. Adopt a hybrid posture licensing high-risk proprietary content, relying on statutory exceptions only for open web data with strict opt-out compliance, and deploying enterprise output filters.

## Analysis

The scenario creates a tension between two priorities of different severity:

| Priority | Authority | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| p95 latency < 1.5s | Director: breaches "unacceptable" | **Hard constraint** |
| Idle GPU spend | Team's "top concern" | Optimization target |

This hierarchy—hard latency filter first, then minimize idle spend among survivors—drives the elimination.

### Elimination

**Option 2 (on-demand-serverless):** Eliminated. A 13B LLM has severe cold-start latency (typically 30–60+ seconds for model weight loading). Bursts begin without warning, so the first requests in every burst hit cold instances, blowing past the 1.5s p95 target immediately.

**Option 3 (autoscaled-dedicated):** Eliminated. The 3-minute replica spin-up is explicitly longer than the burst onset. During the first 3 minutes of each burst, baseline capacity (sized for ~5 req/s) would serve a 120 req/s load—roughly 4% of demand—causing catastrophic latency spikes.

**Option 5 (dedicated-plus-serverless-overflow):** Eliminated. This creates a catch-22. If the dedicated baseline is small (to minimize idle spend), the overflow fraction is large and those requests hit on-demand serverless cold starts, breaching p95.
